article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel , independent researcher. Published 22 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 7 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Further research · Collaboration

The expected root degree of the free uniform spanning forest need not be invariant under squaring an infinite connected locally finite simple vertex-transitive graph. For the binary grandparent graph G , of degree 8, two explicit free-exhaustion reductions give E deg FUSF(G) ( o ) = (24 − √2)/7 > 3.22. For its simple square G 2 , of degree 40, a finite rational-current certificate proves E deg FUSF(G²) ( o ) ≤ 3208526010913748780/10 18 < 3.21. All currents, divergences and energies are verified with integer arithmetic; the passage to the infinite free forest is justified by finite-support flows and free exhaustion. With the explicitly adopted normalization b F ( X ) = ½ E deg FUSF(X) ( o ) − 1, this gives b F ( G ) − b F ( G 2 ) > 1/200, a negative answer to the unrestricted vertex-transitive assertion in Abért’s Question 24. The graph and electrical/forest principles are established background; no new general forest mechanism or exhaustive priority claim is made.

Start with an infinite network that looks the same from every vertex. Its “square” adds a direct connection wherever two vertices were previously two steps apart. In this example, each vertex goes from having 8 neighbors to having 40.

Now consider a random forest obtained by taking uniform random spanning trees on larger and larger finite pieces, leaving their boundaries free. Count how many forest edges touch a fixed vertex, and average over the randomness. Even with all those extra available connections, this expected count decreases .
Quantity Original G Square G 2
Available neighbors 8 40
Expected forest degree 3.226540… ≤ 3.208526…
The original value is exact: (24 − √2)/7. The square’s displayed value comes from a proved upper bound; its exact expected degree is not computed.

The surprise is a failure of invariance for this infinite free-forest statistic. It is not a claim about the average degree of a finite spanning tree, or a general rule that adding edges always lowers forest degree.

Take the 3-regular tree, choose an end, and let p ( v ) be the neighbor of v toward that end. The binary grandparent graph joins each vertex to its parent and grandparent. Every edge has unit conductance.
For this graph G and its simple square H = G 2 :

Both graphs are infinite and vertex-transitive. The original graph is nonunimodular : its symmetries distinguish the unique parent from the two children. The result makes no claim of failure in the unimodular or Cayley-graph subclasses.

Abért’s 2010 Question 24 asks about squaring arbitrary vertex-transitive graphs. The paper proves unequal expected degrees directly and states its forest-derived normalization explicitly. Its contribution is this specific comparison; the grandparent graph and the electrical-network tools are established prior work.

Calculate the original value. Two finite-network reductions, with explicit convergence arguments, give the exact free effective resistances in G . Summing the edge-inclusion probabilities gives (24 − √2)/7.

Certify an upper bound for the square. A finite network contains all 40 edges incident to the root. Explicit rational currents satisfy the required unit-flow equations, and their total energy is checked exactly.

Pass to the infinite free forest. The currents have finite support and extend by zero to larger finite free networks. Thomson’s principle and the free limit transfer the energy bound to the expected root degree.
This last step is essential. An unrestricted infinite-network flow calculation would generally concern wired resistance and would not establish the free-forest bound used here.

This is an unrefereed preprint. AI tools were used extensively in the research, proof development, computation, literature review, and writing. The source package includes the manuscript, exact certificate, and verification code.
Can squaring ever increase expected free-spanning-forest degree? For an infinite, connected, locally finite, simple vertex-transitive graph X , can
E deg FUSF(X²) ( o ) > E deg FUSF(X) ( o )?
Here X 2 is the simple square, and every edge in both graphs has unit conductance.

This paper establishes a strict decrease but does not resolve the opposite direction. A general nonincrease theorem would replace the failed invariance statement with a weaker law. An increasing example would show that squaring can change the expectation in either direction. I see this as a research question; the present evidence does not favor a conjectured answer.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 21 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 10 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We construct an associative pointed free product system of separable complex Hilbert spaces whose maximal ordered tensor subsystem does not generate the whole free system. Its tensor core is the time-ordered finite-word Fock system, and the closed free subsystem generated by that core is precisely the full finite-word Fock system. The ambient system has, in addition, nonzero orthogonal sectors of words of ordinal length below ω². A recoverable Gaussian mixture supplies a sigma-finite measure class invariant under finite-prefix absorption. Finite monochromatic-run charts turn concatenation into the free product structure. We prove separability, an explicit continuous Hilbert-field structure including time zero, and continuity of the full structural maps and their inverses. This gives a negative answer, in the scalar specialization, to the universal tensor-core generation question stated by Skeide in 2009. It does not answer the separate adapted-cocycle or forward tensor-recovery questions. The argument is analytic; accompanying finite computations do not certify its infinite-dimensional assertions. This draft is unrefereed and extensively AI-assisted.

A product system describes how mathematical spaces for shorter time intervals combine into a space for a longer interval. There are different ways to combine them. Tensor products impose one kind of ordering; free products allow a richer collection of alternating combinations.

The question is whether the largest tensor subsystem inside a free product system always contains enough information to rebuild the whole free system. This paper constructs an example where it does not. Its tensor core generates all the finite-word sectors, but the full system also contains orthogonal sectors made from infinite words. Taking limits of the finite-word sectors cannot reach those extra sectors.
The construction retains separable Hilbert spaces and proves a specified continuous dependence on time, including at time zero. The obstruction therefore persists beyond a purely algebraic example.

There exists an associative pointed free product system E of separable complex Hilbert spaces with the following structure at every positive time t. Its maximal ordered tensor subsystem F is the time-ordered finite-word Fock system. The closed free subsystem generated by F is the full finite-word Fock system K, and K_t is a proper subspace of E_t. A nonzero grade-ω sector remains orthogonal to K_t.
The system has a continuous vacuum and norm-continuous support-subspace sections, is locally trivial at positive time, and has jointly continuous structural maps and inverses, including at time zero.
This gives a negative answer in the scalar case to the universal tensor-core generation question stated by Michael Skeide in 2009.
A recoverable Gaussian mixture gives a sigma-finite measure class on convergent infinite sequences that is preserved under finite-prefix absorption.
Words of ordinal length below ω² split at a time cut into finitely many monochromatic runs, producing associative pointed free-product unitaries and the specified continuity structure.
Intersecting ordered tensor ranges leaves decreasing finite words. Their free hull contains exactly finite words, while a positive finite-measure grade-ω set supplies a nonzero orthogonal remainder.
The continuity claim uses the explicit Hilbert-field convention stated in the paper. Stronger regularity requirements would need to be checked separately.
The result concerns tensor-core generation. The adapted-cocycle and forward tensor-recovery questions remain separate, as does a classification of free product systems.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 22 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 11 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Let t be an actual involution in a natural finite symplectic or orthogonal group over a field of odd order, with both eigenspaces of dimension between one third and two thirds of the natural dimension n. For each eigenspace separately we prove an unconditional c/log n lower bound for the probability that the even branch of Bray’s construction induces a strong involution on that eigenspace. A graph chart reduces the problem to squarefree polynomials and self-adjoint operators. articles.header: Missing faces and topological embeddings of sphere skeleta By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 12 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 8 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Let S be a finite simplicial triangulation of the topological sphere S^(2d), and let T be a missing d-face. We prove that adjoining T to the d-skeleton of S prevents a topological embedding in S^(2d). For d ≥ 3, a graded Koszul calculation combines with established ambient-completion, anisotropy and metastable embedding theorems. For d = 2, we apply the Nevo–Wagner bistellar transfer theorem in the PL class supplied by the given triangulation: a contractible complementary manifold supplies the required disk map, and a flag subdivision supplies the base. This proves the statement of their Conjecture 1.3 without a standard PL structure assumption on the source. No claim of first priority or a new general method is made.

A triangulation builds a shape from vertices, edges, triangles and their higher-dimensional counterparts. Its skeleton retains only pieces up to a chosen dimension. A missing face is a piece that is absent even though its entire boundary is already present.

For an ordinary triangulated sphere, the edge network cannot be drawn on the sphere without crossings after adding any missing edge. This paper proves the corresponding statement in every even dimension: add a missing middle-dimensional face to the skeleton, and the enlarged space cannot fit into the original sphere without identifying distinct points.

Nevo and Wagner’s earlier theorem already rules out arbitrary continuous embeddings when the source has the standard piecewise-linear sphere structure. This result allows any finite triangulation of a topological sphere.

Let d ≥ 0, let S be a finite simplicial complex whose realization is homeomorphic to S^(2d), and let T be a missing d-face on its actual vertex set. Then the realization of S^(d) ∪ {T} has no topological embedding into S^(2d).

The theorem establishes the statement of Nevo–Wagner Conjecture 1.3. For d = 2, the proof also gives a nonzero mod-2 van Kampen obstruction. The d = 0 statement is vacuous under the actual-vertex convention.

Adding the missing face creates one extra class in a graded face-ring quotient. An embedding into a suitable PL sphere would force a surjective multiplication map between graded pieces of incompatible dimensions.
For d ≥ 3, a topological embedding supplies deleted-product data. Weber’s metastable theorem would then produce the PL embedding already ruled out by the algebraic argument.

Dimension four needs a separate argument. Nevo–Wagner transfer carries the obstruction through bistellar moves within the source’s own PL class, starting from a flag subdivision. A contractible complement supplies a disk map without requiring a standard PL complementary ball.
The source must be a finite triangulation of a topological even-dimensional sphere; the statement is not a theorem for every complex with the same homology.
The added simplex must be a missing face: every proper face must already be present, and its vertices must belong to the original complex.
The distinction from the earlier theorem concerns the source triangulation. Nevo and Wagner’s result for PL spheres already excludes arbitrary topological embeddings.
The proof combines established algebraic and topological theorems, including Nevo–Wagner transfer in dimension four and the ambient Lefschetz mechanism in higher dimensions.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 12 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 5 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Let X be a smooth integral projective variety over an algebraically closed field of arbitrary characteristic. We prove that positivity of the relative Seshadri constant of T_X at one closed point implies X ≃ P^(dim X), resolving the conjecture of Fulger and Murayama. An absolute minimum of ample degree among rational curves through the specified point gives a proper pointed family without boundary. Its very-free members yield surjective evaluation. A contracted marking section and line-bundle descent force Picard number one and ampleness of −K_X, reducing the problem to the established Fano case. No general-point or characteristic-zero assumption is used. This is an unrefereed preprint developed and checked extensively with AI tools.
Projective space is one of algebraic geometry’s basic spaces. A central question is how to recognize it from properties of a space that may initially look quite different.

The tangent bundle records the infinitesimal directions available at each point. Its relative Seshadri constant tests positivity using curves through a chosen point. Although the constant is attached to that point, computing it involves whole curves rather than only a small neighborhood.

The paper proves that a positive value at just one closed point already forces a smooth integral projective variety to be projective space. Earlier results required additional assumptions, such as being Fano, being a surface, or choosing a general point in characteristic zero. This argument retains the chosen point and works in every characteristic.

Let X be a smooth integral projective variety of dimension n ≥ 1 over an algebraically closed field k of arbitrary characteristic. If the relative Fulger–Murayama Seshadri constant ε(T_X; x) is positive at one closed point x, then X is isomorphic over k to P^n.

For a vector bundle E, let ρ: P(E) → X parametrize one-dimensional quotients and let ξ = c₁(O_{P(E)}(1)). The relative constant is ε(E; x) = inf_Γ (ξ·Γ)/mult_x(ρ_*Γ), where Γ ranges over integral curves in P(E) whose images are curves containing x. If Γ maps to C with total generic degree q, then ρ_*Γ = q[C], including any inseparable degree.

The theorem establishes the statement of Fulger–Murayama Conjecture 4.9 without assuming that X is Fano, that its tangent bundle is globally nef, that the field has characteristic zero, or that x is a general point.

Positivity forces the tangent bundle pulled back to the normalization of every rational curve through x to split into positive-degree line bundles. Among these curves, choose one with the smallest degree for a fixed very ample line bundle.

Absolute degree minimality rules out broken curves and multiple covers in the corresponding one-marked stable-map family. Deformation theory makes its evaluation map cover X while its marking section stays at x.

The contracted section lets line bundles descend and forces all numerical divisor classes to be proportional. The anticanonical divisor is then ample, so the established Fano case identifies X with projective space.
Smoothness, integrality, projectivity, an algebraically closed base field, and positive dimension are explicit hypotheses.

The constant is the relative Seshadri constant of Fulger and Murayama, with the quotient convention for the projectivized tangent bundle. The result should not be transferred silently to another positivity invariant.
The smoothness hypothesis cannot simply be dropped: Chang gives a singular projective toric threefold with a positive tangent-sheaf Seshadri constant that is not projective space.
The proof uses established rational-curve and moduli theory, and concludes by applying the previously proved Fano case.

This is an unrefereed preprint. AI tools were used extensively in the research, proof development, computational checks, literature review, and writing. The supporting package contains the published source and verification materials.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 15 September 2026 · Version 1.1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 13 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We construct a finite group G for which p = 1009, |G| = |Aut(G)| = 1009^52359. The group is the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff group of an explicitly specified rank-31 Lie ring modulo 1009^1689. Its nilpotency class is at most 846 < 1009. An asymmetric lattice forces every automorphism of the finite Lie ring into an integral logarithm–exponential neighborhood. This gives a bijection between the full automorphism set and the kernel of a linear derivation matrix. Exact independently implemented Python and C++ computations establish the Smith valuations of that matrix. The resulting computer-assisted proof answers the existence question affirmatively. The construction and all exact certificates are supplied with separately implemented verification software.

An automorphism is a way to relabel every element of a group while preserving its multiplication. The question is whether a nontrivial group whose size is a power of an odd prime can have exactly as many of these symmetries as it has elements.

This paper constructs an example with 1009^52359 elements and the same number of automorphisms. The number is enormous, but the construction has a finite description: an element is a list of 31 numbers taken modulo 1009^1689, with a specified rule for multiplying two lists.

The main difficulty is accounting for every automorphism. The proof uses a deliberately asymmetric lattice to constrain them all, then turns their count into an exact linear-algebra calculation. The paper presents this as an affirmative answer to D. MacHale’s Kourovka Notebook problem 16.63.
For p = 1009, the paper constructs a finite nontrivial p-group G with |G| = |Aut(G)| = 1009^52359, where Aut(G) is the full automorphism group.

The group is G = BCH(L/p^1689 L), where L is the explicit rank-31 Lie lattice in Definitions 2.1 and 5.1. Its nilpotency class is at most 846, below p, so the finite Lazard correspondence preserves its order and full automorphism group.

For this fixed Lie lattice and every integer i ≥ 7, the full Lie-ring automorphism group of L/p^i L has order p^(30i + 1689), while L/p^i L has p^(31i) elements. Choosing i = 1689 makes the two counts equal.

The exact derivation matrix has 14,415 rows, 961 columns, rank 931, and nullity 30. Its nonzero p-primary Smith valuations have multiplicities 87, 55, 758, 6, and 25 at valuations 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4; their sum is 1689.

Begin with the rank-31 Lie-algebra template of Omirov and Ruan. A chosen flag has no nonidentity stabilizer in its full finite-field automorphism group. Weighting the lattice along this flag forces every automorphism of a sufficiently deep finite quotient into a domain where logarithms are integral.

Within that domain, logarithm and exponential preserve the required precision and give a bijection between all automorphisms and solutions of a linear derivation equation. This is the bridge from a nonlinear symmetry problem to an exact matrix count.

The matrix’s nullity contributes 30i to the exponent of the automorphism count, while its Smith valuations contribute 1689. The ring itself has order p^(31i), so the counts meet at i = 1689. The class bound then lets the Lazard correspondence transfer the equality to a finite group.
This gives one example at p = 1009. It does not establish an example for every odd prime, and it makes no minimality claim for the prime, group order, or number of generators.
The equality is between orders. The paper does not claim that G and Aut(G) are isomorphic.

The construction is explicit through its Lie bracket and finite Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff rule. It does not enumerate the group’s multiplication table or its automorphisms. Exact computation certifies the matrix data; the full-automorphism reduction and the correspondence with groups also require the written proof.
The Lie-algebra template is due to Omirov and Ruan. This paper supplies its integral normalization, finite-characteristic arguments, asymmetric lattice, and exact count of finite automorphisms.
The Kourovka Notebook lists this manuscript as an AI-proposed solution awaiting confirmation by mathematicians. Its listing should not be read as external validation or journal peer review.

This is an unrefereed preprint whose construction, proof development, and initial verification software were generated using AI tools; subsequent checks are not external human peer review or proof-assistant formalization.

E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), The Kourovka Notebook, 21st edition, October 2026 update-3 : Problem 16.63, on printed page 106, asks the odd-prime equality question and links this manuscript with the marker for an AI-proposed solution awaiting mathematician confirmation. Archive 12.77 concerns the separate divisibility question.

Bakhrom Omirov and Jie Ruan, On Lie Algebras with Only Inner Derivations (2026) : Theorem 4.8 supplies the rank-31 characteristic-zero Lie-algebra template. The present construction credits that input and separately establishes the finite-characteristic facts it needs.

Jon González-Sánchez and Andrei Jaikin-Zapirain, Finite p-groups with small automorphism group (2015) : Constructs families with fewer automorphisms than elements and disproves the general divisibility conjecture. That result and its Lie-theoretic method are important background; it does not establish the exact equality sought in Problem 16.63.

M. Shabani-Attar, On equality of order of a finite p-group and order of its automorphism group (2015) : Classifies equality in specified classes and excludes odd-prime examples of maximal class, with cyclic Frattini subgroup, or of class two with cyclic centre. These restrictions are not a general nonexistence result.

Serena Cicalò, Willem A. de Graaf, and Michael Vaughan-Lee, An effective version of the Lazard correspondence (2012) : Explains the correspondence between finite p-groups and Lie rings of nilpotency class below p, including preservation of automorphism groups. That class restriction is checked explicitly here.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 12 September 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 37 pages) · Reproducibility package (ZIP) · Technical supplement (PDF, 27 pages) · Complete TeX source (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We determine the exact population-level information in multilocus sequence alignments generated by a temporal species network under the independent-lineage Network Multispecies Coalescent (NMSC), without treating estimated gene trees or concordance factors as observed data. With known nonrecombining locus boundaries, contemporaneous labelled sampling, and one shared irreducible stationary reversible finite-state continuous-time Markov chain, the indexed family of length-L locus laws is equivalent to the stationary distribution, the trace-normalized substitution generator, and the mutation-scaled metric-genealogy law. The first step is a compact moment theorem for the random conditional site-pattern tensor. A determinant coordinate then recovers each realized additive gene-tree metric, while a continuum in the ancestral coalescence tail identifies the shared generator, including JC, K2P, K3P, and repeated-eigenvalue GTR strata.

We compile every finite temporal NMSC presentation into a finite typed continuous-time response system on partition–occupancy states. Its canonical reachable–observable residual behavior, denoted CCR, is coordinate independent, removes analytically invisible event times, and is unique up to typed linear isomorphism. Equality of CCR is equivalent to equality of normalized metric-genealogy laws. The minimal time-indexed realization has an intrinsic positive cone, but its finite analytic encoding does not supply a stochastic occupancy basis or an NMSC graph. Literal graph recovery is impossible on the strict physical domain: arbitrary sample-unary temporal funnels have identical response in every context. Species trees are nevertheless recovered pointwise with all exposed population rates. For one-reticulation presentations we give an exact finite port-response quotient and a graph theorem on the incidence-separated subclass; the reduced level-1 result additionally assumes scalar-separator faithfulness, and no unconditional level-1 or level-2 graph theorem is claimed.

The finite-locus hierarchy has two complementary conclusions. On every fixed finite union of compact semianalytic finite-presentation charts, one finite locus length determines the complete indexed family. The proof uses the Frisch–Siu Noetherian ring of analytic germs along a compact set and remains valid at coalescent–substitution resonances. No determining length can depend only on the number of sampled taxa, reticulations, alphabet size, and sampling design if demographic epoch count is unbounded. For every L we construct two strict two-taxon, zero-reticulation, known-JC demographic histories with identical laws through length L and different length-(L + 1) laws. A Vandermonde Jacobian and the implicit-function theorem make the collision exact. We finally separate Borel inversion, finite proposed-model equivalence testing, moment approximation, and statistical consistency.

Different stretches of DNA can have different family trees, even when sampled from the same species. This paper asks what could be learned from the exact probabilities of every possible DNA alignment, while keeping track of which sites belong to the same nonrecombining stretch.

Under the stated evolutionary model, the complete collection of these probabilities contains exactly the information in the distribution of gene family trees, including their branching times, together with a normalized mutation model. It does not require treating estimated gene trees as observed facts. This is an ideal population-level statement, not a claim that one finite dataset reveals every hidden genealogy.

That information still need not identify a unique species network. Some different histories produce exactly the same distribution of observations. The paper describes the common observable behavior in a finite mathematical representation, called canonical coalescent-response behavior, or CCR.

One especially striking result concerns the length of each DNA stretch. For any chosen length L, the paper constructs two different demographic histories for just two taxa that agree on every alignment probability through length L but disagree at length L + 1. A universal length guarantee therefore has to account for demographic complexity. On a fixed compact class with finitely many specified presentations, a sufficiently long finite locus does determine the full observational equivalence class.

Fix a finite labelled sampling design with at least two sampled lineages and at least one sample from every terminal taxon. The principal model uses a finite temporal population network, positive finite coalescence rates and epoch durations, inheritance probabilities strictly between zero and one, independent routing of ancestral lineages, independent loci with known nonrecombining boundaries, contemporaneous samples, and one shared irreducible stationary reversible finite-state substitution generator Q.

The complete indexed family of length-L alignment laws is equivalent to the triple (π, Q₀, μ̄), where π is the stationary distribution, Q₀ = Q/(−tr Q), and μ̄ is the law of rooted metric gene genealogies in mutation units. The equivalence is pointwise, including reversible models with repeated eigenvalues, rather than only a generic claim.

Two normalized genealogy laws agree exactly when their CCR representations are isomorphic as typed linear response systems. CCR retains observable coalescence behavior and removes analytically invisible event times; it is not a canonical species graph. The paper proves contextual invisibility of sample-unary funnels and recovers sampled-complete species trees with exactly the demographic rates exposed to at least two ancestral lineages.

Every at-most-one-reticulation presentation has a complete finite port-response quotient. Graph incidences and inheritance weights are recovered on the incidence-separated subclass. The reduced level-1 graph result additionally requires scalar-separator faithfulness and local incidence separation. Parent-corridor demographic histories remain classified by their full response equations, which can have genuine ambiguities.

For each fixed finite union K of compact semianalytic normalized finite-presentation charts, some finite length L*(K) determines the entire indexed family. The proof gives no practical numerical bound. Conversely, with demographic epoch count unbounded, no determining length can depend only on taxon count, reticulation count, alphabet size, and sampling design: exact two-taxon, zero-reticulation collisions exist at every prescribed finite order.

Within one locus, all sites share a random genealogy. Their joint probabilities give mixed moments of the conditional site-pattern probabilities. Compact moment determinacy recovers the distribution of those conditional probabilities from all indexed lengths.

Pairwise determinants then give additive gene-tree distances. Contemporaneous sampling restores the root, while reversibility lets a matrix logarithm recover the normalized substitution generator. Finite partition-and-population states describe the resulting coalescence densities; reachable and observable future responses define CCR.

Analyticity on fixed presentations and the Frisch–Siu compact-germ theorem reduce equality of all sequence coordinates to finitely many coordinates on the stated compact classes. For the opposing result, Jukes–Cantor pair probabilities reduce to moments of a transformed coalescence time; a Vandermonde Jacobian produces exact demographic collisions through any chosen order.

The data object is the exact collection of population alignment laws indexed by locus length. It is stronger than pooled single-site frequencies, gene-tree topology summaries, or a finite empirical alignment.

The principal equivalence assumes a shared stationary reversible mutation process, contemporaneous samples, known locus boundaries, and no recombination within loci. Unknown nonreversible generators, unspecified rate mixtures, and within-locus recombination are outside that theorem.
A change of physical time unit remains possible unless an external calibration fixes it. Other indistinguishable network or demographic histories can remain even after this scale is fixed.

CCR is a finite analytic linear representation of behavior. Its positive cone does not provide a stochastic occupancy basis or an NMSC graph realization. No unconditional level-1, level-2, or general-network graph-recovery theorem is claimed.

Finite determination requires the stated compact semianalytic classes and fixed finite presentations. It does not supply a usable locus-length bound, a global noncompact theorem, or numerical stability. Finite testing of two proposed models additionally assumes exact inputs with a terminating equality test.

The consistency results concern the observational equivalence class under the stated sampling and estimation conditions. The released finite computations support specific identities and examples; they do not certify all universal theorems or establish performance on biological datasets.

Allman, Baños and Rhodes (2022), Identifiability of species network topologies from genomic sequences using the logDet distance : Earlier direct-sequence work recovers substantial level-1 topology from logDet distances. The present paper instead studies the full indexed collection of within-locus laws under its shared-generator assumptions.

Zhu and Degnan (2017), Displayed Trees Do Not Determine Distinguishability Under the Network Multispecies Coalescent : Distinguishability depends on the stochastic observation model, branch-length information, and sampling. The present funnel theorem should not be read as the first discovery of network ambiguity.

Yang and Flouri (2022), Estimation of Cross-Species Introgression Rates Using Genomic Data Despite Model Unidentifiability : Full-likelihood introgression models already exhibit exact label-switching ambiguities. This provides an important precedent for separating observable behavior from a unique biological parameterization.

Allman, Baños, Garrote-López and Rhodes (2024), Identifiability of Level-1 Species Networks from Gene Tree Quartets : Quartet concordance factors identify network features while retaining specific ambiguities. Those topology summaries are a different observation object from complete metric-genealogy or indexed sequence laws.

Allman, Ané, Baños and Rhodes (2025), Beyond Level-1: Identifiability of a Class of Galled Tree-Child Networks : Graph-identifiability results beyond level 1 already exist for restricted network classes and data conditions. The present paper makes no unrestricted higher-level graph claim.

Bhaskar and Song (2014), Descartes’ rule of signs and the identifiability of population demographic models from genomic variation data : Earlier demographic identifiability bounds explicitly depend on the number of pieces in the history. Their expected site-frequency-spectrum setting differs from the finite linked-locus laws studied here.

Siu (1969), Noetherianness of Rings of Holomorphic Functions on Stein Compact Subsets : Siu’s real-analytic Theorem 2 and compact-semianalytic consequence, following Frisch, provide the established analytic foundation for finite determination on the paper’s compact classes.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 30 July 2026 · Archive label v1.1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 34 pages) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Vértesi and Bene exhibited a 3 × 2 Bell scenario in which qubit positive-operator-valued measurements (POVMs) outperform qubit projection-valued measurements (PVMs). We prove the matching setting lower bound. For arbitrary finite, input-dependent output alphabets, the shared-randomness convex hulls of bipartite qubit-POVM and qubit-PVM behaviors are equal when both parties have two inputs. Equivalently, no two-input linear Bell functional separates the two convexified sets.

We also give a rational 3 × 2 functional, an exact qubit-POVM strategy, and a global analytic qubit-PVM upper bound with a strict exact gap. Hence 3 × 2 is the minimum input architecture, up to exchanging the parties.

The equality proof combines a one-binary-party Lorentz-cone simulation, an extremal binary–ternary reduction, a physically exact Lorentz incidence manifold, finite-POVM duality, and a rank trichotomy based on the incidence second variation. The result concerns convexified behavior sets; it does not assert equality of the raw nonconvex strategy images or same-state simulation.

In a Bell experiment, two separated observers each choose a measurement and record an outcome. Generalized quantum measurements, called POVMs, allow more possibilities than projective measurements, called PVMs. This paper asks how many measurement choices are needed before that extra freedom changes the observable correlations when each observer’s quantum system is a qubit.

With only two choices for each observer, the paper shows that any probability table produced by qubit POVMs can also be produced by a shared-randomness mixture of qubit PVM strategies. This holds for every finite number of declared outcomes, even when the outcome lists differ between measurements.

The mixture may use different states and measurements on different runs. The result concerns reproducing the joint probabilities; it does not turn every individual POVM into a projective measurement on the original state.

Three choices on one side and two on the other are enough for a strict advantage. Vértesi and Bene established that phenomenon in 2010. The proposed advance here is the matching two-choice lower bound, together with an explicit rational Bell expression and exact bounds certifying a three-by-two gap.

For every bipartite architecture with two inputs per party and arbitrary finite, input-dependent output alphabets (A₀, A₁; B₀, B₁), conv Q₂ᴾᴼⱽᴹ(A, B) = conv Q₂ᴾⱽᴹ(A, B). Each strategy has local Hilbert-space dimension at most two. The convex hull permits a shared classical variable to select the state and all measurements simultaneously.

The PVM class includes zero projectors, deterministic measurements, all labelled support patterns, and stochastic output postprocessing. Dimension-increasing ancillary systems are excluded. Equivalently, every linear Bell functional with two inputs per party has the same qubit-POVM and qubit-PVM optimum.

For the rational three-by-two Bell functional in equation (1), the paper gives an attained POVM value L₀ = 20√2 + 16/25 and a global PVM upper bound U = 20√2 + 3/5 + (4 + 3√2)/250. The certified gap is L₀ − U = 3(2 − √2)/250 > 0.

The witness has output architecture (2, 2, 3) for one party and (2, 2) for the other. Together with the two-input equality and the locality of one-input scenarios, it gives the minimum input architecture 3 × 2, up to exchanging the parties. The numbers 3 and 2 count measurement settings, not outcomes.

If one observer has only binary outcomes, the other observer’s steered states can be compressed into a three-dimensional cone. Decomposing relations in that cone gives one common mixture of complete projective strategies, preserving the whole probability table.

A hypothetical two-input Bell separator can then be reduced to one binary and one ternary measurement on each side. The remaining physical strategies admit exact Lorentz-metric coordinates. At a strict nonprojective maximum, duality forces positive multipliers, and an exhaustive rank analysis either produces an improving physical direction or an explicit projective simulation.

For the three-by-two witness, a CHSH term constrains the state and measurement geometry while an additional three-outcome measurement gains a state-discrimination advantage. Exact algebra bounds every projective alternative, including zero effects and deterministic cases.

The equality is between shared-randomness convex hulls. It does not establish equality of the raw nonconvex strategy images, a simulation using the same state, or projective simulability of an individual POVM as an operator-valued measurement.

The classification is bipartite and restricted to local Hilbert spaces of dimension at most two, finite output alphabets, and ordinary single-round Bell behaviors. It does not extend here to higher dimensions, multiple parties, or sequential measurements.

The three-by-two certificates provide an attained lower bound and a global upper bound. Neither is claimed to be the exact global optimum. The paper also derives no private-randomness entropy guarantee.

The code checks finite identities and explicit constructions. Compactness, extremal reduction, physical reconstruction, multiplier positivity, and exhaustion of the rank cases require the written proof. The paper remains unrefereed and was developed with extensive AI assistance.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 22 August 2026 · Version 1.2.4 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 16 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Supplementary note (PDF, 2 pages) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Stochastic mass-action reaction networks are chemical-master-equation models of low-copy-number biochemical systems. Anderson and Kim conjectured that weak reversibility implies positive recurrence. We prove this for finite bimolecular networks with one linkage class, removing the earlier requirement that every species occur in a pure unary or pure-double complex. Under weak reversibility, the states reachable from each initial population form a closed communicating class. Under the additional one-linkage and bimolecular hypotheses, for every positive rate vector each nonabsorbing reachable class is positive recurrent, whereas an absorbing singleton carries its point-mass law; consequently every reachable class has a unique stationary probability distribution. The closure statement follows by lifting directed return paths of complexes to population states.

For recurrence, the proof marks the target of the most recently fired channel and applies a log-factorial potential after subtracting that target. Its increment is exactly the logarithm of a target/source falling-factorial ratio, so following the carried target has zero reward. Finite target-following paths propagate the negative drift of a rare terminal source, while a normalized-log compactification and a bimolecular top-complex alternative rule out all other divergent sequences. The same return-cycle construction recovers nonexplosion directly. Multiple linkage classes and molecularity above two remain open.

A stochastic reaction network describes molecules being created, consumed, and transformed by random reaction events. This paper asks when such a system has a stationary probability distribution: a consistent long-run distribution of molecule counts within the states it can reach.

The theorem applies when every complex contains at most two molecules and the reaction diagram is strongly connected, so any complex can return to any other through a directed sequence of reactions. It works for any finite number of species and every choice of positive reaction-rate constants. It removes an earlier extra requirement that each species appear by itself in a one- or two-molecule complex.

The surprising point is that stability can emerge over several reactions even when the next jump pushes the population outward. For example, in 0 → A + B → B → 0, a state containing many A molecules but no B can initially only gain molecules. The newly created B then enables a reaction that consumes A. The proof tracks these delayed effects instead of requiring every state to have an immediate inward drift.

For every initial population, the reachable states form one closed communicating class. A nonabsorbing class has finite mean return times and one stationary law; an absorbing state has its point-mass law. This does not mean that individual trajectories stay bounded, that all molecule-count moments are finite, or that equilibrium is reached quickly.

Let a finite stochastic mass-action reaction network be weakly reversible, have exactly one linkage class, and have molecularity |y| ≤ 2 for every complex y. For every positive rate vector and initial population x₀, the set Γ(x₀) of states reachable by enabled reactions is a closed communicating class. On a nonabsorbing Γ(x₀), the minimal continuous-time Markov chain is nonexplosive and positive recurrent. An absorbing singleton carries its point-mass stationary law.

Consequently, every reachable class has a unique stationary probability distribution. The claim is class-wise: different initial populations can belong to different classes, for example because of conservation or lattice restrictions.

Compared with the single-linkage binary theorem of Anderson, Cappelletti and Kim, the result removes the condition that each species Sᵢ have Sᵢ or 2Sᵢ among the complexes. It retains weak reversibility, one linkage class, and bimolecularity.

The reachability statement uses only weak reversibility: every enabled reaction can be followed by a directed return path that remains enabled at the population level. Positive recurrence requires the additional hypotheses above. Combinatorial return-path existence and finite expected stochastic return time are distinct assertions.

blocks.text: A stochastic reaction network describes molecules being created, consumed, and transformed by random reaction events. This paper asks when such a system has a stationary probability distribution: a consistent long-run distribution of molecule counts within the states it can reach.

The theorem applies when every complex contains at most two molecules and the reaction diagram is strongly connected, so any complex can return to any other through a directed sequence of reactions. It works for any finite number of species and every choice of positive reaction-rate constants. It removes an earlier extra requirement that each species appear by itself in a one- or two-molecule complex.

The surprising point is that stability can emerge over several reactions even when the next jump pushes the population outward. For example, in 0 → A + B → B → 0, a state containing many A molecules but no B can initially only gain molecules. The newly created B then enables a reaction that consumes A. The proof tracks these delayed effects instead of requiring every state to have an immediate inward drift.

For every initial population, the reachable states form one closed communicating class. A nonabsorbing class has finite mean return times and one stationary law; an absorbing state has its point-mass law. This does not mean that individual trajectories stay bounded, that all molecule-count moments are finite, or that equilibrium is reached quickly.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 12 September 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 21 pages) · LaTeX source (ZIP) · Technical supplement (PDF, 11 pages) · Reproducibility materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We classify the observable rooted graph and parameters of finite strict temporally separated binary strongly tree-child species networks of level at most two under the independent-lineage Network Multispecies Coalescent (NMSC), with a fixed known surjective taxon sampling map. Equality of complete normalized rooted metric-genealogy laws is equivalent, pointwise on the full positive domain, to an explicit quotient generated by eight move types.

The proof recovers current pair co-occupancy from the analytic germ of a finite positive Kingman mixture. Signed jumps reveal every tree event and every pair-exposed reticulation. Descendant clusters, chronology, tree-childness and level-two shortcut completion then reconstruct the retained graph, including arbitrary decorations. Deterministic witnesses and actual three-lineage merger densities recover oriented inheritance weights and the entire finite demographic rate words on exposed populations. Scalar propagation through ancestral reticulations links both incoming arms, including equal rates and inheritance one-half. The indexed collection of all genealogy marginals on at most three sampled lineages suffices for the complete quotient.

A reticulation with one descendant sampled lineage retains its two typed first-exposure outlets and route weights, while its internal clock and singly occupied demographic words are unobservable. Sister-transfer direction is invisible exactly when both sides are sample unary; the corresponding reversal transfers the whole exposed donor rate word. Together with presentation suppression, equal-rate composition, unary-corridor replacement, parent exchange and labelled isomorphism, these responses exhaust the quotient. Exact hidden-clock and rank-one nonbridge examples explain essential obstructions. A separate graph argument derives the five cores and twelve minimum strong repairs.

The companion study transfers the classification to all indexed ordered locus laws with known boundaries, jointly with the stationary distribution and trace-normalized shared irreducible stationary reversible substitution generator. The reconstruction uses observable current-grouping scalars throughout.

A species history can contain both branching and gene flow between branches. Different genetic lineages can therefore trace different family trees through the same species network. The question here is what the complete probability distribution of those genealogies could reveal about the underlying history.

For a restricted class of networks, the paper classifies exactly which changes leave that distribution unchanged. It claims recovery of the retained rooted graph, inheritance probabilities and the histories of coalescence rates in populations that can contain two sampled ancestral lineages.

The distinction between visible and invisible history is central. An event carrying only one sampled lineage can retain identifiable route probabilities while its internal timing remains invisible. In a sister-transfer triangle, direction is ambiguous when each side supplies only one sampled lineage; additional exposure can distinguish the directions. These are statements about ideal probability laws under the model, not guarantees for a finite genetic dataset.

The main theorem considers finite rooted binary strongly tree-child networks of level at most two under the independent-lineage Network Multispecies Coalescent. Samples are contemporaneous, and the known sampling map is surjective onto the terminal taxa. Finite population durations and piecewise-constant Kingman pair rates are positive, inheritance weights lie strictly between zero and one, and distinct internal biological events have distinct ages. The above-root population eventually has a positive constant coalescence rate.

Strongly tree-child means that the semi-directed reduction is tree-child under every admissible rooting, which is stronger than checking the supplied rooting alone. Level at most two limits each blob to two reticulations; it does not limit the entire network to two reticulations. Raw reticulations have distinct parents.

Two such models have the same complete normalized rooted metric-genealogy law exactly when they agree under eight specified equivalence moves, Q1–Q8. These include harmless presentation changes, parent exchange, replacement of unobservable single-lineage corridors and two-outlet routing fans, and reversal of a bi-unary sister triangle with its entire exposed donor rate history transferred.

The indexed collection of every labelled genealogy marginal on at most three sampled lineages suffices for this quotient. The result is pointwise on the stated positive domain, including equal population rates and inheritance probability one-half. It concerns the observable equivalence class, not unique recovery of every raw event and parameter.

Through the companion paper, the classification also applies to all indexed ordered locus laws with known boundaries under a shared irreducible stationary reversible substitution generator. This additionally identifies the stationary distribution and trace-normalized generator; physical time and rate retain the common scale ambiguity.

The companion’s finite-determination theorem further gives a finite determining locus length on each fixed finite union of compact semianalytic normalized finite-presentation charts in this class. It provides no effective practical sequence-length bound.

On a short interval with no population boundary, pair survival is a finite sum of positive exponentials plus a constant. The constant corresponds to ancestral lineages in separate populations. Exact local analytic information therefore determines their current co-occupancy probability without observing their routes.

A tree join produces a positive co-occupancy jump; independent splitting at an exposed reticulation produces a negative one. With distinct biological event times, these jumps reveal descendant clusters and chronology. Tree-child witnesses and the level-two graph restrictions then determine the retained graph up to the stated sister-triangle ambiguity.

Ordinary population rates come from a merger density divided by co-occupancy. Three-lineage merger densities distinguish incoming reticulation arms; forward propagation of already recovered parameters recovers the remaining arm histories. These are observable scalar calculations, not measurements of historical route labels.

Single-lineage regions cannot contain a coalescent merger. Their observable effect reduces to how they deliver a lineage to its first exposed outlets. Keeping those weighted outlets while discarding invisible internal clocks explains why the theorem identifies an equivalence class.
This is an unrefereed preprint developed with extensive generative-AI assistance. The author is responsible for its claims and welcomes independent expert review.

The theorem requires the strong tree-child, binary, level-at-most-two, strict positivity, temporal-separation and sampling hypotheses. It does not classify arbitrary reticulate species histories, simultaneous biological events or limiting zero-duration or zero-rate models.

The observations are exact rooted metric-genealogy probability laws, including merger times. Recovering analytic germs and their continuations is a theoretical identifiability argument. No sample-size guarantee, noise-stability bound or efficient practical estimator is supplied.

Some clocks and rate histories are intrinsically unobservable when only one sampled lineage traverses a population. Sister-triangle reversal can also preserve the law when both sides are sample unary. All claims about recovered demographics are modulo the stated equivalence moves.
The small-marginal statement requires all relevant labelled pairs and triples. It does not say that one triple, three nucleotide sites or three observed genealogies determine a network.

The sequence-law corollary relies on the companion preprint and its additional model assumptions. Unknown locus boundaries, recombination, nonreversible substitution and arbitrary demographic mixtures are outside this result. Finite computational checks support the arguments within their declared domains and do not prove the universal theorem.
This is an unrefereed preprint developed with extensive generative-AI assistance. The author is responsible for its claims and welcomes independent expert review.

Alec Kriebel, Direct Sequence Laws under the Network Multispecies Coalescent (2026) : The companion preprint supplies the sequence-law to normalized metric-genealogy equivalence used by this paper. The graph classification and its sequence corollary therefore have different dependency chains.

Marc Hellmuth, David Schaller and Peter F. Stadler, Clustering systems of phylogenetic networks (2023) : Develops the relationship between descendant clusters and network structure. This is background for the tree-child cluster arguments; clusters alone do not identify arbitrary networks.

Ziheng Yang and Tomáš Flouri, Estimation of cross-species introgression rates using genomic data despite model unidentifiability (2022) : Earlier work analyzes parameter ambiguities and sampling in coalescent introgression models. The present paper should be read as an exact quotient for its larger specified network class, not as the first observation of introgression nonidentifiability.

Yuttapong Thawornwattana and colleagues, Inferring the Direction of Introgression Using Genomic Sequence Data (2023) : Already explains the sister-species direction ambiguity with one sequence per species and the value of additional sampling. Here that phenomenon is incorporated into a graph-and-demographic classification with finite rate histories.

Elizabeth S. Allman, Cécile Ané, Hector Baños and John A. Rhodes, Beyond Level-1: Identifiability of a Class of Galled Tree-Child Networks (2025) : Establishes topology identifiability for restricted galled tree-child semi-directed networks, including networks of arbitrary level, from suitable data such as quartet concordance factors. Its network class and recovered information differ from this metric-genealogy quotient.

Niels Holtgrefe and colleagues, Distinguishing Phylogenetic Level-2 Networks with Quartets and Inter-Taxon Quartet Distances (2025) : Characterizes a canonical form for outer-labelled planar galled semi-directed level-2 networks using displayed quartets. The present result uses richer metric-genealogy laws and retains rooted numerical information within its own restrictions.

Aviva K. Englander and colleagues, Identifiability of Phylogenetic Level-2 Networks under the Jukes-Cantor Model (2025) : Gives generic identifiability of triangle-free strongly tree-child semi-directed level-2 topology under a Markov DNA-evolution model. This is relevant prior level-2 identifiability work; its model and topology target differ from the NMSC demographic classification here.

Jari Brits, Niels Holtgrefe, Leo van Iersel and Samuel Martin, On Tree-Network Distinguishability and Full Identifiability of Phylogenetic Networks (2026) : Studies pointwise level-1 topology identifiability, modulo triangle redirection, under JC, K2P and K3P Markov models. It is further context for avoiding a broad claim to the first pointwise network-identifiability result.

blocks.text: A species history can contain both branching and gene flow between branches. Different genetic lineages can therefore trace different family trees through the same species network. The question here is what the complete probability distribution of those genealogies could reveal about the underlying history.

For a restricted class of networks, the paper classifies exactly which changes leave that distribution unchanged. It claims recovery of the retained rooted graph, inheritance probabilities and the histories of coalescence rates in populations that can contain two sampled ancestral lineages.

The distinction between visible and invisible history is central. An event carrying only one sampled lineage can retain identifiable route probabilities while its internal timing remains invisible. In a sister-transfer triangle, direction is ambiguous when each side supplies only one sampled lineage; additional exposure can distinguish the directions. These are statements about ideal probability laws under the model, not guarantees for a finite genetic dataset.

blocks.text: The main theorem considers finite rooted binary strongly tree-child networks of level at most two under the independent-lineage Network Multispecies Coalescent. Samples are contemporaneous, and the known sampling map is surjective onto the terminal taxa. Finite population durations and piecewise-constant Kingman pair rates are positive, inheritance weights lie strictly between zero and one, and distinct internal biological events have distinct ages. The above-root population eventually has a positive constant coalescence rate.

Strongly tree-child means that the semi-directed reduction is tree-child under every admissible rooting, which is stronger than checking the supplied rooting alone. Level at most two limits each blob to two reticulations; it does not limit the entire network to two reticulations. Raw reticulations have distinct parents.

Two such models have the same complete normalized rooted metric-genealogy law exactly when they agree under eight specified equivalence moves, Q1–Q8. These include harmless presentation changes, parent exchange, replacement of unobservable single-lineage corridors and two-outlet routing fans, and reversal of a bi-unary sister triangle with its entire exposed donor rate history transferred.

The indexed collection of every labelled genealogy marginal on at most three sampled lineages suffices for this quotient. The result is pointwise on the stated positive domain, including equal population rates and inheritance probability one-half. It concerns the observable equivalence class, not unique recovery of every raw event and parameter.

Through the companion paper, the classification also applies to all indexed ordered locus laws with known boundaries under a shared irreducible stationary reversible substitution generator. This additionally identifies the stationary distribution and trace-normalized generator; physical time and rate retain the common scale ambiguity.

The companion’s finite-determination theorem further gives a finite determining locus length on each fixed finite union of compact semianalytic normalized finite-presentation charts in this class. It provides no effective practical sequence-length bound.

blocks.text: On a short interval with no population boundary, pair survival is a finite sum of positive exponentials plus a constant. The constant corresponds to ancestral lineages in separate populations. Exact local analytic information therefore determines their current co-occupancy probability without observing their routes.

A tree join produces a positive co-occupancy jump; independent splitting at an exposed reticulation produces a negative one. With distinct biological event times, these jumps reveal descendant clusters and chronology. Tree-child witnesses and the level-two graph restrictions then determine the retained graph up to the stated sister-triangle ambiguity.

Ordinary population rates come from a merger density divided by co-occupancy. Three-lineage merger densities distinguish incoming reticulation arms; forward propagation of already recovered parameters recovers the remaining arm histories. These are observable scalar calculations, not measurements of historical route labels.

Single-lineage regions cannot contain a coalescent merger. Their observable effect reduces to how they deliver a lineage to its first exposed outlets. Keeping those weighted outlets while discarding invisible internal clocks explains why the theorem identifies an equivalence class.

blocks.text: This is an unrefereed preprint developed with extensive generative-AI assistance. The author is responsible for its claims and welcomes independent expert review.

The theorem requires the strong tree-child, binary, level-at-most-two, strict positivity, temporal-separation and sampling hypotheses. It does not classify arbitrary reticulate species histories, simultaneous biological events or limiting zero-duration or zero-rate models.

The observations are exact rooted metric-genealogy probability laws, including merger times. Recovering analytic germs and their continuations is a theoretical identifiability argument. No sample-size guarantee, noise-stability bound or efficient practical estimator is supplied.

Some clocks and rate histories are intrinsically unobservable when only one sampled lineage traverses a population. Sister-triangle reversal can also preserve the law when both sides are sample unary. All claims about recovered demographics are modulo the stated equivalence moves.
The small-marginal statement requires all relevant labelled pairs and triples. It does not say that one triple, three nucleotide sites or three observed genealogies determine a network.

The sequence-law corollary relies on the companion preprint and its additional model assumptions. Unknown locus boundaries, recombination, nonreversible substitution and arbitrary demographic mixtures are outside this result. Finite computational checks support the arguments within their declared domains and do not prove the universal theorem.

blocks.text: Alec Kriebel, Direct Sequence Laws under the Network Multispecies Coalescent (2026) : The companion preprint supplies the sequence-law to normalized metric-genealogy equivalence used by this paper. The graph classification and its sequence corollary therefore have different dependency chains.

Marc Hellmuth, David Schaller and Peter F. Stadler, Clustering systems of phylogenetic networks (2023) : Develops the relationship between descendant clusters and network structure. This is background for the tree-child cluster arguments; clusters alone do not identify arbitrary networks.

Ziheng Yang and Tomáš Flouri, Estimation of cross-species introgression rates using genomic data despite model unidentifiability (2022) : Earlier work analyzes parameter ambiguities and sampling in coalescent introgression models. The present paper should be read as an exact quotient for its larger specified network class, not as the first observation of introgression nonidentifiability.

Yuttapong Thawornwattana and colleagues, Inferring the Direction of Introgression Using Genomic Sequence Data (2023) : Already explains the sister-species direction ambiguity with one sequence per species and the value of additional sampling. Here that phenomenon is incorporated into a graph-and-demographic classification with finite rate histories.

Elizabeth S. Allman, Cécile Ané, Hector Baños and John A. Rhodes, Beyond Level-1: Identifiability of a Class of Galled Tree-Child Networks (2025) : Establishes topology identifiability for restricted galled tree-child semi-directed networks, including networks of arbitrary level, from suitable data such as quartet concordance factors. Its network class and recovered information differ from this metric-genealogy quotient.

Niels Holtgrefe and colleagues, Distinguishing Phylogenetic Level-2 Networks with Quartets and Inter-Taxon Quartet Distances (2025) : Characterizes a canonical form for outer-labelled planar galled semi-directed level-2 networks using displayed quartets. The present result uses richer metric-genealogy laws and retains rooted numerical information within its own restrictions.

Aviva K. Englander and colleagues, Identifiability of Phylogenetic Level-2 Networks under the Jukes-Cantor Model (2025) : Gives generic identifiability of triangle-free strongly tree-child semi-directed level-2 topology under a Markov DNA-evolution model. This is relevant prior level-2 identifiability work; its model and topology target differ from the NMSC demographic classification here.

Jari Brits, Niels Holtgrefe, Leo van Iersel and Samuel Martin, On Tree-Network Distinguishability and Full Identifiability of Phylogenetic Networks (2026) : Studies pointwise level-1 topology identifiability, modulo triangle redirection, under JC, K2P and K3P Markov models. It is further context for avoiding a broad claim to the first pointwise network-identifiability result.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 17 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 5 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We give a negative answer to the comparison question of Gishboliner and Shapira in Oberwolfach Report 19/2019, Problem 5, and their later Problem 5.6. The fixed property consisting of K₄-free graphs that become 3-colorable after deleting at most one vertex has a polynomial classical canonical tester, for every input size. In the vertex-distribution-free model, every adaptive two-sided tester has superpolynomial total sample-plus-adjacency cost as the proximity parameter tends to zero. The lower bound follows by an elementary tripartite-cover and heavy-apex reduction from the established two-sided triangle-testing lower bound. All distances allow arbitrary edge additions and deletions. The reduction remains valid when the tester is given the vertex set, its size, the full positive rational distribution, and the heavy vertex. A self-contained classical sampling argument and exact finite verification materials accompany the note.

Graph property testing asks whether a large network has a specified feature, or is far from having it, while inspecting only a small part of the network. Usually every vertex receives equal weight. The vertex-distribution-free model allows vertices to have very different weights, which affect both sampling and the cost of changing edges.

This paper constructs one fixed feature that is relatively cheap to test with uniform samples but much more expensive with arbitrary vertex weights. The feature has two conditions: no four vertices form a complete clique, and deleting at most one vertex makes the graph colorable with three colors.

The key example gives a single vertex half of the sampling weight. Its connections force the rest of the graph to obey a difficult triangle-free condition. That one vertex has little influence under uniform sampling in a large graph, yet it is expensive to disconnect under the weighted distance.

The separation persists even if the tester is told every vertex name and the entire distribution. The obstruction is therefore not just ignorance of the sampling weights. The result measures how many samples and adjacency questions are required; it makes no claim of a polynomial running-time algorithm.

Fix the property P of finite simple undirected K₄-free graphs that become 3-colorable after deleting at most one vertex. It is hereditary, closed under edge deletion, and extendable by adding an isolated vertex.

For every nonempty input size, a one-sided classical canonical tester uses O(ε⁻⁶ log(1/ε)) independent uniform samples and O(ε⁻¹² log²(1/ε)) adjacency queries. It does not need to know the number of vertices.

Along a sequence of positive rational ε tending to zero, every randomized adaptive two-sided vertex-distribution-free tester has worst-case total sample-plus-adjacency cost exp(Ω(log²(1/ε))). This remains true with the full vertex set, its size, the complete positive rational weight vector, and the distinguished heavy vertex supplied.

The distance is the sum of D(u)D(v) over unordered changed vertex pairs, minimized over graphs with the property on the same vertex set; additions and deletions are both allowed. For uniform D this is the number of changed edges divided by n². Testers accept members and reject ε-far inputs with probability at least 2/3.

Consequently no fixed polynomial in classical canonical complexity and 1/ε can bound the VDF complexity for every extendable hereditary property, even after a fixed positive constant rescaling of the classical proximity parameter. This addresses the comparison question in Gishboliner–Shapira Problem 5.6 and the earlier Oberwolfach problem.

The classical tester looks for two disjoint subgraphs that each fail 3-colorability. Deleting one vertex cannot remove both obstructions. A color-list sampling argument finds these witnesses in large inputs; sufficiently many samples collect every vertex of a small input.

For the lower bound, a tripartite cover makes any graph 3-colorable while preserving triangle-freeness and retaining a constant fraction of its distance from that property. After adding a universal vertex with weight 1/2, the new graph’s distance from P is exactly one quarter of the tail’s triangle-free distance.

The composition loses only a factor of 36 in proximity. Sampling the constructed graph needs no access to the original edges, and each adjacency query costs at most one original adjacency query. The established adaptive two-sided triangle lower bound therefore transfers to the weighted testing problem.
This is a separation for one fixed property. It does not classify which other properties have a gap, or settle every question about forbidding one fixed subgraph.

The lower bound counts samples and adjacency queries together. It is not a sample-only bound when unlimited arbitrary-name adjacency queries are free. Its displayed quantitative bound is stated along a sequence of proximity parameters.
The classical tester can use exhaustive membership checking on the sampled graph. Polynomial oracle complexity does not imply polynomial running time.

The proof imports the established two-sided triangle-testing lower bound of Alon and Shapira. The contribution is the property and the reduction that place known triangle hardness against a polynomial classical tester, not a new triangle lower bound.

The literature comparison is bounded. No claim of exhaustive priority certification, independent human peer review, or formal proof verification is made. The finite programs supplement the written proof and its cited theorem.

AI tools were used extensively in development, verification, literature review, and writing. The author is responsible for the claims. AI-assisted reviews and finite verification programs are not independent human peer review or formal proof certification.

Authorship and responsibilities would be discussed in relation to the substantive contributions made.

Gishboliner and Shapira, Testing Graphs against an Unknown Distribution : Defines the VDF framework and states the uniform-versus-VDF comparison as Problem 5.6. Its positive result for blowup-avoidable properties does not cover every extendable hereditary property.
Gishboliner, joint work with Shapira, Oberwolfach Report 19/2019 : The original comparison appears as Problem 5 on printed page 1139. The model counts vertex samples and edge queries.
Alon and Shapira (2004), Testing subgraphs in directed graphs : Theorem 4(ii) and its two-sided lower-bound argument supply the classical triangle-testing hardness used by the reduction.

Alon and Krivelevich (2002), Testing k-colorability : Part of the established polynomial colorability-testing theory. The note includes a conservative sampling proof that explicitly handles every input size.

Fei (2026), Testing Properties of Edge Distributions : Studies distributions on edges with a different default sampling oracle and arbitrary edge weights. Those results should not be conflated with vertex-product distance and counted adjacency access here.

blocks.text: The classical tester looks for two disjoint subgraphs that each fail 3-colorability. Deleting one vertex cannot remove both obstructions. A color-list sampling argument finds these witnesses in large inputs; sufficiently many samples collect every vertex of a small input.

For the lower bound, a tripartite cover makes any graph 3-colorable while preserving triangle-freeness and retaining a constant fraction of its distance from that property. After adding a universal vertex with weight 1/2, the new graph’s distance from P is exactly one quarter of the tail’s triangle-free distance.

The composition loses only a factor of 36 in proximity. Sampling the constructed graph needs no access to the original edges, and each adjacency query costs at most one original adjacency query. The established adaptive two-sided triangle lower bound therefore transfers to the weighted testing problem.
