article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 13 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We construct a compact smooth Riemannian sphere and a smooth homeomorphism from the round sphere which locally minimizes Reshetnyak energy against every same-trace Sobolev competitor, but has essentially unbounded infinitesimal distortion. This gives a negative answer for the Reshetnyak member of the general-energy harmonic-sphere question posed in the inspected 2025 texts of Meier–Vikman–Wenger. Scalar calibration on a flat belt and an exact two-form calibration on conformal caps prove the full local comparison. The map does not minimize energy in its homotopy class and is not Korevaar–Schoen harmonic. Separately, an angular-stress argument gives the nonsharp bound 4 + √17 for locally Korevaar–Schoen-minimizing spheres into complete metric spaces; the sharper classical SL(2)-minimal bound also applies. Classical ingredients are credited; first priority is not claimed.

An energy-minimizing map can be thought of as a way of placing one surface onto another that cannot be improved by changing a small patch while keeping its boundary fixed. Whether that condition prevents severe stretching depends on which energy is being minimized.

The paper constructs a smooth map from the round sphere onto a smooth Riemannian sphere. It is a homeomorphism: it is one-to-one, onto, and has a continuous inverse. It locally minimizes Reshetnyak energy, which measures the square of the greatest infinitesimal stretch, yet its stretching can be arbitrarily unequal in different directions.

Near the equator, one direction is compressed by a factor proportional to the square of the distance from the equator while the other is left unchanged. The ratio of the two stretches exceeds every finite bound on a region of positive area. This is a distortion phenomenon, even though the map and both surfaces are smooth.

The choice of energy matters. The example does not minimize the usual Dirichlet, or Korevaar–Schoen, energy and does not minimize energy globally within its homotopy class. A separate argument in the paper establishes bounded infinitesimal distortion for locally Korevaar–Schoen-minimizing spheres into complete metric spaces.

There is a compact smooth Riemannian surface X diffeomorphic to S² and a smooth homeomorphism u from the round S² to X that locally minimizes Reshetnyak energy E₊² but has essentially unbounded infinitesimal distortion.

Local minimization has the full fixed-trace meaning: each source point has a neighborhood U such that, for every Lipschitz domain Ω compactly contained in U, u has no larger energy than any W¹,²(Ω, X) competitor with the same boundary trace. Competitors need not be continuous, remain in the chosen image patch, or share a prescribed homotopy class.

The target is geodesic, satisfies a local quadratic isoperimetric inequality, and every sufficiently small-diameter continuous sphere in it is null-homotopic. Thus the counterexample satisfies the target assumptions of the general-energy harmonic-sphere question in the inspected Meier–Vikman–Wenger arXiv v1 and Oberwolfach texts.

On a punctured equatorial band the ratio of largest to smallest infinitesimal stretch is 1/t² in cylindrical coordinates. Every proposed finite distortion bound fails on a set of positive area. The inverse homeomorphism need not be smooth.

Separately, for a complete metric target in the standard metric-Sobolev framework, a locally Korevaar–Schoen-minimizing W¹,² map from S² has infinitesimal distortion at most 4 + √17. The stress argument also gives SL(2)-minimality, so the sharper established Lytchak–Wenger bound 2√2 + √6 applies. The displayed elementary constant is not claimed as an improvement or an optimum.

The target sphere has a flat cylindrical belt and smooth conformal caps. The map compresses one belt coordinate by h(t), with h′(t) = t² near the equator, while preserving the angular coordinate. It becomes conformal away from the compressed region.

On the belt, a globally 1-Lipschitz extension of the angular coordinate turns every competitor into a scalar Sobolev function with the same boundary data. Its Dirichlet energy gives a lower bound attained by the constructed map. This comparison still works when a competitor leaves the local image patch.

On the caps, an exact two-form with comass at most one agrees with the area form near the image. Pullback and trace-gluing identities make its integral depend only on the fixed boundary trace, giving the required lower bound for arbitrary Sobolev competitors.

For the separate KS result, inner variations yield an angular stress tensor. On the sphere it defines a holomorphic quadratic differential and therefore vanishes. The resulting balance of the infinitesimal seminorm bounds distortion; the established SL(2)-minimal theory gives the sharper constant.

The counterexample uses Reshetnyak energy, the integral of the squared operator norm. It is not Korevaar–Schoen harmonic, where the smooth-target energy instead sums the squares of both singular values. Comparable energies can have different minimizers.

The map is a local fixed-trace minimizer, not a global minimizer in its homotopy class. A conformal homeomorphism in the same class has strictly lower total energy, so the example does not contradict the established theory of global homotopy minimizers.

The negative answer is tied to the Reshetnyak member of the general-energy question in the inspected 2025 arXiv version and workshop contribution. The revised journal body was not available for comparison, and neither unchanged final wording nor continued open status is asserted.

The positive Korevaar–Schoen statement gives bounded distortion in general metric targets, not conformality of every tangent seminorm. The smooth Riemannian-target conformality phenomenon and the sharper SL(2)-minimal bound are classical ingredients.

First priority and optimal constants are not claimed. Finite algebra checks and numerical diagnostics support the construction but do not certify the universal Sobolev comparison or the global stress argument.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 18 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 11 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

For a nearest-neighbor walk on Z in a fixed i.i.d. space-time environment with transition probabilities strictly between zero and one, we prove that its quenched and averaged endpoint laws agree, after coarse graining into deterministic intervals of any diverging length, outside an environment event of probability smaller than every inverse power of time. No uniform ellipticity or quantitative rate of divergence of the interval length is required. This is the affirmative one-dimensional assertion contrary to Conjecture 1 in Berger’s contribution to Oberwolfach Report 38/2009. The proof combines replica overlap estimates, environmental martingales, same-parity coalescence and concentration over a short final segment. Priority qualification: novelty and historical priority remain unresolved. A bounded literature audit established no exact full anticipation, but four relevant older original full texts could not be accessed. article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 15 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 5 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

For every integer d ≥ 2 we construct a bond percolation on Zᵈ that is invariant under all lattice automorphisms, mixing under translations, and has ordinary finite energy. Almost surely it has a unique infinite component, yet every independent Bernoulli thinning with retention p < 1 destroys all infinite components. The construction perturbs a one-ended spanning tree, using the maximum finite-past size along each non-tree edge’s tree path to suppress every bypass of large tree cuts. This answers the historical ordinary-energy question of Benjamini, Häggström and Schramm. We also make explicit a planar threshold-one consequence of Häggström–Mester’s earlier construction. No first-priority claim is made.

Percolation studies which connections survive in a random network. This paper constructs a random network on the integer lattice that has one infinite connected component, yet is so fragile that independently deleting each edge with any fixed positive probability destroys every infinite component.

The network has no preferred location or lattice direction. It also has ordinary finite energy: even after all other edges are revealed, any particular edge still has a positive conditional chance of being either present or absent. Those probabilities need not share a common bound away from zero and one.

The construction leaves a sequence of bottlenecks on every route to infinity. Beyond a sufficiently large scale, each such boundary has exactly one surviving crossing edge. Independent thinning eventually breaks these indispensable connections, however close its retention probability is to one.

The result works in every dimension at least two. It develops Häggström and Mester’s earlier one-ended-tree perturbation mechanism and makes a further threshold consequence of their planar example explicit. The note does not claim a verified first resolution of the historical question.

For every integer d ≥ 2, there is a bond-percolation law on the nearest-neighbor edges of Zᵈ that is invariant under every graph automorphism and mixing under translations. For each edge e, its conditional probability of being open, given all other output edges, lies strictly between zero and one almost surely.

Almost surely the realized graph X has a unique infinite component C, and p_c(X) = p_c(C) = 1 for independent internal bond thinning. The internal site thresholds of both graphs also equal one. These statements are quenched: X is fixed before the independent thinning is introduced.

More generally, the perturbation applies to any countably infinite connected simple bounded-degree graph with a one-ended spanning tree T. If deleting a tree edge t leaves a finite side of size s_T(t), retain it with probability 1 − 2^(−s_T(t)). Insert a non-tree edge e with probability 2^(−M_T(e)), where M_T(e) is the maximum finite-side size along its connecting tree path. Conditional on T, these choices are independent.

The all-dimensional lattice input comes from Timár’s established factor-of-iid one-ended spanning-tree theorem. The note also derives a planar threshold-one conclusion from the exact fixed-phase midpoint projection of Häggström–Mester’s older model, preserving its original flip rates.

In a one-ended tree, each edge on a ray separates off a finite set, and those sets grow to exhaust the graph. Any extra edge crossing one of these boundaries has a tree path that includes its separating tree edge.

The insertion rule uses the largest finite-side size along that path. The probabilities of deleting the essential tree edge or adding any bypass have a summable total along the ray. Borel–Cantelli therefore leaves eventual singleton boundaries and retained infinite ray tails.

The retained tails coalesce, yielding one infinite component. Once the graph is fixed, any infinite path must use infinitely many distinct bottleneck edges. Independent retention with p < 1 has probability at most pᵏ of preserving the first k of them, which tends to zero. The same argument uses their vertices for site thinning.

Every conditional edge probability is strictly between zero and one even after the hidden tree is averaged out. Equivariance of the tree input and perturbation preserves all lattice symmetries, while their representation as a measurable factor of iid marks gives translation mixing.

The energy condition is ordinary finite energy. The paper neither proves a uniform positive lower bound on the marginal conditional probabilities nor proves that every such uniform bound fails. Small probabilities conditional on the hidden tree do not alone decide the marginal question.

Finite components are allowed. Existence of a unique infinite component does not say that every lattice vertex belongs to it. The external random process is a bond law; the additional site assertion concerns independent thinning inside its realized graph.

The perturbation theorem requires a connected one-ended spanning tree and bounded ambient degree. A disconnected uniform spanning forest in higher dimensions cannot be substituted, since some non-tree edges would have no connecting tree path.

The planar midpoint law is a coordinate marginal of a fixed-phase site construction, with all coarse vertices present. It is not the induced bond graph of the final open sites, and the old site/bond threshold comparison alone does not provide an external finite-energy bond law.

The planar perturbation mechanism is due to Häggström and Mester. The note supplies an additional bounded-cutset deduction and a dimension-independent bypass rule with eventual singleton cuts. Neither first priority for the historical answer nor certified novelty of that rule is claimed. No finite coding radius or quantitative mixing rate is asserted.

OpenAI tools were used extensively in solving, proof development, drafting, coding, and adversarial verification. The author is responsible for the claims. No completed external human peer review or formal proof-assistant verification is claimed; package checks authenticate files rather than the infinite mathematical proof.

Benjamini, Häggström and Schramm, On the effect of adding ε-Bernoulli percolation to everywhere percolating subgraphs of Zᵈ : Poses the historical ordinary-finite-energy bond question. Its separate sprinkling setting adds fixed-density noise to an everywhere-percolating graph.

Benjamini and Tassion, Homogenization via sprinkling : Question 1 restates the exact existence problem and defines finite energy as insertion and deletion tolerance. The sprinkling theorem has different hypotheses from this tree-dependent perturbation.

Häggström and Mester, Some two-dimensional finite energy percolation processes (2009) : Section 2 supplies the prior summable finite-past site-flip mechanism. The post-flip threshold-one deduction supplied in this note is not a theorem stated in the inspected antecedent; the original mechanism deserves explicit credit.
Timár, One-ended spanning trees in amenable unimodular graphs : Theorem 1 provides the equivariant factor-of-iid connected one-ended spanning tree used on every Zᵈ with d ≥ 2.

Pemantle, Choosing a spanning tree for the integer lattice uniformly : Provides the classical uniform spanning-tree alternative in dimensions two through four and the planar primal/dual input behind the earlier construction.

Almost surely the realized graph X has a unique infinite component C, and p_c(X) = p_c(C) = 1 for independent internal bond thinning. The internal site thresholds of both graphs also equal one. These statements are quenched: X is fixed before the independent thinning is introduced.

More generally, the perturbation applies to any countably infinite connected simple bounded-degree graph with a one-ended spanning tree T. If deleting a tree edge t leaves a finite side of size s_T(t), retain it with probability 1 − 2^(−s_T(t)). Insert a non-tree edge e with probability 2^(−M_T(e)), where M_T(e) is the maximum finite-side size along its connecting tree path. Conditional on T, these choices are independent.

The all-dimensional lattice input comes from Timár’s established factor-of-iid one-ended spanning-tree theorem. The note also derives a planar threshold-one conclusion from the exact fixed-phase midpoint projection of Häggström–Mester’s older model, preserving its original flip rates.

blocks.text: In a one-ended tree, each edge on a ray separates off a finite set, and those sets grow to exhaust the graph. Any extra edge crossing one of these boundaries has a tree path that includes its separating tree edge.

The insertion rule uses the largest finite-side size along that path. The probabilities of deleting the essential tree edge or adding any bypass have a summable total along the ray. Borel–Cantelli therefore leaves eventual singleton boundaries and retained infinite ray tails.

The retained tails coalesce, yielding one infinite component. Once the graph is fixed, any infinite path must use infinitely many distinct bottleneck edges. Independent retention with p < 1 has probability at most pᵏ of preserving the first k of them, which tends to zero. The same argument uses their vertices for site thinning.

Every conditional edge probability is strictly between zero and one even after the hidden tree is averaged out. Equivariance of the tree input and perturbation preserves all lattice symmetries, while their representation as a measurable factor of iid marks gives translation mixing.

blocks.text: The energy condition is ordinary finite energy. The paper neither proves a uniform positive lower bound on the marginal conditional probabilities nor proves that every such uniform bound fails. Small probabilities conditional on the hidden tree do not alone decide the marginal question.

Finite components are allowed. Existence of a unique infinite component does not say that every lattice vertex belongs to it. The external random process is a bond law; the additional site assertion concerns independent thinning inside its realized graph.

The perturbation theorem requires a connected one-ended spanning tree and bounded ambient degree. A disconnected uniform spanning forest in higher dimensions cannot be substituted, since some non-tree edges would have no connecting tree path.

The planar midpoint law is a coordinate marginal of a fixed-phase site construction, with all coarse vertices present. It is not the induced bond graph of the final open sites, and the old site/bond threshold comparison alone does not provide an external finite-energy bond law.

The planar perturbation mechanism is due to Häggström and Mester. The note supplies an additional bounded-cutset deduction and a dimension-independent bypass rule with eventual singleton cuts. Neither first priority for the historical answer nor certified novelty of that rule is claimed. No finite coding radius or quantitative mixing rate is asserted.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 12 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We give polynomial-time exact linear optimization, strong separation and membership for mixed-integer bipartite covers with arbitrary rational edge demands, unrestricted variable signs and any selected integer coordinates. All data and query points are rational in the total binary-input model; dimension and demand denominators vary. This resolves the finite rational interpretation of Conforti’s 2008 hull-membership problem. A direct specialized proximity proof localizes integer labels to intervals of length 2n and proves attainment. Exact continuous completion yields a submodular value oracle on a polynomial-size threshold lattice. A bounded-core argument establishes closedness of the actual hull and a polynomial facet-encoding bound, allowing classical optimization–separation equivalence to apply. The result is an explicit application of classical mixed proximity, discrete-convex and submodular-minimization ideas. It does not prove the separate subtree-hull conjecture or assert a compact formulation or strongly polynomial total algorithm.

A bipartite graph has two groups of vertices, with edges only between the groups. Assign a number to each vertex so that the two numbers at each edge add up to at least its prescribed demand. Some chosen vertices must receive integers; the other values may be fractional, and negative values are allowed.

The paper gives a polynomial-time method to minimize any rational linear cost under these rules, or certify that the cost can decrease without limit. It also decides exactly whether a rational point is an average of feasible assignments, including points on the boundary of that convex hull.

Large denominators are the key complication. Earlier formulations could require work proportional to a numerical common denominator, which may be exponentially larger than its binary description. Here each integer coordinate needs only a short interval of candidate values around a continuous optimum, and established submodular optimization handles the combined choices.

The contribution is a complete application and bit-complexity argument for this precise rational model. The proximity, partial-minimization and optimization–separation tools are classical and receive explicit credit; a separate conjecture about intersecting subtree hulls is not proved.

Let U and V be disjoint vertex sets, E ⊆ U × V a finite bipartite edge set, I any subset of vertices, and b a rational demand for each edge. The feasible set is S = {x ∈ Rⁿ : x_u + x_v ≥ b_uv for uv ∈ E, x_i ∈ Z for i ∈ I}. Variables have unrestricted signs.

For every rational objective c, Theorem 1 gives an exact rational minimizer of cᵀx on S, or a feasible point and an integral improving recession direction when the objective is unbounded below. The time is polynomial in the total binary encoding of the graph, demands, objective and integer-coordinate choices. Dimension, integer-coordinate count and denominators may all vary.

The actual convex hull conv(S) is a closed rational polyhedron with a polynomially computable bound on the binary encoding of each facet inequality. Exact strong separation and membership at every rational query point, including boundary points, follow in polynomial total binary-input time.

After changing signs on one vertex class, at least one mixed optimum lies at sup-distance less than n from a continuous optimum. Integer labels consequently lie in intervals of width at most 2n. A threshold representation uses at most 2n|I| nodes and exact rational linear-programming completion values.

The finite rational interpretation of Conforti’s Problem 1 in Oberwolfach Report 51/2008 is the stated target. The result allows empty edge or integer-coordinate sets and handles the zero-dimensional case separately.

Changing signs on one side of the graph turns sums into difference constraints. A signed-threshold argument moves feasible mixed assignments toward a continuous optimum without worsening their cost and proves that an optimum is attained nearby.

Fixing the short-range integer labels leaves an exact rational linear program. Its optimum value is submodular because the difference-constraint system is closed under coordinatewise minima and maxima.

Threshold nodes and implication arcs encode all feasible label choices in a polynomial-size ring family. Established submodular minimization then searches that family without enumerating every assignment or denominator residue.

A uniformly bounded mixed core plus the recession cone equals the actual convex hull. The resulting closedness and facet-encoding bound make classical exact optimization–separation applicable, including rational boundary queries.
The theorem uses explicit rational inputs and rational query points measured in binary. It does not claim an algorithm for arbitrary unencoded real data or a strongly polynomial total running time.

The graph is bipartite and the variables have unrestricted signs. The proof uses that structure to complete integer assignments and compare boundedness with the continuous relaxation; arbitrary additional constraints or bounds are not included.

Only existence of at least one nearby mixed optimum is asserted. Coordinatewise minimum/maximum closure applies after the bipartite sign change, and only constraints joining two integer coordinates are rounded upward.

The closed-hull and facet-encoding proofs do not enumerate all vertices or facets and do not supply a polynomial-size extended formulation or a facet classification. The separate subtree-hull Conjecture 2 remains unaddressed.

Classical mixed proximity, hybrid partial minimization, ring-family submodular minimization and exact optimization–separation are inherited ingredients. The note supplies the explicit rational application, denominator-independent label count and actual-hull encoding argument; exhaustive novelty and historical first priority are not certified.

The supplied exact-arithmetic checkers enumerate small cases and boundary examples. They do not implement the full polynomial-time LP, submodular-minimization and separation algorithm, and their observed runtime is not a proof of the complexity claim.

AI tools were used extensively in solving, verifying, source auditing and preparation. The adversarial reviews are AI reviews. Conventional human peer review, journal acceptance and formal proof-assistant certification are not claimed.

Conforti, Combinatorial Mixed-Integer Programming (2008) : Printed pp. 2904–2905 pose the hull-membership problem and a separate subtree-hull conjecture. This note addresses the finite rational version of Problem 1.

Cook, Gerards, Schrijver and Tardos, Sensitivity theorems in integer linear programming : The mixed-integer proximity result in p. 258, Remarks (1), is an established predecessor. The note gives a direct specialization that also supplies attainment.

Takamatsu, Hara and Murota, Continuous/Discrete Hybrid Convex Optimization and Its Optimality Criterion : Proposition 2 gives the prior hybrid partial-minimization mechanism; the linked text is the authors’ English translation.

Murota, On Steepest Descent Algorithms for Discrete Convex Functions : Section 4.1 records the earlier scaling and polynomial-size ring-family lineage. The note does not claim to invent that abstract method.

Conforti, Di Summa, Eisenbrand and Wolsey, Network Formulations of Mixed-Integer Programs : Earlier network formulations give polynomial bounds in a numerical common denominator and identify settings with short fractional-part lists.

Conforti, Wolsey and Zambelli, Projecting an extended formulation for mixed-integer covers on bipartite graphs : The revised November 2009 author manuscript explicitly distinguishes its pseudopolynomial formulation from a binary-encoding polynomial bound.

Schrijver, A combinatorial algorithm minimizing submodular functions in strongly polynomial time : Section 6 supplies the ring-family interface; the current note makes its required closure data explicit and accounts for the bit cost of rational LP oracle values.

Grötschel, Lovász and Schrijver, Geometric Algorithms and Combinatorial Optimization : The classical exact rational submodular and strong optimization–separation framework is imported, with the needed hull-description and encoding bounds established in the note.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 16 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 4 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Let g be a finite-dimensional complex unimodular Lie algebra and n a complex semisimple Lie algebra of the same dimension. We prove that if two Lie algebra homomorphisms j₁, j₂ : g → n have invertible difference, then g is semisimple. The integrated left-right action has a holomorphic infinitesimal determinant. Unimodularity makes this determinant invariant, and its constancy on an open orbit extends to the whole target group. Transitivity and simple connectedness then identify the source and target manifolds; their compact-form homology rules out a nonzero source radical. Consequently a perfect nonsemisimple complex source and a semisimple target admit no post-Lie algebra structure.

A Lie algebra describes infinitesimal symmetries. A post-Lie product is an extra operation that makes two Lie brackets on the same vector space compatible. This paper asks when that compatibility is impossible.

The result rules out every finite-dimensional complex pair whose source is perfect but not semisimple and whose target is semisimple. In this language, perfect means generated by its brackets, while semisimple means having no nonzero solvable ideal. The paper actually proves a stronger obstruction using the weaker source condition called unimodularity.

The striking step is geometric: a local compatibility condition would force two associated symmetry spaces to be the same manifold. Their topology then detects the source’s solvable part and shows that it must vanish. This turns a problem about algebraic identities into a short obstruction from geometry and homology.

The argument addresses the semisimple-target conjecture described by Burde and Dekimpe, extending earlier special cases. It adapts a determinant method with an explicit predecessor in Baues’s work and uses established Lie theory; historical first priority is not claimed.

Theorem 1: let g and n be complex Lie algebras of the same finite dimension. If tr(ad_g x) = 0 for every x ∈ g, n is semisimple, and homomorphisms j₁, j₂ : g → n have an invertible linear difference, then g is semisimple.

Corollary 3: if a post-Lie structure exists on (g, n), with g unimodular and n semisimple, then g must be semisimple. Every perfect Lie algebra is unimodular, so a perfect nonsemisimple source admits no such structure with any semisimple target.

The homomorphisms need not be injective, algebraic, or have closed integrated images. Their invertible difference is the transversality assumption. The zero-dimensional case is included, with the zero algebra semisimple by convention.
The result supplies the semisimple-target conclusion conjectured on printed p. 2689 of Oberwolfach Report 46/2023. The separate conjectures there concerning nilpotent targets are outside this result.

Integrate the two homomorphisms to simply connected complex groups. Their left-right action has a globally holomorphic determinant measuring whether its infinitesimal orbit directions span the target tangent space.

Unimodularity makes this determinant invariant. It is a nonzero constant on an open orbit, so the holomorphic identity theorem makes it that same constant everywhere. All orbits are open, forcing transitivity on the connected target.
The stabilizer is closed and discrete. The orbit map is therefore a covering, and simple connectedness makes it a diffeomorphism of the source and target manifolds.

A simply connected solvable radical is contractible. The source retracts onto the compact form of its semisimple Levi factor, while the target has a nonzero homology class in the degree of its full complex dimension. A nonzero source radical would make those homology groups incompatible.
For a semisimple post-Lie target, inner derivations yield the established pair j₁ = R + I and j₂ = R. Their difference is the identity, so the obstruction applies.
The published theorem is stated for finite-dimensional complex Lie algebras. It does not provide a separate treatment of arbitrary real forms, positive characteristic or infinite dimension.
Unimodularity cannot simply be omitted. Remark 4 supplies a three-dimensional nonunimodular solvable source with two homomorphisms into sl₂(C) whose difference is invertible.

A merely reductive target is not covered. Central directions change both the inner-derivation reduction and the topological obstruction; earlier literature contains perfect-source examples with reductive nonsemisimple targets.

The orbit map identifies manifolds, and is not asserted to be a group homomorphism. The proof’s conclusion is semisimplicity of the source; a Lie algebra isomorphism is not inferred solely from that manifold identification.

The determinant method, transverse-pair formulation and Lie-theoretic and topological inputs have substantial predecessors. The literature comparison is bounded, and the original body of Onishchik’s 1969 decomposition paper was not accessible in this review. No exhaustive novelty or first-priority certificate is given.

Exact finite diagnostic checks accompany the paper. They cannot establish the global integration, transitivity, covering-space or homology arguments, which depend on the analytical proof and its cited classical results.

AI systems were used extensively in solving, checking and writing the work. The paper describes AI audits; these do not constitute independent human peer review or formal proof-assistant verification.

articles.header: Property (T) above one-third density in random free-product quotients By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 15 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint Read the paper (PDF, 7 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 15 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 7 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Fix at least three nontrivial finitely generated groups and a finite inverse-closed generating alphabet of nonidentity elements in each factor. At every fixed density 1/3 < d < 1, their random free-product quotient, formed from independent uniform cyclically reduced syllable relators of exact length with replacement, has Kazhdan’s property (T) with probability tending to one through all integer lengths. This answers the property-(T) question in Problem 16 of the 2026 Oberwolfach report on median geometry. The proof completes model-specific steps of an earlier proposed syllable-block spectral program: a weighted endpoint calculation handles unequal alphabets, torsion, and all three length residues. It uses the established triangular-link criterion and matrix concentration. The conclusion includes fixed-radius word-ball alphabets and makes no uniform assertion for growing parameters.

Start with at least three groups, combine them in a free product, and impose many randomly chosen equations. The question is whether the resulting group usually has Kazhdan’s property (T), a strong form of rigidity: in unitary representations, almost-invariant vectors force a genuinely invariant vector.

For the precise sampling rule in this paper, the probability of property (T) approaches one whenever the fixed density is greater than one-third. Density controls the number of random equations as a power of the available relator count; it is not the fraction of all available equations that is sampled.

The result allows unequal finite syllable alphabets, torsion in the factors and every sufficiently large integer relator length. It answers the at-least-three-factor question in the 2026 Oberwolfach report. The new density range includes one-third < d ≤ one-half, since an earlier collapse theorem already covers d > one-half.

The general strategy was proposed earlier by Montee and Steenbock. This paper supplies the calculations and transfer argument needed for that strategy in the stated model, with explicit credit for earlier spectral criteria, block constructions and concentration inequalities.

Fix n ≥ 3 nontrivial finitely generated groups Gᵢ and nonempty finite inverse-closed generating sets Bᵢ ⊂ Gᵢ ∖ {1}. For each ℓ ≥ 2, Sℓ consists of rooted syllable words of length exactly ℓ whose adjacent factors differ, including the last–first boundary. Words are not identified under rotation or inversion.

For a fixed density 1/3 < d < 1, sample ⌊|Sℓ|ᵈ⌋ independent uniform elements of Sℓ with replacement and quotient G₁ ∗ ⋯ ∗ Gₙ by their normal closure. Theorem 1 states that the probability of Kazhdan’s property (T) tends to one as ℓ tends to infinity through all integers.

The factors, alphabets and density remain fixed throughout the limit. Fixed-radius word-ball alphabets with positive integer radius are included, and factors may have torsion, be infinite or fail to be finitely presented.

The proof supplies a weighted endpoint kernel, deletion estimates for blocks equal to their inverses, spectra for all three length residues, concentration for independent whole-relator Laplacians, and a quotient onto a subgroup of index at most two.

Section 6 also treats the distinct sampling law of independent uniform linear reduced words, which omits the wrap-around condition, by retaining cyclic words at a slightly smaller density and then passing to a further quotient.

A complete multipartite alphabet matrix counts legal syllable sequences. Its Perron eigenvector supplies the correct endpoint weights when the factors have different alphabet sizes. Blocks fixed by inversion are exponentially scarce and can be discarded.

Cut each relator into three almost-equal blocks. The mean link compresses exactly to a matrix indexed by block type and endpoints. Its limit has a spectral gap strictly greater than one-half for all three length residues.

Expected minimum degree grows exponentially when d > 1/3. Matrix concentration for the independent relator contributions and a separate degree bound transfer the mean spectral gap to the actual random link.

The classical triangular-link criterion gives property (T) to the block presentation. Carefully chosen common suffixes show that its image in the desired quotient has index at most two, so property (T) passes to the whole quotient.

The result requires at least three factors. It does not resolve the full two-factor version of Question 1.9 in Random Quotients of Free Products; for two factors the odd-length cyclic universe is empty.

There is no conclusion at d = 1/3, no finite-length guarantee, and no uniform estimate when the factors, alphabet sizes, ball radius or density vary with relator length. The one-third bound is sufficient, not claimed sharp.

The law is uniform sampling with replacement from rooted cyclically reduced syllable words of exact length. It must not be silently replaced by uniform conjugacy classes, ordinary free-group words, a different word metric, or sampling without replacement.

The theorem proves property (T), not infinitude or factor embeddings. Above one-half, known collapse already implies property (T); those facts and the models to which they apply require their own hypotheses.

The three-block spectral strategy, almost-equal blocks, common-suffix finite-index method, link criterion and matrix concentration have explicit predecessors. The contribution is their model-specific completion. No exhaustive novelty, historical firstness or universal Gromov-model threshold is claimed.
The finite verification routines test exact formulas and artifact integrity. They cannot certify the asymptotic theorem, property (T), external proof dependencies or priority.

OpenAI tools were used extensively in solving the problem, developing and checking the proof, drafting, coding and adversarial verification. AI reviews and finite diagnostic checks do not constitute external human peer review or formal proof-assistant certification.

blocks.text: Fix n ≥ 3 nontrivial finitely generated groups Gᵢ and nonempty finite inverse-closed generating sets Bᵢ ⊂ Gᵢ ∖ {1}. For each ℓ ≥ 2, Sℓ consists of rooted syllable words of length exactly ℓ whose adjacent factors differ, including the last–first boundary. Words are not identified under rotation or inversion.

For a fixed density 1/3 < d < 1, sample ⌊|Sℓ|ᵈ⌋ independent uniform elements of Sℓ with replacement and quotient G₁ ∗ ⋯ ∗ Gₙ by their normal closure. Theorem 1 states that the probability of Kazhdan’s property (T) tends to one as ℓ tends to infinity through all integers.

The factors, alphabets and density remain fixed throughout the limit. Fixed-radius word-ball alphabets with positive integer radius are included, and factors may have torsion, be infinite or fail to be finitely presented.

The proof supplies a weighted endpoint kernel, deletion estimates for blocks equal to their inverses, spectra for all three length residues, concentration for independent whole-relator Laplacians, and a quotient onto a subgroup of index at most two.

Section 6 also treats the distinct sampling law of independent uniform linear reduced words, which omits the wrap-around condition, by retaining cyclic words at a slightly smaller density and then passing to a further quotient.

blocks.text: A complete multipartite alphabet matrix counts legal syllable sequences. Its Perron eigenvector supplies the correct endpoint weights when the factors have different alphabet sizes. Blocks fixed by inversion are exponentially scarce and can be discarded.

Cut each relator into three almost-equal blocks. The mean link compresses exactly to a matrix indexed by block type and endpoints. Its limit has a spectral gap strictly greater than one-half for all three length residues.

Expected minimum degree grows exponentially when d > 1/3. Matrix concentration for the independent relator contributions and a separate degree bound transfer the mean spectral gap to the actual random link.

The classical triangular-link criterion gives property (T) to the block presentation. Carefully chosen common suffixes show that its image in the desired quotient has index at most two, so property (T) passes to the whole quotient.

blocks.text: The result requires at least three factors. It does not resolve the full two-factor version of Question 1.9 in Random Quotients of Free Products; for two factors the odd-length cyclic universe is empty.

There is no conclusion at d = 1/3, no finite-length guarantee, and no uniform estimate when the factors, alphabet sizes, ball radius or density vary with relator length. The one-third bound is sufficient, not claimed sharp.

The law is uniform sampling with replacement from rooted cyclically reduced syllable words of exact length. It must not be silently replaced by uniform conjugacy classes, ordinary free-group words, a different word metric, or sampling without replacement.

The theorem proves property (T), not infinitude or factor embeddings. Above one-half, known collapse already implies property (T); those facts and the models to which they apply require their own hypotheses.

The contribution is their model-specific completion. No exhaustive novelty, historical firstness or universal Gromov-model threshold is claimed.
The finite verification routines test exact formulas and artifact integrity. They cannot certify the asymptotic theorem, property (T), external proof dependencies or priority.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 15 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

For every dimension at least two, we construct a connected open quasi-conical domain whose Dirichlet Laplacian has a complete orthonormal eigenbasis, although its spectrum and essential spectrum are the entire nonnegative half-line. Its positive eigenvalues are dense, zero is not an eigenvalue, and both continuous spectral subspaces vanish. We use the expanding-cube and shrinking-window geometry of Krejčířík and Lotoreichik, choosing both cube sizes and positive apertures inductively. The additional construction transports a growing family of complete finite spectral clusters with summable norm errors. A repeated dense test family proves completeness and excludes singular continuous spectrum. This answers the existential spectral-type question in their discussion and the corresponding Oberwolfach contribution.

Think of an infinite chain of increasingly large rooms, connected through increasingly small openings. Waves vanish on the walls. The rooms become large enough to contain balls of any radius, yet the whole connected space has a complete collection of square-integrable standing-wave modes.

The surprising point is that these individual modes suffice to represent every square-integrable state, even though the spectrum fills the whole nonnegative half-line. The eigenvalues are dense: there are eigenvalues arbitrarily close to every positive energy. This does not mean that every energy is itself an eigenvalue.

Krejčířík and Lotoreichik introduced this domain geometry and proved that it can retain an embedded eigenvalue while excluding the absolutely continuous part. Their remaining spectral-type question concerns the singular continuous part. This paper addresses that question by constructing a complete eigenbasis, choosing the room sizes as well as the openings.

The additional ingredient is to preserve an expanding collection of whole finite-dimensional spectral clusters and repeatedly test it against a dense family of states. Keeping just one mode, or even many modes without proving completeness, would leave the central question unanswered.

For every integer d ≥ 2 there is a connected open quasi-conical set Ω ⊂ Rᵈ whose Dirichlet Laplacian A has a complete orthonormal eigenbasis. The operator is defined by the closed energy form with domain H₀¹(Ω).

The spectrum and essential spectrum are [0, ∞), which is also the closure of the point spectrum. All eigenvalues are positive, zero is not an eigenvalue, and both the absolutely continuous and singular continuous spectral subspaces vanish.

The domain consists of expanding cubes joined through positive shrinking windows in their common faces. Both cube widths and window widths are chosen inductively. The result gives an existential construction within this geometric family.
Pure point here describes spectral type and the existence of a complete eigenbasis. It does not mean an isolated sequence of eigenvalues or compact resolvent.

At a finite stage, closing one window separates two bounded pieces. Shrinking-window convergence gives norm control of resolvents and of whole isolated finite spectral clusters, including their multiplicities.
The next cube size avoids the finite set of protected spectral values. Its opening is then small enough that every previously protected projection changes by a summable amount.

New finite spectral families capture successively larger portions of a countable dense collection of cube-supported states. Repeating this requirement prevents states from escaping the protected subspaces.

At the infinite limit, each protected finite-dimensional subspace remains invariant under the resolvent and is spanned by eigenvectors. The dense test family proves that these subspaces together fill the Hilbert space, which removes both continuous spectral parts.

The arbitrarily large cubes supply Weyl sequences throughout the nonnegative half-line. The zero-energy equation would require an L² constant on the connected infinite-volume domain, so zero is not an eigenvalue.
The construction chooses future cube sizes to avoid finitely many protected eigenvalues. It does not prove the same conclusion for every prescribed sequence of cube sizes.

The published proof uses windows in zero-thickness interface screens and does not establish a smooth-boundary or positive-length-passage version of the complete-eigenbasis result. Extensions of earlier embedded-eigenvalue results do not automatically give those stronger variants.
The aperture choices are existential, without explicit numerical bounds that guarantee the infinite construction. The statement concerns the Dirichlet Laplacian, not arbitrary boundary conditions.
The positive eigenvalues form a dense set whose closure is the half-line. The point spectrum itself is not asserted to equal the whole half-line.

The geometry, shrinking-window perturbation theory and spectral-projection approach have substantial predecessors. The added claim is exhaustive cluster transport and completeness; the bounded literature comparison does not certify historical first priority.
Finite diagnostic calculations in the archive cannot certify Mosco convergence, the infinite limiting operator or completeness. Those conclusions rely on the analytical argument.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 16 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 5 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We construct smooth nonintegrable almost complex structures on the product of a genus-two curve and an elliptic curve with at least three independent real anti-invariant de Rham classes. The structures converge smoothly to the product complex structure and equal it outside one coordinate ball. The construction gives a negative answer to the unrestricted integrability conjecture of Draghici–Li–Zhang. The separate generic-vanishing statement is a prior theorem of Tan–Wang–Zhang–Zhu.

An almost complex structure tells a real even-dimensional space how multiplication by the imaginary unit should act on tangent directions. Integrability is the extra condition that makes this local rule come from actual complex coordinates.

An influential conjecture proposed that, on a compact four-dimensional manifold, three independent anti-invariant cohomology classes would force integrability. These classes are global geometric data represented by closed differential forms with a particular symmetry under the almost complex structure.

The paper constructs a small deformation of a product of two complex curves that preserves three such global classes but becomes nonintegrable. The deformation is confined to one coordinate ball and can be made arbitrarily small in the smooth topology.

The key distinction is between global classes and pointwise forms. The three classes are independent globally, while their local representatives fit into a two-dimensional plane through a relation with varying coefficients. This leaves room to preserve all three classes while breaking integrability.
Let Σ be the smooth compact completion of y² = z⁶ − 1, let E = C/(Z + iZ), and let J₀ be the product complex structure on M = Σ × E. Theorem 1 constructs ε₀ > 0 and a smooth family Jε for |ε| < ε₀.
Every Jε agrees with J₀ outside one fixed coordinate ball and Jε → J₀ in C∞. Three fixed, linearly independent classes in H²_dR(M; R) have closed Jε-anti-invariant representatives.
Every nonzero sufficiently small ε gives a nonintegrable structure. Consequently h⁻_Jε ≥ 3; the paper gives this lower bound, not an exact dimension.

This is a counterexample to the unrestricted compact-four-manifold integrability conjecture of Draghici–Li–Zhang. The separate theorem that h⁻_J = 0 is open and dense among almost complex structures is prior work of Tan–Wang–Zhang–Zhu and is compatible with this exceptional family.

Two holomorphic one-forms on the genus-two curve, paired with the elliptic-curve differential, supply three closed real forms. Positivity of the square of a real holomorphic two-form and Stokes’ theorem establish independence of their de Rham classes.

In one coordinate ball the forms satisfy γ = uα − vβ. A compactly supported perturbation changes β and γ by exact terms while preserving the corresponding identity γε = uα − vβε, so all three global classes stay fixed.

For a sufficiently small parameter, α and βε span a positive two-plane. Normalizing this plane gives a decomposable complex two-form whose contraction kernel defines the new almost complex structure. The construction agrees smoothly with J₀ near the ball’s boundary.

The local relation puts the third representative in the same anti-invariant plane. On the region where the cutoff is one, an explicit coframe has a nonzero integrability obstruction for every nonzero parameter, proving that the new structure is nonintegrable.
The construction is on the specified genus-two-curve times elliptic-curve product. It does not assert that every compact four-manifold admits such a deformation.

Three independent de Rham classes do not mean three pointwise independent anti-invariant forms. The local anti-invariant plane has real dimension two, and the third representative is a variable-coefficient combination of the other two.
The theorem proves h⁻_J ≥ 3, without computing the exact value. It concerns smooth almost complex structures and does not impose compatibility with a fixed symplectic form.

The deformation is not metric related to the original complex structure: there is no common positive compatible metric. Thus it lies outside the hypotheses of the earlier Draghici–Li–Zhang metric-related obstruction.

Although the starting real pair is closed, variable normalization produces a complex two-form that is not closed. The established closed normalized-pair integrability criterion therefore does not apply.

Earlier work includes compact nonintegrable examples with h⁻ = 2, higher-dimensional and noncompact examples, and nonintegrable structures on products of curves with many pluricanonical sections. Those sections are not automatically closed real anti-invariant de Rham classes. The bounded comparison does not certify exhaustive novelty or exclude further deductions from older examples.

AI tools were used extensively in the construction, drafting, literature checking and internal adversarial review. The note is unrefereed, and no independent human peer review or formal verification is claimed.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 6 October 2026 · Manuscript dated 6 October 2026 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 10 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We extend the signed-impulse proof of the one-species three-dimensional relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell theorem in OpenAI’s family 362 manuscript to a fixed finite collection of particle species. Mass normalization gives a common velocity law and constant species-dependent accelerations. The entire source–receiver cancellation has coefficient eₐe_b/mₐ; the source acceleration cancels before its sign is discarded. A positive mass-weighted energy controls a disjoint union of species label spaces, and the angular occupation and selected receiver coefficient use one simultaneous momentum bootstrap. We prove the resulting global classical theorem for nonnegative smooth compact phase data and compatible C_b^∞ ∩ L² Maxwell fields, without smallness, symmetry or neutrality. The universal geometric identity is inherited; the new estimates keep all source and receiver coefficients explicit and close the shared-field bootstrap.

The relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell equations describe a collisionless population of charged particles and the electromagnetic field they create. Several particle species share the same field, but their masses and charges make them respond differently. The question is whether initially smooth data can develop a singularity in finite time.

This paper claims global smooth evolution for a fixed finite collection of species under its stated regularity assumptions, without requiring the particles to be dilute, symmetric or electrically neutral overall. It extends the signed-impulse argument in a specific OpenAI one-species manuscript; that upstream analytical argument is an essential dependency.

The useful cancellation occurs before taking absolute values. Electric and magnetic contributions that look large separately can partly cancel in the accumulated change of a particle’s momentum. With several species, the signs and mass factors must stay attached to the correct source and receiving particle throughout that calculation.

The added problem is a shared-field estimate when charge-to-mass ratios differ. Simply adding all species into one density does not generally produce a one-species equation. The paper instead combines their positive energies and controls every species in one momentum argument.

Fix a finite number of species in three space dimensions, each with a positive mass and a real charge, including zero charge. Their initial phase densities are nonnegative smooth functions with compact support in position and momentum.

The initial electric and magnetic fields lie in C_b^∞(R³) ∩ L²(R³): every spatial derivative is bounded, and the fields have finite L² norm. They satisfy the Maxwell divergence constraints for the initial charge density.

Under these assumptions, the published theorem asserts a unique global classical solution that is smooth on every finite time interval, with compact phase support on each such interval and fields continuous in time with values in L². No smallness, symmetry or neutrality condition is imposed.

Mass normalization gives all species the same velocity law u(v) = v/√(1 + |v|²), with acceleration coefficient eₐ/mₐ. The complete interaction between a receiver of species a and a source of species b carries eₐe_b/mₐ; positive mass-weighted energy controls all species together.

The argument imports the geometric cancellation and analytical framework of the pinned OpenAI family 362 manuscript. Its claimed addition is the explicit coefficient bookkeeping and simultaneous closure needed for a fixed finite multispecies system.
Normalize momentum by each species’ mass. This produces a common relativistic velocity law while leaving the distinct charge-to-mass ratios explicit in the acceleration.

Apply the inherited source–receiver identity to each pair of species before estimating magnitudes. The source acceleration cancels within the identity, leaving the correct receiver-dependent factor eₐe_b/mₐ.

Combine the separate species label spaces using their positive mass-weighted energy. One common momentum bound then controls angular occupation across the shared field without pretending that the sum of the densities solves a scalar transport equation.

The paper transfers the direct-force and selected-receiver estimates with this common bound. The selection gain offsets the angular loss, allowing the signed-impulse bootstrap to improve itself for every species simultaneously.

The resulting momentum-growth control rules out finite-time momentum blowup. A local theory compatible with nonneutral fields and the bounded-momentum continuation criterion then give the asserted global solution.

This is an extension of a specific upstream proof. Its conclusion depends on the analytical estimates in that proof; it is not an independent proof of the one-species theorem obtained from the headline existence statement alone.

The data assumptions include compact phase support and bounded derivatives of all orders for the initial fields. The theorem does not cover arbitrary smooth finite-energy data, noncompact momentum tails, collisions or a different spacetime model.

The number of species and their masses and charges are fixed. Constants may depend on these parameters, the initial data and the time horizon. No uniform infinite-species or zero-mass limit, or uniform-in-time momentum bound, is established.

When all charged species have the same nonzero charge-to-mass ratio, a weighted reduction already gives a one-species problem. The substantive extension concerns differing ratios, including mixtures of opposite charges.

Classical bounded-momentum continuation results, the retarded division identities and the upstream signed-impulse mechanism are prior inputs. This bounded literature review does not establish exhaustive historical priority.

The finite algebraic and rational checks in the archive do not verify the full analytical theorem. No independently reproduced proof-assistant certificate or completed external human peer review is claimed.

AI tools were used extensively in developing, checking and presenting the argument. Internal AI-assisted review and finite computational checks are not external human peer review or formal verification of the analytical theorem.
The manuscript is dated 6 October 2026. Neither the printed paper nor the Zenodo record supplies a numbered version.

Luk and Strain, A new continuation criterion for the relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell system : Reviews bounded-momentum continuation and explicitly notes the multispecies setting in Remark 1.2. Continuation once momentum stays bounded is a classical input, not the new step here.

Those hypotheses and conclusions should not be conflated with arbitrary-size finite-time regularity.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 23 September 2026 · Version 1.0.1 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 9 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Let b(G) be the largest size of an inclusion-minimal base, over all permutation representations of a finite group G, with bases taken for the permutation image. Let μ′(G) be the largest size of an independent subset of G, not necessarily generating G. We construct an explicitly specified affine group of order 100920 for which b(G) = 3 < 4 = μ′(G). The upper bound covers faithful and nonfaithful actions and does not depend on enumerating the subgroups of the affine group. Exact, independently implemented Python and C++ verifiers certify the small matrix-group inputs and the explicit witnesses. The obstruction is a subgroup of order two that is central in the complement but not normal in the ambient affine group.

There are two ways to measure how much independent information a finite group can contain. One asks how many group elements can be chosen so that none can be generated from the others. The other looks at actions by permutations and asks how large a set of observed points can be when every observation is essential to distinguish the permutations.

Peter Cameron asked whether the largest possible values always agree. This paper gives an explicit group with an independent set of four elements, while every inclusion-minimal permutation base has at most three points, across all actions. It also constructs an action that attains three, so both values are exact.

The obstruction is a small subgroup that behaves differently inside the matrix part of the construction and inside the full affine group. It is central in the former but not normal in the latter. This realizes the precise normality obstruction in Cameron’s earlier formulation of the question.

The official Kourovka Notebook now records the negative answer, cites this Zenodo paper and reports confirmation by P. J. Cameron. The paper remains an unrefereed preprint; that recorded confirmation is distinct from journal publication.

The group is G = F₂₉² ⋊ H, where H is generated over F₂₉ by A = [[0,28],[1,0]] and B = [[2,7],[12,28]]. This specifies the actual matrix action. H is isomorphic to SL₂(5), and |G| = 29² · 120 = 100920.
For this group, b_f(G) = b(G) = 3 and μ′(G) = 4. Here b_f uses faithful permutation actions, b allows all actions, and μ′ is the maximum size of an independent subset, whether or not it generates G.

Minimal means inclusion-minimal: every selected point is essential. For a possibly nonfaithful action, a base has pointwise stabilizer equal to the action kernel, or equivalently trivial stabilizer in the permutation image.

The paper gives an independent generating four-set and a faithful inclusion-minimal three-point base in a disjoint-union coset action. Structural subgroup and normal-subgroup arguments supply the upper bounds for every action.

The four omission subgroups of the independent set have a nonnormal intersection of order two. The corresponding Boolean meet-semilattice has rank four, but no rank-four realization can have normal bottom. This gives the negative answer to Problem 16.45.

The complement H has a unique involution. Every even-order subgroup contains it, which sharply limits families of subgroups whose intersection is trivial, while the quotient H/{±I} supplies a larger base in a nonfaithful action.
Over F₂₉, a line stabilizer in H is cyclic of order dividing four. This bounds the faithful base invariant of every subgroup of G that does not contain the full translation subgroup.

A faithful irredundant intersection family must contain such a subgroup. Restricting the other members to it gives the upper bound of three. Every nontrivial normal subgroup of G contains the translation subgroup, so nonfaithful actions reduce to the already controlled complement.

Explicit matrix and translation elements give the independent four-set, and three explicit affine subgroups give the faithful three-point base. Their omission intersection is central only in the complement. Taking normal cores destroys the four-way irredundancy rather than converting it into a larger base.
The construction is not claimed to have the smallest possible group order. It does not classify all counterexamples or determine the largest possible gap between the invariants.

The result concerns inclusion-minimal bases maximized over all actions. It should not be described as a result only about transitive actions, minimum-size bases in one fixed action, or ordered irredundant bases.
Faithful and arbitrary actions must remain distinct. For the complement H itself, b_f(H) = 2 while b(H) = 3; omitting nonfaithful actions would change the problem.
The characteristic matters. The paper exhibits a related characteristic-11 construction with a faithful minimal base of size four, so the same conclusion is not established for every finite field.

Finite exact verifiers check the explicit matrix groups and witnesses. The upper bound for every subgroup and action of the full affine group relies on the structural proof, rather than exhaustive enumeration of its subgroup lattice.

The official notebook’s reported confirmation is evidence of external recognition, not a journal acceptance or proof-assistant certificate. This page does not claim an exhaustive priority search beyond the cited primary sources.

The publication revision and verification were prepared with extensive OpenAI Codex assistance, including separate AI agents and exact Python/C++ checks. Those internal checks are distinct from the confirmation reported in the official notebook and from journal peer review.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 1 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 5 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We prove that a finite two-dimensional simplicial complex can have minimum piecewise-linear embedding dimension three and minimum original-simplex linear embedding dimension five. This answers affirmatively the minimum-dimension question posed by Brehm in 2006, already in dimension two. The construction makes the random affine obstruction used by Newman uniform under small facet deletions, then removes triangles sharing an edge. The resulting linear hypergraph admits a PL embedding in three dimensions. We include an elementary embedding of its first barycentric subdivision and a finite parameter choice with exact arithmetic checks. The existence proof does not generate an explicit facet list.

A finite simplicial complex is built by joining vertices, edges and triangles along specified faces. There are two different embedding rules: keep each original triangle flat, or first divide the triangles into smaller pieces and place those pieces consistently. The second rule is called a piecewise-linear embedding.

This paper proves the existence of a two-dimensional complex whose minimum ambient dimension drops from five to three when subdivision is allowed. Four dimensions do not suffice under the original-triangle rule, while the first barycentric subdivision already embeds in three dimensions.

The construction starts with a random family of triangles whose crossings cannot all be avoided in four dimensions. It strengthens that obstruction so it survives every small deletion. The first barycentric subdivision of K admits a linear embedding in R³. Its new vertices are freely assigned positions in space; they need not be arithmetic barycenters of the images of original vertices.
The construction gives a family of triangles in which distinct triangles share at most one vertex. The generated complex has a nonplanar one-skeleton, forcing the lower bound e_PL(K) ≥ 3.

The finite existence calculation uses n = 2²⁵⁶ vertex labels, triangle-selection probability p = 2⁻³⁸⁴ and deletion allowance m = 2³²⁰. It establishes a positive-probability outcome without generating its facet list.

Every seven generic points in R⁴ contain two disjoint triples with intersecting convex hulls. This supplies many potential crossing pairs in every placement, whose pattern is determined by the labeled order type.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 12 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We apply Fawzi’s established obstruction for normalized complex separable states to the oriented real Grassmann orbitope C₄,₁₂. Two affine hyperplanes select a section real-linearly isomorphic to Sep(3,3), so this mass ball has no finite projected semidefinite lift. A compact first-moment argument then disproves the universal degree-one supporting sum-of-squares assertion formulated by Sanyal, in joint work with Rostalski. It also gives a negative answer in general to Harvey–Lawson’s Question 6.5: some constant comass-one four-form on R¹² has no pointwise or local norm completion. The failing unnormalized functional may have rational coefficients, but no explicit coefficient list or exact comass is supplied. The reduction combines classical Kähler faces, established fermionic projector bodies and the prior tensor-to-wedge lemma with Fawzi’s theorem; worldwide priority of this assembly is not certified.

Semidefinite programming describes a convex set through positivity conditions on a finite matrix, possibly with extra variables that are later projected away. Such descriptions can turn geometric optimization into a standard computational problem. This paper shows that one natural geometric body has no exact description of this kind, regardless of matrix size.

The body is built from all oriented four-dimensional planes in twelve-dimensional real space. The key observation is that two linear conditions select a piece that is equivalent to the set of separable states of two three-level quantum systems. Fawzi had already proved that this quantum-state set has no finite semidefinite description.

That obstruction also answers two geometric questions in the negative. A proposed universal sum-of-squares certificate for supporting inequalities fails, and some calibration—a differential form used to certify volume-minimizing geometry—cannot have the norm-completion identity asked for by Harvey and Lawson.

The proof establishes existence. It does not write down the coefficients of the failing calibration or claim that twelve is the smallest possible ambient dimension. The contribution is a reduction linking established results and transferring their obstruction to this particular geometric setting.

Let C₄,₁₂ be the convex hull of all unit decomposable real four-vectors in Λ⁴R¹², including both orientations. The paper identifies C₄,₁₂ ∩ {Φ = 1, Q = 0} with normalized complex Sep(3,3) through an injective real-linear map.

Consequently C₄,₁₂ has no finite projected semidefinite lift, even when arbitrary auxiliary variables and affine equalities are allowed. The conclusion concerns every finite lift, not just one chosen relaxation hierarchy.

There exists a real linear functional ℓ, with δ = max ℓ on the unit decomposable four-vectors, for which δ − ℓ is not a sum of squares of affine-linear polynomials modulo the full real vanishing ideal. The coefficients of the unnormalized ℓ can be rational.

There exists a constant closed four-form φ on R¹² of comass one for which φ(p)² + Σψⱼ(p)² = ‖p‖² cannot hold on all decomposable four-vectors for any finite collection of linear four-forms ψⱼ. Failure at each point also rules out a local differential-form completion.

The classical Wirtinger inequality selects the positively oriented complex two-planes as a face of the real mass ball. A real-linear projector map identifies that entire face with the standard convex hull of decomposable bivector projectors.

Split C⁶ into two orthogonal copies of C³. A zero-trace condition on the two pure exterior blocks forces every positive-weight generator into the mixed block. There, the prior tensor-to-wedge lemma identifies decomposable bivectors exactly with product tensors.
The resulting section is normalized Sep(3,3). Affine sections and linear maps preserve finite semidefinite lifts, so a lift of the mass ball would contradict Fawzi’s theorem.

A first-moment matrix constrained by all degree-two vanishing relations has fixed trace and a compact feasible set. If every supporting inequality had an affine SOS certificate, its projection would equal the mass ball and provide the forbidden lift.

Strict separation supplies a failing support, with rational coefficients before normalization. A norm-completion identity would turn its normalized supporting inequality into an affine SOS, giving the calibration contradiction.

The nonrepresentability theorem for normalized complex separable states is Fawzi’s established result. The paper applies that theorem; it does not prove a new quantum-state nonrepresentability theorem.
The two hyperplane equations are imposed inside the oriented mass ball. They alone do not characterize separable states, and Q is only required to be nonnegative on the selected Kähler face.

The failing calibration is existential. No coefficient list, exact comass, explicit separating certificate or rational normalized calibration is supplied. The classical Kähler form used to expose the face is not the failing form.

The counterexample occurs at (k,n) = (4,12). No claim is made that this is the least dimension, that lower-dimensional cases fail, or that earlier experiments in dimensions at most seven were incorrect.

The relevant SOS polynomials have degree at most one, including constants, and equality is taken modulo the full real vanishing ideal. Earlier obstructions for homogeneous quadratic Grassmann cones concern a different representation and do not by themselves establish this oriented mass-ball claim.

Earlier work already supplied the Kähler-face geometry, fermionic projector body, tensor-to-wedge lemma and SOS/completion connection. The claimed addition is their explicit assembly with Fawzi’s obstruction. This bounded comparison does not establish worldwide first priority, formal verification or completed human peer review.

AI tools were used extensively in developing the argument, checking proofs, reviewing literature and preparing the paper. Internal AI reviews and exact-coordinate checks do not constitute conventional human peer review or formal certification.

Fawzi, The Set of Separable States has no Finite Semidefinite Representation Except in Dimension 3 × 2 : Theorem 1 excludes arbitrary finite projected Hermitian semidefinite representations of normalized complex Sep(3,3). This is the decisive imported obstruction, first public in 2019.

Sanyal, Grassmann Orbitopes, Oberwolfach Report 13/2015 : Printed pages 708–709 state the universal degree-one SOS conjecture, credit joint work with Philipp Rostalski and connect it with Harvey–Lawson’s question.

Harvey and Lawson, Calibrated geometries : Question 6.5 asks for a local differential-form norm completion on simple vectors. Their classical Kähler examples have such completions; the present existential obstruction concerns other constant four-forms.

Vrana and Lévay, Special entangled quantum systems and the Freudenthal construction : Section 3.1, equation (25) and its lemma establish the tensor-to-wedge decomposability interface used here in the C³ ⊕ C³ case.

Grabowski, Kuś and Marmo, Segre maps and entanglement for multipartite systems of indistinguishable particles : Definition 4.2 and Theorem 5.1 give the established fermionic separable-state body as the convex hull of normalized decomposable projectors.
Sanyal, Sottile and Sturmfels, Orbitopes : Theorem 7.6 shows that the (3,6) Grassmann orbitope is not a spectrahedron. That unprojected obstruction does not exclude all finite projected lifts.

Bettiol, Kummer and Mendes, Convex algebraic geometry of curvature operators : Corollary 4.2 and Remark 4.3 already exclude finite shadows for cones of nonnegative homogeneous quadratics on Grassmannians. Their representation is Sym²(ΛᵏRⁿ), distinct from the oriented mass ball in ΛᵏRⁿ.
