article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 4 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 5 pages) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

The distributed dense-coding question posed by Bruß and collaborators asks whether the symmetric four-qubit W state gives a strict advantage when two independent senders each transmit one qubit to a different receiver and the receivers decode using local operations and classical communication (LOCC). We give an affirmative answer in their asymptotic unitary-encoding model. Independent Pauli encodings followed by a complete Bell measurement at one receiver produce a finite classical–quantum multiple-access channel whose entire output is local to the other receiver. Winter’s coding theorem gives an achievable sum-rate supremum of 3/2 + h₂(1/4) = 2.311278… bits per resource copy. In particular, both senders can transmit 9/8 bits per copy with vanishing average error. This settles the stated W-state classification question using established measurement and coding ingredients; it does not determine the optimal LOCC capacity or assert a one-copy advantage.

Two senders and two receivers share a four-qubit W state. Each sender encodes an independent message and sends one qubit to their own receiver. The receivers can exchange ordinary classical messages, but cannot send quantum systems to each other.

The paper shows that, by coding across many copies, they can transmit more than the two-bit total available without the shared entangled resource. Its protocol approaches a combined rate of about 2.311278 bits per copy. A concrete rate safely inside the proven region is 1.125 bits per sender, or 2.25 bits in total.

One receiver measures in the Bell basis and forwards the outcome. The other keeps their quantum systems and decodes them together across many copies. Keeping those systems quantum until the final decoding step is what allows a standard multiple-access coding theorem to be used.

The result answers the specified W-state classification question in an asymptotic unitary-encoding model. It does not say that a single copy beats two bits, or that 2.311278 is the best possible rate for all allowed protocols.

For the symmetric state |W₄⟩ = (|1000⟩ + |0100⟩ + |0010⟩ + |0001⟩)/2 in the order A₁A₂B₁B₂, sender i initially holds Aᵢ and receiver i holds Bᵢ. Each sender transmits their encoded qubits noiselessly to their corresponding receiver.

With independent uniformly distributed messages, separate fixed codebooks and local unitary encoders, every nonnegative rate pair with R₁ < 3/2, R₂ < 3/2 and R₁ + R₂ < 3/2 + h₂(1/4) is achievable with vanishing uniform average decoding error.

The protocol’s achievable sum-rate supremum is 3/2 + h₂(1/4) ≈ 2.311278 bits per resource copy, giving a lower bound on the optimal LOCC capacity. In particular, R₁ = R₂ = 9/8 gives a total rate of 9/4 bits per copy.

Independent single-qubit Pauli operations suffice for encoding. A complete Bell measurement at the first receiver, classical forwarding and a collective local measurement at the second receiver implement the decoder; no extra shared entanglement or quantum communication between receivers is supplied.

This places the symmetric W₄ state in the LOCC-dense-codeable class of the stated original unitary-encoding model. The paper also connects its vanishing-error rate statement to the source’s asymptotic accessible-information formulation.

A paired Bell decomposition makes the effect of independent Pauli encodings explicit. The first receiver performs a complete Bell measurement and forwards every outcome, without postselecting successful events.

That measurement produces a finite classical–quantum multiple-access channel. The classical outcome and remaining quantum state are both held by the second receiver, so Winter’s ordinary single-output coding theorem applies to this channel.

The channel output entropy is 3/2 for each input pair. Averaging over either sender gives entropy 3, while averaging over both gives 3 + h₂(1/4). These yield the two individual bounds 3/2 and the sum bound 3/2 + h₂(1/4).

The many-copy decoder can be conditioned on the forwarded classical outcome string, leaving its quantum measurement entirely inside the second receiver’s laboratory. Separate Pauli codebooks implement independent senders.

The rate pair (9/8,9/8) lies strictly inside the achievable region and exceeds the two-bit classical benchmark. A Fano inequality transfers reliable message decoding to the accessible-information formulation of the original question.

The rate is asymptotic over many independent resource copies and allows collective quantum decoding inside a receiver’s laboratory. It is not a one-copy advantage, a finite-block performance guarantee or an explicit practical family of codebooks.
The theorem gives a capacity lower bound. It does not prove that 3/2 + h₂(1/4) is the optimal LOCC capacity, characterize every achievable rate pair or rule out better protocols.
The error criterion is uniform average error over independent messages. Zero-error and maximal-error coding are not established.

The ownership and routing are fixed: each independent sender sends one qubit per copy to their own receiver, and receiver operations are local across A₁B₁ : A₂B₂. There is no sender message disclosure, feedback to senders, additional shared entanglement or quantum communication between receivers.

The two-bit calculation when both receivers immediately use Bell measurements concerns that particular one-copy measurement and input ensemble. It is not a converse bound for arbitrary one-copy LOCC strategies.

Bell forwarding and multiple-access dense coding have earlier precedents. The claimed addition is the specific retained-quantum-output channel and its achievable region for this W₄ problem, using Winter’s established coding theorem. This bounded comparison does not certify worldwide first priority, formal proof verification or completed human peer review.

Bruß and collaborators, Distributed quantum dense coding : Introduces the distributed task, unitary-encoding framework and usefulness classification. Several-receiver bounds must be distinguished from achieved rates.
Bruß, distributed dense-coding contribution, Oberwolfach Report 4/2005 : Printed pages 203–205 explicitly ask whether the four-qubit W state belongs to the LOCC-dense-codeable class.

Winter, The capacity of the quantum multiple-access channel : Theorem 9 gives product-prior multiple-access achievability with separate encoder maps and vanishing uniform average error. Its single quantum output must be available in one receiver’s laboratory.

Pradhan, Agrawal and Pati, Teleportation and superdense coding with genuine quadripartite entangled states : Section 4.2.3 already uses Bell measurements and classical forwarding for a two-bit W-state protocol. The present protocol retains the second receiver’s quantum output for many-copy decoding.

Cao and Song, Quantum secure direct communication with W state : An earlier W-state communication scheme using Bell measurements and classical communication, credited by the manuscript for its paired Bell decomposition. Its security task is distinct from the independent-message rate theorem here.

Huang, Zhang and Hou, Classical capacity of a quantum multiple-access channel : Earlier work already connects multiple-access coding with dense coding. That general connection is not claimed as a new idea here.

Hayashi and Wang, Dense Coding with Locality Restriction on Decoders : Studies a sender, receiver and helper with a different ownership and transmission arrangement. Its capacity formula cannot be imported without checking the receiver partition used here.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 5 October 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 8 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We give an almost surely consistent spectral-equation estimator for a general smooth symmetric diffusion tensor and an unknown smooth invariant density on a known bounded connected smooth domain. Observations are stationary exact positions at one known fixed positive lag; reflection is conormal, and fixed ellipticity and density bounds are known. A symmetric finite-rank estimate of the stationary pair kernel supplies all its positive empirical eigenpairs. Transition-eigenvalue fourth powers and vanishing ridge regularization give a basis-invariant fit. We prove full spectral-jet excitation and construct the required derivative-consistent kernels from the dependent data. The tensor and its separately fitted divergence converge locally uniformly; an ellipticity-clipped tensor converges globally in L². This provides a convergence analysis for the spectral reconstruction question posed by Reiß in OWR24/2017, in the explicit smooth model stated here. No rate or numerical implementation is claimed. Spectral fitting and eigenvalue-power weighting have established predecessors.

Suppose a particle moves randomly inside a known smooth region, with its direction and speed of spreading depending on location. You see its exact position at regular time intervals, but never the path between observations. The paper studies how to recover the matrix that governs this spatially varying, direction-dependent motion.

The method estimates the transition pattern between successive observations and uses all of its positive spectral modes to fit the unknown coefficients. It proves that the fitted tensor approaches the true one as the observation record grows, under smoothness, reversibility, reflection and known positive-bound assumptions.

Reversible dynamics were already known to be identifiable from one fixed observation lag. The contribution here is a convergence proof for a particular spectral reconstruction method, including repeated eigenvalues and dependence between consecutive observations.

The result gives eventual consistency rather than a usable sample-size guarantee. It does not provide a numerical implementation, an error rate, or a theorem for noisy positions, an unknown boundary or arbitrary nonreversible motion.

Let D be a known bounded connected C∞ domain in Rᵈ, d ≥ 2. The unknown symmetric tensor S and invariant density μ are smooth up to the boundary, with known positive ellipticity and density bounds. The reversible generator is L = μ⁻¹ div(S∇), with conormal reflection n·S∇u = 0.

From stationary exact positions observed at one known fixed lag Δ > 0, the estimator uses a symmetric finite-rank stationary pair-kernel estimate, a density estimate and every positive empirical eigenpair. Fourth powers of the transition eigenvalues weight a ridge-regularized spectral-equation fit. Any strictly positive deterministic ridge sequence tending to zero is allowed.

Almost surely, on every compact subset of the interior, the tensor estimate converges uniformly to S and a separately fitted vector converges uniformly to div(S). The density estimate converges in C² on the closure; after clipping eigenvalues to the known ellipticity interval, the tensor converges globally in L²(D).

The physical interior covariance is Σ = 2S/μ and drift is β = div(S)/μ, so their fitted versions converge locally uniformly as well. The fitted divergence is a separate estimate, not a claim about differentiating the estimated tensor.

The construction is basis-invariant and measurable through a finite-feature formula. Repeated eigenvalues, changing rank and eigenvalues crossing zero do not require consistent labeling of individual eigenvectors.

A boundary-corrected symmetric kernel estimate learns the stationary pair law from dependent, overlapping observation pairs. Smoothness and reversible mixing allow the required mixed derivatives to converge almost surely.

The spectral equations are rewritten using continuous functions of the estimated transition operator. Their behavior at zero controls small eigenvalues and avoids choosing matching eigenvectors across repeated eigenvalues.

Completeness of the true eigenfunctions and elliptic regularity let compactly supported affine and quadratic test functions prescribe every needed gradient and Hessian direction. This gives full local excitation of the tensor and divergence coefficients.

The limiting local normal matrix is positive definite. Convergence of its estimated entries and a vanishing ridge then give local uniform consistency; ellipticity clipping supplies a bounded global estimate for the L² conclusion.

The model assumes stationarity, reversibility, exact positions, a known fixed lag, a known smooth domain, smooth coefficients and known positive bounds. Nonreversible dynamics, measurement noise, unknown geometry and weaker regularity are not covered.
Reflection is conormal and depends on the tensor. Ordinary normal reflection is not an interchangeable boundary condition for anisotropic diffusion.

The raw tensor and separately fitted divergence converge locally uniformly in the interior. The global tensor conclusion is L² convergence after ellipticity clipping, not uniform boundary convergence or convergence of tensor derivatives.

No convergence rate, finite-sample guarantee, class-uniform conditioning bound, efficient numerical scheme or general-domain implementation is supplied. The all-mode estimator is a mathematical construction involving known-domain integrals.

Fixed-lag identification, spectral fitting and eigenvalue-power weighting have established predecessors. The claimed addition is consistency of this specific fit in the stated general tensor model, rather than the first multidimensional diffusion estimator.

The supplement also discusses a different estimator obtained from classical variational regularization. That argument does not prove consistency of the main spectral fit, and internal AI audits or finite controls do not constitute human peer review or formal proof certification.

AI tools were used extensively in deriving, checking and writing the work, including internal adversarial mathematical and priority audits. Those checks are AI-assisted verification rather than independent human peer review; finite controls supplement the analytic proof.

The present paper specifies an estimator and an explicitly smooth reversible model.

Crommelin and Vanden-Eijnden, Reconstruction of diffusions using spectral data from timeseries : An established spectral-fitting approach to diffusion reconstruction, including nonparametric formulations.

Crommelin and Vanden-Eijnden, Diffusion estimation from multiscale data by operator eigenpairs : The inspected 2011 author manuscript includes eigenvalue-power weighting and discusses finite-expansion estimation. The publisher-final body was not assumed identical without inspection.

Nickl, Consistent inference for diffusions from low frequency measurements : Earlier multidimensional low-frequency consistency in a scalar-diffusivity setting. It prevents treating multidimensional consistency itself as new.

Giordano and Wang, Statistical algorithms for low-frequency diffusion data: A PDE approach : Develops low-frequency inference algorithms and discusses anisotropic extensions. Its setting and computational contribution differ from the present tensor-estimator theorem.

Alberti, Barnes, Jambhale and Nickl, On low frequency inference for diffusions without the hot spots conjecture : Lemma 3.8 supplies a close predecessor for spectral excitation of gradients. Here the fitted vector requires the full Hessian-and-gradient jet.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 12 September 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0.11 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 19 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Mathematical supplement (PDF, 19 pages) · Data and certificate tables · Complete reproducibility package · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Multicomponent Turing theories often seek a lower-dimensional unstable subsystem responsible for patterning. For every n ≥ 4, we construct an n-species binary-complex classical mass-action topology for which, throughout every positive-equilibrium realization, every principal subsystem below order n−1 is Hurwitz while one order-(n−1) subsystem is unstable. We prove a general principal-minor diffusion-ray theorem and obtain an exact network law: for any homogeneously stable realization, a stationary crossing occurs along a positive diagonal diffusion ray exactly when d_Z > 8h_Z ∑_{j=2}^{n−2} d_j/h_j. This gives the nonattained fixed-equilibrium contrast infimum, the unit-equilibrium value 8(n−3), and the topology-wide stationary trade-off χ_Dχ_H > 8(n−3). At unit equilibrium, an exact rational design undergoes a primary supercritical bifurcation with locally exponentially stable positive patterns in the fixed-integrated-mass class. A second exact family redistributes heterogeneity between diffusion and equilibrium concentrations so that both contrasts are Θ(√n), matching the topology-specific stationary minimax lower bound in exponent. The proof uses explicit flux-cone design, exhaustive strongly connected block classification, conservation-compatible center-manifold reduction, and inspectable symbolic certificates. The networks are synthetic; the bifurcation, stability, and robustness conclusions are local for each fixed dimension, and the stationary diffusion law does not classify arbitrary wave instability.

Diffusion usually smooths out differences, but in a reacting system it can destabilize a uniform state and create a spatial pattern. Many explanations trace that instability to a small group of interacting components. This paper constructs systems in which the smallest unstable group contains all but one of the species.

For every number of species n ≥ 4, the construction uses ordinary mass-action reactions with at most two molecules on either side. Its collective character holds at every positive equilibrium realization of that fixed reaction topology. The networks are mathematical designs, not identified biochemical systems.

The paper derives an exact threshold for stationary instability in terms of diffusion rates and equilibrium concentrations. It then separately proves that particular designs produce small, positive, locally stable patterns near their first stationary bifurcation.

A second design shares the required variation between diffusion rates and concentrations. Both contrasts grow like the square root of the number of species, reaching the best possible growth exponent for stationary instability within this topology. The optimal constant and the best possible stable-pattern threshold remain undetermined.

For every n ≥ 4, an explicit n-species binary-complex classical mass-action topology has every principal subsystem of order below n−1 Hurwitz at every positive-equilibrium realization, while one subsystem of order n−1 has a positive real eigenvalue.

Write h_i = 1/x_i* for inverse equilibrium concentrations and D = diag(d_i) for strictly positive diffusion coefficients. At a homogeneously stable realization, a stationary crossing along the diffusion ray occurs exactly when d_Z > 8h_Z ∑_{j=2}^{n−2} d_j/h_j.

The fixed-equilibrium stationary diffusion-contrast infimum is 8h_Z ∑_{j=2}^{n−2} 1/h_j and is not attained. At unit equilibrium it equals 8(n−3). Across this topology, diffusion contrast χ_D and equilibrium-concentration contrast χ_H satisfy χ_Dχ_H > 8(n−3) for stationary instability.

An exact rational unit-equilibrium design on a one-dimensional Neumann interval undergoes a primary supercritical stationary bifurcation. For each fixed n, sufficiently small positive distance past onset gives positive patterns that are locally exponentially stable in H¹ within the fixed-integrated-mass class defined by the semipositive conservation law.

A second exact family adjusts equilibrium concentrations and physical diffusion together. Both contrasts are Θ(√n), matching the topology-specific stationary minimax lower bound in exponent. This does not establish the optimal constant or the complete trade-off frontier.

An explicit positive flux cone describes every equilibrium realization of the chosen topology. The resulting Jacobian factorization lets the proof classify every possible strongly connected principal block and show that all blocks smaller than n−1 are stable.

The signed principal minors make the determinant along a positive diagonal diffusion ray especially simple. After removing the conservation factor, every higher coefficient is positive, leaving a single first coefficient to decide the unique positive stationary crossing.

For the selected rational design, separate half-plane certificates control every noncritical Fourier mode. A conservation-compatible center-manifold calculation then establishes a positive crossing derivative and negative cubic coefficient, yielding the locally stable supercritical branch.

The second family changes concentrations, diffusion and the conservation gauge consistently. Exact spectral and cubic-sign certificates persist over a specified parameter interval, allowing the two contrasts to be balanced at square-root growth.

The topology is synthetic and the reaction law is classical mass action. The result does not classify arbitrary networks, establish biological realizability or provide a universal diffusion threshold.

The exact ray law concerns stationary zero-eigenvalue crossings. It does not rule out every oscillatory or wave instability, and it does not alone prove the existence or stability of nonlinear patterns.

Homogeneous stability is imposed on the stoichiometric subspace because the full Jacobian has a conservation zero. The conserved quantity has zero weight on X₁; fixed integrated mass is not total mass of all species or a global concentration bound.

Stable-pattern and robustness conclusions are local for each fixed dimension and fixed conserved integral. They do not give global attraction, a dimension-uniform basin, or stability for arbitrary perturbations of the conserved mass.

The interval has Neumann boundary conditions and discrete spatial modes. The construction tunes a diffusion multiplier to onset and does not claim intrinsic finite wavelength selection as the domain grows.

The stationary contrast infimum is strict and unattained. The threshold for a locally stable nonlinear branch can be higher, and its exact infimum is not determined. The square-root construction is exponent-optimal only within this topology and stationary setting.

Subsystem theories, topology-based diffusion constraints, monomial equilibrium parametrizations and local bifurcation theory have established predecessors. Exact symbolic checks supplement the proof; they are not human peer review or a formal proof-assistant certificate.

AI systems assisted with exploratory theorem discovery, symbolic derivation, code generation, adversarial testing, proof organization and prose editing. The author takes responsibility for the content. Exact computations and internal AI checks supplement the mathematical arguments and do not constitute conventional human peer review.

Satnoianu, Menzinger and Maini, Turing instabilities in general systems : General multicomponent theory already allows an unstable principal subsystem as large as n−1. The present construction realizes that endpoint throughout a constrained mass-action topology.

Anma, Sakamoto and Yoneda, Unstable Subsystems Cause Turing Instability : Established subsystem criteria distinguish stationary and wave mechanisms. The present exact diffusion-ray law addresses the stationary case.

Diego, Marcon, Müller and Sharpe, Key Features of Turing Systems Are Determined Purely by Network Topology : Earlier graph methods relate reaction-network topology to diffusion constraints and pattern properties. Topology-based Turing design itself is not new here.

Haas and Goldstein, Turing’s Diffusive Threshold in Random Reaction–Diffusion Systems : Studies diffusion thresholds and collective behavior in random systems, providing context distinct from an exact family of mass-action realizations.

Conradi, Mincheva and Uecker, Conditions for Spatial Instabilities and Pattern Formation from Monomial Steady State Parameterizations : Develops related steady-state and mass-action methods for spatial instability, with a nine-species application and numerical nonlinear analysis.

Crandall and Rabinowitz, Bifurcation from Simple Eigenvalues : The local branch construction relies on classical simple-eigenvalue bifurcation hypotheses, together with conservation-compatible parabolic stability theory.

blocks.text: Multicomponent Turing theories often seek a lower-dimensional unstable subsystem responsible for patterning. For every n ≥ 4, we construct an n-species binary-complex classical mass-action topology for which, throughout every positive-equilibrium realization, every principal subsystem below order n−1 is Hurwitz while one order-(n−1) subsystem is unstable. We prove a general principal-minor diffusion-ray theorem and obtain an exact network law: for any homogeneously stable realization, a stationary crossing occurs along a positive diagonal diffusion ray exactly when d_Z > 8h_Z ∑_{j=2}^{n−2} d_j/h_j. This gives the nonattained fixed-equilibrium contrast infimum, the unit-equilibrium value 8(n−3), and the topology-wide stationary trade-off χ_Dχ_H > 8(n−3). At unit equilibrium, an exact rational design undergoes a primary supercritical bifurcation with locally exponentially stable positive patterns in the fixed-integrated-mass class. A second exact family redistributes heterogeneity between diffusion and equilibrium concentrations so that both contrasts are Θ(√n), matching the topology-specific stationary minimax lower bound in exponent. The proof uses explicit flux-cone design, exhaustive strongly connected block classification, conservation-compatible center-manifold reduction, and inspectable symbolic certificates. The networks are synthetic; the bifurcation, stability, and robustness conclusions are local for each fixed dimension, and the stationary diffusion law does not classify arbitrary wave instability.

blocks.text: Diffusion usually smooths out differences, but in a reacting system it can destabilize a uniform state and create a spatial pattern. Many explanations trace that instability to a small group of interacting components. This paper constructs systems in which the smallest unstable group contains all but one of the species.

For every number of species n ≥ 4, the construction uses ordinary mass-action reactions with at most two molecules on either side. Its collective character holds at every positive equilibrium realization of that fixed reaction topology. The networks are mathematical designs, not identified biochemical systems.

The paper derives an exact threshold for stationary instability in terms of diffusion rates and equilibrium concentrations. It then separately proves that particular designs produce small, positive, locally stable patterns near their first stationary bifurcation.

A second design shares the required variation between diffusion rates and concentrations. Both contrasts grow like the square root of the number of species, reaching the best possible growth exponent for stationary instability within this topology. The optimal constant and the best possible stable-pattern threshold remain undetermined.

blocks.text: For every n ≥ 4, an explicit n-species binary-complex classical mass-action topology has every principal subsystem of order below n−1 Hurwitz at every positive-equilibrium realization, while one subsystem of order n−1 has a positive real eigenvalue.

Write h_i = 1/x_i* for inverse equilibrium concentrations and D = diag(d_i) for strictly positive diffusion coefficients. At a homogeneously stable realization, a stationary crossing along the diffusion ray occurs exactly when d_Z > 8h_Z ∑_{j=2}^{n−2} d_j/h_j.

The fixed-equilibrium stationary diffusion-contrast infimum is 8h_Z ∑_{j=2}^{n−2} 1/h_j and is not attained. At unit equilibrium it equals 8(n−3). Across this topology, diffusion contrast χ_D and equilibrium-concentration contrast χ_H satisfy χ_Dχ_H > 8(n−3) for stationary instability.

An exact rational unit-equilibrium design on a one-dimensional Neumann interval undergoes a primary supercritical stationary bifurcation. For each fixed n, sufficiently small positive distance past onset gives positive patterns that are locally exponentially stable in H¹ within the fixed-integrated-mass class defined by the semipositive conservation law.

A second exact family adjusts equilibrium concentrations and physical diffusion together. Both contrasts are Θ(√n), matching the topology-specific stationary minimax lower bound in exponent. This does not establish the optimal constant or the complete trade-off frontier.

blocks.text: An explicit positive flux cone describes every equilibrium realization of the chosen topology. The resulting Jacobian factorization lets the proof classify every possible strongly connected principal block and show that all blocks smaller than n−1 are stable.

The signed principal minors make the determinant along a positive diagonal diffusion ray especially simple. After removing the conservation factor, every higher coefficient is positive, leaving a single first coefficient to decide the unique positive stationary crossing.

For the selected rational design, separate half-plane certificates control every noncritical Fourier mode. A conservation-compatible center-manifold calculation then establishes a positive crossing derivative and negative cubic coefficient, yielding the locally stable supercritical branch.

The second family changes concentrations, diffusion and the conservation gauge consistently. Exact spectral and cubic-sign certificates persist over a specified parameter interval, allowing the two contrasts to be balanced at square-root growth.

blocks.text: The topology is synthetic and the reaction law is classical mass action. The result does not classify arbitrary networks, establish biological realizability or provide a universal diffusion threshold.

The exact ray law concerns stationary zero-eigenvalue crossings. It does not rule out every oscillatory or wave instability, and it does not alone prove the existence or stability of nonlinear patterns.

Homogeneous stability is imposed on the stoichiometric subspace because the full Jacobian has a conservation zero. The conserved quantity has zero weight on X₁; fixed integrated mass is not total mass of all species or a global concentration bound.

Stable-pattern and robustness conclusions are local for each fixed dimension and fixed conserved integral. They do not give global attraction, a dimension-uniform basin, or stability for arbitrary perturbations of the conserved mass.

The interval has Neumann boundary conditions and discrete spatial modes. The construction tunes a diffusion multiplier to onset and does not claim intrinsic finite wavelength selection as the domain grows.

The stationary contrast infimum is strict and unattained. The threshold for a locally stable nonlinear branch can be higher, and its exact infimum is not determined. The square-root construction is exponent-optimal only within this topology and stationary setting.

Subsystem theories, topology-based diffusion constraints, monomial equilibrium parametrizations and local bifurcation theory have established predecessors. Exact symbolic checks supplement the proof; they are not human peer review or a formal proof-assistant certificate.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 28 August 2026 · Zenodo version 1.2.6; manuscript 1.2.7 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 20 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Displayed-tree clarification (PDF, 2 pages) · Technical summary (PDF, 2 pages) · Original archive checksums · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We construct exact distributions shared by a phylogenetic tree and a binary semi-directed strict level-two theta network under the Kimura two-parameter (K2P) and three-parameter (K3P) substitution models. The compact three-leaf K2P construction lies in the strict stochastic interior and is an exact counterexample to the formal K2P lemma and the K2P part of the corresponding global corollary removed between Versions 2 and 3 of Brits, Holtgrefe, van Iersel, and Martin. Because K2P is nested in K3P, this collision alone answers both high-level Kimura tree–trinet disjointness questions posed in Version 3 negatively. We additionally give an exact K3P theta realization whose network parameter lies outside every globally character-relabelled K2P specialization, while openly identifying its shared distribution as globally character-relabelled K2P. Full-rank Jacobians show that the fixed theta images are Zariski dense in the effective K2P and K3P Fourier spaces. Locally, the collision loci have dimensions 17 and 23 and project submersively onto the tree models, with 11- and 14-dimensional fixed-output network fibers. Consequently, a relatively open dense set of nearby K3P tree distributions outside every globally character-relabelled K2P submodel also has theta realizations. These conclusions persist in edgewise strictly continuous-time chambers, where generators and rate ratios may vary by edge and no clock or global timing is imposed. Finally, a common-subtree argument replaces any chosen internal vertex of any labelled unrooted binary tree by one theta blob while preserving the full leaf-pattern distribution; hence exact strict-interior collisions occur for every number of leaves. For the compact K2P and quartic K3P witnesses, exact verifiers separately reconstruct the retained-graph Fourier coordinates and perform ordinary-state Markov pruning in every pattern.

A phylogenetic tree describes an evolutionary history of branching lineages. A network can also include reticulation events, where lineages join. The paper constructs a tree and a network with two such events that predict exactly the same probability for every observed DNA pattern under the specified Kimura substitution models.

The equality is exact and uses strictly positive transition probabilities and nonzero inheritance weights. For these constructed histories, even an unlimited amount of sequence data from the model cannot distinguish the tree from the network.

These are families of exceptional coincidences, rather than a claim that most networks look like trees. Nearby tree distributions also have network realizations, but a generic choice of parameters on the network is not tree-equivalent.

The three-leaf construction can be inserted at one chosen internal vertex of any binary tree topology, giving examples with any number of leaves. The stronger continuous-time version allows each edge to have its own rates and duration; it does not impose a common rate matrix or molecular clock.

An explicit three-leaf K2P tree and binary semi-directed strict level-two theta network have identical values for all 64 site-pattern probabilities. All edge transition entries are positive, both inheritance probabilities are 1/2, and the exact minimum pattern probability is 1188799/79626240.

This disproves the arbitrary-level K2P disjointness statement in Lemma 5.6 and the K2P part of Corollary 5.8 of Brits and collaborators’ Version 2, which were removed in Version 3. Since K2P is a submodel of K3P, the same example gives a negative answer to both high-level Kimura trinet-disjointness questions stated in Version 3.

A separate quartic K3P network parameter lies outside every globally character-relabelled K2P specialization, although its shared tree distribution itself is relabelled K2P. Local full-rank arguments additionally produce nearby shared distributions outside all those observable K2P symmetry strata.

The fixed theta maps have ambient ranks 9 under K2P and 15 under K3P. Near the witnesses, the tree-collision parameter loci have dimensions 17 and 23, and the network realizations of a fixed nearby tree distribution have dimensions 11 and 14, respectively.

Strictly positive-rate continuous-time versions exist edge by edge. A common-subtree argument gives parameter choices with the same full leaf-pattern distribution after replacing one chosen internal vertex of any labelled unrooted binary tree topology by one theta blob.

The network has four retained-parent choices. The proof derives each corresponding Fourier monomial from the actual graph, including branches with no observed descendants, and averages them with the inheritance weights.

Special algebraic edge parameters make that averaged expression factor exactly into the three edge contributions of a tree. Exact ordinary-state Markov pruning provides a separate way to compare every pattern probability.
The quartic derivation uses the equal-coordinate comparison factor displayed in equation (17).

Nonzero Jacobian minors show that the unrestricted theta map is locally onto its effective Fourier space. The preimage and constant-rank theorems then give the collision dimensions and nearby tree coverage; an implicit-function argument moves into strict continuous-time chambers.
Attaching the same three conditional Markov subtrees applies the same linear map to both equal interface distributions. This preserves equality on any number of leaves after one theta insertion.

The theorem concerns a displayed-tree mixture substitution model with uniform root distribution and independent reticulation choices. It is not a theorem about every model of evolutionary history or the network multispecies coalescent.

The failure is pointwise distinguishability. Tree-equivalent theta parameters form a proper lower-dimensional subset, so the paper does not prove generic tree equivalence or generic nonidentifiability of all network topologies.

The theta admits no tree-child rooting. These examples do not contradict results restricted to tree-child or strongly tree-child networks, the retained level-one Kimura results, or the Jukes–Cantor tree–network theorem.

A K3P network parameter with three distinct edge eigenvalues need not produce an observably genuine K3P distribution. The closed-form quartic example has a relabelled K2P output; observable symmetry breaking is supplied by a separate local argument.

Edgewise continuous time allows different generators, rate ratios and durations on different edges. No common generator, molecular clock, global temporal compatibility or standard common-rate-matrix GTR conclusion is established.

The all-leaf theorem gives suitable parameter choices on every binary tree topology and one chosen vertex. It does not cover every preassigned tree distribution, independently composable replacements at several vertices, or genuine four-attachment blobs.

Zariski density excludes additional polynomial equalities only in the effective Fourier spaces. It does not fill the probability simplex, remove positivity inequalities or eliminate tree-model invariants.

Finite exact calculations verify the explicit witnesses and algebraic inputs. Local family and all-leaf conclusions also require the stated analytic and common-kernel proofs; stored verifier reports and AI checks are not formal proof certification or journal peer review.

AI-assisted analysis was used for exploratory symbolic and numerical search, code assistance, adversarial checking and editorial review. The manuscript supplies exact constructions, source code and analytic arguments. Internal AI checks and verifier transcripts do not constitute conventional journal peer review.

Brits, Holtgrefe, van Iersel and Martin, On Tree–Network Distinguishability and Full Identifiability of Phylogenetic Networks, Version 2 : The earlier Lemma 5.6 and K2P part of Corollary 5.8 claimed the general disjointness contradicted by the compact K2P example.

Brits, Holtgrefe, van Iersel and Martin, Version 3 : Removes those formal K2P claims, explains the leaf-order obstruction and asks about high-level K2P/K3P trinet distinguishability. Its level-one and Jukes–Cantor results remain distinct.

Ardiyansyah, Distinguishing Level-2 Phylogenetic Networks Using Phylogenetic Invariants : Studies restricted nice level-two networks through variety noncontainment. Lemma 5.1 excludes all simple nice strict level-two trinets, so that setting does not cover this theta.

Englander and collaborators, Identifiability of Phylogenetic Level-2 Networks under the Jukes–Cantor Model : Theorem 3.2 in the July 2026 version proves generic identifiability for binary triangle-free strongly tree-child level-two networks under JC, with different topology and model hypotheses.

blocks.text: The theorem concerns a displayed-tree mixture substitution model with uniform root distribution and independent reticulation choices. It is not a theorem about every model of evolutionary history or the network multispecies coalescent.

The failure is pointwise distinguishability. Tree-equivalent theta parameters form a proper lower-dimensional subset, so the paper does not prove generic tree equivalence or generic nonidentifiability of all network topologies.

The theta admits no tree-child rooting. These examples do not contradict results restricted to tree-child or strongly tree-child networks, the retained level-one Kimura results, or the Jukes–Cantor tree–network theorem.

A K3P network parameter with three distinct edge eigenvalues need not produce an observably genuine K3P distribution. The closed-form quartic example has a relabelled K2P output; observable symmetry breaking is supplied by a separate local argument.

Edgewise continuous time allows different generators, rate ratios and durations on different edges. No common generator, molecular clock, global temporal compatibility or standard common-rate-matrix GTR conclusion is established.

The all-leaf theorem gives suitable parameter choices on every binary tree topology and one chosen vertex. It does not cover every preassigned tree distribution, independently composable replacements at several vertices, or genuine four-attachment blobs.

Zariski density excludes additional polynomial equalities only in the effective Fourier spaces. It does not fill the probability simplex, remove positivity inequalities or eliminate tree-model invariants.

Finite exact calculations verify the explicit witnesses and algebraic inputs. Local family and all-leaf conclusions also require the stated analytic and common-kernel proofs; stored verifier reports and AI checks are not formal proof certification or journal peer review.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 6 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 7 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Let G be a locally compact second countable Hausdorff Abelian group, acting jointly measurably on an arbitrary measurable space. Let Q be sigma-finite and let ξ be a covariant locally finite Radon random measure, nonzero Q-almost everywhere. We prove that full ambient Q-invariance under every invariant, ξ-preserving, ξ-measurable Markov transport kernel implies the joint Mecke identity, and hence mass-stationarity. Together with known transport invariance this answers Last–Thorisson's Problem 7.3 in the stated setting. The argument uses oriented local symmetric transports away from periods of the measure and normalized period-subgroup transports on the remaining set. It requires neither a standard Borel ambient space nor a sigma-finite law of ξ, and imposes no finite-intensity assumption.

Imagine a landscape whose mass sits at isolated points, spreads continuously, or does both. A mass-stationary origin is a location that is typical of that mass. This paper gives a way to recognize such an origin using randomized changes of viewpoint.

The allowed rules inspect the mass measure, choose a random displacement, and move the origin. Each rule must respect translations and redistribute the existing mass while preserving that same measure. If every allowed rule leaves the full environment’s governing measure unchanged, the origin is mass-stationary.

The interesting part is that the rules see only the mass, while the conclusion concerns the entire environment. For example, a translation can leave a periodic mass pattern unchanged while moving other information attached to the landscape. The proof accounts for that hidden information too.

Let G be a locally compact second countable Hausdorff Abelian group acting jointly measurably on an arbitrary measurable space Ω. Let Q be a sigma-finite measure on Ω, and let ξ be a measurable, covariant, locally finite Radon random measure that is nonzero Q-almost everywhere. Q may be infinite; expectations below mean integration with respect to Q.

The test class consists of every invariant, pointwise ξ-preserving, ξ-measurable Markov transport kernel T. Markov means each row has mass one; ξ-measurable means the rule depends on the ambient state only through ξ. Pointwise preservation requires ∫ T(ω,s,B) ξω(ds) = ξω(B) for each state ω and measurable set B. The hypothesis is full ambient invariance: E_Q ∫ f(θ_tω) T(ω,0,dt) = E_Q f for every nonnegative measurable function f on Ω.

This hypothesis implies the joint Mecke identity, or Campbell reversal: E_Q ∫ g(θ_tω, −t) ξω(dt) = E_Q ∫ g(ω,t) ξω(dt) for every nonnegative measurable g on Ω × G. The classical Mecke/Palm and Palm/mass-stationarity equivalences then give mass-stationarity. Together with the known converse transport invariance, this answers Last and Thorisson’s Problem 7.3 from 2009 in the stated setting.

The proof separates displacements that change the mass measure from its periods, the translations that leave the measure unchanged. Away from periods, oriented local symmetric transports recover reversal on pieces that can be distinguished by observing the measure. Normalization and a holding probability turn these tests into genuine Markov kernels.

On the remaining set, normalized transports along the period subgroup recover reversal even when a shift changes hidden parts of the environment. The two arguments combine to give the joint identity for the whole ambient state. Standard Borel structure is used for the space of Radon measures; it is not imposed on Ω.

The theorem requires an Abelian group, sigma-finite Q, and a locally finite Radon measure that is nonzero Q-almost everywhere. Atoms, diffuse or mixed mass, periodic measures, infinite total mass and infinite Q are included. There is no finite-intensity assumption and no assumption that the marginal law of ξ is sigma-finite. The theorem does not cover non-Abelian groups or the zero random measure.

The hypothesis tests the full ambient measure against every admissible Markov transport. Invariance of the law of ξ alone is not a substitute. A converse based only on deterministic transports, or on the narrower class arising from Cox allocations, is outside this result.

The new step is deriving joint Mecke reversal from measure-only Markov tests. The Palm equivalences and converse transport theorem are established inputs, and earlier discrete, aperiodic and positive-density cases receive credit in the paper. This page does not certify exhaustive novelty, historical first priority or the present status of related open questions.

Discovery, checking and manuscript preparation were extensively AI-assisted. This is an unrefereed preprint without independent human peer review or a formal proof-assistant certificate. The supporting package contains the published source and finite controls; those computations do not prove the general theorem.

Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

The biconstrained reachability function ψ(x, y) is the largest fraction of the first part that some vertex of the third part must reach in two steps, over all finite tripartite graphs satisfying minimum-degree conditions in both directions on each adjacent pair. We answer its symmetry question negatively: |ψ(13/27, 14/27) − ψ(14/27, 13/27)| ≥ 1/108. The proof establishes the exact rational-boundary formula ψ(1 − θ, θ) = 1 − θ/d(θ), where d(θ) is a minimum integer degree of a positive rational regular incidence template. An existing seven-type example and its complement bound both relevant integers by four, making equality impossible. Neither exact value nor their ordering is needed or asserted.

Imagine three groups of vertices, with connections between neighboring groups. Each adjacent pair must meet a minimum connection requirement in both directions. How large a fraction of the first group must at least one vertex in the third group be able to reach in two steps?

Exchanging the two thresholds can change that guarantee. At thresholds 13/27 and 14/27, the guarantees differ by at least 1/108. This is a statement about all eligible finite graphs; looking at two individual examples would not suffice.

The surprising feature is that the proof establishes a definite gap without finding either exact guarantee or deciding which is larger. It obtains an exact boundary formula involving an integer, then uses a known small construction to restrict the possible integers.

The graph is finite and simple, partitioned into nonempty stable parts A, B and C, with no A–C edges. An (x,y)-biconstrained graph satisfies all four conditions: every A vertex has at least x|B| neighbors in B; every B vertex has at least x|A| neighbors in A and y|C| neighbors in C; every C vertex has at least y|B| neighbors in B.

For each graph, take the largest fraction of A reachable from any single C vertex through B. Each reached A vertex is counted once, however many paths reach it. The function ψ(x,y) is the infimum of this maximum over all eligible finite graphs and partitions. It is the best universal guarantee; its attainment is not assumed in the definition.
The main separation is |ψ(13/27,14/27) − ψ(14/27,13/27)| ≥ 1/108. Neither exact value nor their ordering is asserted.
More generally, for every rational θ with 0 < θ < 1, the paper proves ψ(1−θ,θ) = 1−θ/d(θ), and this value is attained by a finite ordinary graph.

Here d(θ) is the minimum unweighted maximum row degree of a finite binary matrix M with distinct columns and strictly positive rational probability vectors b and q satisfying Mq = θ1 and Mᵀb = θ1. A row degree counts column types, not weighted mass. Rows may repeat and the matrix may be rectangular.

On the boundary x+y=1, a vertex in C that misses a vertex in A forces their middle neighborhoods to be complementary. If the maximum reach is below one, this applies to every C vertex and forces exact degree equalities between B and C. Grouping identical neighborhoods produces a regular incidence template. The reverse degree condition from B to A bounds the smallest missed class, giving a lower bound valid for every finite graph.

For the matching upper bound, a template attaining the least integer degree gives weighted vertex types. Strictly positive middle weights preserve the paths between distinct types, and rational weights turn the construction into an ordinary finite graph by replacing types with integer numbers of vertices. This proves the formula and finite attainment.

The seven-type construction of Chudnovsky, Hompe, Scott, Seymour and Spirkl, together with its complement, gives d(13/27) ≤ 4 and d(14/27) ≤ 4. The formula then leaves only finitely many integer possibilities; none give equal guarantees, and every possible absolute gap is at least 1/108.
The boundary formula is stated for rational θ strictly between zero and one. The page makes no claim about irrational boundary parameters, the endpoints, or the full function away from this boundary.

The two integer minima, the two exact ψ-values and their ordering remain unevaluated here. The displayed finite graphs supply upper bounds only and are not claimed to attain the infima. The bound 1/108 is not claimed to be the exact gap.

All four degree inequalities and strict positivity of the rational template weights matter. The known symmetry of the related one-direction function φ is a different result. The inherited seven-type example is credited prior work; the contribution here is the universal rational-boundary formula and its quantitative asymmetry consequence. No exhaustive priority or current-openness certification is claimed.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 6 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

For a fixed odd integer q, consider the nonnegative real homogeneous forms whose qth powers are sums of squares. We give a negative answer to the general-dimensional convexity question recorded by Reznick in 2023. For sextics and q = 3, the cone is nonconvex in the explicit finite dimension 3 · 10^62. For every odd q ≥ 3, it is nonconvex in some finite dimension depending on q. The proof combines a classical modified Motzkin form with an SOS cube, separation from the SOS cone, positivity of product truncated functionals, and elementary distinct-index counting. An explicit rational moment functional gives the displayed dimension; its 220 × 220 local positivity certificate can be checked without floating-point arithmetic. No ternary or smallest-dimension conclusion is made.

A sum of squares is a particularly transparent way to show that a polynomial is never negative. Some nonnegative polynomials do not have such a representation themselves, but their cubes do. This paper asks whether averaging polynomials with that property preserves it.

The result is that it can fail. The construction takes many separate copies of one classical polynomial, each with a sum-of-squares cube. Their average remains nonnegative, yet its cube cannot be written as a sum of squares. The displayed example uses 3 · 10^62 variables: a finite existence result, not a small or practical example.

The same obstruction works for every fixed odd exponent at least three, in a finite number of variables that may depend on the exponent. Keeping the exponent fixed is essential. Earlier convexity results allow a larger odd power after the polynomials are added.

The classical polynomial and its sum-of-squares cube come from earlier work. This note uses them with established separation and product arguments to address the general convexity question recorded by Reznick in 2023. It does not settle the three-variable case or claim a verified first resolution.

For real homogeneous forms f of positive even degree m, let C(n,m,q) consist of those that are nonnegative on R^n and whose fixed positive odd qth power is a finite sum of squares of real polynomials. Nonnegativity follows automatically from the power condition when q is odd. These sets are closed and stable under nonnegative scaling; addition is the issue under investigation. Here n counts variables.

Put N = 10^62 and use N disjoint triples of variables. For each triple define p_i = x_i^4 y_i^2 + x_i^2 y_i^4 + z_i^6 − x_i^2 y_i^2 z_i^2. Each p_i belongs to C(3N,6,3), but N^−1 times their sum does not. Thus C(3 · 10^62,6,3) is nonconvex.

For every fixed odd q ≥ 3, there is a finite n(q) for which C(n(q),6,q) is nonconvex. The construction may use a different separating functional and a different number of variable blocks for each q. Each counterexample also persists after adding unused variables.

For q = 3, the paper supplies a rational linear functional on polynomials of degree at most 18 in three variables. Its order-nine moment matrix has 220 monomials and splits into eight parity blocks. The accompanying archive contains the manuscript source, the exact local certificate and a standalone rational-arithmetic checker.

Start with the classical coefficient-1 modified Motzkin sextic p. It is nonnegative and not itself a sum of squares, while its cube has an explicit sum-of-squares identity. Multiplying that identity by the square of p^((q−3)/2) supplies an SOS representation at every odd q ≥ 3.

For a chosen exponent q, separate p from the finite-degree sum-of-squares cone. This gives a normalized linear functional L that is nonnegative on the necessary squares but has L(p) < 0. Taking finite products of this functional preserves positivity on squares involving separate variable blocks.

When the qth power of a sum of many disjoint copies is expanded, terms using q different copies give the leading contribution. Their coefficient is L(p)^q, which is negative because q is odd. Terms that repeat a copy grow at a lower rate, so the product functional eventually assigns a negative value to the entire power. That excludes every sum-of-squares representation.

For the cube, a displayed rational moment table makes the argument finite and explicit. With L(p) = −1 and the specified second and third moments, the resulting cubic expression is negative at N = 10^62. The local positivity certificate and the written product argument play separate roles.

The explicit number of variables is a sufficient bound, with no claim of optimality. The theorem does not prove nonconvexity for three variables, for a prescribed small dimension, or in one common dimension that works for all odd exponents.
The result concerns sextics and a prescribed odd exponent. It is not a classification of all degrees, dimensions and exponents. The ordinary sum-of-squares cone at q = 1 remains convex.

Failure at one odd power does not say that every odd power fails. The established convexity of the union over odd exponents is consistent with the result, and no stubbornness claim is made for the constructed average.

The separating functional is positive on squares within its specified degree range. It is not integration against a positive measure: it assigns a negative value to a nonnegative polynomial. The enormous product matrix is handled by a finite algebraic argument, not materialized numerically.

The seed, its cube identity, SOS separation, product positivity and distinct-index counting have earlier sources. The contribution is their application to a fixed-exponent obstruction and the explicit finite cube certificate. The bounded literature comparison does not establish worldwide priority.

AI tools were used extensively in derivation, literature comparison, reproduction, writing and adversarial verification. This is an unrefereed preprint without human peer review or formal proof-assistant verification. Its mathematical and source claims remain open to independent correction.

Reznick, The Odd Powers of the Motzkin Polynomial, etc. (2023) : The contribution on pp.778–781 records the general fixed-odd-power convexity question and the modified Motzkin cube example. The fixed-power question appears on p.779.

Blekherman, Kozhasov and Reznick, On odd powers of nonnegative polynomials that are not sums of squares (2026) : Theorem 5.3 proves convexity when the odd exponent may increase. Section 6 repeats the fixed-exponent question and gives the credited cube identity for the modified Motzkin family.

Berg, Christensen and Jensen, A remark on the multidimensional moment problem (1979) : Lemma 1 gives exactly the dehomogenized coefficient-1 seed used here. Theorems 3–4 provide classical closure and positive-functional separation results.

Barak, Kelner and Steurer, Rounding Sum-of-Squares Relaxations (2013) : Appendix A, Lemma A.5, proves the established product-positivity property for truncated pseudoexpectations used by the disjoint-copy argument.
Acevedo and Blekherman, Power Mean Inequalities and Sums of Squares, v1 (2023) : Lemma 2.1 is a precedent for separating the leading contribution of distinct indices from lower-order collisions.

Blekherman and Riener, Symmetric Nonnegative Forms and Sums of Squares, v4 (2020) : Proposition 6.4 provides another related distinct-index asymptotic argument. It is credited as an ingredient, not as the fixed-power nonconvexity theorem.

Baldi, Blekherman, Kozhasov, Plaumann, Reznick and Sinn, Stubborn Polynomials, v1 (2026) : Theorem 2.2 establishes convexity of the nonstubborn cone by allowing the odd exponent to increase; this is a different statement from fixed-power convexity.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 3 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 8 pages) · Source and exact finite controls (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

The union of complete affine lines tangent to three pairwise disjoint convex subsets of ℝ³ has Lebesgue outer measure zero. Tangency means meeting the set while lying in a supporting plane. The sets may be nonclosed, unbounded, lower dimensional or nonsmooth. For compact sets, two tangency constraints admit countably many Lipschitz two-parameter covers after contact localization. At almost every tritangent parameter, the transverse derivative at each of three distinct contacts has rank at most one. A quadratic determinant then vanishes identically along the line, and the area formula makes its swept locus null. Countably many compact caps give the arbitrary-set statement. This proves the measure-zero formulation of Goaoc's Conjecture 4 in Oberwolfach Report 44/2008; it does not prove the stronger countable-union-of-2-manifolds formulation.

Take three convex sets in three-dimensional space, with no point belonging to more than one set. A convex set contains the straight segment between any two of its points. Here a tangent line must actually meet the set and lie in a supporting plane: a plane with the entire set on one side.

Now collect every line tangent to all three sets and extend each line infinitely in both directions. The paper proves that the whole collection occupies zero three-dimensional volume. This remains true for unbounded sets, sets missing some boundary points, nonsmooth shapes, and even sets lying in a plane or a line.

The striking point is the change from two sets to three. Common tangents to two disjoint rectangles can fill a region of positive volume. A third disjoint convex set imposes an additional contact condition that forces the volume swept out by the common tangents to vanish. Zero volume does not mean there are only finitely many lines.

For every three pairwise disjoint convex subsets K₁, K₂ and K₃ of ℝ³, the union of all complete affine lines tangent to each set has three-dimensional Lebesgue outer measure zero. Equivalently, this union is contained in a Lebesgue-measurable null set. If any set is empty, the union is empty.

Tangency requires actual intersection with the set and containment of the line in a supporting plane. Contacts and supporting planes need not be unique, and a contact may be an entire segment. The sets need not be closed, bounded, full dimensional, strictly convex or smooth; their closures may intersect.

This is the measure-zero statement of Xavier Goaoc’s Conjecture 4 in Oberwolfach Report 44/2008, section 13, page 2552. The paper does not establish the separate countable-union-of-2-manifolds statement in Conjecture 3.

The proof first localizes actual contacts to countably many disjoint compact caps. After separating the lower-dimensional cases, it constructs countably many Lipschitz families of lines tangent to two compact convex sets, each described by two parameters. The construction uses support inequalities and a contraction argument, so it does not require smooth boundaries or differentiable support functions.

At almost every parameter corresponding to a common tangent, each contact forces a transverse derivative to have rank at most one. The determinant that measures the volume swept out along the line is a polynomial of degree at most two in the height coordinate. The three distinct contacts give it three distinct roots, so it vanishes identically. The area formula then gives zero volume. Separate cases handle points, segments and planar sets.

Nullness is a statement about ordinary three-dimensional volume. The paper does not prove containment in countably many 2-manifolds, a Hausdorff-dimension bound of two, or a description by smooth surfaces.

Pairwise disjointness and supporting tangency are essential to the stated theorem. Lines that merely pass through the interiors of the sets are not covered. Contact with a closure alone is not enough when the original set omits that contact point.
For nonclosed inputs the union of tangent lines need not itself be closed. The outer-measure conclusion avoids assuming either input measurability or closedness of that union.

This is a geometric existence theorem, not an algorithm for enumerating tangents, a bound on their number, or a theorem in arbitrary ambient dimensions. The source package’s exact finite checks support algebraic and rational steps; they do not replace the proof for arbitrary convex sets.

The attribution to the 2008 conjecture identifies the historical question answered by the stated theorem. It is not a certification of first priority, an exhaustive literature search, or a claim that the question remained unresolved until this preprint.

This is an unrefereed preprint. Extensive AI assistance was used in solving, drafting and internal mathematical verification. It has not undergone conventional external human peer review or formal proof-assistant verification.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 13 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 9 pages) · Source and verification (tar.gz) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

For explicitly listed rational bimatrix games of variable positive dimensions and exact rank rank(A + B) = 1, deciding whether there is exactly one mixed-strategy equilibrium pair is coNP-complete. Its nonuniqueness counterpart is NP-complete. Arbitrary degeneracy is allowed. A polynomial reduction from nonempty positive-integer Partition produces a known strict pure equilibrium and an additional equilibrium exactly when the source instance admits a partition. The construction applies the signed flow counter of Disser and Skutella and the auxiliary zero-sum representation of Adsul and coauthors. A comparison-preserving rational perturbation isolates every real-demand flow optimum, an injective simplex encoding transfers diagnostic arc flow to a scalar consistency equation, and a uniform polynomial-bit exact penalty controls every auxiliary minimizer. Rational support-polytope certificates establish membership, including positive-dimensional equilibrium sets. A bounded source audit found no matching proof among the inspected bodies; worldwide priority remains unknown.

A Nash equilibrium is a pair of strategies in which neither player can improve their expected payoff by changing strategy alone. Players may randomize. In a rank-one bimatrix game, the two payoff tables have a special algebraic relationship that allows one equilibrium to be found in polynomial time.

This paper asks whether that equilibrium is the only one. It proves that deciding uniqueness is coNP-complete, while deciding whether a second equilibrium exists is NP-complete. The difficulty persists even when the input supplies a known strict pure equilibrium.

The construction turns a Partition problem into a game with a specified equilibrium. A second equilibrium exists exactly when the original integers can be split into two groups of equal total weight. This separates the task of finding one equilibrium from the task of ruling out every alternative.

The input consists of explicitly listed rational payoff matrices A and B of variable positive dimensions, encoded in binary, with exact rank(A + B) = 1. Uniqueness concerns the entire mixed-strategy equilibrium pair, including pure strategies.

On these inputs, uniqueness is coNP-complete and nonuniqueness is NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions. Arbitrary degeneracy is allowed, including positive-dimensional equilibrium sets. Hardness also holds when a known strict pure equilibrium is supplied.

For a nonempty list of n positive integers, the reduction constructs a game with (8n + 9) rows and (16n + 22) columns. Its rational entries have polynomial total binary encoding length. No partition gives exactly the specified equilibrium; a partition gives at least one additional equilibrium.

The formal languages reject malformed encodings and games whose payoff sum does not have exact rank one. The two languages are complements within the valid rank-one input class; rank-invalid inputs belong to neither.

The proof starts from Disser and Skutella’s signed counting flow network. Flow through a designated bridge detects a partition. A small rational perturbation preserves the decisive comparisons while making the minimum-cost flow unique at every real demand.

An injective encoding places those flows inside a strategy simplex. A uniform exact penalty excludes infeasible minimizers, and the auxiliary zero-sum representation of Adsul and coauthors translates the bridge condition into the scalar consistency equation for a rank-one equilibrium.

The proof controls every auxiliary minimizer and every equilibrium, including degenerate cases. Rational certificates for two distinct equilibrium pairs establish membership in NP for nonuniqueness; checking input validity completes the coNP membership argument for uniqueness.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 14 October 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 5 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We give an explicit family of counterexamples to the proposed lower bound ε(S,L;x) ≥ (2+|K_S²|^(1/4))⁻¹ for minimal complex projective surfaces. For every integer d ≥ 7, a classical plane-pencil construction followed by a double base change gives a smooth surface with ample canonical bundle, K_S² = 6(d−1)(d−3), and an ample integral line bundle L with L² = 6 and ε(S,L;x) ≤ 1/(d−1). Already d = 7 contradicts the bound. The pencil and covering ingredients are classical; historical priority has not been fully cleared. This unrefereed note used AI tools extensively and has not received human peer review.

A Seshadri constant measures how positive a line bundle is near one point of an algebraic surface. One way it becomes small is when a curve has little intersection with the line bundle but many branches through that point.

A proposed lower bound tied this local quantity to the surface’s canonical self-intersection. This paper gives a family that falls below that bound, while keeping the line bundle’s self-intersection equal to 6.

The surfaces are minimal in the algebraic-geometric sense: they contain no smooth rational curve of self-intersection −1. The small value occurs at a deliberately chosen singular point of a curve on the smooth surface.

For every integer d ≥ 7, the paper constructs a smooth integral complex projective surface S with ample canonical bundle K_S, an ample integral line bundle L and a point x such that K_S² = 6(d−1)(d−3), L² = 6 and ε(S,L;x) ≤ 1/(d−1) < 1/(2+(K_S²)^(1/4)).
At d = 7, the displayed curve has L-degree 1 and multiplicity 6 at x. Thus ε(S,L;x) ≤ 1/6, while K_S² = 144 and the proposed lower bound is larger than 1/6.

The target is Szemberg’s arbitrary-point bound for minimal surfaces, restated as Conjecture 2 in Oberwolfach Report 21/2009 and Question 6.1.6 of the cited primer. The additive 2 is outside the fourth root.

The proof starts from Miranda’s classical pencil construction. A finite-degree argument chooses a plane pencil whose fibres are all integral and reduced. Blowing up its simple base points gives a surface Y with fibre F and a section E₁; the divisor A = 2F+E₁ is ample and has degree 1 on the chosen singular fibre.

A double base change, branched at four smooth fibres and away from the chosen singular fibre, produces a smooth surface with ample canonical bundle. The chosen fibre splits into two isomorphic copies, so its degree 1 and multiplicity d−1 survive on either copy.
Pulling back A gives L² = 6. The curve then supplies the stated upper bound directly from the definition of the Seshadri constant, and the strict comparison holds for every d ≥ 7.
Only an upper bound for ε(S,L;x) is asserted; the paper does not determine its exact value.

The surfaces vary with d and x is a special point. This does not establish vanishing of the infimum on one fixed complex surface, or contradict very-general-point, Picard-rank-one, canonical or adjoint polarization bounds.
The second pencil member and branch values are chosen through nonempty-open existence arguments; the paper does not list explicit coefficients for every choice.
The pencil, polarization and covering methods are classical. Historical priority and the problem’s status immediately before this note have not been fully established.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 16 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 7 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We give a self-contained proof that ordinary conservative chip-firing halting is NP-complete on finite loopless simple strongly connected digraphs. Hardness holds with polynomial numerical total initial chips and a specified vertex whose deletion leaves an acyclic graph of depth at most one. A separate construction forbids antiparallel arcs. The proof combines the primed-toppler mechanism of Holroyd–Levine–Winkler with the classical prime/Boolean/clause encoding of Stockmeyer–Meyer, also reconstructed by Gramlich. We prove the physical conservative realization, its legal checkpoint dynamics and the arbitrary-schedule implication in full; NP membership is credited to Farrell–Levine and reproved with an explicit certificate bound. This is an attributed proof of the historical simple-digraph question. Exact full-result and realization priority and preexisting worldwide openness remain unknown after a bounded audit; no firstness is claimed. AI tools were used extensively. The paper is unrefereed and has not received external human peer review.

Place a pile of chips at each vertex of a directed graph. A vertex can fire when it has enough chips to send one along every outgoing arrow. Firing moves chips without creating or removing any. The question is whether the game can eventually reach a position where no vertex can fire.

This paper proves that deciding whether the game halts is NP-complete even when the graph has no loops or repeated arrows and every vertex can reach every other vertex. A separate construction also forbids arrows pointing in opposite directions between the same two vertices.

The difficulty persists with polynomially many initial chips and a graph that becomes very shallow after removing one specified vertex. The construction encodes a Boolean formula through counters that cycle modulo small primes: a stable position can be reached exactly when the formula has a satisfying assignment.

The input is a finite loopless simple strongly connected digraph with at least two vertices and an arbitrary nonnegative integer chip configuration encoded in binary. Each vertex fires at its actual outdegree and sends one chip along each outgoing arc. There is no dissipative sink.

HALTING asks whether some finite legal firing sequence reaches a stable configuration. The problem is NP-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The same conclusion holds for the oriented subclass, which additionally forbids antiparallel arcs.

Hardness holds when a specified root r is supplied and deleting r leaves an acyclic graph with no directed path of two arcs. The reduction also has polynomial numerical total initial chips in the source 3-SAT input length, so the hardness persists when chip counts are written in unary.

Membership in NP covers arbitrary binary chip counts. A certificate records how many times each vertex fires, with polynomially many bits, and certifies a nonnegative stable endpoint. It need not list the full firing sequence.

A modular bank stores a number of chips that is largest exactly at selected residues. Its priming specializes the established primed-toppler construction of Holroyd–Levine–Winkler. The prime/Boolean/clause encoding is due to Stockmeyer–Meyer and is also reconstructed by Gramlich.

The proof realizes these counters as an ordinary conservative graph. At each checkpoint, every emitted chip has returned to the correct part of the graph. The root becomes unable to fire precisely when all residue conditions hold. The Chinese remainder theorem connects such a checkpoint to a satisfying Boolean assignment.

A legal checkpoint sequence establishes both directions of the reduction. Classical least action relates this sequence to all legal firing orders, without a fairness assumption. The proof also gives an explicit bound for a short firing-count certificate, using the NP-membership method of Farrell–Levine.

These are worst-case complexity statements. Unless P = NP, no polynomial-time algorithm solves every valid input. This does not mean that every instance is difficult, and the polynomial-bit certificate does not give a polynomial-time simulation of the game.

The theorem does not claim bounded-degree or Eulerian hardness, and it does not concern a fixed graph, a dissipative-sink model, weighted firing thresholds or a specified target configuration. The oriented construction is separate from the simple construction, which allows antiparallel arcs.

The primed-toppler mechanism, prime-residue encoding, root-last stabilization, least action, tree periods and NP-membership method have prior sources. The paper supplies a complete conservative graph realization and halting reduction with those antecedents credited.

Exact full-result and realization priority remain unknown. A bounded source comparison does not establish that the historical question was still open worldwide immediately before this work. Finite computational checks support the written proof; they do not establish the universal theorem by exhaustion.

AI tools were used extensively in solving, checking, adversarial review, source comparison, programming and writing. The author is responsible for the claims. The paper has not received external human peer review or journal acceptance and is not formally certified in a proof assistant.
