article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Zenodo date 23 August 2026 · Zenodo version 1.1.7 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 33 pages) · Paper and reader source (ZIP) · Reader supplement (PDF, 7 pages) · Verifier entrypoints (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Reticulate evolutionary histories encode hybridization, recombination, and lateral transfer, but such histories are scientifically recoverable from sequence data only when distinct networks induce distinguishable site-pattern distributions. We determine this information limit for binary, LSA-rootable, already-simple semi-directed strongly tree-child level-2 networks under the fixed one-step reticulation-preserving semi-directed convention used here and the open four-state Jukes–Cantor model. A source-relative full-dimensional regular stochastic containment occurs if and only if the labelled reduced bridge trees agree and every pair of corresponding blobs is labelled-isomorphic or differs by ordinary triangle redirection. Hence no proper one-sided generic containment exists, and an exact generic distribution determines a unique topology modulo that redirection. Fourier cut ranks recover the bridge tree, while positive rank-one factorizations recover only projective local tensors modulo the full incidence-scaling group; physical bridge multipliers are not identified. A graph-to-algebra classification of cycle and theta factors, together with marginal submersions and coherent bounded probes, reconstructs arbitrary subdivisions.

The boundary is sharp even without triangles. For every n ≥ 4 we construct two triangle-free networks that are weakly but not strongly tree-child, nonisomorphic, and not triangle-related, yet whose open JC images share a regular relatively open subset of full dimension 2n + 1. A second triangle-containing family exhibits a distinct pendant-transfer mechanism. All finite-atlas, class-membership, Fourier-equality, sign, and Jacobian claims are supported by exact primary and separately implemented replay certificates.

An evolutionary network allows two ancestral lineages to merge, as they can during hybridization. Even with unlimited sequence data, two different networks might predict exactly the same distribution of DNA patterns. This paper studies when that ambiguity remains under the Jukes–Cantor substitution model.

The distinction is between a network that has a tree-child rooting and one whose every admissible rooting is tree-child. In a tree-child rooting, each internal vertex has at least one child that is not a merger. Under the paper’s precise graph convention, the stronger condition permits generic recovery of level-2 networks, apart from changing the orientation inside an ordinary triangle.

The surprising part is the boundary: allowing just the weaker rooting condition admits triangle-free examples that remain ambiguous on a full-dimensional open region of distributions. These are not isolated coincidences or cases where a parameter is forced to zero. The construction works for every number of leaves from four onward.

Earlier work already establishes generic recovery for triangle-free networks in the strong class and explains local triangle ambiguity. This paper extends the proposed classification to triangles at level two and supplies explicit weak-class counterexamples. It addresses an exact mathematical model; it is not a test of a particular biological history.

The positive theorem concerns binary, LSA-rootable, already-simple semi-directed networks of level at most two. Reticulation arrowheads are preserved under the specified one-step root suppression, and every admissible rooting must be tree-child. The model uses a uniform root distribution and a displayed-tree mixture. Each edge has a Jukes–Cantor Fourier multiplier strictly between zero and one, and every inheritance probability is also strictly between zero and one.

Within that class, a regular neighborhood of a source model’s full dimension lies in another network’s stochastic image exactly when their labelled reduced bridge trees agree and corresponding blobs are labelled-isomorphic or differ by ordinary triangle redirection. Thus the directed full-dimensional containment relation has no proper one-sided cases.

Outside a proper algebraic exceptional set, the exact site-pattern distribution determines the semi-directed topology within this class, modulo ordinary triangle redirection. The bridge cuts themselves have a pointwise criterion throughout the strictly open parameter domain: their Fourier flattenings have rank at most four, while non-bridge splits have larger rank.

For every n ≥ 4, the paper constructs two labelled triangle-free level-2 networks that are weakly but not strongly tree-child, are nonisomorphic and not triangle-related, and share a regular relatively open region of JC distributions of dimension 2n + 1. A separate triangle-containing family shares such a region of dimension 2n.

The manuscript gives written reductions and a computer-assisted finite classification. The reader supplement explains the proof dependencies and explicit witnesses. The small source and entrypoint ZIPs accompany the paper; the full exact certificate and replay package is archived separately at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22064121.

First, Fourier rank conditions identify the bridges that connect the network’s reticulate components. Positive rank-one factorizations then separate the local component tensors, while keeping the full freedom to rescale their incidences. Those rescalings must be tracked because the physical bridge multipliers are not uniquely determined.

Each level-2 component reduces to a cycle or a theta shape with labelled attachment ports. The finite exact classification records the graph, all physical port arms, incoming roles and relevant marginal completions. Bounded probes recover the order of arbitrary subdivisions and test local containment modulo the allowed positive scaling.

The ordinary triangle ambiguity is realized on a regular physical open region. Compatible positive scalings then join local matches across the recovered bridge tree. Conversely, nonmatching local structures must be separated by the finite classification. This is the computational part on which the global theorem depends.

For the negative examples, explicit rational or algebraic parameter choices produce identical complete Fourier tensors on two different labelled networks. Rank witnesses and local parameter arguments extend those equalities to regular open regions. Attaching the same cherry at corresponding leaves extends the construction to larger numbers of taxa.
Generic topology recovery allows a proper algebraic exceptional set. The pointwise bridge-cut theorem does not turn the entire topology theorem into an everywhere-identifiable result.

The comparison class matters. The theorem does not classify all level-2 networks, arbitrary rooted refinements, or alternative semi-directed cleanup conventions. The weak-class counterexamples show that the strong hypothesis cannot simply be replaced by the whole weak class; they do not show that every weakly tree-child network is ambiguous.

Triangle redirection is a specific change of the reticulation placement and its arrowheads within a triangle, with the labelled underlying graph and outside attachments fixed. The theorem concerns full-dimensional regular overlap, not equality of entire stochastic model images. A particular distribution can distinguish triangle orientations even when the models overlap elsewhere.

Root location and all numerical parameters are not recovered. Positive factorization determines local tensors only up to the full incidence-scaling action, and physical bridge multipliers remain unidentifiable by that factorization.

The strictly open four-state JC model excludes zero or infinite edge lengths and inheritance probabilities zero or one. The result does not transfer automatically to K2P, K3P, coalescent models, rate mixtures, or sampled data with estimation error.

The constructive discussion assumes an exact full distribution with 4^n entries. Its bounded local probes do not provide a polynomial-time-in-n method for finite DNA samples. The bounded primary-literature comparison also does not establish worldwide priority.

AI tools assisted the mathematics, code, drafting and internal review. The separately implemented replay is a second code implementation, not independent human peer review. The author is responsible for the work.

Theorem 3.1 gives the level-1 triangle quotient; Corollary 2.12 already recovers blob-tree structure from exact JC data.

Currie et al., Semialgebraic Conditions for Identifying Triangles in Phylogenetic Networks, v1 (2026) : Theorem 3.2 proves that pairs of differently oriented triangle models have both full-dimensional overlap and full-dimensional differences. Holtgrefe et al., Characterizing Semi-Directed Phylogenetic Networks and Their Multi-Rootable Variants (2026) : Theorem 5 gives the no-omnian characterization of strong tree-childness. The present paper specializes this established structural idea to its binary, LSA-rootable fixed-graph convention.

Huber et al., When Are Quarnets Sufficient to Reconstruct Semi-Directed Phylogenetic Networks? (2025) : Lemma 4.2 and Figure 8 give the two underlying semi-directed level-2 generator shapes. The four directed theta cases here additionally record the incoming source position and ports.

Ardiyansyah, Distinguishing Level-2 Phylogenetic Networks Using Phylogenetic Invariants, v1 (2021) : Earlier invariant-based generic distinguishability for specified nice level-2 classes provides context; its class restrictions and algebraic statements differ from the open-image containment classification here.

sections.text: Abstract Reticulate evolutionary histories encode hybridization, recombination, and lateral transfer, but such histories are scientifically recoverable from sequence data only when distinct networks induce distinguishable site-pattern distributions. We determine this information limit for binary, LSA-rootable, already-simple semi-directed strongly tree-child level-2 networks under the fixed one-step reticulation-preserving semi-directed convention used here and the open four-state Jukes–Cantor model. A source-relative full-dimensional regular stochastic containment occurs if and only if the labelled reduced bridge trees agree and every pair of corresponding blobs is labelled-isomorphic or differs by ordinary triangle redirection. Hence no proper one-sided generic containment exists, and an exact generic distribution determines a unique topology modulo that redirection. Fourier cut ranks recover the bridge tree, while positive rank-one factorizations recover only projective local tensors modulo the full incidence-scaling group; physical bridge multipliers are not identified. A graph-to-algebra classification of cycle and theta factors, together with marginal submersions and coherent bounded probes, reconstructs arbitrary subdivisions. The boundary is sharp even without triangles. For every n ≥ 4 we construct two triangle-free networks that are weakly but not strongly tree-child, nonisomorphic, and not triangle-related, yet whose open JC images share a regular relatively open subset of full dimension 2n + 1. A second triangle-containing family exhibits a distinct pendant-transfer mechanism. All finite-atlas, class-membership, Fourier-equality, sign, and Jacobian claims are supported by exact primary and separately implemented replay certificates.

blocks.text: An evolutionary network allows two ancestral lineages to merge, as they can during hybridization. Even with unlimited sequence data, two different networks might predict exactly the same distribution of DNA patterns. This paper studies when that ambiguity remains under the Jukes–Cantor substitution model.

The distinction is between a network that has a tree-child rooting and one whose every admissible rooting is tree-child. In a tree-child rooting, each internal vertex has at least one child that is not a merger. Under the paper’s precise graph convention, the stronger condition permits generic recovery of level-2 networks, apart from changing the orientation inside an ordinary triangle.

The surprising part is the boundary: allowing just the weaker rooting condition admits triangle-free examples that remain ambiguous on a full-dimensional open region of distributions. These are not isolated coincidences or cases where a parameter is forced to zero. The construction works for every number of leaves from four onward.

Earlier work already establishes generic recovery for triangle-free networks in the strong class and explains local triangle ambiguity. This paper extends the proposed classification to triangles at level two and supplies explicit weak-class counterexamples. It addresses an exact mathematical model; it is not a test of a particular biological history.

blocks.text: First, Fourier rank conditions identify the bridges that connect the network’s reticulate components. Positive rank-one factorizations then separate the local component tensors, while keeping the full freedom to rescale their incidences. Those rescalings must be tracked because the physical bridge multipliers are not uniquely determined.

Each level-2 component reduces to a cycle or a theta shape with labelled attachment ports. The finite exact classification records the graph, all physical port arms, incoming roles and relevant marginal completions. Bounded probes recover the order of arbitrary subdivisions and test local containment modulo the allowed positive scaling.

The ordinary triangle ambiguity is realized on a regular physical open region. Compatible positive scalings then join local matches across the recovered bridge tree. Conversely, nonmatching local structures must be separated by the finite classification. This is the computational part on which the global theorem depends.

For the negative examples, explicit rational or algebraic parameter choices produce identical complete Fourier tensors on two different labelled networks. Rank witnesses and local parameter arguments extend those equalities to regular open regions. Attaching the same cherry at corresponding leaves extends the construction to larger numbers of taxa.

blocks.text: Generic topology recovery allows a proper algebraic exceptional set. The pointwise bridge-cut theorem does not turn the entire topology theorem into an everywhere-identifiable result.

The comparison class matters. The theorem does not classify all level-2 networks, arbitrary rooted refinements, or alternative semi-directed cleanup conventions. The weak-class counterexamples show that the strong hypothesis cannot simply be replaced by the whole weak class; they do not show that every weakly tree-child network is ambiguous.

Triangle redirection is a specific change of the reticulation placement and its arrowheads within a triangle, with the labelled underlying graph and outside attachments fixed. The theorem concerns full-dimensional regular overlap, not equality of entire stochastic model images. A particular distribution can distinguish triangle orientations even when the models overlap elsewhere.

Root location and all numerical parameters are not recovered. Positive factorization determines local tensors only up to the full incidence-scaling action, and physical bridge multipliers remain unidentifiable by that factorization.

The strictly open four-state JC model excludes zero or infinite edge lengths and inheritance probabilities zero or one. The result does not transfer automatically to K2P, K3P, coalescent models, rate mixtures, or sampled data with estimation error.

The constructive discussion assumes an exact full distribution with 4^n entries. Its bounded local probes do not provide a polynomial-time-in-n method for finite DNA samples. The bounded primary-literature comparison also does not establish worldwide priority.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 17 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 5 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We construct a finite two-dimensional abstract simplicial complex that is doubly Cohen–Macaulay over every field of characteristic zero, but contains no two-dimensional homology-sphere subcomplex over any field. This gives a negative answer to Nevo's question asking whether every doubly Cohen–Macaulay complex admits a decomposition into homology spheres with specified overlap properties. We use a finite quotient of an affine building, with all links equal to the incidence graph of the projective plane of order eleven. A direct spectral estimate controls the links after any vertex deletion; a weighted cocycle argument verifies the required homology vanishing. The sphere obstruction is an Euler-characteristic count. The construction and the spectral and curvature mechanisms build on established work, credited below.

A simplicial complex is built from vertices, edges, triangles and their higher-dimensional counterparts. Doubly Cohen–Macaulay complexes satisfy strong homological conditions that survive removal of any single vertex.

Nevo asked whether every such complex could be assembled from homology-sphere pieces with specified overlap properties. This paper gives a two-dimensional counterexample with no permitted sphere piece at all. The obstruction therefore appears before the overlap requirements can even be considered.

The construction uses a finite quotient of a well-studied geometric object called an affine building. Earlier building theory, spectral estimates and a curvature argument supply the main tools. The contribution is their application to the precise decomposition question, including the conditions after every vertex deletion.

There exists a finite pure two-dimensional abstract simplicial complex K that is doubly Cohen–Macaulay over every field of characteristic zero and contains no two-dimensional homology-sphere subcomplex over any field.

Here a homology sphere must have the homology of a sphere both globally and in every face link. The excluded sphere subcomplex need not be induced. Having sphere homology only globally is a weaker condition and is not the definition used in the theorem.

The example gives a negative answer to Nevo’s homology-sphere replacement question, recorded as Problem 8 in the 2005 Oberwolfach report and Problem 3.7 in the 2008 paper. It does not contradict Nevo’s earlier decomposition into minimal cycle complexes, which are a broader class of pieces.

Every vertex link of K is the incidence graph of the projective plane of order eleven. After a vertex deletion, the relevant links are either that graph or the graph with one vertex removed. Both have normalized Laplacian gap strictly greater than one half.

The construction starts with the vertex-regular affine-building lattice and faithful polynomial matrix representation of Lubotzky, Samuels and Vishne. Reducing those matrices modulo t⁹ gives a finite quotient. A degree bound excludes short identifications, so the quotient retains its projective-plane links.

The projective-plane incidence matrix satisfies an exact Gram identity. This controls the spectral gap even after one link vertex is removed. A finite weighted-cocycle argument then gives the required first-homology vanishing for K and every vertex deletion; connectivity and the remaining face-link conditions complete the doubly Cohen–Macaulay property.

Any homology-sphere subcomplex would have exactly two triangles on each edge and a cycle around each vertex. Those cycles have length at least six because they lie in the projective-plane links. Counting vertices, edges and triangles forces Euler characteristic at most zero, whereas a homology two-sphere has Euler characteristic two.

The doubly Cohen–Macaulay assertion is proved for characteristic-zero coefficient fields. It is not a claim over every field of positive characteristic. The field of order eleven in the geometric construction is distinct from the field used to compute homology.

The sphere exclusion uses the local-link definition of a homology sphere. It concerns actual subcomplexes of this finite complex, without subdivision or an enlarged ambient complex; it does not exclude all possible immersed or topologically embedded spheres.

The ambient complex is two-dimensional but is not a surface: each of its edges belongs to twelve triangles. The construction is an existence argument using a finite quotient; the accompanying finite checks do not enumerate that quotient or replace the proof.

The building, congruence method, spectral vanishing mechanism and curvature obstruction have substantial earlier sources. The paper applies them to the stated decomposition question. Its bounded literature search is not a certificate of worldwide priority.

AI tools were used extensively in the argument, writing, literature research, computation and internal review. These internal reviews do not constitute independent human peer review or formal proof verification. The author is responsible for the work.

Nevo, Rigidity and the lower bound theorem for doubly Cohen–Macaulay complexes (2008) : Theorem 3.4 gives the minimal-cycle decomposition. Problem 3.7 asks whether homology spheres can replace those pieces; this is the question addressed here.
Nevo, Discrete Geometry, Oberwolfach Report 17/2005 : Problem 8 on printed page 961 is the earlier workshop formulation of the homology-sphere replacement question.

Swartz, g-elements, finite buildings and higher Cohen–Macaulay connectivity, v1 : Section 4 states the local-link convention for homology spheres used in the decomposition literature. Global sphere homology alone is insufficient.

Lubotzky, Samuels and Vishne, Explicit constructions of Ramanujan complexes of type Ãd, v2 : Sections 2–4 supply the affine building, vertex-regular lattice and faithful polynomial representation. The present paper does not need the later global Ramanujan spectrum results.

Lubotzky and Meshulam, A Moore bound for simplicial complexes (2007) : The polynomial-degree versus congruence-divisibility method is an antecedent. The present paper gives its own short-displacement argument for the particular nonreduced quotient modulo t⁹.

Ballmann and Świątkowski, On L²-cohomology and property (T) for automorphism groups of polyhedral cell complexes : The strict link-gap threshold is part of the established Garland-type spectral method. The present manuscript includes a finite two-dimensional weighted-cocycle proof.

Januszkiewicz and Świątkowski, Simplicial nonpositive curvature (2006) : Example 1.8(5) records the curvature obstruction to triangulated two-spheres with sufficiently long links. The manuscript uses a direct Euler count for its arbitrary, possibly non-induced sphere subcomplexes.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 21 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 7 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Consider power reinforcement with exponent α>1 on a finite simple loopless graph: vertices fire at positive rates and select an incident edge proportionally to its current count to the power α. We prove that the infinitely reinforced edges almost surely form a forest for α>4/3, for arbitrary positive vertex rates and positive integer initial counts. The known triangle obstruction shows that the constant 4/3 cannot be decreased; its equality case is excluded. For equal rates we prove that every surviving component has diameter at most three when α≥17/4. The main deterministic step excludes an arbitrary weighted odd support cycle of length m when α>sec²(π/(2m)); the corresponding uniform cycle threshold and the even-cycle method are known. We use the published finite WARM convergence and support theorems, and credit the earlier least-weight and champion arguments. The forest result answers the forest-bound improvement requested in Oberwolfach Reports 12/2023; the suggested sharp whisker bound remains open. AI tools were extensively involved. This is an unrefereed preprint.

Imagine a finite network in which each vertex has its own clock. When a clock rings, one incident edge is reinforced. An edge chosen often becomes more likely to be chosen again; the exponent α controls how strongly past choices are favored.

The paper studies the edges that continue to be reinforced forever. When α is greater than 4/3, those surviving edges almost surely contain no cycles, even when vertices fire at different rates. This strict threshold cannot be lowered: for 1 < α < 4/3, an equal-rate triangle starting with one count on every edge can keep all three edges with positive probability.

When all vertices fire at the same rate and α is at least 17/4, each surviving component is a tree whose farthest vertices are at most three edges apart, a shape called a whisker. A whisker can still have many leaves; the bound concerns diameter rather than the number of vertices.

The model is a finite simple undirected loopless graph. Each nonisolated vertex has an independent Poisson clock with a fixed positive finite rate. Each edge starts with a fixed positive integer count. At a firing, an incident edge is selected with probability proportional to its current count raised to α, and that count increases by one.

For every such graph and initial count vector, α > 4/3 implies that the edges reinforced infinitely often almost surely form a forest. If the vertex rates are equal, α ≥ 17/4 implies that every surviving component is a tree of diameter at most three.

The forest constant is sharp as a strict sufficient bound. The known equal-rate triangle obstruction has positive probability of retaining all three edges for every 1 < α < 4/3 when initialized at unit counts. The paper makes no assertion at α = 4/3.

The deterministic contribution excludes an arbitrary weighted odd support cycle of length m from a limiting equilibrium when α > sec²(π/(2m)). It allows unequal rates, chords and attachments. The triangle sets the largest odd-cycle threshold, 4/3; the corresponding uniform bare-cycle spectrum and the even-cycle method come from earlier work.

A weighted cycle inequality supplies a positive direction for the Hessian of the reinforcement potential. For odd cycles, paired sine and cosine perturbations give the stated threshold independently of the equilibrium weights. The resulting positive Jacobian eigenvalue excludes the equilibrium even when other directions are critical.

Published finite WARM convergence and support-identification theorems turn this equilibrium exclusion into an almost-sure statement about surviving edges. A finite prescribed sequence of reinforcements transfers the required almost-sure tail conclusions from unit initialization to any fixed positive integer initial counts.

For equal rates, the whisker argument sharpens the earlier least-weight and champion methods. Exact interval estimates and an analytic bound for all sufficiently large α force internal support edges to form a matching. This rules out cycles and paths of four edges, leaving trees of diameter at most three.

The claims concern finite simple undirected graphs with positive rates and fixed positive integer initial edge counts. Loops, infinite graphs, zero initial counts and noninteger initial offsets are outside the stated model.
The stochastic equality case α = 4/3 is unresolved here. The paper also does not establish the suggested sharp equal-rate whisker conclusion throughout 4/3 < α < 17/4.

Equal rates are essential to the whisker claim; unequal-rate whisker conclusions are false in general. The triangle obstruction is a positive-probability statement from unit counts, not almost-sure triangle survival or a claim about every initialization.
These are asymptotic structural results. The paper gives no finite-time convergence rate, general survival probabilities or unique limiting shape, and makes no empirical biological claim.

The stochastic convergence and support theorems, uniform cycle spectrum, triangle obstruction, even-cycle method and least-weight/champion arguments have earlier sources. The bounded literature comparison does not certify worldwide priority. Finite checks supplement the universal proof rather than establish it.

AI tools were used extensively in mathematical research, proof development, symbolic and computational checks, adversarial auditing, literature investigation and writing. Internal AI reviews are not independent human peer review, journal acceptance or proof-assistant certification. This is an unrefereed preprint.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Published 17 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 5 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We give a negative answer to Cedó's Problem 9 in Oberwolfach Report 51/2019. An explicit left brace of order 20 000 is nontrivial and simple, has metabelian multiplicative group with abelian Sylow subgroups, and is not an asymmetric product of two trivial braces. The obstruction is intrinsic: every such two-factor product has zero triple star products within each additive Sylow subbrace, whereas the constructed brace has (x*x)*x=x³≠0 in its 5-primary subbrace. The obstruction covers the full admissible symmetric-cocycle definition, not only a chosen bilinear construction family. All operations and the simplicity argument are given directly; exact verification programs and independent adversarial audits accompany the note.

A brace is a set with two compatible group operations. Such structures connect algebra with the Yang–Baxter equation. Here “simple” means that there is no nonzero proper ideal compatible with both operations; it does not mean that the multiplicative group is simple.

Cedó’s 2019 question asks whether all finite nontrivial simple left braces with two specified restrictions on their multiplicative group come from one construction: an asymmetric product of two trivial braces. The restrictions are that the group is metabelian and that every one of its Sylow subgroups is abelian.

The paper presents a 20,000-element counterexample. Its distinguishing feature is an internal calculation that survives every change of coordinates: a triple star product is nonzero in the 5-primary part, whereas the proposed two-factor construction forces all such products to vanish there.

Theorem 1 specifies a left brace B with additive group C₅⁴ × C₂⁵ and multiplicative group (C₅³ ⋊ C₂) × (C₂⁴ ⋊ C₅), with the two actions explicitly given. It is nontrivial and simple, and its multiplicative group is nonabelian and metabelian with all Sylow subgroups abelian.

Lemma 2 is a presentation-independent obstruction. In any finite asymmetric product of two trivial braces with abelian multiplicative Sylow subgroups, (a∗b)∗c = 0 whenever a, b and c lie in one additive Sylow subbrace. The constructed brace instead has (x∗x)∗x = x³ ≠ 0 in its 5-primary subbrace, ruling out every such presentation.

The construction combines the truncated ring xF₅[x]/(x⁵) with a four-dimensional binary space and one extra binary coordinate. A finite logarithm change of coordinates identifies the multiplicative group explicitly; no infinite series or division by five is used.
The simplicity argument starts with an arbitrary nonzero ideal and forces it to contain generators of both primary parts. It does not assume that ideals are coordinate subspaces.

The obstruction begins with a normalized symmetric cocycle in the general asymmetric-product definition. Brace compatibility forces biadditivity in the two-trivial-factor setting. The abelian multiplicative Sylow condition then forces the indicated primary triple products to vanish.
The result is one explicit counterexample of order 20,000. It makes no smallest-order claim and does not classify all finite simple braces.
The excluded presentations have exactly two trivial factors. The paper does not exclude asymmetric products with nontrivial factors, more elaborate products, or general matched-product descriptions.

The universal obstruction assumes a finite left brace and abelian multiplicative Sylow subgroups. It concerns the left-associated product (a∗b)∗c with all three elements in the same additive primary part; it does not assert that every mixed-primary triple product vanishes.
The paper is an unrefereed, extensively AI-assisted preprint. Its historical-priority discussion is explicitly bounded, and it does not claim a new general construction formalism.

The obstruction is intrinsic: every such two-factor product has zero triple star products within each additive Sylow subbrace, whereas the constructed brace has (x*x)*x=x³≠0 in its 5-primary subbrace. The obstruction covers the full admissible symmetric-cocycle definition, not only a chosen bilinear construction family. All operations and the simplicity argument are given directly; exact verification programs and independent adversarial audits accompany the note.

blocks.text: A brace is a set with two compatible group operations. Such structures connect algebra with the Yang–Baxter equation. Here “simple” means that there is no nonzero proper ideal compatible with both operations; it does not mean that the multiplicative group is simple.

Cedó’s 2019 question asks whether all finite nontrivial simple left braces with two specified restrictions on their multiplicative group come from one construction: an asymmetric product of two trivial braces. The restrictions are that the group is metabelian and that every one of its Sylow subgroups is abelian.

The paper presents a 20,000-element counterexample. Its distinguishing feature is an internal calculation that survives every change of coordinates: a triple star product is nonzero in the 5-primary part, whereas the proposed two-factor construction forces all such products to vanish there.

Lemma 2 is a presentation-independent obstruction. In any finite asymmetric product of two trivial braces with abelian multiplicative Sylow subgroups, (a∗b)∗c = 0 whenever a, b and c lie in one additive Sylow subbrace. article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript dated 15 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 5 pages) · Source and verification (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We give a complete smooth compact-support proof of the classification asked for in the historical integrable-systems problem source: a real Jordan type occurs on a nonempty open subset of ℝⁿ for a compactly supported smooth Nijenhuis operator exactly when its spectrum is real. The construction realizes arbitrary specified numerical real Jordan data in a commuting local frame. On a same-dimensional torus collar, the torsion equation reduces to (A-λ I)A'=0; an ordered finite path removes every Jordan block and reaches an exact zero band. The nonreal obstruction and earlier semisimple and two-dimensional examples are prior results. We include the precise zero-point rigidity deduction needed for necessity. The historical priority of the full result and of this construction remains unestablished. Extensive AI tools assisted solving, verification and writing. This preprint is unrefereed and has no external human peer review or formal proof-assistant certification.

A Nijenhuis operator assigns a linear transformation to each point of a space while satisfying a differential compatibility condition. This paper asks which matrix patterns can hold throughout an open region when the entire field must become exactly zero outside a bounded region.

Every pattern with real eigenvalues can be realized. The construction allows repeated eigenvalues and Jordan blocks of any size, including matrices that cannot be diagonalized. It fixes both the numerical eigenvalues and the block pattern in a suitable local frame.

The difficult step is turning the field off without breaking its compatibility condition. The paper makes that transition in a thin neighborhood of a torus, removing the connections within each Jordan block in a controlled order.

Outside the chosen region, the matrix pattern is allowed to change. The converse is an established obstruction: a smooth compactly supported real Nijenhuis operator cannot have a nonreal eigenvalue anywhere.

For every integer n ≥ 1 and every prescribed numerical real Jordan matrix J whose eigenvalues are all real, there is a globally C∞, compactly supported real Nijenhuis operator on ℝⁿ whose matrix is J in a smooth commuting local frame on a nonempty open domain.
The construction includes repeated eigenvalues, multiple blocks belonging to the same eigenvalue, blocks of arbitrary size, negative or zero eigenvalues and the zero matrix.

Conversely, every eigenvalue at every point of any smooth compactly supported real Nijenhuis operator on ℝⁿ is real. Together, these statements give the classification asked for in the printed historical problem.

The prescribed numerical matrix is realized on an open domain in the same dimension. The theorem does not prescribe the ambient Cartesian-frame matrix or require one Jordan type throughout the whole space.

In dimensions two and higher, a thin torus neighborhood lets all coefficients depend on one transverse variable. For the block matrix L = [[A(t), b(t)], [0, λ(t)]], the Nijenhuis condition reduces to the ordered equation (A − λI)A′ = 0.

A finite sequence first removes the transverse coupling, then turns off each Jordan block’s arrows in order and moves its scalar part to zero. Smooth transitions with constant end intervals join these stages and leave exact zero bands at both ends.

In these dimensions, an embedded torus collar lies in ℝⁿ in the required dimension. The tensor is pushed into that collar and extended by zero; the zero bands make the extension smooth and compactly supported. In dimension one, a smooth compactly supported scalar function suffices.

For necessity, the paper uses the established local splitting and holomorphic structure of nonreal spectral blocks in a zero-point rigidity argument. Compact support allows extension to a sphere with a neighborhood on which the tensor is zero.
The result is C∞ smooth. It does not give a nonzero real-analytic compactly supported operator.
The matrix J appears in a smooth commuting local frame on a domain chosen by the construction. The ambient Cartesian-frame matrix and an arbitrarily preassigned realization domain are not prescribed.

Rank, eigenvalues and Jordan type may change outside the realization domain. Global algebraic regularity and a single global Jordan type are not guaranteed; algebraic regularity is distinct from smoothness.
The nonreal obstruction concerns globally compactly supported operators. It does not forbid local models with nonreal eigenvalues or operators without compact support.

Earlier work supplies the nonreal obstruction, real semisimple and two-dimensional examples, local point realizations, and the splitting and holomorphic tools. Historical priority of the full result or this construction is not established.

Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · LaTeX source (ZIP) · Verification package (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We construct a finite locally CAT(0) unit cube complex with one vertex, seven edges, eight squares, and two three-dimensional cubes, whose fundamental group is the mapping torus of a→ a, b→ ab, c→ bcb. Its universal cover gives a proper cocompact cubical action of the exact group in AIM Question 5.2. All attaching maps, signed vertex links, and reversible presentation changes are given explicitly. We also explain a qualitative existence deduction from earlier WPD, Morse, and cubical completion theorems. The contribution presented here is the explicit small finite model; no historical firstness or minimality claim is made.

Some groups can be understood through the geometry of spaces assembled from squares and cubes. A useful arrangement has nonpositive curvature and repeats so that a finite quotient describes the entire infinite space.

This paper gives an explicit construction for one group in the AIM problem list. Its finite model has one vertex, seven edges, eight squares and two three-dimensional cubes. The face identifications and the resulting fundamental group are specified. The universal cover is the infinite CAT(0) cube complex on which the group acts freely, properly and cocompactly.

The compact description is the interesting feature. “Two cubes” counts the three-dimensional cells in a quotient that allows boundary identifications. It does not mean that every point on the boundaries of two ordinary solid cubes remains distinct.
Let F be the free group on a, b and c, with automorphism φ(a)=a, φ(b)=ab and φ(c)=bcb. The mapping torus uses the convention tut⁻¹=φ(u); the final b in bcb is positive.

There is a finite locally CAT(0) unit cube complex Z of dimension three, with cell counts (1,7,8,2) and fundamental group isomorphic to the full group F⋊φZ. Its universal cover carries a free, proper and cocompact action of that exact group by cubical isometries.

The finite quotient uses the general cube-complex convention allowing isometric boundary-face identifications. The stated cell counts are before subdivision; the CAT(0) universal cover satisfies the stricter embedded-cube convention.
A base built from two squares admits a cubical involution. A second two-square complex has infinite cyclic fundamental group and two compatible local-isometry maps into the base.

Attaching the ends of its product with an interval gives the finite quotient. The links are checked with signed edge directions and all repeated corner occurrences retained; the unique vertex link is an actual flag simplicial complex.

Reversible presentation changes identify the entire fundamental group, including the positive final b in the automorphism. Standard cubical geometry then gives the CAT(0) universal cover and the proper cocompact deck action.
A separate argument explains qualitative existence using earlier WPD, Morse and cubical-completion theorems. Those prior tools do not supply the displayed small cell counts.
The result concerns this exact marked automorphism. The workshop summary also discusses a related example with b↦aba; that formula is distinct from the b↦ab target here.
No minimum dimension, minimum cell count, virtual specialness or theorem for a whole family of free-by-cyclic groups is claimed.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript dated 20 October 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Source and verification package (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We prove positive recurrence at every fixed positive arrival rate for the four-population deterministic-first-chunk chain described by Norros, Reittu and Eirola. This answers the stability conjecture in Norros's 2010 Oberwolfach contribution and the retained 2011 author proof, for the exact six-rate model with a permanent seed and invisible empty waiting rooms. A single coercive Foster function combines remaining workload, rounded cohort imbalance, and two bounded finite birth–death Poisson correctors. Monotone ratio cutoffs make every first-download interface error nonpositive. The other interface errors are controlled pointwise. The proof requires no stationary averaging, moment assumption, or uniformity in the arrival rate. Exact finite controls supplement the analytic proof. The contribution is the all-load extension of the stated historical conjecture; classical methods and source-version limits are explicit.

Imagine a file split into two pieces. Each arriving participant independently chooses at random which piece to fetch first and keeps that first choice. Participants leave as soon as both pieces are obtained, while one permanent seed always has both pieces.

The paper proves stability for a particular continuous-time random model at every fixed positive arrival rate. Stability here means positive recurrence and a unique stationary probability distribution. It does not imply a bound on average population or download time.

The exact model matters: empty participants are excluded from the contact denominator, and the permanent seed has no separate aggregate upload cap. Many empty participants can contact it at once. This result is not a stability theorem for a capped-seed model.

The associated large-system differential equations can have trajectories growing without bound. For this model, that behavior does not force instability of the random chain. The paper extends the elementary small-load argument to every fixed positive load.

For every fixed real λ>0, Theorem 1 states that the continuous-time chain on N₀⁴ is nonexplosive, irreducible and positive recurrent, and therefore has a unique stationary probability distribution. The conclusion covers every finite initial state.

The state (a,b,x,y) records empty participants assigned to each first-chunk choice and participants holding only each respective chunk. With D=x+y+1, the two arrivals have rate λ/2, the first downloads have rates a(x+1)/D and b(y+1)/D, and departures have rates x(y+1)/D and y(x+1)/D. A transition decrementing a zero coordinate has rate zero.

The seed contributes the +1 terms. The empty populations a and b do not enter D, and these rates allow unbounded aggregate seed upload as the waiting populations grow. The theorem applies to this literal generator.
The proof combines the amount of unfinished downloading with a smoothed measure of imbalance between the two participant groups. Two bounded corrections handle states in which one piece is scarce.

The corrections are activated by monotone cutoffs. The first-download transitions change those cutoffs in a favorable direction; the remaining changes are bounded explicitly. One global function then has negative expected drift outside a finite set.
The argument uses localized stopping times and a finite-mean return cycle to obtain recurrence. It does not assume in advance that a stationary distribution or a stationary population moment exists.

The model has exactly two chunks, one permanent seed, independently uniform fixed first choices, immediate departure on completion and empty waiting rooms excluded from the contact denominator. It does not cover arbitrary file-sharing software or other chunk-selection rules.
The six rates impose no fixed aggregate seed-capacity bound. This is not a solution for a capped-seed or finite-bandwidth missing-piece model.

The arrival rate is fixed and strictly positive, and the proof constants can depend on it. No bound uniform in λ, stationary population moment, completion-time estimate, convergence rate or geometric ergodicity is established. At λ=0 the zero state is absorbing and the stated irreducibility conclusion does not apply.

The historical target is the 2010 Oberwolfach stability conjecture and the retained 2011 author-proof model. The 2009 preprint conjectured high-load instability instead. These source versions must be distinguished.

The classical Foster–Lyapunov method and finite birth–death Poisson equation are prior tools. The paper claims the all-load pointwise certificate for this model, and does not certify worldwide priority or continued openness.

Let k be any field of characteristic zero and let 0≠h∈k[x]. For A_h=k⟨x,Y⟩/(Yx−xY−h(x)), the ordinary Hochschild cohomology, with its canonical cup product and Gerstenhaber bracket, admits a Batalin–Vilkovisky generator if and only if h is squarefree. In the squarefree case its bracket is zero. A repeated irreducible factor produces a cup-zero, noncommuting pair of degree-one classes, and a central annihilator forces every putative generator to vanish on degree one. Thus in that case no degree-minus-one bracket generator exists, even without requiring its square to be zero. The argument uses the published resolution and derivation structure of this family, and answers the concrete-family question recorded by Lopes in Oberwolfach Report 46/2023, p. 2702, Question (2).

Hochschild cohomology packages information about an algebra and its possible deformations. It comes with both a product and a bracket. A Batalin–Vilkovisky, or BV, generator is a single operator that recovers the bracket from the product and whose square is zero.

This paper considers a family of algebras governed by one polynomial h. The classification is simple to state: a BV generator exists exactly when h has no repeated irreducible factor. Nonzero constant polynomials are included in the positive case.

The negative case is stronger than failure to find a suitable formula. A repeated factor produces cohomology classes whose product is zero but whose bracket is nonzero. Together with a central annihilating class, these relations rule out every degree-minus-one bracket generator, even if its square is not required to vanish.

For any characteristic-zero field k and nonzero h∈k[x], let A_h=k⟨x,Y⟩/(Yx−xY−h(x)). Theorem 1 states that h being squarefree, the canonical Gerstenhaber bracket on ordinary HH•(A_h,A_h) being zero, existence of a bracket generator, and existence of a BV generator are equivalent.

For squarefree h, the zero operator is a BV generator. If h has a repeated irreducible factor over k, no bracket generator exists. The argument works over the original field and does not require the polynomial to split into linear factors.
Published results describe the algebra’s resolution and derivations. The paper compares that resolution with normalized bars to identify the canonical cup product needed for the obstruction.

When d=gcd(h,h′) is nonconstant, a central degree-one class annihilates every other degree-one class under the cup product. This forces any possible bracket generator to vanish on degree one. An explicit cup-zero pair with nonzero bracket then gives a contradiction.
When d=1, the second and higher cohomology groups vanish and the remaining degree-one derivations commute. The entire bracket is therefore zero.

The classification concerns this one-variable polynomial family over fields of characteristic zero, with its ordinary Hochschild cohomology and canonical product and bracket. It does not classify arbitrary Weyl subalgebras, positive-characteristic cases, twisted-coefficient variants, or Poisson analogues.

For h≠0, A_h is the subalgebra of the first Weyl algebra generated by x and yh(x). The literal embedded h=0 case instead gives k[x], which the paper treats separately using Δ(f∂x)=−f′. Setting h=0 in the abstract two-generator presentation gives a different algebra, k[x,Y].

The result uses established resolution and derivation theorems. The accompanying finite exact computations support selected identities; they are not proof-assistant certification or a replacement for the universal argument.

Earlier work already ruled out bracket generators for other ordinary Hochschild cohomology algebras. This paper gives a classification for the stated family, with bounded historical coverage. It makes no first-discovery claim.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript dated 15 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Source and verification package (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Ordinary legal chip-firing reachability is coNP-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions for finite loopless strongly connected directed multigraphs, with binary adjacency entries and nonnegative binary initial and target configurations. We give an explicit reduction from the complement of the halting problem of Farrell and Levine. A finite-state cutoff controls an exact simulation, a gate supplies a cleanup reserve, and a marker forces that gate to have fired in every target-reaching word. Together with the prior coNP-membership theorem of Hujter, Kiss and Tóthmérész, this answers the historical general-digraph hardness question in the stated model. We credit earlier period, recurrence and reserve-simulation arguments. Exact-result, gadget and method priority, independence of discovery, and present-day openness remain unknown after a bounded source audit. This extensively AI-assisted note is unrefereed.
In a chip-firing game, a vertex with enough chips can send chips along all its outgoing arcs. This paper asks whether some finite sequence of legal moves can reach a specified final arrangement.

The result classifies this question as coNP-complete for a precise family of directed multigraphs. Arc multiplicities and chip counts are written in binary, so a compact input can describe very large numbers of parallel arcs and chips. The graph is loopless and strongly connected: every vertex can reach every other along directed paths.

The proof turns the question of whether legal play can continue indefinitely into a specified-target reachability question. It computes the new graph and target directly, without first finding a recurrent arrangement or writing out the potentially very long sequence of moves.

For finite nonempty loopless strongly connected directed multigraphs, deciding whether a finite sequential legal firing word takes a nonnegative initial configuration to a specified nonnegative target is coNP-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions.

The number of vertices varies with the input. Adjacency entries, including arc multiplicities, and both configurations are encoded in binary. The empty firing word is allowed, and a word may stop even when another move remains available. Malformed inputs are rejected. In the one-vertex loopless case, reachability is exactly equality of the two configurations.
The reduction supplies coNP-hardness. Prior work by Hujter, Kiss and Tóthmérész supplies coNP membership; the paper explains the earlier certificate argument with attribution.

Conservation bounds the number of possible source configurations. A legal word that is long enough must repeat a state, so it can be continued forever. This cutoff can be numerically large while its binary representation stays short.

The new graph simulates the source until a gate has collected enough chips. Firing the gate releases a reserve that lets the remaining prescribed moves reach an explicitly calculated target. A marker ensures that every target-reaching word has fired the gate, even if its other firing counts differ from the intended ones.

The graph and target use polynomially many bits. The reduction computes them without executing the long simulation. The earlier coNP-membership argument gives polynomial-size certificates of nonreachability using reduced firing counts.
Parallel arcs, large degrees and large chip counts are used. No corresponding classification is established for simple graphs, unary encodings, bounded degrees or bounded total chip counts.
The theorem concerns legal reachability of a specified target on a varying input graph. It is not a halting or rotor-routing classification, or a claim about all configurations on one fixed graph.
Both input configurations are nonnegative. Signed intermediate normalization in the hardness proof does not establish coNP membership for every signed formulation.
The cutoff bounds a simulation horizon, not the running time of a reachability algorithm. Finite verification controls supplement the written proof and do not certify it formally.

Source hardness, coNP membership, period deletion, recurrence and reserve-simulation arguments are earlier work. Priority of the complete result or gate/marker mechanism, independent discovery and present worldwide openness remain unestablished.

AI tools were used extensively in solving, checking, source comparison, programming and writing. Internal AI reviews and finite computational controls do not constitute external human peer review, journal acceptance or proof-assistant certification.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript dated 15 October 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 4 pages) · Source and verification package (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Let A_n(k) be the integral Andreadakis filtration of the automorphism group of a free group, and let D_n(k) be the kernel of its action on J/J^{k+1} in the rational SL(2,ℂ) matrix-entry algebra at the trivial representation. We construct elements of D_n(5) \ A_n(5) for every n≥4, and of D_n(6) \ A_n(6) for every n≥3. Thus the equality in all degrees conjectured in Satoh’s 2018 report is false at every rank in its stated range. The construction uses a classical degree-five Lie identity, elementary free-group automorphisms, and integral Magnus coefficients. The proof works with actual powers of J, rather than only values along one-parameter representations.

A free group starts with symbols that can be combined into words, with no relations beyond cancellation. An automorphism changes the generators while preserving the group. Two filtrations measure how hard such a change is to detect: one uses successive group quotients, while the other uses two-by-two matrix representations near the trivial representation.

The paper gives explicit changes that the matrix test misses to a specified order even though the corresponding group quotient detects them. It treats degree five for every rank at least four, and degree six for every rank at least three.

The key idea is that a classical identity holds for two-by-two matrices but not for freely noncommuting symbols. Turning this mismatch into words gives counterexamples to the all-degree equality stated in Satoh’s 2018 report.

For the free group F_n, let A_n(k) be the kernel of the action on F_n/Γ_{k+1}F_n, using the integral lower central series. Let D_n(k) be the kernel of the action on the entire J/J^{k+1}, where J is the augmentation ideal in the rational algebra of SL(2,ℂ) matrix-entry functions.
With group commutator [g,h]=ghg⁻¹h⁻¹, set w=[[[x₁,x₂],[x₁,x₃]],x₁]. For every n≥4, the automorphism x₄↦x₄w fixing the other generators lies in D_n(5) but not A_n(5).

Set v=[[[x₁,x₂],[x₁,[x₁,x₂]]],x₁]. For every n≥3, the automorphism x₃↦x₃v fixing the other generators lies in D_n(6) but not A_n(6). Thus equality in all degrees fails at every rank n≥3 covered by the stated conjecture.

The classical identity [[[X,Y],[X,Z]],X]=0 for two-by-two matrices follows here directly from Cayley–Hamilton over any commutative coefficient ring. Substituting Z=[X,Y] gives the weighted degree-six identity.

A filtered group-commutator calculation transfers these identities to actual powers J⁶ and J⁷ in the matrix-entry algebra. It controls the whole ideal quotient, rather than only selected representations or one associated graded piece.

Integral Magnus expansions retain a nonzero degree-five coefficient for w and degree-six coefficient for v. These obstruct membership in the next lower central subgroup. Each word omits the generator that is moved, so the displayed substitutions have explicit inverses.

This is a result about the rational SL(2,ℂ) matrix-entry algebra and the full ideal quotient J/J^{k+1}. It is not a theorem about a trace algebra, a character algebra or a Grothendieck representation ring.
The theorem does not establish a degree-five counterexample at rank three, failure in every degree, or an extension to larger matrix sizes.
It addresses the representation-filtration equality formulated in 2018. It is distinct from the comparison of the Andreadakis filtration with the lower central series of IA_n.

The matrix identity and the general algebraic tools are classical. The stated contribution is their explicit application to this equality; no new polynomial identity, historical firstness, exhaustive novelty clearance or continuing worldwide openness is claimed.

articles.header: Deep derived pure braids need not be 1-solvable By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript dated 15 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 4 pages) · Source and verification package (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

For every m≥3 and every finite k≥1, the kth ordinary derived subgroup of the pure braid group contains a braid whose standard closure is not integrally smoothly 1-solvable. Consequently P_m^{(n+2)}⊄F_n^m for every integer n≥1, answering negatively the derived-series containment question in the Harvey–Park–Ray Oberwolfach contribution. The proof combines established signature-quasimorphism results with amenable-quotient rigidity and a pointwise signature obstruction to 1-solvability. The general quasimorphism ingredients are prior results. An accompanying exact verification package also preserves an explicit 104-crossing example in P_3^{(3)}.

Pure braids return each strand to its starting position. Repeatedly taking commutators creates the derived series, an increasingly restrictive sequence of subgroups. A separate notion, called 1-solvability, asks whether the closed braid fits into a four-dimensional construction with specified surfaces and intersection properties.

The paper shows that for every number of strands at least three, a braid can lie arbitrarily far down the derived series and still fail 1-solvability. For each finite depth there is a witness; the argument does not use one braid that works simultaneously at every depth.

The general argument connects established results about braid signatures and quasimorphisms. The supporting materials also give a concrete three-strand word with 104 crossings at the third derived level. That finite example illustrates one case of the broader existence theorem.

Let P_m be the classical disk pure braid group, with P_m^(0)=P_m and P_m^(k+1)=[P_m^(k),P_m^(k)]. For every m≥3 and every finite integer k≥1, some braid in P_m^(k) has standard oriented closure that is not integrally smoothly 1-solvable in the sense of Otto Definition 2.3.

Equivalently, the string-link concordance classes represented by P_m^(k) are not all in F₁^m. Since F_n^m⊂F₁^m for integers n≥1, this gives P_m^(n+2)⊄F_n^m for every m≥3 and integer n≥1, a negative answer to Question 3 in the Harvey–Park–Ray Oberwolfach contribution.

For the explicit third-derived example, set a=σ₁², b=σ₂², c=[a,b], d=a⁻¹ca, e=b⁻¹cb, u=[c,d], v=[d,e] and β=[u,v], using [x,y]=xyx⁻¹y⁻¹. The paper gives a 104-letter freely reduced Artin word for β with closure signature −2.

The ordinary signature s of a three-strand braid closure has bounded failure of additivity. Its homogenization q is a homogeneous quasimorphism, exactly linear on powers. Published signature formulas show that q restricted to the pure braid group P₃ is not a homomorphism.

A nonhomomorphic homogeneous quasimorphism cannot vanish on a finite derived subgroup. Otherwise it would descend to a solvable, hence amenable, quotient, where homogeneous quasimorphisms are homomorphisms. The general ingredients are established results.

The ordinary signature and its homogenization are distinct. A suitable positive power is essential: nonzero q on a braid does not by itself give nonzero ordinary signature on that same braid. The powered braid has nonzero ordinary signature and zero pairwise linking numbers. A pointwise signature obstruction rules out an integral smooth 1-solution; adding split trivial strands reaches every m≥3.

The result uses the ordinary derived series of classical disk pure braid groups and integral smooth solvability of standard closures. It makes no claim for power subgroups, lower central series, rational derived series, surface braid groups, rational solvability or a merely topological solvability category.

The witness may depend on the finite depth k. No single braid in the intersection of all derived subgroups is asserted, and the explicit 104-crossing word is supplied only for k=3. No minimal crossing number or effective word-length bound at arbitrary depth is claimed.

For m=1 and m=2, the positive derived subgroups are trivial. The consequence for the solvable filtration is stated for integers n≥1; it does not contradict the prior n=0 containment discussed in the original report.

The general signature, quasimorphism and amenable-group tools are credited prior results. The contribution presented is their application to this particular containment question, together with the explicit finite example. No historical firstness, exhaustive novelty clearance or continued worldwide openness is claimed.

For the separate explicit example, the supporting derivation reconstructs the Goeritz form from crossing geometry and records a printed index discrepancy in Erle’s matrix formula. A separate Burau–Meyer calculation gives the same signature. This qualification concerns the finite example; the arbitrary-depth existence proof is independent of that calculation.

blocks.text: Pure braids return each strand to its starting position. Repeatedly taking commutators creates the derived series, an increasingly restrictive sequence of subgroups. A separate notion, called 1-solvability, asks whether the closed braid fits into a four-dimensional construction with specified surfaces and intersection properties.

The paper shows that for every number of strands at least three, a braid can lie arbitrarily far down the derived series and still fail 1-solvability. For each finite depth there is a witness; the argument does not use one braid that works simultaneously at every depth.

The general argument connects established results about braid signatures and quasimorphisms. The supporting materials also give a concrete three-strand word with 104 crossings at the third derived level. That finite example illustrates one case of the broader existence theorem.

blocks.text: The ordinary signature s of a three-strand braid closure has bounded failure of additivity. Its homogenization q is a homogeneous quasimorphism, exactly linear on powers. Published signature formulas show that q restricted to the pure braid group P₃ is not a homomorphism.

A nonhomomorphic homogeneous quasimorphism cannot vanish on a finite derived subgroup. Otherwise it would descend to a solvable, hence amenable, quotient, where homogeneous quasimorphisms are homomorphisms. The general ingredients are established results.

The ordinary signature and its homogenization are distinct. A suitable positive power is essential: nonzero q on a braid does not by itself give nonzero ordinary signature on that same braid. The powered braid has nonzero ordinary signature and zero pairwise linking numbers. A pointwise signature obstruction rules out an integral smooth 1-solution; adding split trivial strands reaches every m≥3.

blocks.text: The result uses the ordinary derived series of classical disk pure braid groups and integral smooth solvability of standard closures. It makes no claim for power subgroups, lower central series, rational derived series, surface braid groups, rational solvability or a merely topological solvability category.

The witness may depend on the finite depth k. No single braid in the intersection of all derived subgroups is asserted, and the explicit 104-crossing word is supplied only for k=3. No minimal crossing number or effective word-length bound at arbitrary depth is claimed.

For m=1 and m=2, the positive derived subgroups are trivial. The consequence for the solvable filtration is stated for integers n≥1; it does not contradict the prior n=0 containment discussed in the original report.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript dated 14 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Source and supporting verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We give an explicit counterexample to retaining ordinary critical-cone strict positivity and strong control-L² quadratic growth after removing quadratic control regularization from the energy-critical quintic-wave problem of Kunisch and Meinlschmidt. On the three-dimensional unit ball, zero is the unique global optimizer for a sufficiently small positive pointwise control cap. Its ordinary critical cone is {0}, so the strict condition is vacuous, but feasible controls converging in L∞ have objective gap o(‖u‖²L²). Nearby radial terminal targets admit global optimizers, and every such optimizer has L² displacement divided by target displacement tending to infinity. Local L¹ quadratic growth survives. The construction realizes the established concentration and noncoercivity mechanism in the actual nonlinear source model, using classical wave estimates.

In optimal control, a control is an input chosen to make a system behave as desired. This paper studies a nonlinear wave equation, where the objective balances a desired final wave profile against penalties on the state and on the amount of control used.

A useful stability property says that moving away from the best control raises the objective by at least a fixed multiple of the squared distance. In this example, doing nothing is the unique global optimum, but increasingly short, small pulses have an objective penalty much smaller than their squared L² size. Uniqueness therefore does not supply that stronger growth property.

The striking feature is that the ordinary critical-cone test still holds: its cone contains only zero, so there are no nonzero directions on which the strict test can fail. The concentrating pulses reveal what this test misses. A weaker L¹ quadratic-growth estimate survives, and the paper also bounds how optimizers respond to nearby terminal targets.

The model is the real defocusing quintic wave equation yₜₜ − Δy + y⁵ = u on the three-dimensional unit ball B, with zero position and velocity initially, homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and final time 1. Let H=L²(B). Controls lie in L²(0,1;H) and obey ‖u(t)‖H ≤ ρ almost everywhere in time. There is ρ*>0 such that the conclusions hold for every fixed 0<ρ≤ρ* and every fixed finite ν≥0.

The objective Jd,ν retains one half of the squared terminal-position tracking error, one quarter of the fourth power of the L⁴(0,1;L¹²(B)) state norm, and the L¹(0,1;H) sparse-control penalty: γ=β₁=1. Only the quadratic control penalty is removed, β₂=0. The optional terminal-velocity term is ν‖yₜ(1)‖²H⁻¹(B)/2.

For target d=πe, with e the normalized first radial Dirichlet eigenfunction, zero is the unique global optimizer over all admissible controls. With A=‖u‖L¹(0,1;H), the objective gap Δ(u)=Jπe,ν(u)−Jπe,ν(0) satisfies Δ(u)≥A³/(12ρ²). The ordinary critical cone is {0}, so the strict substitute second-variation condition is vacuous. The cap threshold and this lower bound can be chosen independently of ν.

The actual nonlinear feasible pulses uₕ=he·1{|t−1/2|<h}, for 0<h<min(ρ,1/2), satisfy ‖uₕ‖L∞(0,1;H)=h, ‖uₕ‖²L²(0,1;H)=2h³ and Δ(uₕ)=(π²/3+2/π²)h⁴+O(h⁶). Strong control-L² quadratic growth therefore fails in both L² and L∞ neighborhoods of zero.

Global optimizers exist for every terminal target d∈H in this fixed small-cap setting. Along dε=(π+ε)e, as ε decreases to zero through positive values, every choice of global optimizers satisfies ‖uε‖L²/ε→∞. No uniqueness of perturbed optimizers is required.

Corollary 3 retains local weaker-norm growth: Δ(u)≥‖u‖²L¹/(4π²) for every admissible control with sufficiently small L¹ norm. For an arbitrary nearby target πe+w, put ε=‖w‖H. Every global optimizer, compared with the fixed zero optimizer, satisfies ‖u‖L¹=O(ε) and ‖u‖L²=O(√ε). The constants and this upper-bound neighborhood can be chosen uniformly over all finite ν≥0.

On the positive radial ray w=εe, every global optimizer satisfies ‖uε‖L¹=Θ(ε) and cε³ᐟ⁴≤‖uε‖L²≤C√ε for sufficiently small ε. The lower-comparison neighborhood may depend on the fixed ν. These bounds do not assert a sharp L² response exponent.

Classical energy and Strichartz estimates make the nonlinear state close to the linear wave for small control mass: the state is O(‖u‖L¹), and the nonlinear remainder is O(‖u‖⁵L¹). This estimate is in a compatible energy-and-Strichartz state space; it does not assume that the nonlinear solution stays in one eigenmode.

The first eigenmode gives an explicit sine kernel for the terminal linear response. At the midpoint in time, the tracking gain exactly meets the sparse-control threshold. A cap-constrained moment estimate proves global optimality of zero, while pulses concentrating at that midpoint make the quadratic-growth quotient vanish.

The terminal tracking square also provides a weaker L¹ quadratic lower bound. A separate pulse comparison for perturbed targets yields the lower response bounds for every optimizer. These arguments use analytic estimates; the accompanying finite algebra checks are not a numerical solution of the nonlinear PDE.

This is a counterexample to retaining the ordinary critical-cone implication unchanged when the quadratic control penalty is removed. It does not rule out adapted sufficient conditions, enlarged cones, nondegeneracy assumptions or growth in weaker norms.
The ordinary critical cone is zero, so strict positivity there is vacuous. The result should not be described as a counterexample with a uniformly positive Hessian on every control direction.

The control cap is pointwise in time on the spatial L² norm. It is not a pointwise bound on |u(t,x)|. Here L¹ and L∞ mean time norms with values in L²(B), while control L² is the time-space L² norm. The state penalty remains present; “unregularized” refers to removing the quadratic control term.

The construction uses the three-dimensional unit ball, the defocusing quintic, zero initial data, a small positive cap and a particular target. It does not assert the same failure for every domain, every target, arbitrary large caps, Neumann conditions or boundary control.

The cap and base-target lower bounds can be chosen independently of ν. Upper target-response estimates and their neighborhood are uniform in finite ν; the radial lower-comparison neighborhood may depend on the fixed ν. No assertion concerns ν = ∞.

The response estimates compare optimizers with the fixed zero optimizer. They do not prove perturbed-optimizer uniqueness, a pairwise Lipschitz selection, L∞ convergence of perturbed optimizers, or a sharp exponent for the L² response.

The paper gives no certified numerical PDE constant or numerical value of the small-cap threshold. Its finite checks do not replace the analytic proof. The historical question and earlier mechanisms are attributed without a worldwide-firstness or present-day-openness claim.

The failure is specific to the selected target. For target d=0 in the same model, J0,ν(u)≥‖u‖L¹≥‖u‖²L²/ρ, so strong quadratic growth does hold. The theorem does not assert failure for all targets or all control caps.

Kunisch and Meinlschmidt, Optimal control of an energy-critical semilinear wave equation in 3D with spatially integrated control constraints : The inspected author preprint is arXiv:1907.02744v1 (5 July 2019). Lemma 2.9 gives the wave estimate; Theorem 4.17 requires a positive quadratic control coefficient. This author edition is distinct from the related 2020 journal publication, whose final body was not inspected.

Meinlschmidt and Kunisch, Optimal Control of a Semilinear Critical Wave Equation (Oberwolfach2021) : Printed pp.438–440 state the historical question about zero quadratic control regularization, and include the optional terminal-velocity term. This paper addresses the unchanged implication, not every possible unregularized theory.

Blair, Smith and Sogge, Strichartz estimates for the wave equation on manifolds with boundary : The classical bounded-domain wave estimates underlying the source model; the L⁴-time/L¹²-space estimate applies in three dimensions.

Herzog, Stadler and Wachsmuth, Directional Sparsity in Optimal Control of Partial Differential Equations : Prior group-sparsity and subgradient calculus. The present construction does not claim that threshold mechanism as new.

Casas and Tröltzsch, Second Order Optimality Conditions and Their Role in PDE Control : Example 4.16 reproduces Dunn’s earlier counterexample to exact-cone sufficiency. Dunn is credited through this inspected source; the concentration and noncoercivity mechanism predates the present nonlinear-wave realization.
Christof and Wachsmuth, No-Gap Second-Order Conditions via a Directional Curvature Functional : Prior nondegeneracy conditions account for normalized directions that converge weakly to zero.

Borchard and Wachsmuth, Second-order conditions for spatio-temporally sparse optimal control via second subderivatives : A second-subderivative framework distinguishing positivity from the additional nondegeneracy condition; original preprint arXiv2311.14538v1.

Wachsmuth and Wachsmuth, Second-order conditions for non-uniformly convex integrands: quadratic growth in L¹ : Prior weaker-norm quadratic-growth theory. The paper’s fixed-basepoint estimate is an explicit estimate within its chosen wave example.

blocks.text: Classical energy and Strichartz estimates make the nonlinear state close to the linear wave for small control mass: the state is O(‖u‖L¹), and the nonlinear remainder is O(‖u‖⁵L¹). This estimate is in a compatible energy-and-Strichartz state space; it does not assume that the nonlinear solution stays in one eigenmode.

The first eigenmode gives an explicit sine kernel for the terminal linear response. At the midpoint in time, the tracking gain exactly meets the sparse-control threshold. A cap-constrained moment estimate proves global optimality of zero, while pulses concentrating at that midpoint make the quadratic-growth quotient vanish.

The terminal tracking square also provides a weaker L¹ quadratic lower bound. A separate pulse comparison for perturbed targets yields the lower response bounds for every optimizer. These arguments use analytic estimates; the accompanying finite algebra checks are not a numerical solution of the nonlinear PDE.

blocks.text: This is a counterexample to retaining the ordinary critical-cone implication unchanged when the quadratic control penalty is removed. It does not rule out adapted sufficient conditions, enlarged cones, nondegeneracy assumptions or growth in weaker norms.
