article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript dated 13 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 5 pages) · Source and verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We give an affirmative answer to Question 3 in Iyer's contribution, joint with Shinko, to Oberwolfach Report 2/2025. A dense Gδ of continuous actions of the restricted wreath product ℤ ≀ ℤ on Cantor space has hyperfinite orbit equivalence relation on the entire space. We specialize established Cantor-action lifting principles to obtain a continuous profinite shift height. Finite-width lamp slabs then satisfy the compatible-metric theorem of Conley–Jackson–Marks–Seward–Tucker-Drob. The full preimage of the embedded integers is treated by a separate finite Borel exhaustion. The auxiliary Borel theorem requires the height factor and allows stabilizers.

A group action describes how transformations move points. Two points lie in the same orbit when one can be moved to the other. Hyperfiniteness means that this orbit relation can be built from an increasing sequence of Borel equivalence relations whose classes are finite.

The group here is the restricted wreath product ℤ ≀ ℤ: an integer shift acts on finitely supported configurations of integer-valued lamps. The paper shows that a generic continuous action on Cantor space has a hyperfinite orbit relation on the whole space. Generic refers to Baire category in the space of all these actions, rather than a probability estimate.

The proof constructs compatible height coordinates modulo successively larger factorials. It cuts the action into finite-width slabs and applies established results on Borel asymptotic dimension. A separate construction handles every point whose profinite height is an ordinary integer.

Let W=(⊕ᵢ∈ℤ ℤ)⋊ℤ be the countable discrete restricted wreath product. There is a dense Gδ subset of the full Polish space Act(W,2^ℕ) of continuous actions, with the subspace topology from Homeo(2^ℕ)^W and compact-open homeomorphism topologies, such that every action in this subset has a hyperfinite orbit equivalence relation on the entire Cantor space 2^ℕ.

More generally, suppose W acts Borelly on a standard Borel space X and admits an actual Borel map p:X→Ẑ satisfying p(gx)=p(x)+χ(g), where χ:W→ℤ is the shift homomorphism and Ẑ=lim ℤ/n!ℤ is the group of profinite integers. Then its orbit equivalence relation is hyperfinite on all of X. The theorem permits stabilizers and does not require freeness, minimality, an invariant probability measure or surjectivity of p.

The main theorem answers Question 3 in Iyer’s contribution, joint with Shinko, to Oberwolfach Report 2/2025. This is the historically posed whole-space generic-action question. The auxiliary Borel result requires the height factor; it does not establish hyperfiniteness for every Borel W-action.

The paper specializes established Cantor-action lifting principles. A direct construction gives compatible height maps modulo successive factorials, using countably many open dense extension conditions in the full action space. Their inverse limit is a continuous equivariant height map; in this compact Cantor setting it is onto.

At each fixed slab width, the lamp directions form a finite-rank free abelian group. Deep results of Conley, Jackson, Marks, Seward and Tucker-Drob give finite Borel asymptotic dimension for its action, including actions with stabilizers. The dimension may grow with the width, and slab components may be infinite. Divisible widths give nested slab graphs with decreasing distances, supplying the exact compatible-metric hypothesis of their Theorem 7.3.

On the full preimage of the embedded integers, which may be uncountable, the proof normalizes to height zero. It combines a finite Borel exhaustion for the lamp subgroup with increasing bounded intervals of integer heights. The height cutoff is essential to keep the pulled-back classes finite. The regular and exceptional pieces are invariant and their finite exhaustions can then be combined.

Genericity concerns a dense Gδ subset of the full space of continuous Cantor actions. Hyperfiniteness holds on every point of the phase space for those actions. The statement does not merely discard a null or meager subset of points, and it does not identify the entire set of hyperfinite actions as Gδ.

The general Borel theorem assumes an actual equivariant profinite height map. Stabilizers and nonsurjective maps are allowed. The onto height obtained for generic continuous Cantor actions is a consequence of that compact setting, rather than an added assumption in the Borel theorem. The paper does not treat all Borel W-actions without a height factor.

Finite Borel asymptotic dimension of each slab does not mean that its orbit components are finite. Dimension bounds need not be uniform across widths. The proof uses a specific compatible-metric theorem, rather than a general theorem about increasing unions of hyperfinite relations.

The proof relies on deep prior Borel theorems. Finite diagnostics in the supporting materials check local group and slab behavior; they do not prove the Baire-category or infinite Borel assertions. No comeager conjugacy class, uniform Borel choice of heights or exhaustions across actions, or clopen finite exhaustion is claimed.
No historical firstness, continued worldwide openness, independent human peer review or formal proof-assistant certification is claimed.

Iyer, joint with Shinko — Generic actions of countable groups : Printed pages 114–115 distinguish the earlier measure-hyperfinite result from the whole-space question; Question 3 asks about ℤ ≀ ℤ.

Conley, Jackson, Marks, Seward and Tucker-Drob — Borel asymptotic dimension and hyperfinite equivalence relations : The author manuscript gives the deep imported results: Corollary 5.5 for each fixed finite-rank abelian action, Theorem 7.3 for compatible metrics, and Corollary 7.5 for the lamp group. The journal article appeared in Duke Mathematical Journal 172 (2023), 3175–3226.

Iyer and Shinko — Asymptotic dimension and hyperfiniteness of generic Cantor actions : The prior generic hyperfiniteness theorem assumes locally finite asymptotic dimension. The pinned manuscript is version 1, September 2024.

Akin, Glasner and Weiss — A homeomorphism of the Cantor set : The linked 2006 author preprint gives the conditional-lifting predecessor in Theorem 3.3 and equation (3.7). The later 2008 journal paper is titled “Generically there is but one self homeomorphism of the Cantor set”; this link points to the 2006 preprint.
Doucha — Strong topological Rokhlin property, shadowing, and symbolic dynamics of countable groups : Proposition 2.12(3) supplies the all-group extension-perturbation background.

Doucha, Melleray and Tsankov — Dense and comeager conjugacy classes in zero-dimensional dynamics : Proposition 3.2, Definition A.3 and Proposition A.7 provide the finite-extension and existential-closure background. The link selects version 2 (2026); the earlier version 1 appeared in 2025.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript dated 11 October 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Source and verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

The closed set of complex monic quadratics with roots in the closed left half-plane is not prox-regular at z². For every fixed positive-definite real inner product on coefficient space, unstable quadratics with multiple attained global nearest stable quadratics occur arbitrarily close to z². The conclusion also holds in the full exact-degree quadratic coefficient space. A direct proof exhibits a limiting normal whose cubic support dominates a quartic squared displacement. The same obstruction disproves set prox-regularity of the whole abscissa epigraph. In contrast, the monic quadratic abscissa is function prox-regular at the origin relative to each finite limiting subgradient. Thus the historical question about local unique stable-polynomial projection has a negative answer for complex coefficients, while this example does not refute the separate function condition.

A polynomial is stable here when all its roots have nonpositive real part. Roots on the imaginary axis count as stable. One way to correct an unstable polynomial is to change its coefficients as little as possible until it becomes stable. The closest stable polynomial can be ambiguous: two different stable polynomials may be equally close.

This paper proves that such ties occur arbitrarily close to z² for complex quadratics. The conclusion holds for every fixed positive-definite real inner product used to measure coefficient changes, including metrics that mix the real and imaginary coordinates. Each neighborhood contains some unstable input with a tie; the theorem does not say that every nearby input has one.

The paper also separates two notions of local regularity. The stable set and the whole epigraph of the root-abscissa function have an obstruction to set prox-regularity. A different function condition still holds after fixing a finite limiting subgradient and allowing its local constants to depend on that subgradient.

For the complex monic quadratic p(z)=z²+az+b, let α(p) be the maximum real part of a root and let S={(a,b)∈ℂ²:α(p)≤0}. Identify ℂ² with ℝ⁴ in the order (Re a, Im a, Re b, Im b). For each fixed real symmetric positive-definite coefficient matrix G, S is not prox-regular at (0,0), and every neighborhood of that point contains some unstable quadratic with at least two distinct attained global nearest points in S. The comparison is with all complex stable quadratics, including repeated and imaginary-axis roots.

The corresponding conclusion holds in the full exact-degree space S_full={(ℓ,a,b)∈ℂ³:ℓ≠0, α(ℓz²+az+b)≤0}, at (1,0,0), for every fixed real symmetric positive-definite coefficient metric on ℝ⁶. Both real leading-coefficient directions are included. The minimizers are attained global nearest points in the original exact-degree set, even though that set is not globally closed.

The entire abscissa epigraph {(c,r):α(c)≤r} fails set prox-regularity at height zero over the monic and full-degree base points, for every fixed positive-definite real metric on the respective coefficient/height space. The metric may mix height and coefficient coordinates. The limiting support covector is horizontal; its representing normal vector can tilt in a mixed metric.

Separately, the monic complex quadratic abscissa is function prox-regular at (0,0), relative to each fixed finite limiting subgradient v₀, in the real Euclidean coefficient metric. The local constants may depend on the chosen v₀. The function condition localizes subgradients, base points and function values; its epigraph normal is (v₀,−1), rather than the horizontal covector used for the set obstruction.

Writing a=x+iy and b=u+iv gives the exact closed-stability chart x≥0, U=u+y²/4≥0 and V²≤x²U, where V=v−xy/2. Both nonnegativity conditions are needed at the singular faces. Along the stable path cₜ=(t²,0,t²,t³), smooth boundary normals converge to a limiting support covector n₀=(0,0,0,1). Its support is n₀·cₜ=t³, while the squared Euclidean displacement is 2t⁴+t⁶. The same cubic-versus-quartic obstruction persists in each fixed positive-definite metric.

The nearby normals are actual proximal normals: a sufficiently small normal step gives a local nearest point, and the triangle inequality excludes more distant competitors. Their limiting normal is not proximal. The classical Poliquin–Rockafellar–Thibault projection characterization then converts failure of set prox-regularity into nearby nonunique global projection. Closedness and a bounded minimizing-sequence argument supply monic attainment.

For full degree, the proof clips the stable set inside a closed metric ball of radius R that stays within ℓ≠0. The clipped set is compact. For a target less than R/3 from the base, points outside that ball are more than 2R/3 away, while the stable base is less than R/3 away. Thus the clipped and original global minimizers coincide. This compact localization supplies the full-degree attainment statement.

For the positive function result, the invertible discriminant-coordinate map (a,b)↦(a,a²−4b) transports lower supports in both directions. Fixing a finite subgradient bounds the scalar subgradients in a small neighborhood. A distance-to-ray estimate and the exact quadratic discriminant remainder then give the required local lower quadratic support.

The claims concern complex quadratics with closed-left-half-plane stability. They give no all-degree or real-only classification. For real monic quadratics the closed stability set is the convex orthant a≥0,b≥0, which has unique projection in every fixed positive-definite inner product.
Each metric is fixed and positive definite. No conclusion is asserted for arbitrary norms, singular or varying metrics, or a general transfer through nonlinear parameter-dependent metrics.

The nonuniqueness statement is existential in every neighborhood. It does not apply to every nearby unstable target, and it concerns global attained minimizers rather than competing local algorithmic minima. No explicit unstable input together with its two minimizing stable polynomials, or algorithm computing such a pair, is supplied.

The full exact-degree set excludes ℓ=0 and is not globally closed. Its global-attainment claim depends on the compact localization argument; treating the entire set as closed would not justify that conclusion.

The positive function claim is restricted to the monic abscissa and real Euclidean coefficient metric, relative to each fixed finite limiting subgradient. It does not give constants uniform over all finite subgradients, a full-degree function theorem, or a function theorem for every mixed coefficient/height metric. Whole-epigraph set failure does not refute this separate function condition.

Poliquin and Rockafellar’s Theorem 3.1 is a prox-regularity composition result under hypotheses; it does not itself state unconditional exact subdifferential equality. The manuscript’s explicit two-sided diffeomorphism and lower-support argument independently supplies the equality used here.

Finite exact rational checks and high-precision Decimal controls supplement the analytic proofs. Decimal controls are not interval-certified bounds, and finite computations do not establish the limiting-normal, universal-metric or global projection conclusions by themselves.

The short 2005 Oberwolfach question does not specify coefficient field, normalization or metric. The comparison here uses the explicit complex monic convention in Lewis’s 2003 Section 8; no unqualified real-only answer is asserted.

The original Cross, Moses–Liu and Bottema bodies were not inspected for the detailed comparisons made in the manuscript. Those exact example and nonuniqueness comparisons are not asserted here. Earlier coefficient-approximation work and related stability-boundary geometry receive credit without an exhaustive absence-of-overlap claim.
No historical firstness, exhaustive novelty clearance or continued worldwide openness is claimed.

Lewis — The mathematics of eigenvalue optimization (2003) : Section 8, printed pp.166–168, specifies complex monic coefficients, a real Euclidean coefficient metric and closed-half-plane stability before asking about set prox-regularity. Quadratics correspond to n=1 in its z^(n+1)+p notation.

Lewis, joint with Burke and Overton — Local Structure and Algorithms in Nonsmooth Optimization (2005) : The original contribution occupies printed pp.104–106; Question 1 on p.106 asks about nearby unique nearest stable polynomials. Its short wording leaves field, normalization and metric unspecified, so the complex convention is qualified through the earlier Lewis source.

Poliquin, Rockafellar and Thibault — Local differentiability of distance functions (2000) : Definition 1.1, Proposition 1.2 and Theorem 1.3(a),(k) supply the classical set prox-regularity and global projection characterization. Closedness is essential, and the additional local weak-closedness condition is automatic in finite dimensions.

Poliquin and Rockafellar — A calculus of prox-regularity (2010) : Definition 1.1 localizes finite subgradients for the function condition; p.205 gives the epigraph correspondence at (v,−1). Theorem 3.1 is a conditional composition result. The present proof supplies its own exact diffeomorphism transport.

Burke and Overton — Variational analysis of the abscissa mapping for polynomials (2001) : Classical complex polynomial-abscissa conventions and first-order variational analysis. Root and normal calculus are prior tools.

Burke, Lewis and Overton — Variational analysis of functions of the roots of polynomials (2005) : Earlier variational analysis in complex exact-degree polynomial coordinates; this background is credited separately from the present local projection argument.

Kirillov and Overton — Robust stability at the Swallowtail singularity (2013) : Related real-quartic Whitney-umbrella stability geometry, including credit to earlier work of Bottema. The differing normalization and open Hurwitz domain are not identified with the present complex quadratic global-projection problem.

Orban de Xivry — Nearest Stable System (2013) : Selected sections of Chapters 2 and 4 document earlier complex monic coefficient approximation, marginal-stability closure, algorithmic methods and weighted objectives. These bounded readings establish prior work without an exhaustive theorem-overlap audit.

Moses and Liu — Determining the closest stable polynomial to an unstable one (1991) : Earlier nearest-stable-polynomial literature cited by the manuscript. The original body was not inspected, so no precise original nonuniqueness statement or example comparison is asserted here.

Quadratics correspond to n=1 in its z^(n+1)+p notation.

Its short wording leaves field, normalization and metric unspecified, so the complex convention is qualified through the earlier Lewis source.

Poliquin, Rockafellar and Thibault — Local differentiability of distance functions (2000) : Definition 1.1, Proposition 1.2 and Theorem 1.3(a),(k) supply the classical set prox-regularity and global projection characterization. Burke, Lewis and Overton — Variational analysis of functions of the roots of polynomials (2005) : Earlier variational analysis in complex exact-degree polynomial coordinates; this background is credited separately from the present local projection argument.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript dated 6 October 2026 · No version number supplied · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 7 pages) · Download PDF · Published source and supporting materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

The finite-energy multimode entropy photon-number inequality proved in the OpenAI mathematics release supplies the sharp entropy premise in the previously conditional pure-loss bosonic dynamic-capacity converses. We give its precise classical, quantum and entanglement consequence under an average photon constraint, including arbitrary entanglement across uses. For public, private and secret-key resources, an operational correction is necessary: the printed catalytic secrecy condition of Wilde–Hsieh protects consumed key jointly with generated secrets and excludes the one-time pad. A zero-energy converse disproves the displayed region under that literal condition. We establish the formula with an explicit generated-secret secrecy criterion, corrected converse accounting, and direct key-assisted coding. The formulas and original conditional reductions are inherited; this is a consequence and operational audit, not an independent proof of EPnI. We rely on the cited unrefereed EPnI proof. Its analytical arguments and formal-source semantics were audited, but its Lean build was not reproduced.

A lossy optical channel can carry ordinary messages, quantum information and shared resources in different combinations. A capacity region describes every combination of rates that can be approached with errors tending to zero. This note identifies the trade-offs for a pure-loss channel under a finite average photon budget, using the cited entropy photon-number inequality (EPnI).

The private-communication part asks what a protocol should protect after it uses up a secret key. A one-time pad keeps a message secret from someone who sees the ciphertext, but the message and the used key are correlated with that ciphertext. Requiring them both to remain jointly secret rules out the one-time pad. The paper proves that this literal requirement also obstructs the claimed private capacity region at zero channel energy.

The positive private theorem therefore states its changed promise explicitly: the generated message and new key are secret, while the used key is discarded. With that convention, the paper establishes the public/private/secret-key trade-off formula. The formulas and their original EPnI-conditional route are credited to earlier work; the note supplies a consequence of the external entropy proof and an operational correction.

Let Lη be the one-mode pure-loss bosonic channel with a fresh independent vacuum environment at each use, 1/2 ≤ η ≤ 1, and 0 ≤ N < ∞ average input photons per use. Arbitrary entanglement among the finitely many channel inputs is allowed. All logarithms are base two. Write g(u) = (u+1) log₂(u+1) − u log₂u, with g(0)=0. Rates are signed forward net rates: positive rates generate resources and negative rates consume them.

For classical communication C, quantum communication Q and entanglement E, the capacity region is the closed union over λ ∈ [0,1] of all triples satisfying the three inequalities simultaneously: C+2Q ≤ g(λN)+g(ηN)−g((1−η)λN); Q+E ≤ g(ηλN)−g((1−η)λN); C+Q+E ≤ g(ηN)−g((1−η)λN). The general equality uses the cited unrefereed finite-energy multimode EPnI proof, together with the named coding results.

For public communication R, private communication P and secret key S, under the explicit generated-secret convention, the capacity region is the closed union over λ ∈ [0,1] of all triples satisfying simultaneously: R+P ≤ g(ηN); P+S ≤ g(ηλN)−g((1−η)λN); R+P+S ≤ g(ηN)−g((1−η)λN). This is the corrected model’s region, rather than the region for the unchanged literal secrecy target in the cited source.

More precisely, the corrected convention requires ‖ω(W,X,Eⁿ)−π(W)⊗ω(X,Eⁿ)‖₁→0, where W=(M,T_A) denotes the jointly uniform generated message and key, X=(K,L) the public data, and Eⁿ Eve’s environment. Consumed private communication and key V=(J,S_B) are traced out and may correlate with W and X. Eve does not additionally receive the consumed key. Generated communication messages are fresh, uniform and initially independent of the preshared key; public common randomness is not counted as communication.

Separately, the literal source target protects U=(M,T_A,J,S_B) jointly and uniformly against Z=(K,L,Eⁿ). At N=0, its secrecy and reliability errors obey 1 ≤ 1/(d_M d_T_A)+(ε_sec+ε_rel)/2, where d_M and d_T_A are the generated message and key register sizes and the errors use the unhalved trace norm. Vanishing errors force d_M d_T_A=1 eventually. The one-time-pad rate vector (−1,1,−1) belongs to the displayed zero-energy private cone but violates this literal promise. For a uniform d-symbol one-time pad, the minimum unhalved trace norm against an independent uniform message/key pair is 2(1−1/d), even after optimizing the comparison public marginal. This obstruction does not depend on EPnI.

The external finite-energy multimode EPnI gives H(L_t^{⊗n}(ρ))/n ≥ g(t g⁻¹(H(ρ)/n)) for every fixed finite n, every finite-energy n-mode input ρ and t ∈ [0,1], with an independent vacuum port. It permits arbitrary internal entanglement. The nondecreasing function f_t(s)=g(t g⁻¹(s)) is convex for 0≤t≤1 and concave for t≥1. This is a use of the cited theorem, not an independent proof of EPnI.

For an arbitrary input ensemble, thermal entropy maximization bounds the average receiver entropy. Choose one common λ by the ensemble’s conditional receiver entropy. Applying the vacuum entropy bound to the channel and its degrading map, followed by Jensen’s inequality, bounds both conditional environment entropy and conditional input entropy using that same λ. Substitution into the regularized dynamic capacity bounds gives the displayed outer regions. The private converse explicitly charges the consumed public, private and key registers; degradability justifies pure spectral refinement.

The known displaced thermal ensemble and classically enhanced father protocol attain the quantum-resource region. For generated-secret private coding, an outer public code is combined with key-indexed private codebooks: Bob decodes using the key, while averaging the unknown key hides the message from Eve. Coherent Gaussian inputs give the stated corner, and the charged noiseless resource conversions give its polyhedron.

Finite ensembles and photon cutoffs are fixed before taking coding limits. A strict mean-energy margin N′<N lets the expected-cost bound and vanishing error bounds select a code that meets the exact average budget. Approximation limits and N′↑N then give the region by closure. Compactness of λ establishes closedness; the entropy parameter gives convexity. The zero-energy refutation instead follows directly from the vacuum input and a decoder-success probability bound.

The exact-region theorems concern the one-mode pure-loss channel with independent vacuum environments, 1/2 ≤ η ≤ 1 and finite N. They do not cover infinite energy, η<1/2, thermal-channel quantum capacity, amplifiers or confidential broadcast.

The photon budget is Tr(G_n ρ̄_n)≤nN, averaged over classical messages, shared key and encoder randomness; G_n is the sum of input photon-number operators. Quantum communication uses the maximally mixed logical source, equivalently half of a maximally entangled reference pair. No peak, per-codeword or arbitrary-source energy constraint, or strong converse, is asserted. Noiseless side resources are charged by rate rather than optical energy.

The resource model has forward communication without free feedback, finite gross generation and consumption rates, and finite resource registers with logarithmic dimensions O(n). Required finite seeds are charged. No free two-way assistance, superlinear catalysts or elimination of all gross seed input is established.

The positive private theorem protects uniform generated messages and keys after consumed registers are discarded. It gives no semantic-security guarantee for arbitrary message distributions and no secrecy guarantee after revealing consumed key. Vanishing trace secrecy gives the normalized information estimates used here; it does not promise dimension-free absolute leakage tending to zero.

At N=0 and at η=1 both complete regions follow without a nontrivial EPnI input. At η=1/2 the complete corrected-private region also does; the full classical/quantum/entanglement equality generally retains its EPnI dependence. At λ=0 and λ=1 the conditional thermal terms are interpreted at their zero and full values.

The general capacity equalities rely on the soundness and stated finite-energy multimode scope of the cited external unrefereed EPnI proof. The note does not supply a new EPnI proof, classify all entropy equality cases or prove uniqueness of Gaussian optimizers. Its finite computational checks supplement analytic arguments.

Wilde, Hayden and Guha already gave the formulas, Gaussian ensembles and original conditional converse route. The entropy result belongs to the cited OpenAI proof, with De Palma’s entropy-bound formulation and the earlier coding literature explicitly credited. No firstness, exhaustive novelty clearance, new ordinary single-resource capacity or general broadcast theorem is claimed.

AI tools were used extensively in research, derivation, drafting, literature comparison and verification, including independent adversarial AI reviews. These reviews are not independent human or journal peer review. This is an unrefereed preprint; its external EPnI dependency is also unrefereed. No reproduced Lean build or proof-assistant certification is claimed. The named author is responsible for the claims and citations.

The manuscript is dated 6 October 2026, matching Zenodo’s declared publication date. Zenodo records creation on 7 October 2026 UTC. Neither the manuscript nor Zenodo metadata supplies a version number. These dates do not establish first priority.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Reviewed edition published 25 August 2026 · Zenodo version 2.0.4; earlier named release 8 August 2026 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 21 pages) · Source and verification materials (tar.gz) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We study fixation from a uniformly random single mutant on finite connected loopless undirected weighted graphs under both Birth–death (Bd) and death–Birth (dB) Moran updating. Let R_sim be the supremum of R for which one fitness-independent graph family eventually amplifies fixation under both rules for every fixed r ∈ (1,R). Let R_hyb be the unique root in (3/2,151/100) of R⁶ − 8R⁵ + 22R⁴ − 30R³ + 21R² − 6R + 1. We construct one fitness-independent family that simultaneously amplifies every fixed 1 < r < R_hyb for all sufficiently large members of the sequence. Therefore R_sim ≥ R_hyb = 1.5028569127905696… > 3/2.

The construction combines a large clique with dilute hub pendants and dilute, internally heavy two-vertex satellites. An exact finite-state derivation of the weak-cut limiting trace, together with uniform establishment, cleanup, and reciprocal-invasion estimates at the scale of the eventual gain, reduces the two normalized fixation corrections to explicit response functions. Optimizing their common positivity interval yields the displayed sextic. The same analysis proves that R_hyb is optimal among fixed positive (σ,λ) in the displayed first-order dilute pair–pendant response model; a specialization with entirely rational edge weights already crosses 3/2. Thus 3/2 is not the exact simultaneous-amplification threshold. The unrestricted value of R_sim, and even a finite universal upper bound, remain open.

In a structured population, a new mutation can disappear or eventually replace every resident. The probability of taking over depends on which individuals can replace which others. It also depends on whether reproduction is chosen before a replacement site, or a vacancy is chosen before its neighbors compete to fill it.

This paper constructs one sequence of weighted population graphs that improves takeover probability under each of these two pure update rules. The entire sequence is chosen independently of the beneficial mutation’s relative fitness. For each fixed fitness strictly between 1 and about 1.5028569, all sufficiently large members improve on a well-mixed population of the same size. The required size can depend on the fixed fitness.

The graph combines a large well-mixed clique with two sparse kinds of peripheral structure. Heavy pairs favor death–Birth fixation, while leaves attached to one hub favor Birth–death fixation. Their small contributions can be balanced to make both improvements positive. Earlier work by Svoboda and colleagues established simultaneous amplification below relative fitness 1.2; a separate earlier construction by the author reached the open interval below 1.5.

The improvement above 1.5 changes what thresholds are possible, although the advantage becomes small as the population grows. This is a mathematical construction with highly separated edge weights. It supplies no empirical prediction or practical population-size requirement.

Let R_hyb be the unique root in (3/2,151/100) of R⁶ − 8R⁵ + 22R⁴ − 30R³ + 21R² − 6R + 1. There exists one fitness-independent sequence of finite connected loopless undirected weighted graphs G_t such that, for every fixed 1 < r < R_hyb, there exists t₀(r) for which every t ≥ t₀(r) strictly amplifies uniformly initialized single-mutant fixation under each pure Bd and dB process. Each comparison uses the complete graph on the same n_t vertices and the matching update rule. Hence R_sim ≥ R_hyb = 1.5028569127905696… > 3/2.

Bd chooses a fitness-weighted parent and then an edge-weighted replacement target. dB first chooses a uniformly random death site and then a neighboring parent with probability proportional to fitness times edge weight. Their finite complete-graph baselines differ: ρ_Bd(K_n,r) = (1−r⁻¹)/(1−r⁻ⁿ), whereas ρ_dB(K_n,r) = ((n−1)/n)(1−r⁻¹)/(1−r⁻⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾). Initialization is uniform over all vertices, with exactly one mutant and resident fitness one.

The sequence uses a unit clique of C_t = t⁴ vertices, m_t = floor(λ_* t) unit hub leaves, and q_t = t two-vertex satellites with internal weight C_t/σ_*. Every satellite vertex connects to every clique vertex by a common positive dyadic weight selected by an exact compact-interval decision procedure. All weights are fixed before r is quantified.

At scale q_t/C_t, the two normalized fixation corrections are B(r) = 2(σ−1)/(1+σ(r²−1)) + λ/(r−1) and D(r) = 2{r(2−r)−σ}/(σ+2r(r−1)) − λ. Their simultaneous positivity produces the sextic threshold. The fixed parameters giving this response-model tangency are approximately σ_* = 0.1306772822870484 and λ_* = 0.7508064830318805.

Within this displayed first-order dilute response model, R_hyb is optimal among fixed positive σ and λ. The rational choice σ = 19/137 and λ = 20/27 already yields an entirely rational-edge graph sequence with threshold (5069 + 12√147001)/6439 = 1.50176815223369… > 3/2.

For fixed finite module sizes, an exact finite-state Schur complement resolves rare migration between the center and satellites. It uses local fixation probabilities to obtain a limiting macro chain while retaining possible reversals of a partially completed sweep.

The center-module argument controls initial establishment, later cleanup, and reciprocal invasion to errors smaller than the eventual gain q_t/C_t. An ordinary approximation with an unspecified error tending to zero would not suffice because the claimed gain itself tends to zero.

The two module types have opposite response signs under the two update rules. The proof balances their densities, optimizes the shared positivity interval, and then selects one positive weak-edge weight for each t on an expanding compact fitness interval. This supplies the required order: one family, then every fixed fitness, then a fitness-dependent size threshold.

The construction uses finite connected loopless undirected weighted graphs, uniform initialization of exactly one mutant, resident fitness one, a fixed mutant fitness r > 1, and the two specified pure Bd and dB rules. No guarantee is supplied for arbitrary initialization, directed or unweighted constructions, empirical evolutionary dynamics, or a process that randomly mixes the update rules.

The theorem concerns each fixed r in the open interval (1,R_hyb). Neutrality r = 1 and the upper endpoint r = R_hyb are excluded; no strict endpoint amplification is established. There is no size bound uniform near either endpoint and no guarantee for fitness varying with population size. The sequence need not contain a graph of every integer order.

For the unrestricted simultaneous-amplification threshold R_sim, the result is a lower bound. Exact optimality applies only to fixed positive σ and λ in the displayed first-order dilute pair–pendant response model. It does not establish optimality over all growing graph families, singular or size-dependent parameter choices, other modules, or higher-order boundary gains. This work supplies no universal upper bound.

For each fixed interior fitness, the normalized fixation gain has order Θ(t⁻³) = Θ(n_t⁻³/⁴) and tends to zero. Pair weights grow with the clique size, and the compact-interval construction may require very small positive weak edges. No useful finite-size onset, fixation-time bound, bounded weight ratio, or practical optimality is established.

The archived exact verifiers check finite labelled transition aggregation, symbolic response identities, rational margins, root isolation, and tangency. They do not machine-verify the manuscript’s weak-cut convergence or population asymptotics.

Svoboda, Joshi, Tkadlec and Chatterjee (2024), Amplifiers of selection for the Moran process with both Birth-death and death-Birth updating : Established simultaneous amplification on 1 < r < 1.2 using weakly connected weighted modules. Its uniform singleton initialization, update rules, and same-order complete-graph benchmarks agree with this paper’s model. The present construction improves the fitness interval.

Kriebel (2026), No universal death–Birth amplifier on a finite weighted population structure : An earlier unrefereed release extends the fixed-graph obstruction to complete directed weighted support and identifies the exact baseline equality class. It addresses a different quantifier order.

Kriebel (2026), A fitness-independent family of simultaneous amplifiers below fitness three halves : The separate center–triangle construction establishes R_sim ≥ 3/2 and suppresses at its own endpoint. The present result crosses that endpoint with a different family.

Brewster, Huang, Mitzenmacher and Nowak (2026), The Mixed Birth-Death/death-Birth Moran Process : Studies a process that independently chooses an update rule at each step. Simultaneous amplification under each pure rule does not by itself prove amplification for every mixture.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 14 October 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 5 pages) · Download PDF · Manuscript source and verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We give negative answers to the two slit-monotonicity questions of P. L. Duren recorded as Problem 6.72 in Hayman–Lingham. Every global maximizer of the real part of a₂+i10⁻²⁴(a₄−3a₃) in the normalized schlicht class omits an arc with nonmonotone continuous argument and nonmonotone radial angle, under both signed and ordinary unsigned conventions. The proof uses classical support-point geometry, a quantitative area-theorem estimate for the actual slit tip, and controlled inversion of the Schiffer differential. It establishes actual extremizers by compactness and does not assume that an arbitrary trajectory is an extremal slit. No formula for the maximizing function or uniqueness is required. This is an unrefereed AI-assisted research note.

A univalent function maps the unit disk into the complex plane without folding it over itself. A support point is such a map that maximizes a linear measurement of the function. Classical results show that its image leaves out a single analytic arc, running from a finite tip to infinity.

Two questions attributed to P. L. Duren ask whether that omitted arc must turn monotonically in its polar direction, and whether the angle between its radius and its tangent must change monotonically. Here monotone allows either increasing or decreasing behavior.

This note chooses one particular measurement of the second, third and fourth Taylor coefficients. Global maximizers exist, and every one of them has an actual omitted slit for which both proposed monotonicity properties fail. The radial-angle failure holds for both the signed outward angle and the ordinary nonnegative angle.

The proof controls all maximizers at once. It does not need to write down a maximizing function or show that it is unique. The polar direction, the tangent direction and the angle between them are different quantities; the theorem addresses the first and the third.

Let S be the analytic injective maps on the unit disk normalized by f(0) = 0 and f′(0) = 1, with f(z) = z + Σₙ≥₂ aₙ(f)zⁿ. Set ε = 10⁻²⁴ and L(f) = a₂(f) + iε(a₄(f) − 3a₃(f)). Global maximizers of Re L on S exist. Every such maximizer omits an actual analytic slit Γ whose continuous polar argument, signed outward radial angle and ordinary unsigned outward radial angle are all nonmonotone.

The polar argument is a continuous real-valued lift along Γ. The tangent used for the signed radial angle points from the finite tip toward infinity. The ordinary radial angle is the nonnegative angle between that outward tangent and the radius vector. Both nondecreasing and nonincreasing behavior are excluded for each of the three quantities.
This supplies counterexamples to the two support-slit monotonicity properties recorded as Hayman–Lingham Problem 6.72. No explicit maximizing map or uniqueness theorem is required.

Compactness of S gives genuine global maximizers. Comparing any maximizer with the Koebe function and using the classical coefficient inequalities gives uniform control of its first coefficients. An odd-root version of the area theorem then controls an analytic tail and places the actual omitted slit tip inside radius 3/10.

The Schiffer differential is expanded exactly for the chosen functional. A controlled inverse natural coordinate constructs a regular arc with modulus greater than 25/81. It agrees with the actual omitted slit near infinity. The separation from the actual tip and local trajectory uniqueness extend that agreement across the tested subarc. This identifies a subarc of each genuine support slit; it does not infer extremality from an arbitrary differential trajectory.

Writing this subarc as W(t) = −V(t)⁻², with 0 < t ≤ 7/4, and Z = tV′/V, the proof bounds Z − 1 − iεq(t) by 2000εη, where η = 10⁻¹² and q(t) = t² − 2t⁴/5. The values q(1) = 3/5 and q(7/4) = −441/640 force opposite strict signs for Im Z and hence opposite signs of the polar-argument derivative.

Increasing t points inward, so the outward tangent is −W′ and its signed radial angle is β = arg Z. This angle tends to zero at infinity and takes both positive and negative values; those facts exclude both monotone directions. Its continuity gives an interior zero between nonzero endpoint values, so the ordinary angle |β| is separately nonmonotone.

The theorem concerns the stated normalized schlicht class, the particular degree-four coefficient functional and the fixed value ε = 10⁻²⁴. It is not a conclusion about every coefficient functional or every support slit. At ε = 0 the strict reversal disappears; no claim for arbitrary larger perturbations is made.
The existence and every-maximizer conclusions do not provide an explicit maximizing function, uniqueness, a numerical extremal solver or a computed extremizer.

The proof uses established compactness, Bieberbach coefficient bounds, the area theorem and classical support-slit and Schiffer geometry. Finite rational checks and numerical diagnostics supplement the analytic estimates; they do not formally certify the universal theorem or the classical foundations.

The historical comparisons are bounded. The manuscript identifies later Duren commentary and Hibschweiler’s 1995 paper as uninspected. No historical firstness, exhaustive priority clearance or claim that the questions remained open worldwide in 2026 is made.

The differential sign is converted to Duren’s convention in this note. Duren (1981), Arcs omitted by support points of univalent functions : Supplies the omitted-arc differential and outward radial-angle convention, and proves positive monotonicity results for restricted evaluation families. Brown (1979), Geometric properties of a class of support points of univalent functions : Establishes positive monotonicity results for point-evaluation support points. This is a restricted family of functionals. de Branges (1985), A proof of the Bieberbach conjecture : The classical coefficient bound |aₙ| ≤ n supplies the bounds for n = 2, 3 and 4 used in the proof. The note’s wider historical comparisons do not constitute exhaustive priority clearance.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 14 October 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 7 pages) · Download PDF · Manuscript source and supporting materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

For two independent standard fractional Brownian motions with the same fixed Hurst parameter H ∈ (1/4,1), we give a localized Gaussian-witness proof that every square-integrable estimator of the canonical iterated integral X_T = ∫₀ᵀ B¹_s dB²_s, based on both complete uniform grids of n observations on [0,T], has root mean-square error at least c_H T^(2H)n^(1/2−2H). The positive constant is explicit and depends only on H; the inequality holds for every T > 0 and integer n ≥ 1, including nonlinear estimators. Smooth compactly supported covariance paths, a Fourier periodization upper Gram bound, and an exact deterministic area pairing provide the witness. The Brownian optimum and the smooth asymptotic rate are prior results. Fourier localization and Gaussian projection have established antecedents; historical theorem and method priority, full novelty, and worldwide current-open status remain unverified. The note uses canonical-area existence and sufficient L² convergence, without endorsing exact Euler-error coefficients of the pinned arXiv v1.
Suppose two independent fractional Brownian paths are recorded at equally spaced times. How accurately can those observations determine the integral of one path against changes in the other?

This note gives a positive lower bound on the root mean-square error of every estimator using both sampled paths. It applies to nonlinear estimators as well as linear ones, and to the conditional expectation that minimizes the error. There are n observations in each component, including the final time T.

For each fixed Hurst parameter H between 1/4 and 1, the lower bound is c_H T^(2H)n^(1/2−2H), with an explicit positive constant depending only on H. The statement holds for every positive T and every integer n ≥ 1.

The proof constructs an auxiliary Gaussian witness that the sampled values cannot detect but that still pairs with the iterated integral. The exact Brownian optimum and the smooth-range asymptotic rate were known previously; this note presents an attributed localized-witness proof.

Fix H ∈ (1/4,1). Let B¹ and B² be independent centered standard fractional Brownian motions with the same Hurst parameter and covariance R_H(s,t) = (s^(2H) + t^(2H) − |s−t|^(2H))/2. Let X_T = ∫₀ᵀ B¹_s dB²_s be the canonical iterated integral, defined by the L² limit of piecewise-linear lifts.

For T > 0 and an integer n ≥ 1, let G_(T,n) = σ(Bⁱ_(jT/n): i=1,2; j=1,…,n). Thus both complete deterministic uniform grids are observed, including T, with n observations per component and deterministic Bⁱ_0 = 0. Every F ∈ L²(G_(T,n)), including every nonlinear square-integrable estimator, satisfies ‖X_T−F‖₂ ≥ c_H T^(2H)n^(1/2−2H).

The explicit positive constant is c_H = 2πa/(D_H√(P̄_fP̄_g)), where a = 4/45045 and D_H = ∫_ℝ |e^(iξ)−1|²|ξ|^(−1−2H) dξ. Put φ(x) = x⁴(1−x)⁴ on [0,1], zero elsewhere, f = φ′, g = φ, α = 2H+1, L_r = ‖r‖₁ and N_r = ‖r‴‖₁, using weak derivatives of the zero extensions. Then P̄_r = π^α L_r² + 2N_r²π^(α−6)(1 + 1/[2(5−α)]) for r=f,g.
Taking F = E[X_T | G_(T,n)] gives the same bound for the optimal conditional root mean-square error. The theorem uses this iterated-integral convention throughout.

Two polynomial covariance paths are placed inside each grid cell and vanish at every observation time. The joint Gaussian structure makes the resulting witness vector independent of both complete observation grids.

A Fourier periodization estimate controls the variance of the sum of witness products by a quantity proportional to n. The argument allows dependence between cells and signed off-diagonal covariances.

For a fixed observation grid, refinement of finite left sums gives an exact deterministic pairing with the iterated integral. That pairing is n a(T/n)^(2H). Cauchy–Schwarz converts the nonzero pairing and variance bound into the displayed error inequality.

Canonical-area existence and identification with the polygonal lift are established external inputs. The paper gives sufficient L² convergence without relying on exact Euler-error coefficients from the pinned arXiv v1 of Neuenkirch–Tindel–Unterberger. It distinguishes that version from the journal-formatted author copy.

The theorem assumes independent standard components with the same fixed H ∈ (1/4,1), observed on both complete deterministic uniform grids. It does not cover unequal Hurst parameters, correlated components, or nonuniform or adaptive sampling.
The positive constant depends on H. No sharp constant, exact normalized-error limit, limiting law, constant uniform in H, or endpoint result is asserted. The statement includes n=1 and all T>0.

The halved antisymmetric area A_T = (I₁₂−I₂₁)/2 equals X_T−B¹_TB²_T/2. The endpoint product is observed, so A_T has the same optimal conditional residual as X_T. The unhalved antisymmetric difference has twice that residual.

The exact Brownian optimum T/(2√n), the smooth H>1/2 asymptotic rate, and Fourier-localization and Gaussian-projection methods are credited prior work. Historical theorem and method priority, full novelty, and worldwide current-open status remain unverified. Broader implications of the Dickinson and Jackowski methods remain unverified; they are attribution limits rather than missing steps in this direct proof.
This is an unrefereed preprint prepared with extensive AI assistance. Finite checks supplement the analytic argument; they do not constitute human peer review or formal proof-assistant certification.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 17 October 2026 · Zenodo metadata version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 7 pages) · Download PDF · Complete source and verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Every discrete initial ordered additive subgroup of the surreal numbers is order-group-isomorphic to a subgroup of the omnific integers that is initial in the surreal numbers. This holds for sets and proper classes in NBG with global choice and answers the discrete-group question posed by Kaplan and Ehrlich. An explicit operation on ordinal-length sign sequences moves the least exponent to zero without creating a right-simplicity-predecessor obligation. Relabeling the actual normal-form supports and normalizing only the bottom coefficient group then gives the required image. An appendix supplies a detailed sufficiency proof of the initial-group characterization used in the argument, addressing support exhaustion and the legality of limit-cut options.

The surreal numbers contain real numbers, infinite quantities and infinitesimals. Each also has a sign sequence describing its position in a construction tree. An initial group contains every proper sign-sequence prefix of each of its elements.

This paper considers actual additive subgroups of the surreal numbers with that closure property and a smallest positive element. It constructs an equivalent copy inside the omnific integers. The copy remains initial in the ambient surreal numbers, and the equivalence preserves addition and numerical order.

The construction relabels the exponents in the normal forms already present and rescales the lowest coefficient group. It applies to sets and proper classes while keeping each individual support set-sized.

Work in NBG set theory with global choice. Let G be an actual initial ordered additive subgroup of No, with addition and order inherited from No. If G is nonzero, assume that it has a least positive element. Then there is an order-group isomorphism T:G→H onto an actual subgroup H⊆Oz that is initial in No. The statement includes set and proper-class groups; the zero group uses the identity.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 17 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 5 pages) · Download PDF · Complete source and verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We give an explicit affirmative answer to Tunçel’s 2017 existential question about algebraic convex cones with negative-curvature normal barriers. The one-sided power cone K = {(x,y,z) ≥ 0: xy² ≥ z³} admits the barrier F = −25 log(z(xy² − z³)) with parameter 100 and D³F(a)[h,u,u] ≤ 0 for every a ∈ int K, h ∈ K, and u ∈ ℝ³. Exact polynomial and positive-semidefinite certificates prove the curvature inequality, including its degenerate directions. A boundary divisibility argument rules out every homogeneous hyperbolic polynomial defining K in ℝ³. The cone itself is a known member of Hildebrand’s classification; the contribution here is the explicit barrier certificate and its verification for the stated existential problem.

Barrier functions grow without bound near the boundary of a feasible region and help optimization methods stay inside it. This paper studies the additional derivative-sign property called negative curvature in conic optimization.

The region is the known cone of nonnegative triples satisfying xy²≥z³. The paper gives a particular logarithmic barrier and proves its sign condition at every interior point, for every direction in the closed cone and every real test vector, including degenerate directions.

It also proves that no homogeneous polynomial of any degree can have this cone as its hyperbolicity cone in the original three-dimensional space. Together, these properties provide the kind of example requested in Tunçel’s 2017 existential question.

The cone and earlier self-concordant barriers were already known. The contribution presented here is the explicit additional third-derivative certificate and the accompanying obstruction, with no first-discovery claim.

Let K={(x,y,z)∈ℝ³:x,y,z≥0, xy²≥z³}. It is a regular algebraic convex cone: closed, pointed and convex, with nonempty interior, defined by homogeneous polynomial inequalities. Its interior is {x,y,z>0:xy²>z³}.

On the entire interior, F(x,y,z)=−25 log(z(xy²−z³)) is a logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant normal barrier with parameter 100. In particular, F(λa)=F(a)−100 log λ for λ>0, and its squared dual Hessian gradient norm is exactly 100.

For every a∈int K, every h∈K and every u∈ℝ³, D³F(a)[h,u,u]≤0. The direction h ranges over the closed cone, including zero and its boundary; the claim is semidefinite and includes the degenerate cases.

There is no homogeneous real polynomial H of any degree in the same ℝ³ for which K is its hyperbolicity cone. This is an obstruction for every possible defining H and interior hyperbolicity direction, rather than only for the displayed cubic xy²−z³.

The weighted geometric mean x^(1/3)y^(2/3) is concave, so its nonnegative hypograph is convex. Writing g=z³/y² and δ=x−g gives a positive Hessian-norm decomposition for f=−log(xy²−z³)−log z. A mixed third-derivative estimate becomes self-concordance after scaling by 25. The degree-four product z(xy²−z³) gives logarithmic homogeneity with parameter 100, and the product tends to zero at every finite boundary point.

A fixed positive diagonal change of coordinates sends any interior base point to (r,1,1), retaining r>1. Every cone direction is a nonnegative combination of (t³,1,t), t≥0, and the x-axis direction. This reduces the mixed sign assertion to an explicit symmetric matrix.

Exact leading-minor and square identities give a positive matrix for t≠1. A separate lower-block certificate at t=1 and a Gram certificate for the x-axis direction supply the semidefinite cases. The reduction includes t=0, h=0 and directions with h_y=0; no strict-definiteness claim is needed there.

Any proposed defining hyperbolic polynomial must vanish on the curved boundary. Substitution x=z³/y² and Gauss’s lemma force the factor p=xy²−z³ to divide it. For every prospective interior direction e, set A=(e_xe_y²)^(1/3)>B=e_z>0. Along v=(0,0,1), the factor p(v+te) has a quadratic factor with discriminant −3A²<0. Multiplication cannot cancel that nonreal root pair, contradicting hyperbolicity.

Negative curvature here means the mixed third-derivative inequality D³F(a)[h,u,u]≤0, equivalently concavity of a↦DF(a)[h] for each fixed h∈K. It does not assert nonpositive sectional curvature of a Hessian metric. Boundary base points are outside the barrier’s domain, while boundary cone directions are included.

The theorem concerns this one-sided nonnegative cone. It makes no assertion for the sign-symmetric power cone, arbitrary exponents or all regular cones. The broader every-regular-cone barrier question remains a separate credited question.

The cone is already in Hildebrand’s classification. Roy–Xiao give a parameter-3 self-concordant barrier on the same cone. Parameter 100 is an explicit sufficient certificate for the displayed barrier and its additional sign property, with no parameter improvement or optimality claim.

The all-degree polynomial obstruction concerns the original three-dimensional ambient space. It does not exclude projections or higher-dimensional lifts. No general new barrier method or practical algorithmic improvement is asserted.

blocks.text: The weighted geometric mean x^(1/3)y^(2/3) is concave, so its nonnegative hypograph is convex. Writing g=z³/y² and δ=x−g gives a positive Hessian-norm decomposition for f=−log(xy²−z³)−log z. A mixed third-derivative estimate becomes self-concordance after scaling by 25. The degree-four product z(xy²−z³) gives logarithmic homogeneity with parameter 100, and the product tends to zero at every finite boundary point.

A fixed positive diagonal change of coordinates sends any interior base point to (r,1,1), retaining r>1. Every cone direction is a nonnegative combination of (t³,1,t), t≥0, and the x-axis direction. This reduces the mixed sign assertion to an explicit symmetric matrix.

Exact leading-minor and square identities give a positive matrix for t≠1. A separate lower-block certificate at t=1 and a Gram certificate for the x-axis direction supply the semidefinite cases. The reduction includes t=0, h=0 and directions with h_y=0; no strict-definiteness claim is needed there.

Any proposed defining hyperbolic polynomial must vanish on the curved boundary. Substitution x=z³/y² and Gauss’s lemma force the factor p=xy²−z³ to divide it. For every prospective interior direction e, set A=(e_xe_y²)^(1/3)>B=e_z>0. Along v=(0,0,1), the factor p(v+te) has a quadratic factor with discriminant −3A²<0. Multiplication cannot cancel that nonreal root pair, contradicting hyperbolicity.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 7 October 2026 · Zenodo metadata version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Download PDF · Complete source and supporting materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We give a complete analytic-transform answer to Georgakopoulos’s question about the lengths of the sets first visited by independent Brownian particles on a circle, with uniform random or equally spaced starting points. For every finite number of particles, the joint Laplace transform is an absolutely convergent series whose coefficients are finite sums of ordinary integrals of explicit interval-exit kernels. The integration regions are specified linear inequalities in cumulative physical hitting times. The outer series has a uniform factorial remainder bound and uniquely determines the probability measure. The result also applies to arbitrary fixed distinct starting points. The construction uses classical heat kernels, strong Markov iteration, and bounded-support moments. Earlier competing-walk painting results are credited and distinguished. No compact density, efficient numerical algorithm, or absolute historical priority is asserted.

Imagine several independent particles moving randomly around a circle. Each point belongs to the particle that reaches it first. The question is how all their territory lengths vary together. The particles keep moving through encounters and already visited territory.

This paper describes the entire joint distribution through a Laplace transform. Its coefficients are finite sums of ordinary deterministic integrals built from classical Brownian interval-exit kernels. Tracking a particle’s cumulative elapsed time preserves the correlations between its visits to different points.

The formula covers every finite number of particles, arbitrary fixed distinct labeled starting points, equally spaced starts and independent uniform labeled starts. A uniform factorial bound controls truncation of the outer series. The coefficient integrals can be high-dimensional; no fast evaluator or compact density is claimed.

Let k≥1 be a finite integer and let p₁,…,p_k be distinct fixed labeled points on the unit circle 𝕋=ℝ/ℤ. The particles are independent standard Brownian motions with generator ½d²/dx² and continue through every encounter and prior visit. Write T_i(x) for particle i’s first physical hitting time of x, assign x to the least label attaining min_i T_i(x), and let L_i be the Lebesgue length of its territory. Almost surely, L lies in the compact simplex {l_i≥0:∑_i l_i=1}.

For real θ_i≥0, set θ_*=max_i θ_i. The joint Laplace transform is ℒ_p(θ)=E_p exp(−∑_i θ_iL_i)=∑_{m=0}∞(−1)^m M_m(θ;p)/m!, with M₀=1. Every coefficient is completely specified by finite permutation and label sums and ordinary spatial/time integrals of explicit scalar interval-exit kernels in equations (2)–(9). No unknown Brownian hitting probability or conditional law remains inside those definitions.

For m queries, a particle’s ordered density is the product of its successive remaining-target kernels. If its discovery order is π_i and elapsed increments are u_ir, its physical hitting time of query j is h_ij=∑_{r≤π_i⁻¹(j)}u_ir. The integration region for owner labels a_j is given by h_(a_j,j)<h_ij for every competing i. These are explicit strict linear inequalities in cumulative clocks, retaining dependence among one walker’s query visits.

For every m≥0, 0≤M_m≤θ_*^m, and the series converges absolutely. For every integer N≥0, |ℒ_p(θ)−∑_{m=0}^N(−1)^m M_m(θ;p)/m!|≤θ_*^(N+1)/(N+1)!. This outer-series bound is uniform over all admissible seed vectors. The entire family of homogeneous coefficient polynomials determines all mixed moments and hence the full joint Borel probability measure on the simplex.

Equally spaced starts use p_i=(i−1)/k. For independent uniform labeled seeds, integrate each fixed-p coefficient over 𝕋^k; the same outer bound holds. Sorting the seeds before assigning labels instead requires the corresponding ordered seed law.

Before reaching the next unvisited query point, one walker stays in an arc whose lift is an interval. The classical killed heat kernel gives its two endpoint exit-time densities. With a single query left, both lifted endpoints represent the same target and their fluxes are added, with total mass one.

The strong Markov property at successive finite discovery times gives each walker’s joint order-and-increment density. Removing a reached query changes only the auxiliary stopping targets: the actual particle continues and can cross earlier queries. Products across independent walkers and comparisons of their cumulative physical clocks give every finite-query ownership probability.

Joint measurability and Fubini show that tie locations have zero spatial measure almost surely; the least-label convention still specifies an owner. Spatial integration gives M_m=E_p Z^m for Z=∑_i θ_iL_i. Since 0≤Z≤θ_*, the exponential expansion is absolutely convergent and Taylor’s theorem gives the exact factorial outer remainder.

All homogeneous moment polynomials recover every mixed moment. Polynomial density on the compact simplex then makes the joint measure unique. The uniform bounds also justify averaging over independent uniform labeled seeds. These are classical heat-kernel, strong-Markov, moment and determinacy tools applied to the explicit cumulative-clock construction.

The model uses finitely many independent continuing Brownian particles with a common diffusivity. Stopping, coalescing or absorption at painted territory changes the model. Common positive diffusivity changes rescale all clocks equally; invariance under different per-particle diffusivities is not asserted.

Fixed starting points must be distinct and labeled. No extension to deterministically coincident seeds is claimed. Random-seed collisions, repeated query points and query/seed coincidences are discarded only on their appropriate Lebesgue-null sets.
Ties have zero spatial measure almost surely. This does not say that ties are absent simultaneously at every point. One particle’s different query hitting times remain correlated throughout.

The scalar spectral kernels are summed at each positive time before improper time integration. The factorial bound controls only the outer series for real nonnegative θ; it supplies no inner Fourier-tail, numerical quadrature or coefficient-evaluation certificate.

No compact or named density, efficient numerical algorithm, large-k asymptotic or discrete-to-Brownian convergence theorem is claimed. The Brownian result follows directly from the analytic construction; finite-model and high-precision diagnostics are supplementary evidence.

Independent uniform labeled starts have full permutation exchangeability. Equally spaced labeled starts have cyclic and dihedral symmetry; unrestricted permutation symmetry is not asserted. Both have mean territory length 1/k. A circle of circumference c has lengths cL_i, so its transform uses cθ.

First-arrival painting, interval kernels, strong Markov iteration, moment expansion and compact-support determinacy are established prior methods. Earlier lattice painting, interface, competitive-range and multitime span results receive credit. Historical priority, full novelty, independent discovery and worldwide current-open status remain unverified; incomplete coverage of the Gomes article and Dicker thesis does not support an exhaustive absence claim.

If its discovery order is π_i and elapsed increments are u_ir, its physical hitting time of query j is h_ij=∑_{r≤π_i⁻¹(j)}u_ir. These are explicit strict linear inequalities in cumulative clocks, retaining dependence among one walker’s query visits. For every m≥0, 0≤M_m≤θ_*^m, and the series converges absolutely. blocks.text: Before reaching the next unvisited query point, one walker stays in an arc whose lift is an interval. The classical killed heat kernel gives its two endpoint exit-time densities. With a single query left, both lifted endpoints represent the same target and their fluxes are added, with total mass one.

The strong Markov property at successive finite discovery times gives each walker’s joint order-and-increment density. Removing a reached query changes only the auxiliary stopping targets: the actual particle continues and can cross earlier queries. Products across independent walkers and comparisons of their cumulative physical clocks give every finite-query ownership probability.

Joint measurability and Fubini show that tie locations have zero spatial measure almost surely; the least-label convention still specifies an owner. Spatial integration gives M_m=E_p Z^m for Z=∑_i θ_iL_i. Since 0≤Z≤θ_*, the exponential expansion is absolutely convergent and Taylor’s theorem gives the exact factorial outer remainder.

All homogeneous moment polynomials recover every mixed moment. Polynomial density on the compact simplex then makes the joint measure unique. The uniform bounds also justify averaging over independent uniform labeled seeds. These are classical heat-kernel, strong-Markov, moment and determinacy tools applied to the explicit cumulative-clock construction.

blocks.text: The model uses finitely many independent continuing Brownian particles with a common diffusivity. Stopping, coalescing or absorption at painted territory changes the model. Common positive diffusivity changes rescale all clocks equally; invariance under different per-particle diffusivities is not asserted.

Fixed starting points must be distinct and labeled. No extension to deterministically coincident seeds is claimed. Random-seed collisions, repeated query points and query/seed coincidences are discarded only on their appropriate Lebesgue-null sets.
Ties have zero spatial measure almost surely. This does not say that ties are absent simultaneously at every point. One particle’s different query hitting times remain correlated throughout.

The scalar spectral kernels are summed at each positive time before improper time integration. The factorial bound controls only the outer series for real nonnegative θ; it supplies no inner Fourier-tail, numerical quadrature or coefficient-evaluation certificate.

No compact or named density, efficient numerical algorithm, large-k asymptotic or discrete-to-Brownian convergence theorem is claimed. The Brownian result follows directly from the analytic construction; finite-model and high-precision diagnostics are supplementary evidence.

Independent uniform labeled starts have full permutation exchangeability. Equally spaced labeled starts have cyclic and dihedral symmetry; unrestricted permutation symmetry is not asserted. Both have mean territory length 1/k. A circle of circumference c has lengths cL_i, so its transform uses cθ.

First-arrival painting, interval kernels, strong Markov iteration, moment expansion and compact-support determinacy are established prior methods. Costabel’s 2022 Oberwolfach report asks for a precise description and proof of the observed approximation of nonreal eigenvalues by the discrete dipole approximation away from a real lattice interval. We give an independent proof for bounded particles whose center-selected cubic voxels converge in volume. This includes every bounded Lipschitz particle, with arbitrary grid translations. At each fixed complex frequency, the actual zero-diagonal matrices have no spectral pollution outside the exact static lattice interval; isolated eigenvalues are approximated with algebraic multiplicity and norm-convergent embedded Riesz projections. The proof combines the established static lattice bound of Costabel–Dauge–Nedaiasl with strong static consistency, Hilbert–Schmidt convergence of the sampled dynamic correction and classical spectral approximation. A separate compact, positive-volume, empty-interior support has a nonreal continuum eigenvalue at frequency 10⁻⁴ while every matrix on the grids n⁻¹ℤ³ is 3 × 3 zero. This example clarifies the geometric hypothesis. The classical ingredients and previously announced dynamic work are explicitly credited; first priority is not certified. AI tools were used extensively, and no external human peer review is asserted.

The discrete dipole approximation replaces a three-dimensional scattering volume by dipoles on a cubic grid. This paper asks when matrix eigenvalues outside a certain real lattice interval track the continuum volume operator as the grid is refined.

The geometric requirement is that the union of cubes whose centers lie in the particle approaches the particle in volume. Bounded Lipschitz particles satisfy it, even when the grid is translated. The actual matrices keep every diagonal block zero.

At each fixed complex frequency, the result gives stable inverses away from the interval and convergence of isolated eigenvalue clusters with their total algebraic multiplicity. A separate irregular compact support shows why arbitrary point-membership sets cannot be included without a geometric qualification.

Let Ω⊂ℝ³ be bounded and measurable, with a chosen representative for deciding center membership. Fix κ∈ℂ throughout the mesh limit. For h>0 choose arbitrary translations a_h, centers x_m=a_h+hm, cells Q_m^h=x_m+h[−1/2,1/2)³ and occupied indices I_h={m∈ℤ³:x_m∈Ω}. Let Ω_h be the union of the occupied cells and assume (G): |Ω_h△Ω|→0.

The matrix is exactly (T_κ^h u)_m=∑_{n∈I_h,n≠m}h³K_κ(x_m−x_n)u_n, with every 3×3 diagonal block zero. Its continuum comparison is S_κ=A_κ−I/3, using the distributional operator and kernel convention in the paper. This shift is part of the statement, rather than a material-contrast conversion.

Let J_lat=cl W(T)=[Λ_−,Λ_+] be the exact closed numerical range of the bounded selfadjoint full static cubic lattice operator. It contains [−1/3,2/3]. Every compact L⊂(ℂ∖J_lat)∩ρ(S_κ) has uniformly bounded discrete inverses for all z∈L and all sufficiently small h. No sequence of matrix eigenvalues can converge to an off-interval point of the continuum resolvent set.

Every continuum spectral point outside J_lat is isolated with finite algebraic multiplicity. For each closed isolating disk whose closure misses J_lat and whose only continuum spectral point is that eigenvalue, the embedded discrete Riesz projections converge in operator norm to the continuum projection. Ranks eventually agree, and enclosed eigenvalues converge with total algebraic multiplicity. Both gap directions for the total generalized spectral subspaces converge, and the matrix norms stay uniformly bounded.

The value-preserving embeddings and continuum projections are extended by zero to the common space L²(ℝ³;ℂ³). The discrete squared norm is h³∑_m|u_m|², making the cell embedding an isometry. An empty occupied set uses the zero-dimensional matrix convention. Bounded sets with boundary of volume zero, including bounded Lipschitz particles, satisfy (G) for arbitrary translations.

Separately, there exists one fixed compact positive-volume support with empty interior for which S_κ has an isolated nonreal eigenvalue at κ=1/10000, while every grid h=1/n, a_h=0 selects only one isolated volume-zero anchor and gives the 3×3 zero matrix. The support is selected at a sufficiently large existential finite index; no effective index or numerical eigenvalue location is claimed.

Exact finite radial-shell cancellation, a smooth-core near/far split and uniform whole-space tails establish strong consistency of the static cubic lattice operators. Condition (G) gives strong convergence of the membership masks. The static lattice bound itself is established prior work of Costabel, Dauge and Nedaiasl.

For the actual sampled dynamic correction R_κ=K_κ−K_0, the near-diagonal squared-kernel mass is O(δ+h), including the omitted same-cell block. Uniform continuity away from the diagonal and volume control of the changing masks give Hilbert–Schmidt convergence. No integrated-cell replacement or inserted self interaction is used.

Factoring out the selfadjoint static resolvent turns compact multiplication into norm convergence of the compact family. On isolating contours the analytic static term integrates to zero. Strong convergence of adjoint resolvents, obtained at the conjugate spectral parameter, supplies the remaining left-compact product. Norm-close Riesz projections then give equal finite ranks, total algebraic multiplicity and both subspace gaps.

For the obstruction, the intrinsic ball has exactly three constant-field zero modes for S_0, with spectral gap 1/15. An explicit perturbation estimate gives Im tr H_κ≤−2κ³/3+1446κ⁴=−(7831/15000)κ³<0 at κ=1/10000, forcing at least one nonreal eigenvalue. Rational holes in the closed ball yield nested compact empty-interior supports; continuum mask convergence retains a nonreal cluster on one sufficiently large fixed support. Restoring the isolated null anchor makes every rational-grid matrix zero.

The affirmative theorem requires the specified center-selected cubic voxels, zero diagonal blocks, a fixed complex frequency and (G). The membership representative matters. The theorem does not classify all irregular compact particles or show that (G) is necessary for every spectral question.

No spectral correctness inside J_lat, convergence rate, mesh-dependent-frequency limit, full operator-norm convergence of the singular static operators or full norm-resolvent convergence is asserted. Individual Jordan block sizes, diagonalizability and individual eigenvector convergence are not promised.
J_lat is the exact closed static lattice interval. Numerically suggested endpoint extrema are not substituted for its definition. Contours and compact resolvent sets must stay outside it.

The irregular support in the separate example fails (G). Its support index and nonreal eigenvalue location remain existential. It neither contradicts the Lipschitz-particle theorem nor proves a necessary geometry condition.

Static lattice bounds, earlier DDA consistency, classical compact spectral approximation, continuum pole theory and sphere perturbation are credited prior work. No new general spectral principle, first DDA consistency analysis or new mechanism for nonreal continuum poles is claimed.

The full announced 2022/2023 time-harmonic DDA manuscript and Rahola’s full article remain outside the bounded source coverage. Their possible overlap and historical priority are unverified; no firstness, exhaustive novelty or worldwide current-open claim is made.

The infinite-dimensional conclusions rest on the analytic proof and credited classical foundations. Finite symbolic, rational and numerical controls are supplementary evidence. This is an unrefereed preprint prepared with extensive AI assistance, without independent human or journal peer review or formal proof-assistant certification.
