article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 16 October 2026 · Version 1.1 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 9 pages) · Download PDF · Complete source and verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Let F=ℚ₃ and let E/F be its unramified quadratic extension. We give an explicit checkable argument that the Langlands quotient with segments [4,6],[2,5],[3,3],[1,4],[0,2] is Galois invariant, is not an entire proper parabolic induction, and has no invariant linear form for any Hermitian stabilizer in GL₁₅(E). The analytic proof assembles the period bases and functional equations of Feigon–Lapid–Offen: two invertible nested-segment swaps expose five necessary opposite-lift conditions forming an odd cycle. Noninduction follows from the Lapid–Mínguez ladder-side matching criterion, with all fifteen partition obstructions displayed. The total multiplicity is zero rather than the two predicted by the historical k=1 multiplicity conjecture. Historical priority and overlap with Luo–Zha, DOI 10.1007/s11464-025-0256-0, remain UNKNOWN: their complete paper was unavailable for comparison. No firstness or worldwide novelty claim is made.

A representation can carry linear measurements that remain unchanged under a subgroup. This note presents a concrete representation for which every such unitary-group measurement vanishes, even though the representation is unchanged by the field’s Galois symmetry.

The example is specified by five integer intervals. It is the unique irreducible quotient of a standard induced representation. The separate noninduction assertion says that this quotient cannot itself be the entire representation obtained by induction from a proper parabolic subgroup.

The argument uses established period bases and functional equations to force five incompatible binary choices around an odd cycle. An established matching criterion, applied to every partition of the five intervals, excludes all entire proper induced realizations.
The result is an attributed instance of classical representation-theoretic tools. Its exact overlap with Luo–Zha’s earlier announced work remains unknown, and no first-discovery claim is made.

Take F=ℚ₃ and its unramified quadratic extension E/F. Work with smooth admissible complex representations. For a≤b, D_K[a,b]=St_(b−a+1)(K)|det|_K^((a+b)/2), using the irreducible-quotient segment convention. Let π be the Langlands quotient of D_E[4,6]×D_E[2,5]×D_E[3,3]×D_E[1,4]×D_E[0,2].

Theorem 1 states that π∈Irr(GL₁₅(E)), π^τ≅π, π is not itself an entire normalized induction from any proper parabolic subgroup, and Hom_(U(V))(π,ℂ)=0 for every nonsingular 15-dimensional Hermitian space V over E/F.

There are two Hermitian isometry classes in this setting. The paper’s total multiplicity is zero rather than two in the historical OWR Conjecture 4 at k=1. The same example is presented as a counterexample to FLO Conjecture 6.12 and the historical unrestricted local unitary converse; established generic and unitarizable positive classes are kept distinct.

For each fixed Hermitian orbit, the FLO no-earlier-relation hypothesis supplies a complete holomorphic basis of periods on each of three induced orders. Two strict-containment swaps are actual isomorphisms with nonzero diagonal coefficients in these bases.

The correctly oriented reverse-intertwiner functional equation and classical segment L-factors force opposite lift labels at five linked adjacencies. Entire independent open-orbit restrictions justify specialization even when unrestricted periods in a linked-swapped order need not be holomorphic. The resulting odd cycle has no consistent binary labels.

Only containment of proper rank-one images in the quotient kernel is used. No general equality generating that kernel is assumed. Langlands classification and the additive constituent property reduce any entire induced realization to a partition of the five segment occurrences. Each partition has a ladder side and an explicit directed matching obstruction under the Lapid–Mínguez criterion.

The stated example uses the specific characteristic-zero p-adic field F=ℚ₃, its unramified quadratic extension, and smooth complex coefficients. It is not an assertion for all fields or coefficient categories.

Unitary periods refer to stabilizers of Hermitian forms. They do not assume π is unitarizable. Unramified character-line data do not assert that π is spherical. The quotient remains a quotient of parabolic induction; only an entire proper induction is excluded.

The written proof uses deep classical FLO, JPSS and Lapid–Mínguez results as explicitly cited dependencies. Finite scalar and graph diagnostics do not compute Hom spaces or prove those source theorems.

Complete periods for a fixed Hermitian orbit, normalized versus unnormalized operators, the extra quadratic-character twist, and the same-parameter ring involution are essential conventions. No separate kernel-generation disproof is claimed.

Historical priority and all substantive overlap with Luo–Zha, DOI 10.1007/s11464-025-0256-0, remain UNKNOWN. Their publisher abstract and dated workshop announcement establish a prior kernel-generation counterexample claim, but not the exact segments, proof mechanism or period consequences. The present construction may overlap, be contained in, or be superseded by that work.

No exhaustive literature absence, independent first discovery or current worldwide-open assertion is made. This is an unrefereed preprint prepared with extensive AI assistance, without external human or journal peer review or formal proof-assistant certification.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 6 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 8 pages) · Complete source and verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We deduce a sharp Cartier-index criterion for complex-structure rigidity on singular Kähler–Einstein Fano varieties. If −K_X = rL with L ample Cartier and r > dim(X)/2 + 1, then the tangent sheaf is stable and every parallel orthogonal complex structure on the regular locus equals the given one or its negative. The proof combines the decomposition theorem of Druel–Guenancia–Păun with a Hilbert-polynomial index bound and local positive-Ricci curvature. Applied to cubic n-fold limits, n ≥ 5, it identifies the ordinary metric Gromov–Hausdorff compactification with cubic GIT modulo conjugation, including the singular boundary. We also record the complex-preserving comparison as an attributed consequence of the unrestricted ordinary-double-point gap, Li–Liu's global Reeb minimum, and Spotti–Sun's established transfer. The complex algebraic comparison is already publicly stated in stronger form by Kong–Shen–Zhao–Zhao; no first-solution claim is made.

A complex algebraic variety also has an underlying real geometric shape. Forgetting the complex structure can identify distinct algebraic varieties with the same metric. This note gives a criterion under which a positive Kähler–Einstein metric determines the complex structure up to conjugation, even when the variety is singular.

The criterion measures how divisible the anticanonical line bundle is by an actual ample Cartier line bundle. Above a strict dimension-dependent threshold, a finite cover cannot split into two positive-dimensional factors. The remaining complex structure is forced to have one global sign.

For cubic hypersurfaces of dimension at least five, the paper applies this criterion to the entire singular boundary of the Kähler–Einstein compactification. Once the stated external normalized-volume gap and established transfer are accepted, two boundary cubics have the same underlying metric exactly when their complex points agree up to conjugation.

The complex cubic comparison is already prior public work, including a stronger result of Kong, Shen, Zhao and Zhao. The additional deductions here are the singular Cartier-index criterion and the argument identifying the metric fibers; first priority is not certified.

Theorem 1 concerns an irreducible normal projective complex klt Fano variety X of dimension m≥1 carrying a positive weak Kähler–Einstein current with bounded potentials, smooth on X_reg. Let L be ample Cartier and let the positive integer r satisfy the actual line-bundle identity ω_X^[−1]≅L^⊗r. If r>m/2+1, then T_X and the tangent sheaf of every irreducible normal finite quasi-étale cover are slope stable for the anticanonical polarization. No such cover is a product of two positive-dimensional normal projective varieties. Every parallel orthogonal complex structure I on (X_reg,g) equals J or −J.

The strict threshold is sharp in this general class: P^(r−1)×P^(r−1), with L=O(1,1) and its equally normalized product Kähler–Einstein metric, has m=2r−2 and admits mixed factor conjugation. This is a general-Fano equality example, not an example among cubic fourfolds.

For n≥5, set G_n=P(H⁰(P^(n+1),O(3)))//SL(n+2), and let σ be coefficientwise complex conjugation. Theorem 2, using the cited unrestricted OpenAI upper-gap theorem in every dimension 2≤k≤n, identifies the complex/polarized Gromov–Hausdorff compactification of smooth Kähler–Einstein cubic n-folds with G_n(ℂ), and the ordinary metric Gromov–Hausdorff compactification with G_n(ℂ)/⟨σ⟩. The closed-point interpretation is the cubic Q-Gorenstein smoothing locus in smoothable K-polystable coarse moduli.

Every metric isometry between the actual Kähler–Einstein cubic boundary varieties is holomorphic or antiholomorphic, including across their singular loci. In the antiholomorphic case it is holomorphic to the conjugate variety. In this formulation the cubic hyperplane Cartier line bundle is preserved, and all fibers of forgetting complex structure are precisely conjugation orbits.

Druel–Guenancia–Păun supply a finite quasi-étale product cover with stable tangent factors. Restricting the genuine Cartier root to each factor, klt Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing gives the r−1 negative integer roots of its Euler-characteristic polynomial. A factor therefore has dimension at least r−1; two factors contradict m<2(r−1). Stability descends through the finite étale big open set and holds on every finite quasi-étale cover.

Local positive-Ricci curvature kills the parallel (2,0) part of g(I·,·), so I commutes with J. Reflexive extension, GAGA and stable-sheaf simplicity then force the single global sign I=±J. This local argument does not require completeness of the regular locus.

The cubic dependency chain is explicit: the external upper bound vol̂(x,X)≤2(k−1)^k for all 2≤k≤n → Li–Liu’s global minimum over all centered real valuations and the identity vol̂(v_ξ)=k^kΘ(C) → the smooth-link singular-cone bound Θ(C)≤2(1−1/k)^k → Spotti–Sun’s iterated-cone and Cartier-root theorem → −K_Z=(n−1)L_Z with L_Z Cartier and L_Z^n=3 → Fujita’s degree-three classification, positive CM polarization and Spotti–Sun’s moduli continuity transfer → the complex/polarized GH/GIT homeomorphism. Proposition 3 and Corollary 4 state the intermediate implications conditionally on the upper gap. Only the gap’s upper bound is used, not its equality classification.

The strict transfer estimate is (1/2)b_n(n+1)^n=(n−1)^n(1+1/n)^n<3(n−1)^n, with b_n=2(1−1/n)^n. The actual Cartier root and the cubic smoothing locus are essential. Li–Liu is applied to the smooth-link case with its canonical-form hypotheses; Spotti–Sun’s iteration handles other singular links.

On the actual cubic GH limits, Donaldson–Sun identify the metric and analytic regular loci. The Cartier criterion fixes the sign there; continuity and normal extension carry the isometry across the singularities. Singular complete-intersection Picard Lefschetz recovers the hyperplane bundle. Polarized compactness and a compact-to-Hausdorff quotient argument finish the ordinary metric comparison.

The general criterion requires a genuine ample Cartier root, a positive Einstein constant, the stated bounded-potential weak metric and the strict inequality r>m/2+1. A merely Q-Cartier divisor or a Ricci-flat analogue is outside its scope.

The cubic compactification application is a deduction at the declared external-theorem level. The pinned unrestricted OpenAI ordinary-double-point upper-gap preprint and its sole dimension-four companion are principal external inputs whose complete proofs are not freshly recertified here. Fujita’s required classification statement and hypotheses are used as an external theorem; its full chapter proof has not been accessed. The general Cartier-index criterion itself does not require the upper-gap theorem.

The metric-isometry application concerns actual polarized GH limits of smooth Kähler–Einstein cubics, for n≥5. It does not classify arbitrary metric completions of nonsmoothable weak Kähler–Einstein varieties. The general sharpness example neither proves nor disproves the cubic-fourfold assertion.

The comparison stated here is topological and concerns the specified smoothable closed points. No scheme or stack equivalence, moduli-functor equivalence, assertion about every nonclosed semistable orbit, effective GH-distance estimate or modulus of continuity is claimed.

The complex cubic K/GIT comparison, smooth tangent stability, smooth metric rigidity, decomposition and conjugation convention retain their prior attribution. No first-solution, first-disclosure, exhaustive worldwide novelty or current global open-status claim is made. Finite arithmetic checks do not prove the geometric source theorems.

Druel, Guenancia and Păun, A decomposition theorem for Q-Fano Kähler–Einstein varieties : Established singular Kähler–Einstein stable-factor product cover, with the bounded-potential and quasi-étale pullback hypotheses used here.

OpenAI, The ordinary-double-point gap in every dimension : Principal external unrestricted upper-gap preprint; its sole companion is The normalized-volume gap in dimension four. These complete proofs are not independently recertified by this note.
Li and Liu, Kähler–Einstein metrics and volume minimization : The established global Reeb minimum over all centered valuations, including the irregular case, and the density normalization.

Spotti and Sun, Explicit Gromov–Hausdorff compactifications of moduli spaces of Kähler–Einstein Fano manifolds : Established gap-to-cubic transfer, singular-cone iteration, limiting Cartier root and moduli continuity.

Fujita, On singular del Pezzo varieties : The degree-three Gorenstein classification. The required definition and statements were checked in the available original preview; the full chapter proof remains an external input.

Kong, Shen, Zhao and Zhao, K-moduli of cubic hypersurfaces : Prior public manuscript stating a stronger complex algebraic comparison, including stacks and good moduli spaces. Earliest public posting and the full separate proof are not certified here.
Donaldson and Sun, Gromov–Hausdorff limits of Kähler manifolds and algebraic geometry, II : The regular-locus identification and normal extension interface for actual GH limits.
Grothendieck, SGA 2, corrected edition : Exposé XII, Corollary 3.7 supplies Picard Lefschetz for global projective complete intersections, including singular ones.

Li, Wang and Xu, On the proper moduli spaces of smoothable Kähler–Einstein Fano varieties : The smoothable K-polystable closed-point interpretation; equal dimension and volume alone do not specify the cubic smoothing locus.
Peternell and Wiśniewski, On stability of tangent bundles of Fano manifolds with b₂=1 : Prior smooth complete-intersection tangent stability.
Spotti, Degenerations of Kähler–Einstein Fano manifolds : Prior smooth positive-KE splitting and rigidity up to factorwise conjugation.

Odaka, Spotti and Sun, Compact moduli spaces of del Pezzo surfaces and Kähler–Einstein metrics : Prior singular del Pezzo compactifications and ordinary metric quotient by conjugation; lower-dimensional cubic comparisons are further credited in the manuscript.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 23 September 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 4 pages) · Complete source and verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Fradelizi, Paouris, and Schütt proved a sharp lower bound for the second moment of a convex body whose extreme points lie outside an open Euclidean ball. They characterized equality for polytopes and conjectured the same characterization for arbitrary convex bodies. We prove this conjecture: equality holds precisely for nondegenerate simplices whose vertices lie on the bounding sphere. The proof extends their simplex argument by an almost-everywhere partition into countably many simplices with extreme-point vertices. An exact nonnegative deficit identity retains the equality information for this partition.

The second moment measures the average squared distance of a body from a fixed origin. Fradelizi, Paouris and Schütt proved a sharp lower bound when every extreme point stays on or outside a specified sphere. They also found exactly which polytopes attain equality.

This note extends that equality characterization to arbitrary convex bodies in every dimension n≥1. Equality holds precisely for nondegenerate simplices whose vertices lie on the sphere. The simplex need not be regular, its centroid need not be the origin, and it need not contain the origin.

The proof keeps a finite or countable collection of simplices whose vertices are actual extreme points of the original body. An exact sum of nonnegative deficits preserves the information needed to recognize equality. A second argument retains a fixed pair of simplices to show that a body which is not a simplex has a strictly positive deficit.

The inequality, simplex moments and polytope equality mechanism are established FPS results. The contribution presented here is the extension retaining equality for general bodies; a bounded literature comparison does not certify first priority.

Let n≥1 and r>0, and let K⊂ℝⁿ be compact and convex with nonempty interior. Assume ‖v‖₂≥r for every actual extreme point v∈ext K. Write |K| for n-dimensional Lebesgue volume, g_K=|K|⁻¹∫_K x dx for its centroid, and C₂(K)=|K|⁻¹∫_K ‖x‖₂² dx for its normalized second moment.

The full inequality is C₂(K)≥[r²+(n+1)‖g_K‖₂²]/(n+2). Equality holds if and only if K is a nondegenerate n-simplex and all its vertices have norm r. The radius hypothesis is non-strict and anchored at the specified origin. If every extreme-point norm is strictly greater than r, equality is impossible.

The weaker inequality C₂(K)≥r²/(n+2) has equality exactly for the same inscribed simplices with centroid zero. In dimension one the equality interval is [−r,r]. Regularity is not required for the strengthened inequality: the triangle with vertices (1,0),(0,1),(−1,0) has centroid (0,1/3), C₂=1/3 and equality at r=1.

If an initial extreme-vertex simplex S differs from K, retain the next visible-facet simplex T formed from an outside extreme point u. With a=|S|>0, b=|T|>0 and v_i the opposite vertex, the deficit has the positive lower bound ab‖u−v_i‖₂²/[(n+1)(n+2)|K|(a+b)]. This is a finite body-dependent strictness witness.

Classical finite-dimensional extreme-point representation and separability give a countable dense choice of actual extreme points. Insert them successively into finite hulls. Strictly visible facet shells split into simplices using only their existing vertices; retaining all earlier cells produces disjoint interiors and covers the body up to its null boundary. No closedness of the extreme set or compatible face subdivisions is required.

For each cell S_j, put w_j=|S_j|/|K|, c_j its centroid and q_j the mean squared norm of its vertices. FPS’s established simplex moment formula and weighted variance give the exact identity Δ_r(K)=[Σ_j w_j(q_j−r²)]/(n+2)+[(n+1)/(n+2)]Σ_j w_j‖c_j−g_K‖₂². Compactness makes all the moment series absolutely convergent, and every displayed term is nonnegative.

If the deficit vanishes, every positive-volume cell has all vertices on the sphere and centroid g_K. Two nondegenerate simplices with that same centroid would share an interior point, contradicting their disjoint interiors. Hence the body is one closed simplex. Conversely, the simplex moment formula proves equality for every inscribed nondegenerate simplex.

The separate finite route retains the same two positive-volume simplices S and T through every larger finite hull. Completing the square in their centroid terms gives the fixed positive witness before taking limits. Bounded moment convergence then preserves it; strictness of unrelated approximating polytopes alone would not suffice.

The theorem uses the Euclidean norm about the specified origin, ordinary Lebesgue volume, compactness and nonempty n-dimensional interior. Degenerate or unbounded bodies, other norms and other probability weights are outside its stated scope.

No centroid-zero, origin-containment, regular-simplex, smooth-boundary, finite-extreme-set or exposed-extreme-point assumption is made. Only the weaker bound without the centroid term requires centroid zero for equality. The countable construction is an analytic existence proof, not a finite algorithm for arbitrary bodies.

The retained finite witness depends on the particular body and chosen simplices. It is not a uniform quantitative stability modulus in a shape distance. Finite exact integration checks corroborate formulas and examples rather than proving the universal theorem.

FPS already proved the inequality, simplex moments, finite vertex decomposition and common-centroid rigidity for polytopes. The original FPS and Oberwolfach formulations identify the historical question; no claim about the current status or wording of an online catalogue is needed. Bounded bibliographic coverage does not certify absence of later equivalent work, first disclosure or current worldwide openness.

Let M be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable n-manifold without boundary, with a positive Riemannian metric and two prescribed, mutually dual, torsion-free connections. For n≥1 we construct a proper smooth embedding into an open subset of ℝ^{binomial(2n+4,3)} carrying one smooth positive Hessian potential. Orthogonal projection of the ambient standard connection and its metric dual induces exactly the ordered pair of given connections. Finite polynomial features provide a smooth global scalar third-jet lifting; a variable tubular neighborhood and a pointwise Schur estimate provide ambient positivity without compactness or uniform bounds. For a general Riemannian dual pair, vanishing of both torsions is necessary and sufficient for such realization. This supplies a self-contained answer in the smooth statistical category to the historical dually flat realization question. Historical novelty and present openness are not asserted; important prior constructions and unresolved primary-source coverage are specified.

A statistical manifold combines a Riemannian metric with two mutually dual ways of differentiating tangent vectors. This note constructs a higher-dimensional space with a single Hessian potential whose metric and projected connections reproduce all that prescribed data.

The construction works for smooth positive statistical manifolds of any fixed finite dimension, including noncompact, disconnected and incomplete ones. It gives a proper embedding and an explicit finite ambient dimension. The surrounding open domain depends on the data and may be nonconvex or incomplete.

Polynomial features lift the required metric and connection data into one finite-dimensional family. A variable normal-neighborhood correction then makes the ambient ordinary Hessian positive along the entire embedded manifold, without assuming uniform geometric bounds.

This is an explicit construction in the historical geometric setting. Substantial prior statistical-embedding, contrast-function and local Hessian constructions are credited. Material earlier final-source coverage remains unresolved, so no first-answer or current-open-status claim is made.

Let (M,g,∇,∇*) be smooth, with M a Hausdorff, second-countable manifold without boundary of one fixed finite dimension n≥1, g positive definite, and ∇,∇* a prescribed ordered mutually g-dual pair of torsion-free connections. There exist N=binomial(2n+4,3)>n, an open U⊂ℝᴺ, one smooth Ψ:U→ℝ with positive ordinary Hessian G=Hess Ψ, and a proper smooth embedding f:M→U such that f*G=g.

The standard ambient connection D and its G-dual D* are both flat and torsion-free on U. Their G-orthogonal tangential projections induce exactly ∇ and ∇*, in that order. Flatness refers to these affine connections; it does not assert vanishing Levi–Civita curvature of the Hessian metric.

For a general smooth positive Riemannian dual pair on the same class of manifolds, realization by orthogonal projection from a torsion-free dually flat statistical manifold is possible if and only if both prescribed torsions vanish. Necessity applies separately to each connection; sufficiency is the construction.

No compactness, connectedness or completeness is required. A second-countable zero-dimensional manifold is treated separately as a countable discrete set, properly embedded in ℝ with Ψ(z)=z²/2; the empty case is vacuous.

Duality and both torsion conditions identify the ordered connections with ∇=L−C♯/2 and ∇*=L+C♯/2, where L is Levi–Civita and C=∇g is totally symmetric. Proper Whitney embedding into ℝ^(2n+1), followed by all polynomial features of degree at most three, supplies the same finite space spanning scalar third jets at every point.

A smooth fiberwise right inverse lifts compatible scalar-jet data without a finite atlas or a uniform inverse bound. Differentiating the frozen-coefficient identities gives the exact metric and connection signs and a global covector field φ with φ·df=0. This vanishing compatibility form avoids a global primitive or period obstruction; global injectivity of φ is not needed.

A variable-radius Euclidean normal neighborhood of the closed embedded image supplies Ψ₀(z)=φ_r(z)(ν(z)). Its tangent Hessian block is the prescribed positive metric, while its mixed block B may be unbounded. Adding λ(r)|ν|² with λ=1+tr(A⁻¹)‖B‖²_HS preserves the first jet and gives a positive normal Schur complement at least (2+t)I, where t=tr(A⁻¹)‖B‖²_HS.

The positive-Hessian locus of this one smooth function is an open U containing the whole image. Its unchanged first jet recovers the metric and the ordered projected connections. The gradient of Ψ gives local affine coordinates for D*, proving dual flatness without a globally injective gradient map. Projecting the two ambient torsion identities proves the two necessity statements.

The result is for smooth positive Riemannian data on Hausdorff second-countable boundaryless manifolds of fixed finite dimension. Boundary, indefinite-metric and lower-regularity extensions are not asserted.

Positive Hessian means positive definiteness of the ordinary second-derivative matrix, not positivity of the scalar value of Ψ. U is data dependent and may be nonconvex and incomplete. The dual affine coordinates are local; neither global injectivity of ∇Ψ nor a global embedding of φ is required or concluded.

The theorem supplies no fixed finite probability model and makes no claim that N is optimal. An unrestricted finite-simplex embedding theorem would already imply the historical existence answer through the Fisher Hessian potential; properness alone does not certify novelty.

The final Lê 2006 article, final Lê 2007 chapter, separate Lauritzen Lancaster pair note and Abe article remain material unverified primary bodies in the bounded priority comparison. The complete Ay–Jost–Lê–Schwachhöfer chapter, including page 239, was not obtained. These are historical attribution limits, not deductive inputs of the explicit proof. No first solution, first priority, absence of earlier equivalent work or current worldwide openness is certified.

The universal claim rests on the written construction and standard differential topology. Exact finite controls and numerical examples corroborate identities. Numerical tolerances are diagnostic choices rather than proved roundoff bounds.

Square-tiled surfaces split into maximal horizontal cylinders. This paper studies the fraction of the total surface area occupied by each cylinder in the principal holomorphic quadratic stratum.

First fix the genus and let the maximum number of squares tend to infinity. Then let the genus grow. At every shrinking area scale that is still large compared with the reciprocal genus, the geometric cylinder-area counts have a Poisson limit.

The conclusion includes the whole rescaled point process and every fixed joint moment of counts in finitely many disjoint compact windows. It is stronger than only identifying the mean in one highlighted window.

Fix g≥2. Sample uniformly from isomorphism classes of square-tiled half-translation surfaces in Q(1^(4g−4)) made from at most N unit squares, allow all positive cylinder heights, count each maximal horizontal cylinder once, and divide its area by total surface area. First N→∞ gives the law ν_g; the customary automorphism weighting gives the same fixed-genus limit. Only afterward does g→∞.

For every deterministic positive s_g with s_g→0 and g*s_g→∞, the actual geometric point measure Σ_i δ_(X_i/s_g) converges vaguely on (0,∞) to PPP(dx/(2x)). This is the marked normalized-area process, not only the auxiliary unmarked component model.

For any fixed finite family of pairwise disjoint compact intervals [a_l,b_l]⊂(0,∞), the counts converge jointly to independent Poisson variables with means (1/2)log(b_l/a_l), and every fixed joint moment converges.

The count in [g^(−1/2),2g^(−1/2)] converges to Poisson((log2)/2); its mean and variance tend to (log2)/2, and its zero-count probability tends to 2^(−1/2). The vertical marginal has the same law by symmetry.

Published geometric graph formulas give a uniform comparison with the prior weighted-permutation law a_j=ζ(2j)/(2j). Its area marks are normalized independent Gamma variables, conditionally giving a Dirichlet vector.

Classical assembly identities give the unmarked intermediate-window law. An expected weighted Gamma-mark error, split across small, intermediate and large component sizes, vanishes even when g*s_g tends to infinity arbitrarily slowly.

Concentration of the total Gamma mass gives the normalized-area process. Uniform bounds on higher compact-window count moments, a uniform good-event density comparison and negligible exceptional moments transfer every fixed joint moment to the geometry; total variation alone is not used to transfer unbounded expectations.

The theorem concerns the principal holomorphic quadratic stratum with the square-count limit before the genus. It supplies neither a diagonal N(g) limit, arbitrary-stratum extension nor a simultaneous all-direction statement on one surface.

The microscopic regime g*s_g=O(1), the macroscopic regime s_g of order1 and relative accuracy for arbitrary rare events are outside the result. The statement addresses intermediate areas rather than every meaning of a full area spectrum.

The exact Gamma total and Liu’s thesis use 6g−6, while the short problem report prints 4g−4. These give different fixed microscopic laws and remain distinct; the paper makes no new microscopic theorem or correction of that report.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 30 September 2026 · Unrefereed preprint, version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 4 pages) · Complete source and verification archive · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We prove that the complex Zariski closure of the exposed points of any finite Minkowski sum of ellipsoidal discs of dimension at least two is irreducible. No genericity or full-dimensionality assumption is needed. This proves the exposed-point irreducibility conjecture stated by Meroni in the 2023 Oberwolfach report. Under an explicit generic condition on the summand spans, we also prove that this closure equals the purely nonlinear part defined by Gesmundo and Meroni, thereby proving their 2022 irreducibility conjecture. The proof uses a connected real-analytic support-point parametrization. A nongeneric example shows why the two varieties must be distinguished.

A discotope is formed by adding centered ellipsoidal balls, which may lie in different linear subspaces. A point is exposed if one nonzero real linear functional has that point as its unique maximizer.

The paper proves that the complex algebraic closure of all exposed points is irreducible whenever every summand has dimension at least two. The conclusion covers arbitrary configurations, including repeated discs and sums lying in a smaller ambient span.

The earlier purely nonlinear part is a different algebraic set. The paper proves equality with the exposed-point closure under an explicit generic-position condition and gives a nongeneric example where equality fails.

For every finite positive sum D=D_1+⋯+D_N⊂R^d of centered ellipsoidal balls whose actual span dimensions are all at least two, E(D)=Zar_C(Exp(D)) is irreducible over C. Exp(D) is the actual set of unique maximizers of nonzero real linear functionals. No genericity or full-dimensionality assumption is required.

Separately, suppose D is full-dimensional and every subset J of summand spans L_i satisfies dim(Σ_(i∈J)L_i)=min(d,Σ_(i∈J)dim L_i). Then S(D)=E(D), where S(D)=Zar_C[(Σ_i ∂_(L_i)D_i)∩∂D] uses the relative boundary in each summand span. Thus S(D) is irreducible under this explicit GP condition.

For every feasible prescribed full-rank summand type, GP is a nonempty real Zariski-open condition. Distinct Vandermonde columns witness every subset rank simultaneously. As in the earlier discotope work, the total span may be used as the ambient space.

Outside generic position, S(D) can strictly contain E(D). Two identical unit xy-discs plus one unit xz-disc give e_3∈S(D) while a polynomial vanishing on E(D) has value 16 at e_3. The separate equality theorem is therefore essential to the earlier S-conjecture application.

Write D_i=A_i(B^(m_i)) with A_i injective. The normal u gives a unique summand support point precisely when A_i^T u≠0, with point A_i A_i^T u/||A_i^T u||. Exposed faces add, so the actual exposed-point set is exactly the image of their summed support map on the complement of the kernels.

Every excluded kernel has codimension at least two, so a two-segment detour makes the real normal domain connected. Positive real radicands make the support map real analytic without a global complex square-root branch.

If a product of two complex polynomials vanishes on the analytic image, one factor vanishes on a nonempty open part of the domain. Analytic uniqueness then forces that factor to vanish throughout the connected domain. The complex vanishing ideal is prime and the closure irreducible.

For S=E, a supporting normal kills a subset of summand spans. GP forces those spans to form a direct sum inside its perpendicular hyperplane. Their joint transpose is onto, allowing one normal perturbation to realize all prescribed unit relative-boundary parameters simultaneously. The resulting exposed points converge to the original boundary sum.

The general theorem assumes each summand has actual dimension at least two. A rank-one interval has two exposed points, and a planar disc plus a nonzero segment has two distinct conic components, so rank-one summands cannot be included indiscriminately.

Equality S=E is asserted under full dimensionality and the every-subset GP condition, with explicit ambient-span reduction. It is not asserted for arbitrary nongeneric sums; the repeated-disc example separates the two varieties algebraically.

The paper establishes no degree formula, birationality statement or irreducibility of the entire complex critical locus. General convex summands, infinite sums and other scope extensions are not part of its theorem.

The connected analytic-image principle, support-gradient parametrization and known discotope special cases are prior work. The contribution is their unrestricted exposed-point application and the generic identification bridge. Historical first priority and current worldwide open status are not asserted.

Every excluded kernel has codimension at least two, so a two-segment detour makes the real normal domain connected. Positive real radicands make the support map real analytic without a global complex square-root branch.

The resulting exposed points converge to the original boundary sum.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 6 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 4 pages) · Complete source and verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

An undirected spanning tree induces an arborescence at every vertex root. Given an independent arc-cost vector for each root, we prove that deciding whether the sum of the costs of these entire rooted orientations is at most a given threshold is NP-complete, even when every cost belongs to {0,1,2}. A reduction from satisfiability uses two hubs, variable vertices, and clause vertices. A symmetric cost vector at one hub forces a tree at threshold to encode an assignment with one selected literal per clause; the corresponding clause-root costs test those literals. Uniformly shifting the costs yields the same conclusion for costs in {1,2,3}. This resolves Problem 1 in Volker Kaibel's November 2018 Oberwolfach workshop contribution, whose report was published in December 2019. Exact finite checks accompany the all-size proof.

Choosing one network tree can become computationally hard when its cost depends on the starting vertex. This note proves strong NP-completeness for the total cost of all rooted orientations, even with costs drawn from three small integers.

Start with a finite connected simple undirected graph with N≥1 vertices. Choose one spanning tree and orient every edge away from a chosen vertex. Do this for every vertex root, keeping the same underlying tree throughout. Each root has its own independently supplied cost for every directed edge, and the objective adds the costs of all edges in all these rooted orientations.

The input explicitly lists all 2N|E| nonnegative integer costs in binary, together with an integer threshold. The decision problem asks whether some common tree has aggregate cost at most that threshold. The theorem proves strong NP-completeness already when every cost is in {0,1,2}. Finding a minimum-cost tree is therefore NP-hard. Adding one to every cost gives strong NP-completeness for the positive alphabet {1,2,3}, because every tree acquires the same total increment N(N−1).

Orienting toward each root gives an equivalent convention when every input arc-cost pair is transposed. The model charges the entire rooted tree at every root; it does not optimize a different tree for each root or charge only a selected destination path.

The reduction starts from satisfiability with at most three literals per clause. Two hub vertices represent the two truth values. Variable vertices attach to hubs, and clause vertices select literals. A symmetric cost table at one hub forces every tree meeting the threshold to contain the hub edge, give each variable exactly one hub attachment, and make every clause vertex a leaf.

The forcing step accounts for every possible spanning tree. If p counts hub–variable edges, q counts clause–variable edges, and h records the hub edge, then the base cost is p+2q=K+(1−h)+(q−m), with K=2m+n and q≥m. Nonnegative costs at the other roots force h=1 and q=m at the threshold. Only after this step is the tree interpreted as an assignment.

When the tree is rooted at a clause leaf, its selected variable's edge points toward that variable's chosen hub. The clause-root table charges one precisely when this selected literal is false. Thus a satisfying assignment supplies a tree at the threshold, and a tree at the threshold supplies a satisfying assignment. The graph, every entry of the cost table, and the threshold have polynomial size. The proof handles clause simplification, empty instances, and sparse variable labels explicitly.

The result answers the whole-orientation objective in Problem 1 of Volker Kaibel's November 2018 Oberwolfach contribution, published in the workshop report in December 2019. The satisfiability machinery is classical, as developed by Cook and Karp. Martin's spanning-tree formulation is also prior work; the note credits the expositions by Conforti, Cornuéjols and Zambelli and by Friesen. Integrality of a formulation's edge projection alone does not settle arbitrary objectives on all its root-orientation variables.

The statement concerns the written finite, explicitly encoded integer-input model. It does not settle Kaibel's neighboring Problem 2 or claim NP membership for arbitrary unencoded real inputs. The false-selected-literal identity applies to the forced structured trees; it is not a formula for the unrestricted optimum in terms of the smallest number of unsatisfied clauses. Historical first discovery and present worldwide open status are not established.
The complete support archive contains the source and exact finite verification material. These checks illustrate and test the construction; the all-size reduction is what proves hardness.

Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

For every fixed compact convex body K⊂ℝⁿ with nonempty interior and every real polynomial f, the normalized Lebesgue sum-of-squares density bound of degree at most 2r has error O_{K,f}(r⁻²) for every integer r≥1. We give a self-contained proof and an explicit constant, using one global square. A quadratic Taylor upper estimator reduces the objective to a scalar endpoint problem. Homothetic contraction compares every sublevel shell with the same core mass that normalizes a fixed power of a Dirichlet polynomial; that mass cancels before summation. This proves the quadratic upper rate in the convex-body/Lebesgue regime of the 2018 Oberwolfach question. A classical interval example shows that the exponent is sharp in the worst case. The proxy and the broad localization and relative-mass mechanisms have established precedents; no firstness or new-method claim is made.

A polynomial can be minimized by concentrating a sum-of-squares probability density near one of its minimizers. This note proves a quadratic error rate on every fixed full-dimensional compact convex body with Lebesgue measure, using a single global square.

Let K⊂ℝⁿ be compact and convex with nonempty interior, with n≥1, and let f be a real polynomial. The bound Hᵣ(f,K) minimizes ∫_K f q dx over global sums of squares q of degree at most 2r subject to ∫_K q dx=1. For every integer r≥1, the error satisfies 0≤Hᵣ(f,K)−f*≤CₙG/r², where f*=min_K f.

For any minimizer a, set H=max_K ‖∇²f‖_op, γ=1+H/2, g(x)=∇f(a)·(x−a)+γ‖x−a‖², and G=max_K g. The theorem gives 0<G<∞ and the explicit constant Cₙ=4(n+2)²(π/2)^(2n+4)(1+2^(n+2)). A single square of a real polynomial, normalized over the whole body, witnesses this upper bound.

The objective need not be convex, and the boundary of K need not be smooth or semialgebraic. The same proof applies to objectives of class C² on an open neighborhood of K. The constants belong to the fixed body and objective; no useful bound uniform over all dimensions or degenerating bodies is asserted.

At a constrained minimizer, the gradient points nonnegatively along every segment into the convex body. Taylor's formula therefore supplies the nonnegative quadratic upper proxy g. After scaling it to u=g/G, contraction toward the minimizer compares every sublevel volume with a smaller one: F(t)≤(t/s)ⁿF(s) for 0<s≤t, where F(t)=volₙ{x∈K:u(x)≤t}.

An explicit Dirichlet polynomial has a positive core of width proportional to the inverse square of its degree and a controlled tail. A fixed even power makes it a global square. Every dyadic tail shell is bounded relative to the same core mass that lower-bounds the normalizing integral. That mass cancels before summation, leaving the quadratic rate. The degree calculation and a constant-density fallback cover every positive integer order.

For K=[0,1] and f(t)=t, the note also proves the classical lower estimate Hᵣ(f,K)≥1/[4(r+1)²]. The same estimate holds for f(t,y)=t on [0,1]×[−1,1]^(n−1). Together with the upper theorem, this gives a fixed worst-case instance of order r⁻² in each dimension. It does not give a positive matching lower rate for every objective; constant objectives have zero error.

The note addresses the convex-body/Lebesgue regime in Laurent's contribution, joint work with de Klerk, to the 2018 Oberwolfach report. It explicitly uses probability densities of unit mass. Slot and Laurent's Theorem 11 gives the earlier O((log r)²/r²) bound for this hierarchy and asks whether the logarithm can be removed.

The constrained-gradient and quadratic-upper-estimator reductions already appear in de Klerk–Laurent and Slot–Laurent. Endpoint polynomial localization and comparison of shell mass with local core mass have classical precedents, including Totik–Varga. Their older endpoint-polynomial theorem, combined with Markov's inequality and the relative-mass argument, also yields the scoped quadratic upper rate. The interval/product worst-case exponent is likewise prior work of de Klerk–Laurent. No firstness or new-method claim is made, and present worldwide open status is not certified.

The theorem uses Lebesgue measure and a quadratic proxy. It does not assert the same rate for arbitrary reference measures or for the restricted hierarchy whose densities must be polynomials of the original objective for general nonconvex f. The construction assumes a global minimizer is available; it does not supply an efficient way to locate one or compute all required integrals. The explicit constant is coarse, rather than an optimal asymptotic coefficient.

The complete source and verification archive accompanies the paper. Finite exact checks and numerical examples supplement the written universal proof; they are not certificates of its infinite quantifiers.

For the characteristic-zero arrangement defined by Q=xy(x-y)(x-2y)zw(x+z+w), the degree-reverse-lexicographic generic initial ideal of the ambient Jacobian ideal has pure-second-variable cutoff 8 and a degree-7 minimal generator whose largest variable is the third. This explicitly contradicts the second-variable bound of Bigatti–Palezzato–Torielli, also stated in OWR Report 5/2021. We prove the generic sectional dimensions on a nonempty open set of compatible flags, using scalar polar syzygies and Hilbert–Burch, and give exact rational checks. The arrangement is a classical parallel connection; the methods and the valid three-variable arrangement theorem are prior work. Historical novelty and independent discovery are not established. This unrefereed note was developed with extensive AI assistance and has not undergone conventional human peer review.

A generic initial ideal records the monomial structure of polynomial equations after a general linear change of coordinates. This note gives a seven-hyperplane arrangement whose Jacobian ideal violates a proposed bound linking a second-variable exponent to the degrees of generators involving the third variable.

Let K be any field of characteristic zero, S=K[x,y,z,w], and Q=xy(x−y)(x−2y)zw(x+z+w). Form the ambient Jacobian ideal J=(∂Q/∂x,∂Q/∂y,∂Q/∂z,∂Q/∂w) using all four partial derivatives before taking any section.

For the degree-reverse-lexicographic generic initial ideal B with variable order x₁>x₂>x₃>x₄, the pure-second-variable cutoff is p=min{d≥0:x₂ᵈ∈B}=8. The full four-variable ideal B has a degree-seven minimal generator in K[x₁,x₂,x₃] divisible by x₃. Its largest variable is therefore x₃, and its degree is strictly below p.

This contradicts the general-dimensional second-variable bound in Bigatti–Palezzato–Torielli's Conjecture 5.7 and the matching Oberwolfach statement. In the former notation, the proposed threshold is d₀+1=p. The theorem holds over every characteristic-zero field, without assuming the field is algebraically closed.

The proof studies compatible binary and ternary linear sections while keeping all four ambient polars. Reducing a linear polar relation modulo each distinct factor turns it into scalar proportionality equations with a trace condition. On the stated open conditions, there are no ternary linear syzygies and exactly one binary linear syzygy.

The binary polars have no common projective zero, so the ideal has height two. The classical Hilbert–Burch theorem forces syzygy coefficient degrees 1,2,3. The resulting Hilbert values are H₂(6,7,8)=(3,1,0) and H₃(5,6,7)=(21,24,24).

An explicit compatible flag shows that the required conditions hold on a nonempty open set. Intersecting that set with the generic-initial open set justifies the generic sectional values. Favorable ranks in one coordinate system alone would not establish this step.

Strong stability and the reverse-lexicographic section identity give the cutoff eight. Multiplication by x₃ in the first-three-variable quotient has kernel dimensions zero at degree six and one at degree seven. A minimal-divisor argument then gives the degree-seven generator and proves its minimality in the full ring: a divisor of a monomial in the first three variables cannot introduce x₄.

The ternary section retains four ambient partial derivatives. It differs from the three-generated Jacobian ideal obtained by restricting the arrangement and then differentiating in three variables. The valid three-variable theorem of Marchesi–Palezzato–Torielli remains intact.

The arrangement is a classical parallel connection of U_(2,4) and U_(3,4) along the shared factor x, as in Falk–Proudfoot. The logarithmic derivation mechanism, Hilbert–Burch theorem, Galligo generic-initial theory, Conca section identity and sectional counting methods are prior work. Tohaneanu explicitly credits Orlik–Terao for the derivation mechanism.

Migliore–Nagel's applicable family theorem already gives the resolution 0→S(−7)³⊕S(−9)→S(−6)⁵→J^(top)→0, where J^(top) is the intersection of the codimension-two primary components of J. This is substantive prior information about the family. That five-generated ideal differs from the four-generated ambient Jacobian ideal studied here.

The full text of Ilardi's 2018 article was unavailable for the priority comparison, so a relevant earlier theorem or family is not excluded. Historical parameter families and code were not exhausted. Firstness, independent discovery, a new arrangement or general method, and present worldwide open status are not established.

The result does not compute the full generic initial ideal, specify an exponent vector for the degree-seven generator, prove a positive-characteristic extension, or claim the smallest possible number of hyperplanes. Exact checks at specified rational coordinates supplement the open-set proof; they are not full-generic-initial or priority certificates.

sections.text: The idea in plain English A generic initial ideal records the monomial structure of polynomial equations after a general linear change of coordinates. This note gives a seven-hyperplane arrangement whose Jacobian ideal violates a proposed bound linking a second-variable exponent to the degrees of generators involving the third variable.

blocks.text: Let K be any field of characteristic zero, S=K[x,y,z,w], and Q=xy(x−y)(x−2y)zw(x+z+w). Form the ambient Jacobian ideal J=(∂Q/∂x,∂Q/∂y,∂Q/∂z,∂Q/∂w) using all four partial derivatives before taking any section.

For the degree-reverse-lexicographic generic initial ideal B with variable order x₁>x₂>x₃>x₄, the pure-second-variable cutoff is p=min{d≥0:x₂ᵈ∈B}=8. The full four-variable ideal B has a degree-seven minimal generator in K[x₁,x₂,x₃] divisible by x₃. Its largest variable is therefore x₃, and its degree is strictly below p.

This contradicts the general-dimensional second-variable bound in Bigatti–Palezzato–Torielli's Conjecture 5.7 and the matching Oberwolfach statement. In the former notation, the proposed threshold is d₀+1=p. The theorem holds over every characteristic-zero field, without assuming the field is algebraically closed.

blocks.text: The proof studies compatible binary and ternary linear sections while keeping all four ambient polars. Reducing a linear polar relation modulo each distinct factor turns it into scalar proportionality equations with a trace condition. On the stated open conditions, there are no ternary linear syzygies and exactly one binary linear syzygy.

The binary polars have no common projective zero, so the ideal has height two. The classical Hilbert–Burch theorem forces syzygy coefficient degrees 1,2,3. The resulting Hilbert values are H₂(6,7,8)=(3,1,0) and H₃(5,6,7)=(21,24,24).

An explicit compatible flag shows that the required conditions hold on a nonempty open set. Intersecting that set with the generic-initial open set justifies the generic sectional values. Favorable ranks in one coordinate system alone would not establish this step.

Strong stability and the reverse-lexicographic section identity give the cutoff eight. Multiplication by x₃ in the first-three-variable quotient has kernel dimensions zero at degree six and one at degree seven. A minimal-divisor argument then gives the degree-seven generator and proves its minimality in the full ring: a divisor of a monomial in the first three variables cannot introduce x₄.

The arrangement is a classical parallel connection of U_(2,4) and U_(3,4) along the shared factor x, as in Falk–Proudfoot. Exact checks at specified rational coordinates supplement the open-set proof; they are not full-generic-initial or priority certificates.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 12 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 3 pages) · Complete source and verification archive (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Liebscher asked whether independence defined by an extreme exchangeable free-product state needs to retain its ambient algebra. We give a state-preserving inclusion of a four-point algebra into M₄(ℂ) for which two distinct proper coordinate subalgebras, intersecting only in the scalars, are dependent downstairs and independent upstairs. Positivity forces every downstairs witness to be the same nontrivial character mixture; upstairs a pure vector state supplies a pure folding witness. Pure folding is an established construction, credited below. We also exhibit an extreme exchangeable algebraic state with no positive extension to a larger algebra, addressing the source's separate non-lifting concern. In contrast, extreme invariant states do lift along equivariant unital C*-inclusions. The definition is unrestricted: extremality is among all exchangeable states, without a fixed-marginal, faithfulness or trace condition.

This paper studies a particular definition of independence based on extreme exchangeable states. It asks whether the answer depends on the larger algebra containing the two observed subalgebras, even when their original joint law is preserved.

An explicit four-point algebra gives a change of answer. Its two coordinate subalgebras are dependent inside that algebra, but become independent after the same algebra is placed diagonally inside the 4-by-4 complex matrices with a coherent pure state.

The paper also separates two directions of state extension. Positive extension can fail for algebraic *-algebras. In the stated C* setting, extreme invariant states do extend, while restriction of an upstairs extreme state can still lose extremality.

Let F(A) be the countable unital free product of copies of A indexed by ℕ, and let E(A) contain all states invariant under finite permutations of its copies. For unital *-subalgebras B,C⊆A, independence means that some ω∈ext E(A) has the entire original B*C joint law when B is put in copy 1 and C in copy 2: ω∘((j₁|B)*(j₂|C))=φ∘(ι_B*ι_C). Extremality is among all exchangeable states, without restricting that convex set to prescribed full-copy marginals. The algebraic category uses positive unital functionals; the C* category uses the universal unital free product and continuous states.

Take the four-point function algebra A=ℂ⁴ on {00,01,10,11}, p(s,t)=s, q(s,t)=t, B=span{1,p}, C=span{1,q}, and φ=(δ₀₀+δ₁₁)/2. Embed A diagonally in M₄(ℂ) in that point order and set u=(e₀₀+e₁₁)/√2 and φ′(T)=⟨u,Tu⟩. The inclusion preserves the state. B and C are distinct proper unital *-subalgebras with scalar intersection. They are dependent in (A,φ) and independent in (M₄(ℂ),φ′), in both free-product categories.

Every possible downstairs exchangeable witness for the full joint law is forced to equal (χ₀+χ₁)/2, where χ₀ and χ₁ evaluate every copy at 00 and 11. This nontrivial character mixture is not extreme. Upstairs, pulling the pure vector state back through the map folding all matrix copies identically gives a pure exchangeable witness, with the correct entire joint law and full-copy marginals φ′.

The pure-state lemma holds in both categories: a pure state pulls back purely along a surjective unital *-homomorphism, and a unit vector state on M_d(ℂ) is pure. The construction extends to every 0<t<1 using φ_t=(1−t)δ₀₀+tδ₁₁ and u_t=√(1−t)e₀₀+√t e₁₁. The forced downstairs mixture then has weights 1−t and t. At t=0 or 1 it is a character. If coincident subalgebras are allowed, A=B=C=ℂ²⊂M₂ supplies the stated smaller variant with a faithful downstairs fair state.

Separately, the algebraic inclusion R=ℂ[x]⊂S=ℂ[x,x⁻¹], with x and x⁻¹ self-adjoint, has an extreme exchangeable all-copy evaluation-at-zero state on F(R) with no positive unital extension to F(S). Evaluation at one is a common state of the two base algebras, but it is different from the forbidden zero-evaluation character.

For an equivariant unital C* inclusion D⊆E under the group of finitely supported permutations of ℕ, every extreme invariant state of D has an extreme invariant extension to E. The canonical map between universal unital free products of a C* inclusion is injective, so this lifting proposition applies to those products. It is compatible with the main example: an upstairs extreme state can restrict to a downstairs nonextreme state.

The full joint law and exchangeability force ∥(P_i−Q_j)Ω∥²=0 for every i≠j in the GNS representation. A third copy index connects all projection vectors to one vector v. Each projection fixes v, so every nonempty finite generator word has moment 1/2, or t in the weighted version. Those words span the free product and determine every possible witness, rather than only testing one chosen fold.

The algebraic GNS null space is a left ideal by Cauchy–Schwarz, which makes the word calculation legitimate. Equality on the cyclic vector is not promoted to equality of operators. Upstairs, positivity makes constituents of a convex decomposition vanish on the folding kernel and descend to the quotient; purity then makes the decomposition trivial. Folding retains each B*C word in its original order.

For the Laurent obstruction, a positive extension would have self-adjoint inverses X,Y with XY=1 and η(X²)=0. Its Gram matrix for X,Y would be [[0,1],[1,η(Y²)]], whose determinant is −1. This contradicts positivity.

In the C* setting, ordinary state extension, averaging over finite symmetric groups and a weak-* cluster subnet give an invariant extension. The fiber over an extreme invariant lower state is a nonempty compact face, so a compact-convex extreme-point theorem gives an extreme upper extension. State extension and cyclic GNS dilations, padded to a common Hilbert space, also prove injectivity of the universal free-product inclusion. These use standard C* state-extension, compactness and Krein–Milman inputs.

The definition concerns countably infinitely many free copies, all exchangeable states and the entire joint law. A two-copy invariant extreme witness can exist downstairs; the third-index step explains why that finite variant differs. A finite collection of word checks cannot replace the all-witness, all-word proof.

Fixing full-copy marginals while still testing extremality in E(A) leaves the upstairs witness valid. Testing extremality inside the fixed-full-marginal convex slice is a different definition: the forced downstairs mixture is extreme in that slice. The counterexample does not assert dependence under that changed convention.

The main example permits nonfaithful states and uses no tracial witness. The smaller coincident ℂ² example has a faithful downstairs state, but supplies no faithful-only theorem with all required states faithful. Faithful-only, tracial-only, trivial-tail and separately specified normal W* definitions remain outside the result.

Commutativity of the single-copy algebra A does not impose commutativity between free copies. A classical commutative or tensor-quotient interpretation changes the state algebra and is not substituted for the printed free-product definition. No arbitrary-group lifting theorem or resolution of the other five workshop questions is claimed.

The algebraic non-extension example concerns the zero-evaluation character, not the different shared evaluation-at-one marginal. It is not a failure of C* state extension. Conversely, existence of extreme C* extensions does not require all extreme-state restrictions to remain extreme.

Pure folding and its maximal-amalgamation setting are established prior work of Dykema, Köstler and Williams. The contribution presented here is the explicit ambient-dependence example, its exclusion of every downstairs witness, the separate algebraic obstruction and the stated lifting deductions. The arguments use classical positivity, GNS, state-extension and compact-convex methods. Historical first priority, independent discovery and current worldwide open status are not asserted.

The paper also separates two directions of state extension. Positive extension can fail for algebraic *-algebras. In the stated C* setting, extreme invariant states do extend, while restriction of an upstairs extreme state can still lose extremality.

sections.text: The idea in plain English This paper studies a particular definition of independence based on extreme exchangeable states. It asks whether the answer depends on the larger algebra containing the two observed subalgebras, even when their original joint law is preserved. An explicit four-point algebra gives a change of answer. Its two coordinate subalgebras are dependent inside that algebra, but become independent after the same algebra is placed diagonally inside the 4-by-4 complex matrices with a coherent pure state. The paper also separates two directions of state extension. Positive extension can fail for algebraic *-algebras. In the stated C* setting, extreme invariant states do extend, while restriction of an upstairs extreme state can still lose extremality.

blocks.text: Let F(A) be the countable unital free product of copies of A indexed by ℕ, and let E(A) contain all states invariant under finite permutations of its copies. For unital *-subalgebras B,C⊆A, independence means that some ω∈ext E(A) has the entire original B*C joint law when B is put in copy 1 and C in copy 2: ω∘((j₁|B)*(j₂|C))=φ∘(ι_B*ι_C). Extremality is among all exchangeable states, without restricting that convex set to prescribed full-copy marginals. The algebraic category uses positive unital functionals; the C* category uses the universal unital free product and continuous states.

Take the four-point function algebra A=ℂ⁴ on {00,01,10,11}, p(s,t)=s, q(s,t)=t, B=span{1,p}, C=span{1,q}, and φ=(δ₀₀+δ₁₁)/2. Embed A diagonally in M₄(ℂ) in that point order and set u=(e₀₀+e₁₁)/√2 and φ′(T)=⟨u,Tu⟩. The inclusion preserves the state. B and C are distinct proper unital *-subalgebras with scalar intersection. They are dependent in (A,φ) and independent in (M₄(ℂ),φ′), in both free-product categories.

Every possible downstairs exchangeable witness for the full joint law is forced to equal (χ₀+χ₁)/2, where χ₀ and χ₁ evaluate every copy at 00 and 11. This nontrivial character mixture is not extreme. Upstairs, pulling the pure vector state back through the map folding all matrix copies identically gives a pure exchangeable witness, with the correct entire joint law and full-copy marginals φ′.

The pure-state lemma holds in both categories: a pure state pulls back purely along a surjective unital *-homomorphism, and a unit vector state on M_d(ℂ) is pure. The construction extends to every 0<t<1 using φ_t=(1−t)δ₀₀+tδ₁₁ and u_t=√(1−t)e₀₀+√t e₁₁. The forced downstairs mixture then has weights 1−t and t. At t=0 or 1 it is a character. If coincident subalgebras are allowed, A=B=C=ℂ²⊂M₂ supplies the stated smaller variant with a faithful downstairs fair state.

Separately, the algebraic inclusion R=ℂ[x]⊂S=ℂ[x,x⁻¹], with x and x⁻¹ self-adjoint, has an extreme exchangeable all-copy evaluation-at-zero state on F(R) with no positive unital extension to F(S). Evaluation at one is a common state of the two base algebras, but it is different from the forbidden zero-evaluation character.

For an equivariant unital C* inclusion D⊆E under the group of finitely supported permutations of ℕ, every extreme invariant state of D has an extreme invariant extension to E. The canonical map between universal unital free products of a C* inclusion is injective, so this lifting proposition applies to those products. It is compatible with the main example: an upstairs extreme state can restrict to a downstairs nonextreme state.

blocks.text: The full joint law and exchangeability force ∥(P_i−Q_j)Ω∥²=0 for every i≠j in the GNS representation. A third copy index connects all projection vectors to one vector v. Each projection fixes v, so every nonempty finite generator word has moment 1/2, or t in the weighted version. Those words span the free product and determine every possible witness, rather than only testing one chosen fold.

The algebraic GNS null space is a left ideal by Cauchy–Schwarz, which makes the word calculation legitimate. Equality on the cyclic vector is not promoted to equality of operators. Upstairs, positivity makes constituents of a convex decomposition vanish on the folding kernel and descend to the quotient; purity then makes the decomposition trivial. Folding retains each B*C word in its original order.

For the Laurent obstruction, a positive extension would have self-adjoint inverses X,Y with XY=1 and η(X²)=0. Its Gram matrix for X,Y would be [[0,1],[1,η(Y²)]], whose determinant is −1. This contradicts positivity.

In the C* setting, ordinary state extension, averaging over finite symmetric groups and a weak-* cluster subnet give an invariant extension. The fiber over an extreme invariant lower state is a nonempty compact face, so a compact-convex extreme-point theorem gives an extreme upper extension. State extension and cyclic GNS dilations, padded to a common Hilbert space, also prove injectivity of the universal free-product inclusion. These use standard C* state-extension, compactness and Krein–Milman inputs.

blocks.text: The definition concerns countably infinitely many free copies, all exchangeable states and the entire joint law. A two-copy invariant extreme witness can exist downstairs; the third-index step explains why that finite variant differs. A finite collection of word checks cannot replace the all-witness, all-word proof.

Fixing full-copy marginals while still testing extremality in E(A) leaves the upstairs witness valid. Testing extremality inside the fixed-full-marginal convex slice is a different definition: the forced downstairs mixture is extreme in that slice. The counterexample does not assert dependence under that changed convention.

The main example permits nonfaithful states and uses no tracial witness. The smaller coincident ℂ² example has a faithful downstairs state, but supplies no faithful-only theorem with all required states faithful. Faithful-only, tracial-only, trivial-tail and separately specified normal W* definitions remain outside the result.

Commutativity of the single-copy algebra A does not impose commutativity between free copies. A classical commutative or tensor-quotient interpretation changes the state algebra and is not substituted for the printed free-product definition. No arbitrary-group lifting theorem or resolution of the other five workshop questions is claimed.

The algebraic non-extension example concerns the zero-evaluation character, not the different shared evaluation-at-one marginal. It is not a failure of C* state extension. Conversely, existence of extreme C* extensions does not require all extreme-state restrictions to remain extreme.

Pure folding and its maximal-amalgamation setting are established prior work of Dykema, Köstler and Williams. The contribution presented here is the explicit ambient-dependence example, its exclusion of every downstairs witness, the separate algebraic obstruction and the stated lifting deductions. The arguments use classical positivity, GNS, state-extension and compact-convex methods. Historical first priority, independent discovery and current worldwide open status are not asserted.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 16 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 4 pages) · Complete source and verification archive (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Given an onto block self-map of a nonempty two-sided irreducible sofic shift, we give a finite, computable criterion for extending that same map from a containing shift of finite type into the original shift. This answers the specified-map question in Boyle's Problem 16.3, including its mixing case. The criterion is locally testable separation of the allowed language from a regular bad-word ideal. An irreducibility argument converts the published Place–van Rooijen–Zeitoun separator bound into a single canonical finite-type approximation test. The result covers every choice of extension radius and local-rule completion. It uses that published theorem; it does not assert a new general separation theorem, historical firstness, or a solution of the separate existence-over-all-maps and cellular-automaton stability questions.

A block code updates a symbolic sequence using a fixed finite window. This paper asks whether one specified onto update rule on an irreducible sofic shift can be extended to a larger shift described by finitely many forbidden patterns, while every output still belongs to the original shift.

The answer is determined by one finite canonical approximation. The proof converts an existing theorem about locally testable languages into a test for forbidden outputs. Success supplies the extension; failure excludes every other choice of completion, radius and containing finite alphabet.
The test is finite and computable, but its monoid and graph can be enormous. The result specifies a decision procedure, without claiming an efficient implementation.

Let T be a nonempty two-sided irreducible sofic shift over a finite alphabet A, and let f:T→T be a specified onto block code with memory a, anticipation b and window length ℓ=a+b+1. Choose any total completion F:A^ℤ→A^ℤ of its local rule on the ℓ-words absent from T. The extension question concerns this same specified f.

Let L=Lang(T), including ε. For a finite input word w, let F_*(w) be its consecutive local-rule outputs, or ε when |w|<ℓ. Set B={w∈A*:F_*(w)∉L}. This is a regular two-sided bad-word ideal disjoint from L. Choose any finite monoid M and morphism α:A*→M recognizing both L and B; minimality of M is not required.

For n≥2, define T[n] to contain exactly those two-sided A-sequences whose every length-n block belongs to Lang_n(T). Put k=4(|M|+1) and N=max{2,ℓ,4(|M|+1)}. Then T[N] is one explicitly determined shift of finite type containing T.

Four statements are equivalent: (1) f extends to a block map G:S→T for some shift of finite type S⊇T; (2) a locally testable language C contains L and avoids B; (3) Lang(T[N])∩B=∅; (4) F(T[N])=T. Containment S⊇T is non-strict. A locally testable language is determined by bounded factors and bounded prefixes and suffixes.

On success, the chosen completion F restricted to T[N] is an extension of f into T. On failure, no other local-rule completion, extension radius or containing finite alphabet can provide an extension. Thus choosing a different completion can change M and N, but cannot change whether an extension exists.

The uniform separator bound is an explicit published input: Place–van Rooijen–Zeitoun, Theorem 4.2 (2014), states that regular languages recognized by a common finite monoid M are locally testably separable if and only if they are LT[k]-separable for k=4(|M|+1). The relevant equivalence records sets of position profiles, without multiplicities. The paper uses this theorem and does not reprove its general algebraic separation argument.

Finite reachability decides condition (3). Enumerate a common transition monoid, the allowed N-words and their overlap graph, mark every vertex initial and final, and label each edge by its appended letter. Its finite-path language is exactly Lang(T[N]), including ε and short words. Product with the bad-word automaton decides emptiness by all-path accepting-state reachability, with no empirical word-length cutoff.

Any proposed extension on a larger alphabet can first be restricted to the original alphabet. Its containing shift of finite type contains every sufficiently high canonical T[n]. Write its local rule and the chosen completion on a common finite interval: they agree on allowed T-words, so agree on sufficiently high T[n]. This normalization closes the quantifier over every possible extension radius and alphabet.

A finite transducer remembers the last ℓ−1 inputs and sends new output letters to an automaton for L, proving regularity of B. Padding a bad input retains its forbidden output as a factor, proving the ideal property. A forbidden output block is equivalent to a bad occurring input interval, so F(T[n])⊆T exactly when Lang(T[n])∩B=∅. Onto f turns that image inclusion into equality.

Irreducibility makes the canonical overlap graph strongly connected, including periodic nonmixing cases. Its paths extend in both directions, and short allowed words have preceding contexts. Consequently Lang(T[n]) is locally testable. A successful canonical extension therefore gives a separator.

For the converse, choose a word U in T containing every allowed n-word. If a bad word w occurred in T[n], overlap paths would place it in W=UcwdU. Independently, irreducibility gives V=UeU in T. For n≥k, these long words have all allowed k-factors and the same long endpoints, so every full or endpoint-truncated k-profile agrees as a set. They have length at least 2k, excluding doubly truncated profiles. A separator cannot distinguish V from W. This saturation argument combines with the published PRZ bound to give the single order N.

The overlap graph and bad-word automaton are finite, so their product search terminates without restricting the length of a witness path. The proof distinguishes profile sets used for LT from profile multiplicities used for locally threshold testable languages. Finite examples support the constructions; the all-word argument and published theorem supply the universal conclusion.

The theorem assumes a nonempty two-sided irreducible sofic target, a finite alphabet and a promised specified onto self-code. Irreducibility suffices; mixing is not required. Empty targets and arbitrary reducible sofic shifts are outside the claim.

Onto is used only to turn F(T[n])⊆T into equality. A constant code to a fixed point can extend from a full shift while its image is only one point, so the image-equality conclusion cannot silently be applied without onto.

If T is already of finite type, S=T is allowed. Conversely, an automorphism is extendible in the stated sense only if T is of finite type: its completed inverse forces T=T[n] once an approximation succeeds. For the mixing non-SFT even shift, every n admits an odd-gap periodic sequence (01^m)^∞ with odd m and m+2>n in T[n] but outside T; its identity therefore has no extension. Periodic irreducible targets and unused alphabet letters are compatible with the theorem.

The result addresses Boyle's specified-map Problem 16.3. It does not select a suitable map as in the separate existence-over-all-maps Problem 16.2, solve Dykstra's broader reducible-sofic homomorphism problem, classify stable cellular-automaton limit sets or extend to higher dimensions.

The decision procedure can involve an enormous monoid and graph. No practical complexity improvement or implemented arbitrary-input solver is claimed. Example programs and finite word tests do not replace unrestricted finite reachability or prove the imported general separation theorem.

Prior machinery is substantial: PRZ supplies the general separator theorem and exact bound; Ballier uses canonical-approximation normalization and develops closing, continuing and cover-based criteria; Dykstra and Barth–Dykstra supply earlier steadiness context. Historical first priority, originality, independent discovery and current worldwide open status are not certified. Possible overlap in the unread final Barth–Dykstra and Ballier journal bodies remains unexcluded; the actual Dykstra thesis and Ballier's version 1 author manuscript are distinct sources.

Zeitoun, On Separation by Locally Testable and Locally Threshold Testable Languages, LMCS 10(3:24) (2014), 1–28 : Theorem 4.2 supplies the indispensable common-monoid bound k=4(|M|+1), with the position-profile conventions of Sections 2–4. It is published prior mathematics explicitly imported here.

M. Boyle, Open Problems in Symbolic Dynamics, Contemporary Mathematics 469 (2008), 69–118 : Section 16, Problem 16.3 asks about a specified onto mixing-sofic self-map, separately from Problem 16.2. The criterion retains the specified map and permits irreducible targets.

A. Dykstra, Two Equivalence Relations in Symbolic Dynamics, Ph.D. thesis, University of Maryland (2007) : Section 3.6, printed pages 46–48, gives earlier steadiness terminology and the broader Problem 3.6.8. The present self-map/irreducible theorem does not settle that unrestricted problem.

J. Barth and A. Dykstra, Weak equivalence for shifts of finite type, Indagationes Mathematicae 18(4) (2007), 495–506 : Earlier terminology is credited through Ballier. The journal body is an explicit remaining source-access limit, distinct from Dykstra's thesis.

A. Ballier, Limit sets of stable cellular automata, ETDS 35(3) (2015), 673–690; online 2013 : Lemma 2.1 supplies prior canonical-approximation normalization; Sections 2–4 give substantial closing/continuing and cover-based results with their stated additional hypotheses.
