blocks.text: Let T be a nonempty two-sided irreducible sofic shift over a finite alphabet A, and let f:T→T be a specified onto block code with memory a, anticipation b and window length ℓ=a+b+1. Choose any total completion F:A^ℤ→A^ℤ of its local rule on the ℓ-words absent from T. The extension question concerns this same specified f.

Let L=Lang(T), including ε. For a finite input word w, let F_*(w) be its consecutive local-rule outputs, or ε when |w|<ℓ. Set B={w∈A*:F_*(w)∉L}. This is a regular two-sided bad-word ideal disjoint from L. Choose any finite monoid M and morphism α:A*→M recognizing both L and B; minimality of M is not required.

For n≥2, define T[n] to contain exactly those two-sided A-sequences whose every length-n block belongs to Lang_n(T). Put k=4(|M|+1) and N=max{2,ℓ,4(|M|+1)}. Then T[N] is one explicitly determined shift of finite type containing T.

Four statements are equivalent: (1) f extends to a block map G:S→T for some shift of finite type S⊇T; (2) a locally testable language C contains L and avoids B; (3) Lang(T[N])∩B=∅; (4) F(T[N])=T. Containment S⊇T is non-strict. A locally testable language is determined by bounded factors and bounded prefixes and suffixes.

On success, the chosen completion F restricted to T[N] is an extension of f into T. On failure, no other local-rule completion, extension radius or containing finite alphabet can provide an extension. Thus choosing a different completion can change M and N, but cannot change whether an extension exists.

The relevant equivalence records sets of position profiles, without multiplicities. The paper uses this theorem and does not reprove its general algebraic separation argument.

Finite reachability decides condition (3). Enumerate a common transition monoid, the allowed N-words and their overlap graph, mark every vertex initial and final, and label each edge by its appended letter. Its finite-path language is exactly Lang(T[N]), including ε and short words. Product with the bad-word automaton decides emptiness by all-path accepting-state reachability, with no empirical word-length cutoff.

blocks.text: Any proposed extension on a larger alphabet can first be restricted to the original alphabet. Its containing shift of finite type contains every sufficiently high canonical T[n]. Write its local rule and the chosen completion on a common finite interval: they agree on allowed T-words, so agree on sufficiently high T[n]. This normalization closes the quantifier over every possible extension radius and alphabet.

A finite transducer remembers the last ℓ−1 inputs and sends new output letters to an automaton for L, proving regularity of B. Padding a bad input retains its forbidden output as a factor, proving the ideal property. A forbidden output block is equivalent to a bad occurring input interval, so F(T[n])⊆T exactly when Lang(T[n])∩B=∅. Onto f turns that image inclusion into equality.

Irreducibility makes the canonical overlap graph strongly connected, including periodic nonmixing cases. Its paths extend in both directions, and short allowed words have preceding contexts. Consequently Lang(T[n]) is locally testable. A successful canonical extension therefore gives a separator.

For the converse, choose a word U in T containing every allowed n-word. If a bad word w occurred in T[n], overlap paths would place it in W=UcwdU. Independently, irreducibility gives V=UeU in T. For n≥k, these long words have all allowed k-factors and the same long endpoints, so every full or endpoint-truncated k-profile agrees as a set. They have length at least 2k, excluding doubly truncated profiles. A separator cannot distinguish V from W. This saturation argument combines with the published PRZ bound to give the single order N.

The overlap graph and bad-word automaton are finite, so their product search terminates without restricting the length of a witness path. The proof distinguishes profile sets used for LT from profile multiplicities used for locally threshold testable languages. Finite examples support the constructions; the all-word argument and published theorem supply the universal conclusion.

blocks.text: The theorem assumes a nonempty two-sided irreducible sofic target, a finite alphabet and a promised specified onto self-code. Irreducibility suffices; mixing is not required. Empty targets and arbitrary reducible sofic shifts are outside the claim.

Onto is used only to turn F(T[n])⊆T into equality. A constant code to a fixed point can extend from a full shift while its image is only one point, so the image-equality conclusion cannot silently be applied without onto.

If T is already of finite type, S=T is allowed. Conversely, an automorphism is extendible in the stated sense only if T is of finite type: its completed inverse forces T=T[n] once an approximation succeeds. For the mixing non-SFT even shift, every n admits an odd-gap periodic sequence (01^m)^∞ with odd m and m+2>n in T[n] but outside T; its identity therefore has no extension. Periodic irreducible targets and unused alphabet letters are compatible with the theorem.

The result addresses Boyle's specified-map Problem 16.3. It does not select a suitable map as in the separate existence-over-all-maps Problem 16.2, solve Dykstra's broader reducible-sofic homomorphism problem, classify stable cellular-automaton limit sets or extend to higher dimensions.

The decision procedure can involve an enormous monoid and graph. No practical complexity improvement or implemented arbitrary-input solver is claimed. Example programs and finite word tests do not replace unrestricted finite reachability or prove the imported general separation theorem.

Prior machinery is substantial: PRZ supplies the general separator theorem and exact bound; Ballier uses canonical-approximation normalization and develops closing, continuing and cover-based criteria; Dykstra and Barth–Dykstra supply earlier steadiness context. Historical first priority, originality, independent discovery and current worldwide open status are not certified. Possible overlap in the unread final Barth–Dykstra and Ballier journal bodies remains unexcluded; the actual Dykstra thesis and Ballier's version 1 author manuscript are distinct sources.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 17 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 7 pages) · Complete source and verification archive (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Let E⊂[0,1] be compact and let F=ℝ∖E be its complement within the real axis. We prove that positive planar 2-modulus of the family joining E to {|z|=2} implies infinite modulus of the family joining E to F. Admissibility is imposed on every curve for pointwise extended Borel densities. A weighted-distance potential and a critical trace estimate first force any hypothetical finite-energy separator to have ℒ¹(E)=0; a separate small-circle argument then treats every such null set, including null sets of positive conformal capacity. The result is stated under explicit conventions for the question recorded as Hayman–Lingham Problem 7.58.

Planar 2-modulus measures the least squared-area cost of a nonnegative density whose line integral is at least one along every curve in a family. This paper compares curves from a compact subset of the real axis to a surrounding circle with curves from that set to its complement on the real axis.

If the first family has positive modulus, the second has infinite modulus. A hypothetical finite-energy density separating the two real sets first forces the compact set to have zero length. A separate small-circle argument then treats the remaining null sets, including ones of positive conformal capacity.
The pointwise and every-curve conventions matter. Infinite density at an endpoint alone adds no line-integral cost, and the proof does not discard exceptional curves or exceptional starting points.

For every compact E⊂[0,1], let F=ℝ∖E be its complement within the entire real axis, and let S₂={z∈ℂ:|z|=2}. Then Mod₂Γ(E,S₂)>0 implies Mod₂Γ(E,F)=∞. The ambient domain for both curve families is the whole plane.

A connector is a continuous curve with its stated endpoints, locally rectifiable on the open parameter interval. Its integral is the increasing limit on compact interior subcurves. Arclength counts multiplicity; constant portions and isolated endpoints have zero arclength measure. The whole connector may have infinite Euclidean length. Intermediate contacts with either plate or the real axis are allowed, including crossings and revisits.

Admissible densities are actual pointwise nonnegative extended Borel functions ρ:ℝ²→[0,∞], required to satisfy ∫_γρ ds≥1 for every connector. Modulus is inf ∫_ℝ²ρ² dA over those densities, with inf ∅=∞. Values may be infinite on area-null sets; replacing a density only almost everywhere need not preserve this every-curve condition.

The complete theorem also holds when both families consistently use globally rectifiable connectors. It does not mix the two conventions or remove a modulus-zero family of exceptional curves. The statement fixes explicit conventions for the geometric implication recorded in Hayman–Lingham Problem 7.58.

The contrapositive is stronger than a length conclusion: a finite-energy density admissible for Γ(E,F) produces q∈L²(ℝ²) with ∫_γq ds=∞ for every γ∈Γ(E,S₂). Therefore q/n is admissible for the entire outer family for every positive integer n, and its energy tends to zero. No extremal density is required.

Empty E has zero outer modulus. Positive-length compact sets without intervals are covered by the trace argument; null compact sets of positive conformal capacity are covered by the separate circle argument. The positive-outer-modulus hypothesis is retained, so the theorem does not assert infinite complement modulus for every compact set without that hypothesis.

On a compact rectangle, dyadic open covers give a lower semicontinuous g≥max{ρ,1} with finite squared integral and pointwise domination everywhere, including infinite values on null sets. Weighted-length lower semicontinuity and the bound g≥1 give compactness of bounded-cost paths. The resulting truncated weighted-distance potential u is an actual Borel function, with u=0 on E and u=1 on F inside the rectangle.

An all-path upper-gradient inequality makes the actual u absolutely continuous on almost every coordinate line and a Sobolev W¹,² function. A compact cutoff of 1−u has actual vertical trace 1_E almost everywhere on the axis. No representative is arbitrarily reset on the axis, and no capacity conclusion is drawn from the exceptional vertical lines.

A Fourier trace estimate and mollification give a finite critical half-order difference seminorm for 1_E, without dividing by the frequency at zero. Telescoping translations of an indicator function give a lower bound proportional to length(E) times ∫₀¹ dh/h. Finiteness therefore forces length(E)=0. This classical rigidity step does not imply zero conformal capacity.

For the remaining null sets, set q=ρ+1_{B(0,3)}. Any finite-q-cost connector to S₂, stopped at its first hit, has finite total variation even at its initial endpoint and can be parametrized by arclength. Fix each actual e∈E separately. Polar integration selects radii r_j↓0 with e+r_j∈F and r_j∫_{|z−e|=r_j}q² ds→0. This is a liminf subsequence, not a claim of a full radial limit or a uniform endpoint selection.

The curve's first-exit initial cost tends to zero, and a circular arc to e+r_j adds cost at most √(2πr_j∫_{|z−e|=r_j}q² ds), also tending to zero. Their concatenation is an actual globally rectifiable E-to-F connector of cost below one, contradicting admissibility. Returns, retracing, winding and intermediate plate contacts do not invalidate this construction. It works at every endpoint and leaves every outer curve in the final scaling argument.

The complement is real, not planar. The result uses whole-plane planar 2-modulus, pointwise extended Borel densities and admissibility on every curve under the stated local-off-endpoint convention or the separately consistent global convention. Other domains, exponents, plate-avoiding interior requirements or density-equivalence-class-only conventions are not asserted.

Zero length and zero conformal capacity are different. The trace step alone does not settle the null positive-capacity case; the endpoint-by-endpoint circle proof is essential. A singleton is consistent with zero outer modulus, and infinity placed only at an endpoint is not a separating line-integral barrier.

The argument uses classical measure theory, weighted-distance/upper-gradient ideas, Arzelà–Ascoli, Sobolev mollification, Plancherel and critical trace rigidity. It makes no new-mechanism claim. Hesse's compact separated-plate theory is background; no capacity identity for the touching real complement is imported.

The question is attributed to A. A. Gonchar, communicated by M. Vuorinen, in the 2018 Hayman–Lingham collection. The full 2019 Springer problem wording and the mathematical contents of the 1982 Goldstein–Jackson item remain unauthenticated. Its programme title does not establish an earlier resolution or its exact relevance. A historical status statement or update-list silence does not establish current worldwide openness.

Historical first priority, independent discovery and current worldwide open status remain undetermined. An indirect deduction assembled from older theory is not evidence that an earlier author printed this exact resolution. The public statement concerns the manuscript's explicit conventions and does not claim to settle every interpretation of unspecified source terminology.

Arclength counts multiplicity; constant portions and isolated endpoints have zero arclength measure. The whole connector may have infinite Euclidean length. Intermediate contacts with either plate or the real axis are allowed, including crossings and revisits.

Admissible densities are actual pointwise nonnegative extended Borel functions ρ:ℝ²→[0,∞], required to satisfy ∫_γρ ds≥1 for every connector. Modulus is inf ∫_ℝ²ρ² dA over those densities, with inf ∅=∞. Values may be infinite on area-null sets; replacing a density only almost everywhere need not preserve this every-curve condition.

The complete theorem also holds when both families consistently use globally rectifiable connectors. It does not mix the two conventions or remove a modulus-zero family of exceptional curves. The statement fixes explicit conventions for the geometric implication recorded in Hayman–Lingham Problem 7.58.

The contrapositive is stronger than a length conclusion: a finite-energy density admissible for Γ(E,F) produces q∈L²(ℝ²) with ∫_γq ds=∞ for every γ∈Γ(E,S₂). Therefore q/n is admissible for the entire outer family for every positive integer n, and its energy tends to zero. No extremal density is required.

Empty E has zero outer modulus. Positive-length compact sets without intervals are covered by the trace argument; null compact sets of positive conformal capacity are covered by the separate circle argument. The positive-outer-modulus hypothesis is retained, so the theorem does not assert infinite complement modulus for every compact set without that hypothesis.

blocks.text: On a compact rectangle, dyadic open covers give a lower semicontinuous g≥max{ρ,1} with finite squared integral and pointwise domination everywhere, including infinite values on null sets. Weighted-length lower semicontinuity and the bound g≥1 give compactness of bounded-cost paths. The resulting truncated weighted-distance potential u is an actual Borel function, with u=0 on E and u=1 on F inside the rectangle.

An all-path upper-gradient inequality makes the actual u absolutely continuous on almost every coordinate line and a Sobolev W¹,² function. A compact cutoff of 1−u has actual vertical trace 1_E almost everywhere on the axis. No representative is arbitrarily reset on the axis, and no capacity conclusion is drawn from the exceptional vertical lines.

A Fourier trace estimate and mollification give a finite critical half-order difference seminorm for 1_E, without dividing by the frequency at zero. Telescoping translations of an indicator function give a lower bound proportional to length(E) times ∫₀¹ dh/h. Finiteness therefore forces length(E)=0. This classical rigidity step does not imply zero conformal capacity.

For the remaining null sets, set q=ρ+1_{B(0,3)}. Any finite-q-cost connector to S₂, stopped at its first hit, has finite total variation even at its initial endpoint and can be parametrized by arclength. Fix each actual e∈E separately. Polar integration selects radii r_j↓0 with e+r_j∈F and r_j∫_{|z−e|=r_j}q² ds→0. This is a liminf subsequence, not a claim of a full radial limit or a uniform endpoint selection.

The curve's first-exit initial cost tends to zero, and a circular arc to e+r_j adds cost at most √(2πr_j∫_{|z−e|=r_j}q² ds), also tending to zero. Their concatenation is an actual globally rectifiable E-to-F connector of cost below one, contradicting admissibility. Returns, retracing, winding and intermediate plate contacts do not invalidate this construction. It works at every endpoint and leaves every outer curve in the final scaling argument.

blocks.text: The complement is real, not planar. The result uses whole-plane planar 2-modulus, pointwise extended Borel densities and admissibility on every curve under the stated local-off-endpoint convention or the separately consistent global convention. Other domains, exponents, plate-avoiding interior requirements or density-equivalence-class-only conventions are not asserted.

Zero length and zero conformal capacity are different. The trace step alone does not settle the null positive-capacity case; the endpoint-by-endpoint circle proof is essential. A singleton is consistent with zero outer modulus, and infinity placed only at an endpoint is not a separating line-integral barrier.

The argument uses classical measure theory, weighted-distance/upper-gradient ideas, Arzelà–Ascoli, Sobolev mollification, Plancherel and critical trace rigidity. It makes no new-mechanism claim. Hesse's compact separated-plate theory is background; no capacity identity for the touching real complement is imported.

The question is attributed to A. A. Gonchar, communicated by M. Vuorinen, in the 2018 Hayman–Lingham collection. article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 22 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Complete source and exact verification archive (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

For a finite 2-vertex-connected graph G, let β(G) be the largest number of consecutive odd ears at the beginning of an open ear decomposition, counting its initial circuit and its one-edge ears. We prove that deciding β(G)≥ t, with t part of the input, is NP-complete even for simple graphs with a universal vertex whose deletion leaves a connected bipartite graph. This answers the variable-threshold complexity question posed by Sebő and by Benchetrit–Sebő. The reduction is from explicitly encoded Set Cover. It uses the classical factor-critical formulation of β, a cone identity, and a block-loss inequality that permits arbitrary partial blocks. In particular, it does not assume an optimal subgraph is a union of whole blocks.

A graph can be built by starting with a cycle and then adding paths whose endpoints are already present and whose internal vertices are new. This is an open ear decomposition. The question here asks how many odd-length ears can occur consecutively at the start, before the first even-length ear.

The initial cycle and paths consisting of a single edge both count. The paper proves that deciding whether this initial odd prefix reaches a requested threshold is NP-complete, even for a restricted family of simple graphs formed by adding a vertex adjacent to every vertex of a connected bipartite graph.

NP-completeness means that a proposed positive answer has a polynomially checkable certificate and that the problem captures the difficulty of all problems in NP through polynomial reductions. An exact polynomial-time algorithm would imply P=NP. The threshold is supplied as part of the input.

Let G be a finite loopless undirected 2-vertex-connected graph with at least three vertices; explicitly listed parallel edges are allowed. An open ear decomposition partitions all edges into an initial circuit and subsequent paths with distinct old endpoints and new internal vertices. One-edge ears are allowed, and oddness means an odd number of edges.

Let β(G) be the largest number of consecutive odd ears at the beginning of such a decomposition, counting the initial circuit and one-edge ears. The first even ear ends the prefix. If no odd initial circuit exists, β(G)=0.

Given G and an integer t in binary, deciding whether β(G)≥t is NP-complete. Hardness holds even when G is simple and has a specified universal vertex z such that G−z is connected and bipartite. Every nonpositive threshold is immediate on valid graph inputs; invalid graph inputs can be rejected in polynomial time.

The proof gives a polynomial reduction from explicitly encoded Set Cover and a polynomial certificate for positive instances. It applies to arbitrary input sizes and arbitrary partial selections of the construction blocks.

The proof uses the classical Lovász characterization of 2-connected factor-critical graphs by all-odd open ear decompositions, in the precise form stated by Benchetrit–Sebő. A graph is factor-critical when deleting any vertex leaves a perfect matching. Each ear contributes one to cycle rank, so β can be expressed by the ranks of suitable factor-critical subgraphs.

For the cone z*B over a connected bipartite graph B with at least two vertices, this becomes β(z*B)=max |E(B[S])| over nonempty S for which B[S] is connected and has a perfect matching. The score counts all induced edges, so both connectedness and the choice of objective matter.

The Set Cover construction uses one complete bipartite block Kₖ,ₖ for the root and each universe element, together with a connector for each set. With T=Σⱼ(1+|Aⱼ|), k=T+n+3, M=(m+1)k² and threshold F=M−ks, a minimal cover supplies distinct private elements and an explicit perfect matching with enough induced edges.

The converse permits arbitrary partial blocks. If aᵢ and bᵢ count omitted vertices on the two sides, the lost internal edges satisfy dᵢ−k(aᵢ−bᵢ)=bᵢ(2k−aᵢ)≥0. Matching balance and the strict threshold gaps force the connector budget; connectedness forces coverage. The argument does not require a selection to be a union of whole blocks.

A positive-instance certificate consists of a suitable subgraph and a perfect matching after each of its vertex deletions. All required conditions can be checked in polynomial time. The accompanying exact finite diagnostics supplement the written universal proof.

The threshold varies with the input. The result does not establish hardness for any fixed threshold and is consistent with the earlier fixed-parameter result of Benchetrit–Sebő. It does not assert P≠NP.

The parameter concerns the initial consecutive odd open ears, with the initial circuit and one-edge ears counted. Closed ears and the total number of odd ears throughout a decomposition are different parameters.
The stated restricted hardness class consists of simple universal-vertex cones over connected bipartite bases. This manuscript does not establish bounded-degree, high-girth or approximation results.

The factor-critical characterization and Set Cover NP-completeness are classical inputs. The exact Lovász statement is used through Benchetrit–Sebő; the original 1972 proof was not obtained. The comparison with Weighted Connected Matchings uses the 2022 arXiv v1 body; its final 2025 journal body was not obtained.

Alper Ferudun’s related preprint gives a different route to the same general classification, using 3-SAT, edge multiplicities and odd subdivisions, with different sparse and high-girth graph restrictions. It is credited as related work; no certification of all its external claims or support is implied.

The observed Zenodo creation dates are 22 October 2026 for this record and 23 October 2026 for Ferudun’s related record. These two bibliographic facts do not establish worldwide firstness or the relationship between the works. Historical priority and present worldwide openness are not certified.

András Sebő (2014), Problems about uniform covers, with tours and detours : Question 4 asks for the complexity of β. The contribution credits joint work with Yohann Benchetrit and Matěj Stehlík; its β discussion identifies the work with Benchetrit.

Yohann Benchetrit and András Sebő (2015), Ear-decompositions and the complexity of the matching polytope, v1 : Gives the open-ear conventions, factor-critical formulation, extension property and Question 3.3. Its fixed-parameter result is consistent with the variable-threshold classification here.

László Lovász (1972), factor-critical characterization, as stated in Benchetrit–Sebő Theorem 3.2 : The classical 2-connected factor-critical/all-odd open-ear theorem is an established input. The original 1972 proof was not obtained; the precise statement used is explicitly given in the cited author manuscript.
Richard M. Karp (1972), Reducibility among combinatorial problems : Supplies the classical NP-completeness of explicitly encoded Set Cover.

Firdovsi Sharifov (2010), Perfectly matchable subgraph problem on a bipartite graph : Optimizes weights of all induced edges on a perfectly matchable selection without requiring connectedness. Connectedness is essential to the cone objective here.

Gomes, Masquio, Pinto, dos Santos and Szwarcfiter (2022), Weighted Connected Matchings, v1 : The objective is the weight of matching edges under endpoint connectedness, whereas the cone identity here counts all induced edges. The 2022 v1 is the comparison body.

Gomes et al. (2025), Weighted connected matchings, journal citation : Published in Theoretical Computer Science 1036, article 115149. The journal citation is authenticated; the final journal body was not obtained or treated as identical to v1.

Frédéric Havet and Nicolas Nisse (2019), Constrained ear decompositions in graphs and digraphs : Studies other length and parity constraints with ear conventions that also allow closed cycle attachments.

Yuhang Bai, Kristóf Bérczi and Chaitanya Nalam (2026), Joins and ear decompositions beyond graphic matroids, v1 : Studies joins and total-even-lobe parameters in matroids, rather than the initial odd open-ear prefix.

Alper Ferudun (2026), Computing the Odd-Ear Prefix Parameter Is NP-Complete, version 1.0 : Related preprint addressing the same general classification by a 3-SAT, multiplicity and odd-subdivision construction. It states hardness for different 2-degenerate apex-bipartite/high-girth classes. Its record was created on 23 October 2026; the current record was created on 22 October. These dates do not establish worldwide priority, independent origin or the relationship of the works, and this citation does not certify the external proof.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 12 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 4 pages) · Complete original source and verification archive (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We prove that, in a finite simple undirected graph with unit edge lengths, finding a minimum edge set whose deletion increases all three distances between three specified terminals by at least one is NP-hard. The budget decision problem is NP-complete even when all deletion costs are one and all three original terminal distances are three. A direct reduction from Vertex Cover passes through a tripartite graph and identifies its vertex-cover number with the minimum shortest-path blocker size. The construction also gives NP-completeness when the terminal distances must remain finite, or must increase exactly from three to four. This provides a classification of the undirected triangle question posed by Krause in 2005, without asserting bibliographic first priority.

Three marked vertices in a graph give three pairs to connect. The question asks for the cheapest set of edges to delete so that the shortest route for every pair becomes at least one edge longer. All edges have length one, and any edge may be deleted.

The paper proves that the budget decision problem is NP-complete even when every deletion costs one and all three original shortest routes have length three. It also proves hardness when the terminal pairs must stay connected or their distances must become exactly four.

A proposed deletion set can be checked in polynomial time, but an exact polynomial-time algorithm for every input would imply P=NP. In the main model a disconnected terminal pair has infinite distance and satisfies the increase requirement. Deletion prices and route lengths are different attributes.

Let G be a finite simple undirected graph with unit traversal lengths and three distinct terminals r, s and t that are initially pairwise connected. All three unordered terminal pairs are demands. A blocker F may delete any edges and must satisfy d(G−F;x,y)≥d(G;x,y)+1 for every demand pair, with infinity greater than every finite distance.

Given a nonnegative binary integer budget B, deciding whether such an F has |F|≤B is NP-complete, even when every deletion cost is one and all three original terminal distances are three. Exact optimization is NP-hard. The decision version with positive binary-encoded rational deletion costs and a rational budget is also NP-complete.

The unit-cost decision problem remains NP-complete when all final terminal distances must remain finite, and when each must increase exactly from three to four. These variants guarantee terminal connectivity; they do not require every remaining vertex to lie in one connected component.

All edges, including terminal spokes, internal construction edges and added backup edges, remain deletable. The result imposes no protected-edge or spoke-only restriction. Its reduction covers arbitrary input sizes and binary budgets without expanding the numeric budget into the graph.

Start from a Vertex Cover instance Q with n vertices and m edges. Replace each edge u−v by a private path u−b−c−v. The resulting tripartite graph H satisfies τ(H)=m+τ(Q). This is the vertex-cover form of Poljak’s classical subdivision identity, and the paper supplies both directions of its proof.

Attach a new terminal to each of the three parts of H. Every original terminal geodesic is a spoke, one H-edge and a second spoke. A vertex cover gives a blocker by deleting its spokes. Conversely, from any blocker choose the vertex of each deleted spoke and one endpoint of each deleted H-edge. These choices form a cover of size at most the blocker, proving opt(G_H)=τ(H) with arbitrary edge deletions.

With budget B=m+k, the two identities preserve the Vertex Cover answer. For m≥1 the graph has n+2m+3 vertices, n+5m edges and all three terminal distances equal to three. A fixed valid yes-instance handles edgeless source graphs. The graph size is independent of the magnitude of binary k.

For the finite-distance and exact-four variants, add a private four-edge backup path between each terminal pair, using nine new internal vertices. No new path of length at most three appears. Any blocker must still hit the old geodesics, while a cover’s spoke deletions leave every backup intact and all three distances exactly four. Krause’s earlier expensive-edge added-path mechanism is credited; this note proves the unrestricted unit-cost specialization directly.

An edge-deletion list, shortest-path searches and exact cost comparisons give polynomial certificates. Positive rational costs inherit hardness from the unit-cost subclass; no weighted spoke-rounding identity is asserted. The finite exact diagnostics accompany the universal written proof.

The theorem concerns finite simple undirected graphs with unit traversal lengths, all three terminal demands and unrestricted edge deletion. It does not claim planar, bounded-degree, weighted-traversal-length or globally connected residual-graph classifications. Directed demands and full-disconnection multicuts require separate model comparisons.

Vertex Cover NP-completeness is the classical complexity input. The paper proves its particular cover, geodesic and backup-path identities directly. Poljak’s subdivision result, Khachiyan and coauthors’ related tripartite attachment, and Krause’s earlier added-path exact-one transfer receive explicit credit.

Krause’s historical sources record the undirected triangle question and separately treat the directed case. A historical open statement is not a claim that the question remained open until this work. The original Bienstock–Díaz body was unavailable; its proposal attribution is through Krause. Broader cut-paper interfaces were read without certifying every auxiliary proof or final journal body.

Alper Ferudun’s related preprint addresses the same general classification through Three-Terminal Cut, with deletion-cost instances at initial distance four and unit-cost bundle instances at distance six. It does not treat exact-one increase. It is positively credited without certifying its entire external proof, archive or solver dependencies.

The present note credits the mechanism and proves its different edge-deletion/unit-length/three-demand transfer.

The inspected introductory interfaces are not an automatic hardness theorem for this three-terminal distance-three restriction; complete auxiliary proofs and final journal identity were not re-audited.

Dvořák and Knop (2015), Parameterized complexity of length-bounded cuts and multi-cuts, v1 : The inspected parameterized multi-terminal interfaces concern broader distance constraints. They are not substituted for the proof of the precise three-demand unit-length theorem here.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 4 October 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 5 pages) · Complete source and verification archive (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

For any fixed finite graph, the binary MTP₂ distributions admitting finite nonnegative unary and edge factors are exactly the pointwise limits of strictly positive attractive Ising distributions on that same graph. In particular, the finite-factor class is closed, answering Conjecture 1 in Lauritzen's 2022 problem statement. The proof handles zero cells by contracting deterministic equalities and aggregating interactions, then uses a classical residual-flow representation to bound local factors without losing normalization. We distinguish this characterization from earlier natural-lattice factorization results and from a previously published counterexample to the accompanying factorization conjectures.

A graphical model writes a joint probability distribution as a product of factors attached to vertices and edges. MTP₂ is a positive-dependence condition. This paper asks what happens when some probabilities are zero or when positive attractive Ising models approach the boundary of the probability simplex.

On every fixed finite graph, the MTP₂ distributions that already have finite nonnegative vertex and edge factors are exactly the limits of positive attractive Ising distributions on that same graph. The result includes deterministic coordinates and tied coordinates, while retaining the original edges.
The finite-factor requirement matters. A globally Markov MTP₂ distribution can fail to have such a factorization; the paper explains an earlier four-cycle counterexample and credits its authors.

Fix any finite simple graph G=(V,E) and binary states Ω={0,1}^V. Let F₂(G) consist of normalized probabilities p satisfying p(x∧y)p(x∨y)≥p(x)p(y) for every x,y∈Ω and admitting an actual product of finite nonnegative unary factors and factors on the original edges. Zeros are allowed.

Let A(G) consist of the strictly positive laws proportional to exp(∑ᵢhᵢxᵢ+∑ᵢⱼ∈EJᵢⱼxᵢxⱼ), with arbitrary finite real fields hᵢ and finite nonnegative couplings Jᵢⱼ. Then F₂(G)=closure A(G) in the fixed finite-dimensional probability simplex. In particular, F₂(G) is closed under pointwise limits. No extra edge or hidden variable is introduced.

The note also gives the exact closure corollary for M_I(G)∩M₂(G) in Lauritzen’s 2022 statement, where M_I uses finite real edge factors only. Signs can be removed by absolute values. When E is nonempty, isolated coordinates are jointly uniform and independent under that edge-only convention; these properties survive limits and the remaining unary factors can be absorbed into incident edges.

For nonempty V and no edges, the literal empty product is not a normalized probability, so the source’s literal edge-only family is empty. With a tacit scalar normalization it contains just the uniform law. For V empty the sole mass is 1. These source conventions are distinct from the main unary-and-edge model, which permits arbitrary independent Bernoulli coordinates on an edgeless graph.

For a nonempty edge set, the supplement also shows that a nonempty Boolean sublattice which is facial for the original-edge design is feasible for that same design. In concrete terms, a lattice zero set of a nonnegative finite original-edge energy is recovered from its original-edge projection constraints. This supplies an attributed support-geometric route to the closure corollary.

Finite local factors identify the support from its actual vertex and edge projections. MTP₂ makes that support a lattice. After pinned coordinates are removed, the edge constraints are implications; strongly connected implication classes represent equal coordinates. On the resulting poset, four allowed support states force each aggregate interaction between incomparable classes to be nonnegative. Individual supplied potentials need not be attractive.

The aggregate interactions can be placed on existing edges. Penalizing the original pin and implication violations then gives positive attractive laws converging to the desired distribution. Their mass on the original support has a strictly positive limiting normalizer.

For the reverse direction, a classical cut representation and maximum-flow residual reparameterization give bounded unary and original-edge factors. Their product is W(x)=exp(−E(x)+min E), so max W=1 and 1≤∑ₓW(x)≤2^|V|. Compactness therefore yields limiting finite factors without losing normalization. The argument allows finite real capacities and does not rely on an integer-capacity algorithm terminating.

This is a finite, binary, pairwise, fixed-graph theorem. It does not assert factorization for every globally Markov MTP₂ law, or extend to arbitrary clique interactions, infinite graphs, nonbinary states, hidden variables or changing graphs. It gives no uniform-in-graph approximation rate or efficient general factor-reconstruction algorithm.

Gandolfi–Lenarda’s earlier four-cycle law illustrates the boundary: its support has x₃=x₄, with mass 2/9 at 1111 and 1/9 at the other seven supported states. It is MTP₂ and globally Markov, but violates an identity obeyed by every original-edge factorization. This is a prior counterexample to separate factorization claims, not a new counterexample or a contradiction to the smaller finite-factor theorem.

The proof uses established toric support geometry, lattice-support ideas, positive-potential theory and graph-cut/flow tools. The comparison with prior work is limited to the cited editions; historical first priority and current worldwide open status are not certified. No new underlying-method or independent-discovery claim is made. Finite computations illustrate examples; the arbitrary-graph theorem rests on the written proof.

D. Geiger, C. Meek and B. Sturmfels, On the toric algebra of graphical models (2006) : The classical distinction between toric closure and finite nonnegative factorization depends on support feasibility and faciality.

T. Kahle and S. Sullivant, Lattice supported distributions and graphical models, arXiv:2411.03139v1 (2024) : Their natural-lattice, clique-factor limit theorem and cover/feasibility framework are prior work. Pins, repeated coordinates and the original-edge design require the additional steps stated in this note.

S. Lauritzen, C. Uhler and P. Zwiernik, Total positivity in exponential families with application to binary variables (2021) : Binary lattice-support reconstruction and compact extended MTP₂ graphical families provide established background; an extended family is distinct from finite original-edge factors.

S. Fallat and coauthors, Total positivity in Markov structures (2017) : The positive-pair-potential criterion is classical. Its cancellation converse is not extended indiscriminately to factors with zero entries.

V. Kolmogorov and R. Zabih, What energy functions can be minimized via graph cuts? (2004) : The binary submodular cut construction is classical; it represents pairwise interactions without extra nonterminal variables.

J.-C. Picard and M. Queyranne, On the structure of all minimum cuts in a network and applications (1979 report; published 1980) : Residual reachability and cut-flow identities supply classical foundations for the bounded-factor gauge.

V. Kolmogorov and C. Rother, Minimizing nonsubmodular functions with graph cuts—a review (2007) : Maximum-flow residual updates as energy reparameterizations are established tools; the separate doubled-node QPBO construction is not needed here.

A. Gandolfi and P. Lenarda, A note on Gibbs and Markov random fields with constraints and their moments, vol. 4 (nominal 2016), pp. 407–422; published 13 April 2017 : Lemma 5.2 gives the exact earlier four-cycle obstruction discussed here. Kahle–Sullivant later give a related equality-support example.

T. Kahle and S. Sullivant, Lattice supported distributions and graphical models, arXiv:2411.03139v1 (2024) : Their natural-lattice, clique-factor limit theorem and cover/feasibility framework are prior work. S. Lauritzen, C. Uhler and P. Zwiernik, Total positivity in exponential families with application to binary variables (2021) : Binary lattice-support reconstruction and compact extended MTP₂ graphical families provide established background; an extended family is distinct from finite original-edge factors.

S. Fallat and coauthors, Total positivity in Markov structures (2017) : The positive-pair-potential criterion is classical. Its cancellation converse is not extended indiscriminately to factors with zero entries.

V. Kolmogorov and R. Zabih, What energy functions can be minimized via graph cuts? (2004) : The binary submodular cut construction is classical; it represents pairwise interactions without extra nonterminal variables.

J.-C. Picard and M. Queyranne, On the structure of all minimum cuts in a network and applications (1979 report; published 1980) : Residual reachability and cut-flow identities supply classical foundations for the bounded-factor gauge.

V. Kolmogorov and C. Rother, Minimizing nonsubmodular functions with graph cuts—a review (2007) : Maximum-flow residual updates as energy reparameterizations are established tools; the separate doubled-node QPBO construction is not needed here.

A. Gandolfi and P. Lenarda, A note on Gibbs and Markov random fields with constraints and their moments, vol. 4 (nominal 2016), pp. 407–422; published 13 April 2017 : Lemma 5.2 gives the exact earlier four-cycle obstruction discussed here. Kahle–Sullivant later give a related equality-support example.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 7 October 2026 · No version number supplied · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 7 pages) · Complete original source and verification archive (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Using OpenAI's all-algebra bounded Hochschild vanishing theorem, we derive local ordinary complex Banach–Mazur rigidity for every von Neumann algebra and its canonical predual. The threshold depends on the algebra; the conclusion is Jordan *-isomorphism. Roydor announced the general cohomological implication in 2020, while his published Theorem 1.2 assumes separable predual. We give an explicit extension of his geometric argument using deformation stability on two fixed source algebras and reconstruction of odd finite type-I summands from full abelian projections. This avoids separability, moving-corner perturbation constants, and enumeration of infinite cardinal degrees. The cohomological input and geometric machinery are attributed external results; no new solution of the underlying cohomology problem or universal numerical threshold is claimed.

A von Neumann algebra carries both a norm and a multiplication. Banach–Mazur distance measures how closely two spaces can match through an invertible linear map, using only their norms. The question is whether a sufficiently close match also determines their algebraic structure.

For each fixed complex von Neumann algebra, this paper obtains a neighborhood in which every other von Neumann algebra has the same Jordan structure. The size of that neighborhood may depend on the fixed algebra. The same conclusion holds when the comparison uses the canonical preduals.

For every complex von Neumann algebra M, there exists ε_M>0 such that, for every complex von Neumann algebra N, either d_BM(M,N)<1+ε_M or d_BM(M_*,N_*)<1+ε_M implies that M and N are Jordan *-isomorphic. Here M_* and N_* are the canonical preduals, and ordinary complex Banach–Mazur distance is the infimum of ||T||·||T⁻¹|| over bounded invertible complex-linear maps T between the spaces.

At this threshold, the two strict distance conditions are equivalent to Jordan *-isomorphism, to a surjective complex-linear isometry between the algebra spaces, and to one between the canonical preduals. The statement includes arbitrary nonseparable centers and preduals, every von Neumann type and every infinite type-I cardinal dimension.

A Jordan *-isomorphism preserves adjoints and the symmetrized product x∘y=(xy+yx)/2. It need not preserve the orientation of the associative product: an algebra and its opposite have the same relevant norm geometry.

The essential input is OpenAI’s bounded Hochschild vanishing theorem for all complex von Neumann algebras. In the ordinary bounded, actual-coboundary sense, its degree-two and degree-three cases provide the estimates needed to correct a small multiplication defect on a fixed source algebra.

The proof extends Roydor’s geometric argument using two fixed source algebras. It handles the part whose unit splits into two equivalent projections, then reconstructs the remaining finite odd type-I degrees using full abelian projections. This treats unbounded finite odd degrees together and avoids constants attached to moving corners. Infinite cardinal dimensions are already included in the first part.

Taking Banach adjoints preserves the norms of a predual isomorphism and its inverse, giving the predual implication. The resulting exact Jordan isomorphism is normal and induces an isometry of the canonical preduals.

The threshold depends on M; the paper gives no universal numerical constant. The comparison spaces must be complex von Neumann algebras or their canonical preduals. The initial near-isometry is measured in ordinary operator norm and need not be normal or completely bounded.

The conclusion is Jordan structure, not recovery of a chosen associative orientation or a claim that the original near-isometry is multiplicative. The inequalities are strict; no threshold-equality result or theorem for arbitrary Banach target spaces is asserted.

The result uses the attributed cohomology theorem and classical geometric machinery. Roydor had already announced the unrestricted conditional formulation; this note supplies an explicit fixed-source extension and records its consequence from the cohomology input. No first-discovery claim is made.

Éric Ricard and Jean Roydor (2014), A non-commutative Amir–Cambern theorem for von Neumann algebras and nuclear C*-algebras : Their unconditional theorem uses completely bounded distance. Its predual observation and conditional two-matrix-level result are prior work; small ordinary distance does not by itself supply their stronger metric hypothesis.

Iain Raeburn and Joseph L. Taylor (1977), Hochschild cohomology and perturbations of Banach algebras : Together with Johnson’s classical perturbation theory, this is prior work on the fixed-algebra deformation mechanism. The note writes out the involution-preserving iteration and its algebra-dependent constants.
David Sherman, Noncommutative Lp structure encodes exactly Jordan structure : Gives the exact isometry–Jordan structure connection, including the algebra and predual endpoints used here.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 3 October 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Complete source and verification archive (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We classify the positive words in the five standard generators of B₆/⟨⟨ch⁻¹⟩⟩ representing c², where c=(a₁a₂a₃a₄)⁵ and h=a₅a₄a₃a₂a₁²a₂a₃a₄a₅. Their lengths are 20, 30, 40, with respectively one, one, and two strict Hurwitz classes. Simultaneous conjugation identifies the two length-40 classes, giving the three representatives proposed in Wajnryb's question. The proof combines classical geometric and braid results with pure-braid linking constraints and an exhaustive, exact 810-word certificate for the length-20 case. The length spectrum and the twice-per-pair crossing theorem used at length 30 have prior sources; a reproducible six-strand certificate for the latter is supplied as additional evidence.
A positive braid word is built from a fixed list of elementary crossings. This paper classifies all such words representing one specified element of Wajnryb’s quotient of the six-strand braid group.

There are two equivalence conventions. Strict Hurwitz moves rearrange adjacent factors while preserving their product. A broader equivalence also permits conjugating every factor by the same group element. The distinction changes the answer: four strict classes become three classes under the broader convention.
Let a₁,…,a₅ be the five standard generators of B₆, and put c=(a₁a₂a₃a₄)⁵, h=a₅a₄a₃a₂a₁²a₂a₃a₄a₅ and z=(a₁a₂a₃a₄a₅)⁶. Work in G=B₆/⟨⟨ch⁻¹⟩⟩. The full-twist identity gives c²=h²=z in G, with z central.

For every literal positive word in these five fixed generators whose product in G is c², its length is 20, 30 or 40. At length 20 there is one strict Hurwitz class, represented by h². At length 30 there is one, represented by z. At length 40 there are exactly two, represented by (a₁a₂a₃a₄)¹⁰ and (a₂a₃a₄a₅)¹⁰.

The length-20 inputs are exactly the ten distinct cyclic rotations of h² as literal words. Simultaneous conjugation identifies the two length-40 classes, leaving exactly one class at each of the three lengths. This gives the three models in Wajnryb’s question under that broader equivalence.

A strict Hurwitz move replaces adjacent factors (x,y) by (xyx⁻¹,x), or applies its inverse. Intermediate tuples may contain conjugates of generators. The classified inputs remain literal positive words in the five fixed standard generators.

Classical chain relations map the quotient to the genus-two mapping class group with one boundary component. The positive boundary-twist length theorem bounds the word length by 40. Abelianization and signed pure-braid linking constraints then rule out lengths 0 and 10 and restrict the crossing patterns at the other three lengths. These constraints are necessary conditions, rather than complete braid invariants.

At length 20, the crossing pattern reduces all inputs to a finite walk problem. A quotient-compatible free-group action rejects the other candidates; centrality separately proves that the ten surviving rotations are genuine and strictly equivalent. At length 30, full free-word identities along every relevant edge of a finite crossing graph prove equality with the full twist. Equal crossing counts alone would not prove this.

At length 40, the noncrossing strand must be an endpoint. The classical four-chain embedding and positive braid relations give one class at each endpoint. Their generated subgroups have different permutation images, so strict moves keep them distinct; an explicit simultaneous conjugation merges them.

The theorem concerns these five fixed standard-generator inputs in this specific six-strand quotient. It does not classify arbitrary products of conjugates of generators, arbitrary nonseparating Dehn-twist factorizations, other ranks or other quotients. Allowing conjugates in intermediate Hurwitz moves does not enlarge the input universe.

The quotient geometry, length spectrum, faithful Artin action, positive monoid embedding and chain embedding are classical inputs. blocks.text: Let a₁,…,a₅ be the five standard generators of B₆, and put c=(a₁a₂a₃a₄)⁵, h=a₅a₄a₃a₂a₁²a₂a₃a₄a₅ and z=(a₁a₂a₃a₄a₅)⁶. Work in G=B₆/⟨⟨ch⁻¹⟩⟩. The full-twist identity gives c²=h²=z in G, with z central.

For every literal positive word in these five fixed generators whose product in G is c², its length is 20, 30 or 40. At length 20 there is one strict Hurwitz class, represented by h². At length 30 there is one, represented by z. At length 40 there are exactly two, represented by (a₁a₂a₃a₄)¹⁰ and (a₂a₃a₄a₅)¹⁰.

The length-20 inputs are exactly the ten distinct cyclic rotations of h² as literal words. Simultaneous conjugation identifies the two length-40 classes, leaving exactly one class at each of the three lengths. This gives the three models in Wajnryb’s question under that broader equivalence.

A strict Hurwitz move replaces adjacent factors (x,y) by (xyx⁻¹,x), or applies its inverse. Intermediate tuples may contain conjugates of generators. The classified inputs remain literal positive words in the five fixed standard generators.

blocks.text: Classical chain relations map the quotient to the genus-two mapping class group with one boundary component. The positive boundary-twist length theorem bounds the word length by 40. Abelianization and signed pure-braid linking constraints then rule out lengths 0 and 10 and restrict the crossing patterns at the other three lengths. These constraints are necessary conditions, rather than complete braid invariants.

At length 20, the crossing pattern reduces all inputs to a finite walk problem. A quotient-compatible free-group action rejects the other candidates; centrality separately proves that the ten surviving rotations are genuine and strictly equivalent. At length 30, full free-word identities along every relevant edge of a finite crossing graph prove equality with the full twist. Equal crossing counts alone would not prove this.

At length 40, the noncrossing strand must be an endpoint. The classical four-chain embedding and positive braid relations give one class at each endpoint. Their generated subgroups have different permutation images, so strict moves keep them distinct; an explicit simultaneous conjugation merges them.

We give a negative answer to the unrestricted fibre-product question for local deformation functors posed by Byszewski. For the weakly ramified action of the additive group of F₄ given by t↦t/(1+at), and its subgroup F₂, restriction–induction cannot be formally smooth over any prorepresentable recipient, regardless of its tangent dimension. The proof combines the known involution deformation pathology with an exact calculation showing that restriction has injective tangent map. The variant assuming prorepresentability of the subgroup and quotient deformation functors is untouched. The involution pathology and additive action are established prior ingredients; the contribution is their use to obstruct the proposed factorization.

Dévissage asks whether deformations of a group action can be assembled from deformations of a subgroup and its quotient. This note gives a characteristic-two action for which the proposed formally smooth fibre-product factorization fails.

The obstruction rules out every prorepresentable recipient in the stated category, regardless of tangent dimension. It combines a known involution deformation pathology with an injective tangent restriction map. The precise coordinate-equivalence category is essential.
Let k=F₄=F₂[u]/(u²+u+1), G=(k,+), N=(F₂,+), Q=G/N, and ρ(a)(t)=t/(1+at). This is the standard weakly ramified additive action on k[[t]].

Work with local Artinian W(k)-algebras with identified residue field k. D_H consists of lifts of the given local action modulo all coordinate changes reducing to the identity, including changes with nilpotent constant terms. D_N^Q is the actual fixed subfunctor of D_N.

There is no prorepresentable recipient F=h_R, with R a complete Noetherian local W(k)-algebra with residue k, and no choice of natural maps f:D_N^Q→F←D_Q:g that makes the actual restriction–induction map D_G→D_N^Q×_F D_Q formally smooth. This holds for every tangent dimension of F, including the one-dimensional recipient prescribed in the refined question.

The theorem uses the actual deformation functors and their fixed subfunctor. It does not replace either component by a versal hull or assume a formula for the tangent maps of arbitrary natural transformations.

The invariant parameter y=t²/(1+t) identifies the subgroup-fixed ring with k[[y]], and the quotient acts by σ(y)=y/(1+y). A nonzero quotient tangent is represented by (y+ε)/(1+y) over k[ε]/ε². The known involution conjugacy, or the known collision under an injection of coefficient rings, forces every natural map to a prorepresentable Hom-functor to send this tangent to the residue basepoint.

Separately, invariant derivations restrict precisely to M=y k[[y]]∂y. With z=y²/(1+y), the quotient action on the complete module M=y k[[z]]∂y⊕y²k[[z]]∂y has kernel equal to image for its characteristic-two cohomology differential. Thus H¹(Q,Θ^N)=0, giving injectivity of tangent restriction. This is a full formal-series argument.

For any proposed recipient maps, the pair (0_N,v) is therefore a genuine point of the fibre product over the dual numbers, with v nonzero. Formal smoothness would lift it to a G-deformation with zero restriction and nonzero induction. Injective restriction forces that deformation to be zero, whose induction is zero, giving a contradiction already over k[ε]/ε²→k.

The statement concerns this specific F₄ additive action and its F₂ subgroup in the original unframed category. Fixing the zero section, choosing a framed category, replacing actual functors by hulls, using global deformation functors, or allowing arbitrary nonprorepresentable recipients changes the problem.

The separate variant assuming that both the subgroup and quotient deformation functors are prorepresentable remains unaddressed. The example uses the exceptional nonprorepresentable involution component and does not contradict the conditional obstruction-space theorems.

The additive action, involution parameter-shift conjugacy, failure to preserve injections and resulting all-recipient tangent collapse are established antecedents. The note combines them with the restriction-kernel calculation to obstruct the proposed factorization. Historical first priority and continued worldwide openness through 2026 are not certified.
Finite exact calculations support explicit identities. The all-formal-series and all-natural-transformation quantifiers depend on the written proof; they do not follow from finite-jet experiments.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 13 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 4 pages) · Complete manuscript source and verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Morpurgo’s volume-normalized weighted Yamabe heat trace comparison, stated for every dimension at least three, is false in dimension three. We specify one smooth positive conformal weight on the round three-sphere whose scaled heat trace exceeds 13/20 at a specified positive time, whereas the round maximum is less than 321/500. The argument applies classical cylindrical conformal geometry and Dirichlet min–max estimates. A finite cylinder length, explicit smooth caps, and exact rational certificates give quantitative separation.

A heat trace adds together the decaying contributions of all the vibration modes of an operator. The Yamabe operator combines the Laplacian with a curvature term. Multiplying its heat trace by a power of time lets us compare the largest value reached by different conformal weights while keeping the volume normalization fixed.

Morpurgo’s comparison asks whether the round sphere gives the largest such value for every smooth positive normalized weight, in every dimension at least three. This note gives a counterexample on the three-sphere.

The construction stretches a region into a very long round cylinder and closes it with smooth caps. It fixes the cylinder length at 10000 and rescales the resulting metric to the round sphere’s volume. The resulting weight stays smooth and strictly positive everywhere.

At a specified positive time, its scaled heat trace is greater than 13/20. The round sphere’s value is less than 321/500 at every positive time. Since 13/20 is larger than 321/500, the weighted example has a strictly larger time maximum. Both maxima occur at finite positive times.

Let g₀ be the unit round metric on S³, let Δg₀ be the positive Laplacian, and define Y₀ = Δg₀ + 3/4 and YW = W^(-1/2) Y₀ W^(-1/2) on L²(dVg₀). There is one specified smooth strictly positive weight W with ∫S³ W^(3/2) dVg₀ = 2π² and an explicitly defined t* > 0 such that (t*)^(3/2) Tr(exp(-t* YW)) > 1106714561/1700054750 > 13/20, while max over t > 0 of t^(3/2) Tr(exp(-t Y₀)) < 321/500.

For the paper’s capped cylinder gL = WL g₀ with L = 10000 and VL = vol(gL), set a = (2π²/VL)^(2/3), W = aWL and t* = 4a. The paper defines WL by an explicit flat smooth cutoff and a convergent volume integral. These expressions specify one finite weight and time.
Both the weighted and round scaled heat traces attain their maxima at positive finite times. The dimension-three example refutes the comparison quantified over all dimensions n ≥ 3.

Classical cylindrical conformal geometry supplies the long product region. The explicit caps extend smoothly over both poles, and the final constant rescaling gives the exact volume normalization. Conformal covariance identifies the geometric Yamabe operator with the stated symmetric weighted operator.

Dirichlet sine functions on the cylinder, extended by zero, belong to the global quadratic-form domain. The min–max principle bounds every eigenvalue needed for an infinite heat-trace lower sum. A Gaussian integral and the finite cap-volume estimate give the displayed weighted lower bound.

The round sphere has an explicit spectrum. Gaussian Poisson summation controls small times, analytic interval and infinite-tail estimates control the middle range, and monotonicity controls large times. Exact rational inequalities complete the bound for every positive time.

The common small-time limit and decay at infinity, together with continuity and values above the small-time limit, ensure that both maxima are attained. The finite arithmetic certificates support these analytic arguments.
The example is in dimension three. The comparison restricted to n ≥ 4 and the separate monotonicity conjecture for n ≥ 4 remain unaddressed.

The theorem uses the specified finite length, smooth caps, exact normalization and witness time. It makes no assertion that the witness time is a maximizing time, that a maximizing time is unique, or that the estimates are uniform over a degenerating family.

The cylindrical geometry, conformal covariance, Dirichlet trial spaces, min–max principle and Gaussian heat estimates are classical. The contribution presented here is a specified finite quantitative application to the historical comparison, with checkable bounds.

The historical source comparison is bounded. The inspected author versions and selected transformed-trace interfaces do not establish exhaustive coverage of the literature. Historical priority, worldwide firstness and continued worldwide openness remain unestablished.

The final 2011 Ammann–Jammes publisher chapter and complete final 2002 Morpurgo journal PDF were not authenticated in the underlying source comparison. The exact author editions and selected web interfaces used are distinguished in the accompanying materials.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 21 October 2026 · Version 1.1 · Unrefereed preprint
Read the paper (PDF, 8 pages) · Complete original manuscript source and verification archive (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

For the fixed birational map L(u,v)=(u,(u^2+1)v), reduction at every prime p≡3(mod 4) permutes all of F_p^2. Its point-weighted distribution of periods divided by p has no limit. At every fixed 1/2≤ x<1, the distribution function is 1-φ(p-1)/(p-1)+o(1), with limsup 1 and liminf at most 23/24. Moreover, neither these distribution-function values nor the period measures converge on any further prime subset of positive upper relative density. The latter statement uses the classical continuous empirical law for φ(p-1)/(p-1). A supplementary proposition treats all odd primes on the invariant regular domain, and under uniform-point deletion or arbitrary exceptional-period completion. These conventions cannot restore convergence on any positive-upper-density prime selection. The contribution is a precisely delimited application to the broad existence assertion in the 2004 Oberwolfach problem on finite-field maps. The triangular family, primitive-value estimates, totient mean and scalar distribution law are established ingredients; no new arithmetic theorem or historical firstness is claimed.

A finite field has only finitely many points, so a permutation eventually repeats every point. One can record the number of steps in each point’s cycle, divide that period by the prime, and ask whether the distribution settles as the prime grows.

This paper studies one fixed map, L(u,v)=(u,(u²+1)v). For primes congruent to 3 modulo 4 it permutes the whole affine plane. Its period distribution keeps changing, even after restricting to any further collection of these primes with positive upper relative density.

The obstruction comes from the classical arithmetic quantity φ(p−1)/(p−1), the proportion of generators of a cyclic group of order p−1. An exact fiber count connects that quantity to the point-period distribution. A separate result shows that changing only the exceptional fibers at other odd primes cannot remove the obstruction under the stated uniform-point conventions.

Set L(u,v)=(u,(u²+1)v), with rational inverse L⁻¹(u,v)=(u,v/(u²+1)). It is a fixed infinite-order birational map over Q with invariant u and genus-zero generic invariant fibers. Put S={p prime : p≡3 (mod 4)}. For every p in S the reduction permutes all of F_p². If T_p(z) is a point’s least positive period, define μ_p=(1/p²)Σ_{z∈F_p²}δ_{T_p(z)/p} and D_p(x)=μ_p([0,x]). These are uniform point weights and normalization by p.

Theorem 1(i). Put θ_p=φ(p−1)/(p−1). For each fixed x∈[1/2,1), eventually as p tends to infinity in S, |D_p(x)−(1−θ_p)|≤1/p+64p^(−1/4). In particular D_p(x)=1−θ_p+o(1). The exact fiber identity is D_p(x)=1−(p−1)P_p/p² once p(1−x)>1, where P_p counts u for which u²+1 has multiplicative order p−1.
Theorem 1(ii). For every such fixed x, limsup_{p→∞, p∈S}D_p(x)=1 and liminf_{p→∞, p∈S}D_p(x)≤23/24.

Theorem 1(iii). For every A⊆S satisfying limsup_{X→∞} #{p≤X:p∈A}/#{p≤X:p∈S}>0, D_p(x) does not converge along A for any fixed x∈[1/2,1). The probability measures μ_p do not converge weakly along A either. Since S has density 1/2 among the primes, the stated relative-density condition also gives positive upper density among all primes.

Proposition 4. For every odd prime p, set N=p−1, θ_p=φ(N)/N, r_p=#{u∈F_p:u²+1=0}∈{0,2}, and Ω_p={(u,v)∈F_p²:u²+1≠0}. Its size is p(p−r_p), and L permutes Ω_p. Here P_p counts nonzero primitive multipliers u²+1. The first coordinate is fixed. On each regular vertical fiber, the map multiplies the second coordinate by u²+1. blocks.text: A finite field has only finitely many points, so a permutation eventually repeats every point. One can record the number of steps in each point’s cycle, divide that period by the prime, and ask whether the distribution settles as the prime grows.

This paper studies one fixed map, L(u,v)=(u,(u²+1)v). For primes congruent to 3 modulo 4 it permutes the whole affine plane. Its period distribution keeps changing, even after restricting to any further collection of these primes with positive upper relative density.

The obstruction comes from the classical arithmetic quantity φ(p−1)/(p−1), the proportion of generators of a cyclic group of order p−1. An exact fiber count connects that quantity to the point-period distribution. A separate result shows that changing only the exceptional fibers at other odd primes cannot remove the obstruction under the stated uniform-point conventions.

For the unit-round sphere and either the unnormalized Hilbert–Schmidt or operator-norm length metric on U(N), we give an explicit strong deformation retraction of the maps with Lipschitz constant at most 1/2 onto the constant maps. At time t ∈ [0,1], the Lipschitz constant is at most (1 − t²)/(1 + t²) times its original value. The formula depends continuously on the entire map and stays in the original U(N). In particular, it answers the literal question [?24](i) in Gromov's 2017 scalar-curvature problem list, with the stronger requirement that the Lipschitz bound be preserved throughout. The proof uses a classical matrix fractional transformation and an elementary resolvent identity.
A map can assign a unitary matrix to each point of a sphere. A small Lipschitz constant means nearby points receive nearby matrices, measured by a specified intrinsic distance on the unitary group.

This note gives an explicit way to deform every such map with Lipschitz constant at most one half into a constant map. At each time the Lipschitz constant is bounded by a known factor times its original value, so the deformation stays inside the same small-map space.

Choose one point on the sphere. The final constant is the matrix originally assigned to that point. Maps that were already constant remain fixed throughout, and the construction uses the original U(N) without enlarging the matrices.

For every finite n ≥ 2 and N ≥ 1, equip the unit-round sphere S^(n−1) with geodesic distance and U(N) with the induced length metric of either the unnormalized Hilbert–Schmidt norm ||X||HS = sqrt(tr(X*X)) or the operator norm ||X||op. Give the space of maps the uniform topology. Fix p ∈ S^(n−1). For every map Φ with intrinsic Lipschitz constant L ≤ 1/2, put A = Φ(p) and WΦ(x) = A*Φ(x). Here * denotes conjugate transpose.

For every t ∈ [0,1], Ht(Φ)(x) = A(WΦ(x) + tI)(I + tWΦ(x))^(−1) is well-defined in U(N) and satisfies Lip(Ht(Φ)) ≤ ((1 − t²)/(1 + t²)) L. It starts at Φ when t = 0 and ends at the constant Φ(p) when t = 1.

This is a jointly continuous strong deformation retraction of the closed L ≤ 1/2 sublevel onto the constant maps, and it restricts to one of the strict L < 1/2 sublevel. Every constant map is fixed at every time. Thus the based subspace Φ(p) = I is contractible; the unbased space retracts onto a copy of U(N). The theorem includes nonsmooth Lipschitz inputs.
The same conclusion holds on the two-point sphere S⁰ when its two points are assigned angular distance π. It does not use the disconnected sphere’s intrinsic path metric.

For any topological parameter space Y, a continuous family Φ: Y × S^(n−1) → U(N) whose slices satisfy the bound gives a continuous family of these deformations. For constant Q,R ∈ U(N), Ht(QΦR) = QHt(Φ)R.

After normalizing by the value at p, the sphere’s diameter and the Lipschitz bound place all image eigenangles in the closed interval [−π/2, π/2]. This keeps the fractional transformation’s inverse uniformly well-defined, including at the terminal time.

A resolvent identity gives the same quantitative differential bound for both stated matrix norms, without assuming that the matrices commute. Integrating that bound along the actual image of a shortest sphere geodesic controls intrinsic curve length and proves the Lipschitz estimate, including for nonsmooth maps.

The construction is a classical Cayley-coordinate scaling. The contribution presented here is the explicit quantitative map-space deformation and its estimate for the two specified length metrics; the Cayley transform, logarithm chart and ordinary local contractibility are classical.

The sphere is unit-round, and the target norms are exactly the unnormalized Hilbert–Schmidt norm or operator norm with their induced length metrics. Dividing the Hilbert–Schmidt norm by sqrt(N), changing the source geometry, or specifying only a shortest-geodesic normalization does not give the stated theorem for an arbitrary metric.

A fixed domain basepoint is chosen. The endpoint constant depends on the input map; the construction does not contract the constant-map copy of U(N) to one prescribed point. No nontrivial sphere-fibration, domain-rotation-equivariant or infinite-dimensional result is claimed.

The result addresses the literal small-map assertion in Gromov’s 2017 question [?24](i). The nearby discussion of the larger Lip < 1 bound and the separate sphere-fibration question are different statements. Ordinary deformation for Lip < 1 already follows from a principal logarithm chart without the same sublevel-preservation assertion.

The method’s classical ingredients are credited below. A bounded primary-source comparison does not establish first-publication priority, exhaustive novelty or continued worldwide openness. Exact algebra and numerical diagnostics in the package supplement the analytic proof; finite tests do not prove its all-dimensional or mapping-space assertions.
