article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher. Manuscript and declared publication date 12 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed research note
Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Complete original manuscript source and verification archive (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0
Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

We apply a negative-mass member of the known Dadhich–Kar–Mukherjee–Visser metric family to the regular-zero-area-singularity conjecture in Burtscher's Oberwolfach report. Its natural static slices have harmonically regular zero-area singularities of mass −2a, but the homogeneous weak second Bianchi identity fails under the boundary-reaching vector-test convention of Burtscher–Kiessling–Tahvildar-Zadeh. We prove absolute convergence of the full scalar contraction for every such compactly supported smooth test and compute its exact boundary functional; a normalized radial test gives −8π. The metric and its Einstein tensor are classical, and the flux method is already present in the cited weak-identity work. The contribution is this explicit counterexample application and its convergence check. The example violates the null energy condition. The conclusion concerns the geometric implication in the cited static-foliation framework, with no specified matter model; it asserts neither regularity on every arbitrary tilted slice nor an identity for tests smooth after collapsing the boundary sphere to a point.

The Bianchi identity is a geometric conservation identity for the Einstein tensor. It holds at every smooth interior point of the spacetime considered here. A weak version also asks what happens when one integrates against smooth test fields that reach a singular boundary.

A zero-area singularity is a boundary approached by surfaces whose physical areas shrink to zero. In this example, each natural static slice has a smooth harmonic resolution of that boundary and negative regular mass. The singular sphere is retained in the background smooth structure used to define the test fields.

Using a known negative-mass metric, the note shows that this slice geometry does not force the homogeneous weak identity under the stated retained-boundary convention. The complete scalar integral converges absolutely for every allowed vector test, but a normalized radial test gives the exact value −8π.

The example violates the null energy condition. It tests the geometric implication in the specified static framework; it does not supply a model of matter or settle variants that impose extra energy conditions or a different boundary-test convention.

Fix any a > 0. Let bar M = R_t × {x ∈ R³: ρ = |x| ≥ a}, M = int(bar M), S_a = {ρ = a}, φ = 1 − a/ρ, δ the Euclidean spatial metric and n = x/ρ. The smooth structure retains the entire boundary sphere S_a. Tests are every ψ ∈ C_c^∞(bar M; T bar M): compactly supported smooth contravariant vector fields on this manifold with boundary, with arbitrary time and angular dependence. Their normal boundary trace may be nonzero; a tangent-bundle section need not be tangent to the boundary.

Use signature (−+++), c = G_Newton = 1 and G_μν = Ric(g)_μν − (1/2)R_g g_μν, with the paper’s Ricci convention R_μν = ∂_λΓ^λ_μν − ∂_νΓ^λ_μλ + Γ^λ_μνΓ^κ_λκ − Γ^κ_μλΓ^λ_νκ. Define I_g(ψ) = ∫_M G^μ_ν ∇_μψ^ν dV_g as the integral of the complete scalar contraction.

For g = −φ^(−2)dt² + φ⁴(dρ² + ρ²dΩ²), the spacetime is static, spherically symmetric and asymptotically flat. Every slice of its natural static foliation is totally geodesic (K = 0) and has a harmonically regular zero-area singularity at S_a of regular mass −2a, including the full C¹ approaching-surface area condition.

For every test ψ in the stated class, ∫_M |G^μ_ν ∇_μψ^ν| dV_g is finite and I_g(ψ) = −(2/a²) ∫_(R × S_a) ⟨ψ_spatial,n⟩_δ dt dA_δ. Here dA_δ is Euclidean sphere area. Choose ψ = η(t)χ(ρ)∂_ρ with smooth compactly supported η, ∫η dt = 1, and smooth compactly supported χ on [a,∞) equal to 1 near a. This admissible normalized radial test gives I_g(ψ) = −8π.

The inner end is a genuine curvature singularity: Ric_μν Ric^μν = 6a²/(ρ⁶φ¹⁰) diverges as ρ decreases to a. Radial null geodesics reach it in finite affine length. It is timelike in the limiting radial conformal sense; no nondegenerate smooth extension of the physical four-metric to the boundary is asserted. The effective tensor T = G/(8π) violates the null energy condition.

The affine-lapse proposition covers every a > 0, A,B ≥ 0 with A + B > 0: set N = A + B(ρ + a)/(ρ − a) and g_N = −N²dt² + φ⁴δ. For every allowed ψ the complete scalar contraction is absolutely integrable and I_gN(ψ) = −(4A/a²) ∫_(R × S_a) ⟨ψ_spatial,n⟩_δ dt dA_δ. The homogeneous identity holds for every test in this family exactly when A = 0. The same radial test gives −16πA; A = B = 1/2 is the main metric and gives −8π. Both the vacuum endpoint A = 0, B > 0 and nonvacuum endpoint B = 0, A > 0 are included; A = B = 0 is excluded.

The spatial metric is the classical negative-mass Schwarzschild zero-area-singularity example. The resolution (δ,φ) has a simple harmonic zero with inward-to-exterior normal derivative 1/a. For every family of boundary graphs approaching in C¹, bounded Euclidean areas and the vanishing φ⁴ factor force the physical areas to zero. The standard regular-mass formula gives −2a.

The classical affine-lapse tensor becomes especially simple after multiplication by the volume density: D^i_j = Nφ⁶G^i_j = (Aa/ρ³)(6n_i n_j − 2δ_ij). This tensor is smooth to the retained boundary, symmetric, tracefree and Euclidean divergence-free. Those properties cancel the entire singular connection contraction pointwise, leaving G^μ_ν∇_μψ^ν dV_gN = D^i_j∂_iψ^j dt d³x.

On compact support the resulting complete scalar density is bounded, so its absolute integral is finite for all the stated tests. Euclidean integration by parts has inner outward normal −n and gives the exact boundary flux. Individual connection summands can have divergent integrals; the proof combines the smooth interior summands before integration. It does not use a principal value or multiply tensor distributions.

The metric and Einstein tensor are due to Dadhich, Kar, Mukherjee and Visser, the spatial regular-ZAS example and mass framework are credited to Bray and Jauregui, and the boundary-flux method is already in Burtscher, Kiessling and Tahvildar-Zadeh. The contribution presented here is the explicit counterexample application and its all-test convergence check.

The conclusion uses the natural static foliation and the retained-sphere smooth contravariant-vector test class. It is not a regularity assertion on every arbitrary tilted spacelike slice, an identity for independently smooth covectors, or an identity for fields smooth after collapsing S_a to a point. Lowering a vector with the singular metric or using the singular areal-radius collapse does not preserve the stipulated boundary smoothness.

Uniformly spacelike local tilts t = t₀ + q s(ρ), |q| < 1, have regular mass −2a/(1 − q²), but arbitrary nearly-null tilts can have a degenerate resolved radial metric. The paper expressly makes no all-arbitrary-tilted-slices claim. Its timelike-end statement concerns a limiting radial conformal causal structure, not a smooth physical extension.

Tests supported strictly inside the smooth interior obey the ordinary classical identity. The failed assertion is the homogeneous zero functional for all allowed boundary-reaching tests; the explicitly computed inhomogeneous boundary-flux identity remains valid. A zero normal boundary trace also gives zero flux.

blocks.text: The spatial metric is the classical negative-mass Schwarzschild zero-area-singularity example. The resolution (δ,φ) has a simple harmonic zero with inward-to-exterior normal derivative 1/a. For every family of boundary graphs approaching in C¹, bounded Euclidean areas and the vanishing φ⁴ factor force the physical areas to zero. The standard regular-mass formula gives −2a.

The classical affine-lapse tensor becomes especially simple after multiplication by the volume density: D^i_j = Nφ⁶G^i_j = (Aa/ρ³)(6n_i n_j − 2δ_ij). This tensor is smooth to the retained boundary, symmetric, tracefree and Euclidean divergence-free. Those properties cancel the entire singular connection contraction pointwise, leaving G^μ_ν∇_μψ^ν dV_gN = D^i_j∂_iψ^j dt d³x.

On compact support the resulting complete scalar density is bounded, so its absolute integral is finite for all the stated tests. Euclidean integration by parts has inner outward normal −n and gives the exact boundary flux. Individual connection summands can have divergent integrals; the proof combines the smooth interior summands before integration. It does not use a principal value or multiply tensor distributions.

The metric and Einstein tensor are due to Dadhich, Kar, Mukherjee and Visser, the spatial regular-ZAS example and mass framework are credited to Bray and Jauregui, and the boundary-flux method is already in Burtscher, Kiessling and Tahvildar-Zadeh. The contribution presented here is the explicit counterexample application and its all-test convergence check.

headings.text: Why the initial affine ray matters

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel · ORCID Original publication date 17 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint

Let G=D ⟨2⟩ ([0,1]) be the compactly supported, locally right 2 ℤ -affine Dlab group. We construct an automorphism preserving both Dlab orders and give a proof that it cannot be implemented after any embedding in either of two explicitly defined groups: all locally right affine increasing interval homeomorphisms, and all locally right affine increasing real homeomorphisms that are affine on an initial ray. The ambient slopes are unrestricted, and the embedding need not preserve an order. Perfectness separates the supports of commuting local groups; a two-tail construction handles both possible orientations of their least action components. This extends a one-tail mechanism used in prior work. The definitions and affine-germ decomposition of the standard Dlab families place them in these ambient groups. Consequently the construction gives an affirmative answer to the corrected Kourovka Problem 21.149, including arbitrary positive-real slope groups and the full and reflected extended-real families.

An automorphism changes the elements of a group while preserving how they compose. Conjugation implements such a change by moving to new coordinates: the same coordinate change is applied before and after every group element. An automorphism can fail to be conjugation inside its own group yet become conjugation in a larger group.

This paper constructs an automorphism of a Dlab group for which that larger-group route also fails in the stated ambient groups. The conclusion holds after every abstract injective embedding, including embeddings that do not preserve an order. The slopes allowed in the ambient group can be any positive real numbers.

The construction uses infinitely many small affine bumps approaching both ends of the source interval. A faithful action can arrange the relevant local regions in either of two orientations. One of the two tails then forces a proposed conjugating map to have a descending sequence of support components, which the ambient endpoint conditions forbid.

articles.name: Exact chordal separation of spherical Fibonacci points
outside_sections: Exact chordal separation of spherical Fibonacci points
Alec Kriebel · ORCID 0009-0001-9320-500X Published 5 October 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

This note proves an exact minimum distance for a spherical Fibonacci configuration. The north pole and the next point are the unique closest pair, for every Fibonacci number of points from two onward. The proof controls every pair, including points far apart in the defining order.
Abstract

We prove the exact finite separation conjecture stated in Brauchart’s 2012 Oberwolfach contribution: the rational, unshifted spherical Fibonacci configuration with Fₙ points has minimum Euclidean chord 2/√Fₙ for every n ≥ 3. A latitude–longitude inequality reduces the lower bound to the classical product separation of Fibonacci lattices. We include an elementary proof of the weaker arithmetic estimate needed here, making the argument self-contained.
The exact point set and result
Let F₀ = 0, F₁ = F₂ = 1 and Fₙ₊₁ = Fₙ + Fₙ₋₁. For every integer n ≥ 3, set q = Fₙ and p = Fₙ₋₁. On the unit sphere, use the points
The minimum Euclidean chord is 2/√Fₙ , uniquely attained by the unordered pair {z₀, z₁} .
A chord is the straight-line distance in three-dimensional space. The corresponding shortest distance along the unit sphere is 2 arcsin(1/√Fₙ), in radians. These are two different metrics.
Why the proof works

The pole and the next point already give the stated distance. The central task is to prove that no other pair is closer. A global latitude–longitude inequality links spherical distance to an integer separation product from the Fibonacci lattice. An elementary argument using a unimodular Fibonacci basis proves the arithmetic bound needed here. Together, the inequalities give the lower bound for all pairs and identify the only equality case.

The supporting archive includes exact arithmetic and rational chord certificates, coordinate-convention controls and reproduction instructions. These finite checks supplement the written proof of the theorem for every n ≥ 3.
Conventions and limits

The formula uses exact rational longitudes 2πpk/q and unshifted heights 1 − 2k/q with the half-open range 0 ≤ k < q. It includes the north pole and excludes the south pole. At n = 2 there is only one point and no pair.

The alternative range 1 ≤ k ≤ q gives an isometric set: relabel k as q − k and apply (x, y, z) ↦ (x, −y, −z). Its closest labels are {z q−1 , z q }. Including both endpoints instead produces a different set of q + 1 points. The reversed planar coordinate order used in the earlier lattice construction also gives an isometric unordered set, after k ≡ pj (mod q); the identity p² ≡ (−1)ⁿ (mod q) requires a reflection of the second spherical coordinate when n is odd.

The theorem does not cover midpoint-shifted heights, an irrational golden angle, arbitrary point counts or arbitrary coprime multipliers. It makes no claim about discrepancy or optimal packing among all point sets on the sphere. An equal-area map is not assumed to preserve distances.
Prior work and related manuscripts

The configuration and the pole upper bound are established ingredients. The exact separation question appears in Johann S. Brauchart’s 2012 Oberwolfach contribution , especially page 2438, published in 2013. The earlier spherical lattice construction is discussed by Aistleitner, Brauchart and Dick . The classical Fibonacci product index is due to S. K. Zaremba , with an explicit modern statement in Suryanarayana, Cools and Nuyens, Theorem 2.2 . This note supplies the all-pair spherical lower bound and its equality analysis.

A later manuscript, Alper Ferudun’s The Minimum Distance of Unshifted Spherical Fibonacci Lattices , version 1.0, dated 27 October 2026, states the same exact minimum and unique closest pair and gives a broader rational-lattice criterion using the Zaremba index. That date follows this note’s 5 October 2026 date. The archive chronology alone establishes neither independence nor influence nor absolute priority.

The note’s historical coverage leaves the fate of the cited Brauchart–Dick work in preparation and some final graphics editions unverified. It does not establish worldwide first priority or certify that the question remained open in 2026.

articles.header: Finite-type invariants on free-exterior string links: low-degree restrictions and an order-seven example Alec Kriebel · ORCID Original publication date: 13 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

article_blocks.text: Alec Kriebel · ORCID
Original publication date: 13 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

We give applications of published finite-type classification and classical genus-two symmetry to the locus of string links with free exterior group. The category is ordinary unframed smooth ordered string links with fixed boundary, upward orientation, and rational invariants. Freeness means that the actual three-dimensional exterior group is abstractly F_k. Recalling a filtered Habegger–Masbaum corollary, the intersection of the entire Milnor algebra with the two-strand order-at-most-two space is span_ℚ{1, ℓ, ℓ²}. Meilhan's classification and known free tangles give a component Conway coefficient outside the Milnor-plus-vanishing span at (k,n)=(2,2), and give zero vanishing kernel for every k ≥ 2 and 0 ≤ n ≤ 2. An exact marked genus-two reversal argument, combined with the prior Duzhin–Karev ordinary orientation detector, gives a nonzero kernel invariant of exact order seven on two strands. The seven-wheel is credited to Bar-Natan following Duzhin–Karev's journal proof. Historical priority of these combined free-exterior applications is undetermined; no firstness is claimed.
A string link is a collection of knotted strands in a cylinder, with labelled endpoints held fixed. Finite-type invariants are numerical probes of how those strands are knotted and linked.

This note studies the links whose surrounding three-dimensional exterior has a free fundamental group. That simple group condition still allows information beyond the linking number: a component Conway coefficient cannot be recovered by combining the relevant Milnor invariants with invariants that vanish on this whole locus.

articles.name: Focal pedal area ratios of closed elliptic billiards
outside_sections: Focal pedal area ratios of closed elliptic billiards
Alec Kriebel · ORCID 0009-0001-9320-500X Published 4 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

A closed billiard path inside an ellipse produces two sets of perpendicular feet from each focus: one on the path’s chord lines and another on the tangents to the ellipse. This note proves that passing from the first construction to the second multiplies both focal signed areas by the same positive factor. That factor stays fixed as the orbit moves through its family, while the ratio between the two foci can change.
Abstract

Reznik, Garcia and Koiller observed equality between the two focal pedal area ratios of a closed elliptic billiard and its outer tangent polygon. We prove this equality for every primitive convex or star orbit with a nondegenerate elliptical caustic. More precisely, the outer and original signed pedal areas are proportional by a positive constant independent of phase and common to both foci. The proof identifies a common pair of simple poles for the two cyclic area traces and matches their residues on a compact torus. It reconstructs previously used local cancellation arguments within established elliptic-function methods. We also give an exact triangular certificate showing that the common focal ratio need not be constant over the billiard family. Known even and triangular cases and classical methods are credited explicitly. This is an extensively AI-assisted, unrefereed research note, with a reproducible verification supplement.
The precise result

Fix a noncircular ellipse and a strictly nested, nondegenerate confocal elliptical caustic. Let a primitive closed orbit have N ≥ 3 sides and coprime turning number 0 < τ < N/2. Both convex and self-intersecting star orbits are included. The outer polygon is formed by consecutive intersections of the boundary tangents at the orbit’s vertices.

For the two foci F₊ and F₋, write A₊ and A₋ for the original chord-pedal areas, and B₊ and B₋ for the outer tangent-pedal areas. A pedal vertex is the perpendicular foot on the infinite supporting line. The vertices retain traversal order, and area means the signed shoelace sum.
B₊(w) = C₀ A₊(w), B₋(w) = C₀ A₋(w), C₀ > 0.

The same C₀ works at both foci and is independent of the phase w within the fixed billiard family. In positive traversal all four signed areas are strictly positive, so the focal ratios are defined at every real phase and satisfy A₊/A₋ = B₊/B₋.

Reversal negates all four areas. A positive integral repetition multiplies all four by the repetition count. The identities and nonvanishing survive both operations. The separate circular regular-star case has coincident foci, both focal ratios equal to one, and C₀ = sec²(πτ/N).
A ratio that can change

The equality of the two focal ratios does not make their common value constant. An exact triangular orbit in x²/21 + y²/16 = 1, with vertices (√21, 0), (−3√21/5, 16/5), (−3√21/5, −16/5), has a confocal caustic with squared semiaxes 189/25 and 64/25. Its multiplier is C₀ = 125/24 and its focal ratio is
Central inversion gives another phase of the same fixed-caustic family and exchanges the foci. Its ratio is the reciprocal, below one. The ratio equality and common multiplier remain valid.
Why the proof works

Canonical Jacobi coordinates turn the two area sums into meromorphic functions of the phase. Local cancellations reduce their possible singularities to the same pair of simple poles. A geometric normal-angle argument proves strict real positivity, including for stars. Matching residues leaves a holomorphic function on a compact torus; the symmetry forces that difference to vanish. This proves the proportionality throughout the family.

The supplement contains exact algebra and finite high-precision real and complex diagnostics. Those diagnostics are not interval-certified bounds and do not establish the universal theorem by sampling. Follow the archive’s reproduction instructions with Python assertions enabled.
Scope and prior work

The theorem concerns signed areas on ordered supporting lines. It excludes hyperbolic or collapsed caustics, two-period diameter walks, unsigned sums of lobe areas and projections clamped to side segments.

The original focal equality is due to Reznik, Garcia and Koiller , observed in April 2020. Their journal Table 7, page 349, labels it k607; the earlier arXiv editions use k605 and k606. Their primitive-even equality proof by central symmetry is prior work. The triangular positive case and classical nonconstancy consequence are also credited as consequences of older results, not separate discoveries.

The canonical coordinates are due to Stachel , with standard Jacobi identities from DLMF . Principal-part and elliptic-function methods are established in Khare, Lakshminarayan and Sukhatme and Roitman, Garcia and Reznik . The specialized local cancellations also appeared in the credited original-foot and outer-foot repository arguments. The supplement explains the triangular deduction from Querret, Fierobe, Garcia–Reznik and Helman and collaborators, including the phase relation needed beyond a locus shape.

Related work includes Alper Ferudun’s Focal Pedal-Antipedal Area Products , Steiner-Centroid Pedal Area Ratios and Outer-Pedal Area Products , all dated 1 October 2026, versions 1.0, 1.0 and 1.1 respectively. These concern related quantities or period classes; earlier even-period multiplier consequences are credited. This note makes no claim to a new observation, new general method, separate triangular novelty or absolute first priority. Historical coverage is bounded, and the old general locus/CAS derivations and every final journal edition have not been independently recertified.

articles.name: Loss of total-space positivity for the normalized relative Kähler–Ricci flow
outside_sections: Loss of total-space positivity for the normalized relative Kähler–Ricci flow
Alec Kriebel · ORCID 0009-0001-9320-500X Published 12 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

A geometric flow can preserve positive curvature inside each fiber of a bundle while losing positivity across the fibers. This note gives an explicit example for the probability-normalized relative Kähler–Ricci flow. The initial metric is positive in every direction on a compact total space. At a specified finite time, an actual horizontal tangent direction has negative curvature, even though the fiberwise curvature stays positive.
Abstract

We give a negative answer to the total-space positivity-preservation question for the relative Kähler–Ricci flow defined by Naumann on O_E(r). For the ample rank-two bundle E = O_{ℙ¹}(1) ⊕ O_{ℙ¹}(1), we construct a smooth strictly positive initial metric on O_E(2) ≃ O_{ℙ¹×ℙ¹}(2, 2). For the defining flow with probability-normalized fiber measures, its horizontal curvature at one point is exactly 1/96 − (1 − e^(−2t))/24, hence equals −1/96 at t = (log 2)/2. The argument uses the exact evolution of a second base derivative along a stationary central fiber and an explicit global positivity certificate.
The explicit counterexample

The base is the projective line S = ℙ¹ and the ample rank-two bundle is E = O(1) ⊕ O(1). With the convention f_*O_E(1) = E, its projectivization is X = ℙ¹ₛ × ℙ¹_z, the tautological line bundle is O_E(1) = O(1,1), and the flow runs on L = O_E(2) = O(2,2).
In finite coordinates s and z, put u = |s|², v = |z|², p = u/(1+u), x = v/(1+v), ε = 1/96 and δ = 1/4. The initial local metric weight is
φ₀ = 2 log(1+u) + (2−ε)/(1+u) + 2 log(1+v) + δ p x².

The logarithms supply the line-bundle transition weights; the remaining terms are globally smooth functions. The same metric extends smoothly through all four coordinate charts, including the joint point at infinity. Its curvature is strictly positive in every complex tangent direction everywhere on the compact X. The square-root metric, with weight φ₀/2, is therefore a positive metric on O_E(1), admissible for the original question.
For the actual nonlinear solution, every finite t ≥ 0 satisfies the exact identity at (s,z) = (0,0):

At t* = (log 2)/2 this coefficient is −1/96. The mixed curvature entry vanishes there, so this is negative curvature on the actual tangent vector ∂/∂s. The coefficient becomes negative for every t > (log(4/3))/2. Vertical curvature stays positive; on the central fiber s = 0 its coefficient remains exactly 2/(1+|z|²)².
Which flow is being solved?

The weight φ is the weight of e −φ on O_E(2). Both fiber measures in the defining equation are probabilities: MA is curvature volume divided by its fixed total mass, and μ uses an evolving fiber integral I(s,t).
∂ₜφ = log(MA(φ)/μ_φ), μ_φ = e −φ dA_z/I(s,t), I(s,t) = ∫ ℙ¹ e −φ(s,z,t) dA_z.

The density is interpreted in compatible anticanonical frames using K⁻¹_X/S = O_E(2) ⊗ f*(det E)⁻¹. It is not a scalar integrated against an arbitrarily fixed global area form. A determinant-frame factor cancels from μ. Locally, with g = φ_z z̄ > 0, this gives ∂ₜφ = log g + φ + log I + C, with a fixed convention constant C. Thus the reaction coefficient is one for this weight and time.

The proof uses the defining equation (13) in Naumann’s published paper . A literal reading of its displayed equation (14) with the same weight and time has a different rank-dependent reaction term. A stationary positive product metric detects that discrepancy; no undocumented intention or editorial explanation is assigned to the source. Changing to a root weight and rescaling time can produce a coefficient r with the corresponding changes. Dropping the evolving log I term instead changes the flow, so the stated exact time and coefficient are not transferred to that different equation.
Why the initial metric is globally positive
In product Fubini–Study unit frames, write A and B for the two diagonal curvature coefficients and Q for the squared modulus of the mixed entry. Direct differentiation gives
Explicit nonnegative-factor identities on the entire closed square 0 ≤ p,x ≤ 1 establish A ≥ ε + (167/48)p, B ≥ 3/2 and Q ≤ p/4. Consequently,
These inequalities prove positivity of the full Hermitian matrix, including mixed directions and the chart boundaries. They do not infer global positivity from sampled points.
How the nonlinear flow gives the exact formula

Uniqueness preserves the initial base-rotation symmetry. Along s = 0 all first base derivatives and the mixed curvature term vanish. The central fiber is exactly stationary because its two probability measures coincide. The actual second derivative w(z,t) = φₛₛ̄(0,z,t) therefore satisfies a closed equation:
∂ₜw = Δ_F w + w − ∫ ℙ¹ w μ_F, w(z,0) = ε + δx².

This is an exact derivative identity for the nonlinear solution, rather than a small-perturbation approximation. The probability μ_F becomes uniform measure dx on [0,1]. The modes P₁ = 2x−1 and P₂ = 6x²−6x+1 have Laplacian eigenvalues −1 and −3, giving

At x = 0 this yields the stated curvature formula. Classical smooth finite-time parabolic existence and parameter regularity, cited through Naumann’s Theorem 5 and the relative anticanonical Kähler–Ricci flow theory, justify the solution and the differentiations. Symbolic verification checks the algebra; it does not prove that analytic existence theorem. No regularity or horizontal convergence of an infinite-time limit is required.
Prior work and limits

Naumann constructed the relative flow in the 2017 Oberwolfach report and the published article ; that construction is prior work. The present example addresses their explicit total-space positivity-preservation question for the defining probability-normalized equation.

Berman’s earlier work distinguishes normalized and nonnormalized weight flows. Its preservation theorem concerns the nonnormalized weight flow, and Remark 4.11 already gives normalized anticanonical negativity in effectively parametrized Fano families. Those statements do not supply this locally isotrivial projective-space bundle example, but they rule out a broad claim of first positivity loss for normalized relative flows.

A relevant Naumann habilitation is listed by the University of Bayreuth with date 4 June 2025. Its text was not recovered for the bounded priority review, and its overlap is unknown. Historical first priority and worldwide absence of earlier examples are not asserted.

The result does not settle the Griffiths conjecture, exclude special positive initial metrics or address every normalization. The example’s bundle itself already has Griffiths-positive metrics. The contribution is this concrete finite-time counterexample with its stated normalization and analytic inputs.

articles.name: Multiplicatively Weighted Centers of Median Graphs in Quasilinear Time
articles.header: Alec Kriebel · 14 October 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0 Multiplicatively Weighted Centers of Median Graphs in Quasilinear Time The manuscript prints 14 October 2026 and no version number. Zenodo identifies this record as version 1.0; the record was created on 15 October 2026, separately from its declared publication date.
outside_sections: Alec Kriebel · 14 October 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0 Multiplicatively Weighted Centers of Median Graphs in Quasilinear Time The manuscript prints 14 October 2026 and no version number. Zenodo identifies this record as version 1.0; the record was created on 15 October 2026, separately from its declared publication date.

article_blocks.text: Alec Kriebel · 14 October 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0
The manuscript prints 14 October 2026 and no version number. Zenodo identifies this record as version 1.0; the record was created on 15 October 2026, separately from its declared publication date.

We record a short reduction from multiplicatively weighted center thresholds to additively weighted eccentricities on a graph with bounded integral distances. Combining it with the algorithm of Bergé, Ducoffe and Habib and a known implicit optimization method gives a deterministic O(n log⁵(2n)) algorithm for a center, the optimum radius and all centers of every finite unit-edge median graph. This answers the finite algorithmic form of Open Problem 1 in Ducoffe’s Oberwolfach report, without a bound on cube dimension. The contribution is the threshold observation and its consequence; neither the additive algorithm nor the optimization mechanism is new. We specify the exact comparison model and give explicit corrections to two estimates in the public preprint proof of the imported algorithm.

A weighted center chooses a vertex that minimizes the worst weighted distance to every vertex of a graph. A larger weight makes distance to that vertex more costly. Median graphs include trees and hypercubes; every three vertices have a unique median on all three pairwise shortest-path intervals.

This note turns each multiplicative distance threshold into an additive arrival-time problem, then combines credited algorithms to find the exact optimum and every vertex attaining it. The graph may have arbitrarily large cube dimension, and no embedding is supplied.

Let G=(V,E) be a finite, nonempty, connected, simple graph with unit edge lengths, n=|V| and shortest-path distance d. Each vertex u has a finite nonnegative real weight w(u). For a candidate vertex x define r_w(x)=max_{u∈V} w(u)d(x,u), the optimum ρ=min_{x∈V} r_w(x), and the full center set C_w={x∈V:r_w(x)=ρ}.

Theorem 1. Given G by adjacency lists, with the promise that G is median, and any such weight profile, a deterministic algorithm computes the exact radius ρ, one vertex in C_w and the entire set C_w in O(n log⁵(2n)) exact operations. No cube-dimension bound or supplied embedding is required. Operations on the original profile only compare bounded integer multiples k w(u), where 0≤k≤n−1.

Zero-weight vertices stay in both the graph and the candidate domain. If n=1 or all weights are zero, the radius is zero and every vertex is a center. The result concerns vertex centers with the original shortest-path distances.

Put D=n−1. For a nonnegative trial radius R, define b_R(u)=max{k∈{0,…,D}:k w(u)≤R} and a_R(u)=D−b_R(u). When w(u)=0, the budget b_R(u) equals D. Bounded binary search finds each budget using comparisons, without a real-division or unbounded-floor primitive.

For every vertex x and every R≥0, w(u)d(x,u)≤R is equivalent to d(x,u)≤b_R(u), hence to d(x,u)+a_R(u)≤D. Taking all u gives the exact identity {x:r_w(x)≤R}={x:E_{a_R}(x)≤D}, where E_a(x)=max_u(d(x,u)+a(u)). This preserves the whole feasible set, rather than only deciding whether it is empty. Negative radii are infeasible.

The imported Bergé–Ducoffe–Habib algorithm computes all additive eccentricities for a nonnegative integer arrival profile on a median graph in O(n log⁴(2n)) time, including preprocessing. Here 0≤a_R(u)≤D. The short threshold identity works for bounded integral graph distances; the efficient median-graph conclusion uses this credited additive oracle.

The optimum is one of the products k w(u). A known implicit optimization mechanism, credited to Ducoffe, searches the n sorted product rows without materializing their n² entries. The note gives a self-contained comparison-only variant: active intervals include their endpoints, lower row middles are weighted by inclusive interval lengths, and feasible equality is saved in an incumbent with a witness before deletion. These rules cover ties and zero rows. Each step deletes at least one quarter of the active entries, so O(log(2n)) oracle calls suffice; a final query at ρ returns every center.

The already published appendix supplies consistent estimates for the recursion in the named author preprint arXiv:2410.10235v1. It uses f(s)=2⌈log₂s⌉ for s≥3, direct base cases for s≤2, and a fixed-root depth estimate. Both original-arrival and fiber-arrival slice calls are retained. Total child volume at each depth is at most the root order and depth is O(log²n), giving the required additive O(n log⁴(2n)) bound. The appendix credits BDH’s algorithm and structural discoveries; it makes no assertion that the inaccessible final SODA chapter contains the same proof errors.

The operation count is an exact comparison model, not an encoding-independent bit-time bound. The optimum can be stored as a pair (k,u) representing k w(u). Overall the search uses O(n log²(2n)) comparisons of original-weight products, in addition to the imported graph operations.

For rational input w(u)=p_u/q_u with positive denominators and numerator and denominator components of at most B bits, comparing k w(u) with j w(v) compares k p_u q_v with j p_v q_u. These integers have O(B+log n) bits; their multiplication and comparison costs, and input reading, must be paid. The additive oracle’s bounded integer labels, including its internal updates, use O(log n) bits. The theorem does not promise unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic or a linear-space oracle.

The graph is finite, nonempty, connected, simple and unit-edge, supplied by adjacency lists and promised median. Recognition of median graphs, arbitrary edge lengths, continuous facilities along edges and an unspecified encoding of infinite median graphs are outside the theorem. The separate unimodality question in Ducoffe’s report is not settled by this global threshold algorithm.

The accompanying package includes exact reference controls, manuscript source and proof comparisons. Its all-pairs and brute-structure routines check finite cases; they are not a fast general implementation or an experimental proof of the asymptotic bound. Reproduction instructions require normal assertion-enabled execution.

The contribution is the short threshold observation and its consequence. The additive algorithm, implicit optimization mechanism and classical median preprocessing are credited prior work. The bounded literature assessment does not establish worldwide firstness or continued open status at a later date. The appendix’s corrections are explicitly limited to the named public author-v1 proof, whose log-base and product estimates it addresses; no claim about errors in the final SODA publication is made.

Ducoffe’s Oberwolfach report asks the finite n-vertex weighted-center algorithmic question, within a discussion that also includes infinite graphs, edge lengths and unimodality. This note answers the finite unit-edge vertex-center form without a cube-dimension bound. It does not claim all the separate questions in that discussion.

Bergé, Ducoffe and Habib provide the additive all-eccentricities algorithm and its median-graph structure. Ducoffe’s ESA 2026 Lemma 2, and Lemma 2.2 of its full author-v1 preprint, already supply the decision-to-optimization mechanism. Classical median algorithms and preprocessing, including the work of Bénéteau, Chalopin, Chepoi and Vaxès, remain dependencies.

For cube-free median graphs, Chalopin, Chepoi, Dragan, Ducoffe and Vaxès already proved the stronger O(n log²n) bound. The present O(n log⁵(2n)) result does not improve that subclass. Algorithms using a supplied tree-product embedding have a stronger representation promise; the unweighted MFCS theorem and the later weighted consequence in the workshop report are not identified as the same statement.

Substantive mathematical verification, extensions within a clearly stated model and collaboration toward journal submission are welcome. Authorship should reflect actual contributions. This is a passive invitation; no claim of an existing collaboration is implied.

Taking all u gives the exact identity {x:r_w(x)≤R}={x:E_{a_R}(x)≤D}, where E_a(x)=max_u(d(x,u)+a(u)). This preserves the whole feasible set, rather than only deciding whether it is empty. Negative radii are infeasible.

The imported Bergé–Ducoffe–Habib algorithm computes all additive eccentricities for a nonnegative integer arrival profile on a median graph in O(n log⁴(2n)) time, including preprocessing. Here 0≤a_R(u)≤D. The short threshold identity works for bounded integral graph distances; the efficient median-graph conclusion uses this credited additive oracle.

The optimum is one of the products k w(u). A known implicit optimization mechanism, credited to Ducoffe, searches the n sorted product rows without materializing their n² entries. The note gives a self-contained comparison-only variant: active intervals include their endpoints, lower row middles are weighted by inclusive interval lengths, and feasible equality is saved in an incumbent with a witness before deletion. These rules cover ties and zero rows. Each step deletes at least one quarter of the active entries, so O(log(2n)) oracle calls suffice; a final query at ρ returns every center.

The already published appendix supplies consistent estimates for the recursion in the named author preprint arXiv:2410.10235v1. It uses f(s)=2⌈log₂s⌉ for s≥3, direct base cases for s≤2, and a fixed-root depth estimate. Both original-arrival and fiber-arrival slice calls are retained. Total child volume at each depth is at most the root order and depth is O(log²n), giving the required additive O(n log⁴(2n)) bound. The appendix credits BDH’s algorithm and structural discoveries; it makes no assertion that the inaccessible final SODA chapter contains the same proof errors.

blocks.text: Ducoffe’s Oberwolfach report asks the finite n-vertex weighted-center algorithmic question, within a discussion that also includes infinite graphs, edge lengths and unimodality. This note answers the finite unit-edge vertex-center form without a cube-dimension bound. It does not claim all the separate questions in that discussion.

Bergé, Ducoffe and Habib provide the additive all-eccentricities algorithm and its median-graph structure. Ducoffe’s ESA 2026 Lemma 2, and Lemma 2.2 of its full author-v1 preprint, already supply the decision-to-optimization mechanism. Classical median algorithms and preprocessing, including the work of Bénéteau, Chalopin, Chepoi and Vaxès, remain dependencies.

For cube-free median graphs, Chalopin, Chepoi, Dragan, Ducoffe and Vaxès already proved the stronger O(n log²n) bound. The present O(n log⁵(2n)) result does not improve that subclass. Algorithms using a supplied tree-product embedding have a stronger representation promise; the unweighted MFCS theorem and the later weighted consequence in the workshop report are not identified as the same statement.

article_blocks.text: By Alec Kriebel · ORCID
Version 1.0.1, 23 September 2026
Unrefereed preprint; version 1.0.1. Developed with extensive AI assistance; no external human or journal peer review, journal acceptance or formal proof-assistant certification is claimed.
Read the complete preprint (PDF, 3 pages) · Complete source and verification package (ZIP) · Original checksums · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0

The universal Harrell–Stubbe bound for a gap between consecutive Dirichlet eigenvalues is never attained on a nonempty bounded open subset of Euclidean space at a finite index. This answers negatively the corrected saturation question recorded in the 2009 Oberwolfach report on low eigenvalues. We prove the stronger statement that Yang’s first inequality is strict at every real threshold above the lowest eigenvalue. The proof uses the classical spectral remainder and a short obstruction to finite spectral support of a coordinate times an eigenfunction. No boundary regularity or connectedness assumption is needed.

For a membrane fixed along its edge, Dirichlet eigenvalues are proportional to squared vibration frequencies. More generally, they describe the Laplacian on a bounded region in any positive dimension.
A classical inequality bounds the gap between consecutive eigenvalues using averages of earlier eigenvalues. This note proves that equality never occurs at a finite index for the Dirichlet Laplacian.
The proof also makes Yang’s first inequality strict at every real threshold above the lowest eigenvalue. It includes disconnected regions, rough boundaries and repeated eigenvalues.

Let n ≥ 1 be an integer and let Ω be any nonempty bounded open subset of Rⁿ. Use the Dirichlet Laplacian defined by the energy form on H₀¹(Ω), and list its eigenvalues 0 < E₁ ≤ E₂ ≤ ⋯ with multiplicity. No boundary regularity or connectedness is assumed.

For every integer J ≥ 1, define A_J = (1/J) Σ_{j=1}^J E_j, B_J = (1/J) Σ_{j=1}^J E_j², M₁ = ((n + 2)/n) A_J and M₂² = ((n + 4)/n) B_J. Then M₁² − M₂² > (E_{J+1} − E_J)²/4. Thus the classical gap bound cannot be attained at any finite index.
More strongly, for every real z > E₁, Σ_{E_j<z} (z − E_j)² < (4/n) Σ_{E_j<z} (z − E_j)E_j. These are finite sums over the eigenvalues strictly below z.
Repeated eigenvalues and zero gaps are included. The proof also covers an index ending inside a repeated eigenspace, including the case E_{J+1} = E₁.
The classical commutator trace identity expresses the difference between the two sides of Yang’s inequality as a nonnegative sum over higher spectral modes.

The equality obstruction is short: multiplying a real Dirichlet eigenfunction by a coordinate cannot produce a finite sum of eigenfunctions. If it did, the differentiated eigenvalue equation and self-adjointness would force a derivative vector to vanish, contradicting an integration-by-parts identity. The argument uses the form-defined operator and distributions, so it does not require a smooth boundary.

The high-mode remainder therefore cannot vanish above the lowest eigenvalue. Completing the square in the resulting quadratic inequality then gives the strict gap bound, with multiplicities handled explicitly.

The theorem concerns the form-defined Dirichlet Laplacian on nonempty bounded open Euclidean sets. Neumann or periodic boundary conditions, unbounded sets and operators with added potentials are different models.

The 2009 Oberwolfach report defines rooted moments M_p but prints M₁² − M₂ in its gap displays. This paper explicitly uses the corrected expression M₁² − M₂², which matches Harrell and Stubbe’s original inequality and scales homogeneously. The negative answer concerns that corrected saturation question.

Finite nonattainment is compatible with sharp leading Weyl asymptotics. It supplies no uniform positive deficit and does not resolve the adjacent quantitative growth question or the separate question about E_J ≤ M_p.

The trace identities and non-strict inequalities are classical and are credited below. The contribution presented here is the explicit nonattainment conclusion and its short equality argument. A bounded source comparison does not certify historical firstness, exhaustive novelty or continued worldwide openness.
Exact algebra and certified box-spectrum checks in the package supplement the analytic proof. They do not machine-prove the theorem for arbitrary domains or provide proof-assistant certification.

headings.text: Why the map vanishes on homology

article_blocks.text: Alec Kriebel · ORCID 0009-0001-9320-500X
17 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
The manuscript prints version 1.0.0 and 17 October 2026, matching the Zenodo version and declared publication date.

Let G be a compact Lie group whose component group is not p-nilpotent, and let k be any field of characteristic p. For R=C_*(Ω((BG)^∧_p);k), we prove that the canonical k-cellularization map ΓₖR→R induces zero in every homotopy degree. This answers Greenlees's Question 2.2 in Oberwolfach Report 9/2026. No adjoint-orientability, component-action, or spectral-sequence-collapse assumption is needed. The proof combines classical proxy-smallness and the finite-ideal theorem for Hopf algebras: each homotopy class in a cellular source factors through a module with finite total homology, whose image in an infinite-dimensional graded Hopf algebra must vanish.

Cellularization is a standard way to approximate a module by objects assembled from the coefficient field. It comes with a canonical map back to the original module. This note proves that, for the completed loop-chain algebras in the theorem, that full map sends every homology class to zero.

The result applies to every prime and every field of that characteristic, including infinite field extensions. It includes both finite and positive-dimensional compact Lie groups with the stated component-group condition. The conclusion concerns induced homology maps; it does not assert that the map itself is zero in the derived category.

Fix any prime p and any field k of characteristic p. Let G be any compact Lie group whose finite group of connected components π₀G is not p-nilpotent. A finite group is p-nilpotent when it has a normal subgroup of order prime to p and index a power of p.

Set X=(BG)^∧_p using Bousfield–Kan p-completion, then R=C_*(ΩX;k). Completion is taken before looping. We work with left modules over this augmented differential graded k-algebra, equivalently with Hk-linear modules. Their homotopy groups π_n are the homology groups of the associated chain complexes.

Theorem 1. For the full canonical k-cellularization map ν:ΓₖR→R, the induced map π_n(ν):π_n(ΓₖR)→π_nR is zero for every integer n. No adjoint-orientability, nilpotent component-action or spectral-sequence/tensor-collapse assumption is imposed. The conclusion is not restricted to a degree range or to a projection into component-group homology.

The note also proves a general cellular vanishing criterion. Let A be an augmented differential graded k-algebra and let Loc_A(k) be the smallest localizing subcategory of left A-modules containing the augmentation module k. Suppose k is proxy-small over A and the multiplication on H_*(A) admits a graded Hopf-algebra structure over k, with Koszul signs, of infinite total dimension. Then every A-linear map f:M→A from every M∈Loc_A(k) induces zero on homology in every degree.

Proxy-smallness means that there is a compact proxy K with K∈thick_A(A)∩thick_A(k) and k∈Loc_A(K). Here thick means finite construction by shifts, finite sums, cones and retracts. Only K is required to be compact; compactness of k is not assumed. Infinite total dimension is distinct from a statement about the dimension of each separate degree.

heading.text: Why the map vanishes on homology

article_blocks.text: The algebraic input is the classical finite-ideal theorem: an infinite-dimensional graded Hopf algebra with Koszul signs has no nonzero finite-dimensional graded left or right ideal. The paper recalls the ordinary argument and treats graded signs by forgetting them in characteristic two or using parity bosonization otherwise. No bijectivity assumption on the antipode is needed.

heading.text: Why the map vanishes on homology

article_blocks.text: Proxy-smallness gives a finite approximation for each homology class separately. If M is k-cellular, each class in H_n(M) comes from some P∈thick_A(K), whose total homology is finite-dimensional. Compact Morita theory and filtered finite constructions supply these stages. This does not say that the whole cellular module has finite homology, or that all its classes pass through one common finite stage.

heading.text: Why the map vanishes on homology

article_blocks.text: For an A-linear map f:M→A, the composite P→M→A has a finite-total-dimensional image in H_*(A). A-linearity makes that image a graded left ideal. The Hopf theorem forces it to vanish, so f kills the chosen class. Applying this argument to every class proves the all-cellular-source, all-map criterion.

heading.text: Why the map vanishes on homology

article_blocks.text: For completed loop chains, the existing Dwyer–Greenlees–Iyengar proxy-smallness result applies to every compact Lie group. Extending chains and a compact proxy from the prime field F_p to k preserves the required finite constructions and homotopy colimits. The argument does not interchange an infinite cochain dual with scalar extension.

heading.text: Why the map vanishes on homology

article_blocks.text: Loop multiplication, diagonal and inversion give H_*(ΩX;k) its graded Hopf structure, with the field Künneth identification. In this application, p-compactness of BG means finite total mod-p homology of Ω((BG)^∧_p). Ishiguro's necessary implication BG p-compact ⇒ π₀G p-nilpotent therefore gives infinite total homology by contraposition under the theorem's hypothesis. Field extension preserves that infinite dimension. The general criterion then applies to the full canonical map ΓₖR→R.

heading.text: Why the map vanishes on homology

article_blocks.text: The proof combines algebraic and topological arguments using the credited classical inputs. The supporting exact finite tests check the graded sign conventions; they do not establish an infinite or topological theorem by sampling.

The coefficient is a field of characteristic p and G is compact Lie with the specified non-p-nilpotent component group. No general coefficient-ring or noncompact-group extension, converse, or transfer to uncompleted loop chains is asserted. Completion before looping is part of the statement.

The theorem gives a homology ghost: all induced homology maps vanish. It does not assert a null morphism in the derived category, and it is not replaced by a statement only about component-group homology. No orientability, component-action or collapse hypothesis is added to the full result.

The general criterion retains its proxy-smallness and infinite-total-dimensional Hopf hypotheses. For example, when A=k the cellularization is the identity, so the infinite-dimensional hypothesis cannot simply be deleted. The approximation is class by class and does not impose finite total homology on arbitrary cellular sources.

The prior-source comparison uses the actual pinned Greenlees v3 and Lomp author-version interfaces and the cited published DGI, BIS and Ishiguro interfaces. It does not claim that every final journal body or the earlier Sweedler, Dwyer–Greenlees and Ishiguro original proofs were freshly read. Historical firstness, exhaustive literature absence and present worldwide openness are not certified.

Greenlees's Question 2.2 in Oberwolfach Report 9/2026, printed page 594, asks the full cellularization-map vanishing question for positive-dimensional compact Lie groups. The note answers that stated question in the non-p-nilpotent component-group setting and also includes finite groups.

The finite-group result is already in Greenlees's arXiv:2504.03050v3, Lemma 6.2. Its Section 6 also contains restricted compact-Lie conclusions with orientability context, nilpotent-action or restricted-image conditions, and an additional tensor-collapse condition in the relevant statements. Those prior results and their ranges remain credited. The inspected author v3 is not silently identified with final journal bytes.

The Hopf finite-ideal input is classical, credited to Sweedler through Lomp's Section 2.4. Compact proxies and Morita machinery are due to Dwyer, Greenlees and Iyengar. Briggs, Iyengar and Stevenson give related filtered finite-construction arguments. The note supplies the class-by-class step explicitly and does not take an unrestricted compactness conclusion from that source. No novelty is claimed for these constituent results.

The topological application uses Ishiguro's published 2007 Proposition 1.3(a), which supplies the necessary p-compactness implication. The cited earlier original proof is treated as prior input rather than claimed to have been newly reproduced. The contribution is the combination giving the stated full-map result, without a worldwide first-priority or continued-open-status claim.

Independent verification of the algebraic or topological argument, a well-supported primary-source comparison, or substantive work toward journal submission would be welcome. Authorship would be considered in relation to actual contributions.

article_blocks.text: Alec Kriebel · ORCID 0009-0001-9320-500X
17 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
The manuscript prints version 1.0 and 17 October 2026, matching the Zenodo version and declared publication date.

We exhibit an eleven-vertex tree T with ordinary L(2,1) initial-segment palette size 5 and arbitrary-list parameter 6. An explicit assignment of five-element positive-integer lists is infeasible by a short forcing argument. An ordinary five-palette labeling and the known Δ+3 tree list bound give the exact values. This contradicts the universal equality stated in Kohl's 2006 Conjecture 4 and dissertation Conjecture 4.4. Independent pendant-path extensions give infinitely many examples of unbounded diameter. Historical priority, minimal order and present openness are not claimed.

Distance labeling assigns integers to vertices with two separation rules: adjacent vertices must be at least two apart, and vertices two edges apart must receive different integers. A list assignment specifies which integers each vertex may use.

This note gives an eleven-vertex tree that can be labeled using the common palette {1,2,3,4,5}, but fails for one assignment of five allowed integers at each vertex. Six allowed integers at each vertex always suffice on this tree, however those positive integers are chosen. The same gap persists after independently extending its six leaves by arbitrary finite paths.

An L(2,1)-labeling of a finite simple graph uses positive integers, with |f(u)−f(v)|≥2 on every edge and f(u)≠f(v) whenever u and v have graph distance two. The ordinary parameter is the least k admitting a labeling from the common initial segment [k]={1,…,k}. The list parameter is the least k for which every assignment of k-element positive-integer sets L(v) admits a labeling f(v)∈L(v). Lists are not restricted to intervals or to a prescribed common bounded palette. These are numerical separation constraints; arbitrary renaming of labels need not preserve them.

The tree T has spine a−b−c−d−e, leaves a₁ and a₂ attached to a, leaf b₁ attached to b, leaf d₁ attached to d, and leaves e₁ and e₂ attached to e. These are all its vertices and edges. Thus T has eleven vertices, ten edges, maximum degree three, radius three and diameter six.
Set A={1,2,3,4,5} and B={1,3,4,5,6}. Assign B to a₁,a₂,e₁,e₂ and A to every other vertex.

Theorem 1. This displayed five-element list assignment has no L(2,1)-labeling. The exact ordinary initial-segment palette parameter of T is 5, equivalently its ordinary zero-based span is λ(T)=4, and its exact arbitrary-list parameter is 6. Palette size and zero-based span differ by one.

Known tree bound. For every nonempty finite tree S, every assignment of (Δ(S)+3)-element positive-integer lists admits an L(2,1)-labeling. In particular, every six-element list assignment works on the displayed tree. The proof includes the singleton case.

Corollary 1. For every independently chosen six-tuple (m₁,…,m₆) of nonnegative finite integers, attach one path of mᵢ new edges outward from the corresponding original leaf of T. Every resulting finite tree S has ordinary initial-segment palette parameter 5, zero-based span 4 and arbitrary-list parameter 6. Zero lengths are allowed, and no parity or equal-length condition is imposed. Allowing one length to grow gives a family of unbounded diameter.

At b, the three neighbors all have list A and must be pairwise distinct. A proposed label 2,3 or 4 leaves at most two choices for them, so b must receive 1 or 5. The same holds at d; since b and d are at distance two, their endpoint labels differ. Reflecting the tree, which preserves the list assignment, permits b=1 and d=5, forcing c=3.

The edge ab and the distance-two pair ac then force a=4 or a=5. If a=4, both a₁ and a₂ have only label 6 available; if a=5, both have only label 3 available. They are at distance two and must differ, giving the contradiction.

An ordinary witness, in vertex order (a,b,c,d,e,a₁,a₂,b₁,d₁,e₁,e₂), is (1,5,3,1,5,3,4,2,4,2,3). A degree-three vertex rules out [4], because each possible center label leaves at most two admissible labels for three mutually distance-two neighbors. This proves the ordinary parameter is exactly five.

For the general list upper bound, root a finite tree and label in breadth-first order. A nonroot vertex has only its parent earlier at distance one, forbidding at most three integers. Its earlier distance-two vertices are its grandparent, if present, and earlier siblings, at most Δ−1 vertices. At most Δ+2 integers are forbidden in total, so any (Δ+3)-element list leaves a choice. This is a self-contained proof of the credited known bound.

The pendant-path extensions preserve all old distances and keep maximum degree three. Along each added path, the parent forbids at most three labels of [5] and the grandparent at most one, so the ordinary witness extends. New vertices on different added paths are at distance at least four. Restriction to the old tree preserves the lower bounds; extending its bad lists by any five-element lists on the new vertices preserves infeasibility. The general upper bound supplies six for every resulting tree.

The argument is elementary and does not depend on computational search. The complete supporting package records the graph, lists, witness, manuscript source and finite exact checks. Those checks support the fixed construction; the written proofs carry the universal list and path-length quantifiers.

The result concerns finite simple trees and the stated positive-integer L(2,1) model. The number five is the ordinary initial-segment palette size, four is the corresponding zero-based span, and six is a list cardinality guarantee. None is substituted for another, and the list theorem is not narrowed to interval lists or a common palette.

No minimum vertex order, historical firstness, new general obstruction mechanism or present worldwide open status is established. The counterexample addresses the universal equality as stated in the cited historical sources. Verification using a supplied construction does not establish independent discovery.

The source comparison used the actual 2006 Oberwolfach and dissertation interfaces and the actual 2001 institutional preprint. Some final journal mathematical bodies were not obtained, and repository deposit-date metadata was not independently authenticated. These access limits are not used to infer priority or to identify a preprint silently with a later journal edition.

A. Kohl's 2006 Oberwolfach contribution states the universal equality between ordinary and arbitrary-list parameters for trees as Conjecture 4, printed page 416. The 2006 dissertation states the matching Conjecture 4.4, printed page 124. The eleven-vertex tree contradicts that stated equality in the same numerical and positive-integer conventions; no claim is made that the question remained open immediately before this note.

The general tree list bound is prior work, credited to Voigt through Kohl's Oberwolfach page 416 and its reference to Kohl, Schreyer, Tuza and Voigt's 2005 paper. The note includes its own short L(2,1) proof for self-contained verification. It does not claim novelty for that bound; the complete 2005 journal mathematical body was not obtained for the source comparison.

General-graph separations were known earlier. Fiala and Škrekovski's 2001 institutional preprint, Figure 4 on printed page 14, gives a ten-vertex cyclic graph with an ordinary five-palette labeling and infeasible five-element lists. That figure is not a tree counterexample. The actual 2001 preprint is credited as such, with no identity asserted with the differently titled 2005 journal version.

Independent verification, a well-supported primary-source comparison or substantive work toward a journal submission would be welcome. Authorship would be considered in relation to actual contributions.

article_blocks.text: Alec Kriebel · ORCID 0009-0001-9320-500X
22 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23578599

We compute the intersection of the closed Nash sets of the complete family of prime divisors obtained by n successive free point blowups over (ℂ²,0), after fixing a prefix of k centers, where 2≤k<n. In suitable coordinates the intersection is {ord x≥⌈n/k⌉, ord y≥n}. For five blowups, fixing two or three centers gives the thresholds (3,5) or (2,5). Neither is q(1,j) for positive integers q,j. These examples disprove the specified-reference-multiple assertion in Conjecture 1 of Fernández de Bobadilla, Pe Pereira and Popescu-Pampu, under each contact and indexing convention explicitly treated here. The source's bare equivalence symbol is undefined and its indexing is inconsistent; no unique author-intended correction is asserted. The intersections are themselves maximal divisorial sets for other toric divisors. Thus the result does not disprove an assertion allowing an arbitrary divisor, or solve the generalized Nash problem.

An arc is a parametrized curve near a point, described here by two formal power series. Blowing up a point replaces it with an exceptional curve that records directions. A sequence of blowups produces divisors, and each divisor determines a closed set of arcs called its Nash set.

This note varies every free continuation of a fixed initial sequence of centers and computes the arcs belonging to every resulting closed Nash set. Five blowups give intersections that cannot be the claimed contact multiple of any divisor in the fixed reference chain.
The conclusion concerns a specified reference divisor. The same intersections do come from other toric divisors, so the result does not rule out an arbitrary-divisor formulation.
Work in the centered complex formal arc space 𝒜={(x(t),y(t)):x,y∈tℂ[[t]]}, with ord 0=+∞. The sets below are Zariski-closed sets of arcs, equivalently reduced supports.

For every n≥3 and 2≤k<n, fix the first k centers c₁,…,cₖ of the length-n free chain following y=0. Let 𝓕ₙ,ₖ be the complete family of final prime divisors with that all-free combinatorial type and fixed prefix. In regular coordinates every member is represented by P(x)=Σᵢ₌ₖⁿ⁻¹aᵢxⁱ and y=P(x)+xⁿw, with every coefficient tuple (aₖ,…,aₙ₋₁)∈ℂⁿ⁻ᵏ allowed. This is the entire free family, not a selected subfamily. Smooth curvettas and further free blowups are included; no restriction to minimal embedded resolutions of singular branches is imposed.

For its final divisor E_P, the closed Nash set is N̄_Eₚ={ord x≥1, ord(y−P(x))≥n}. Taking the intersection over all coefficients gives Iₙ,ₖ=⋂_{E′∈𝓕ₙ,ₖ}N̄_E′={ord x≥⌈n/k⌉, ord y≥n}. Requiring exactly k common centers means aₖ≠0 and gives the same closed intersection.

Let Dⱼ be the divisor created at the jth center of the zero reference chain, continued further if necessary. For every positive j and q, the closure of exact-contact-q arcs is Cont̄^q(Dⱼ)={ord x≥q, ord y≥jq}. Closing the at-least-q contact locus gives the same formula.

For n=5,k=2 the intersection is {ord x≥3, ord y≥5}; for n=5,k=3 it is {ord x≥2, ord y≥5}. Neither threshold pair is (q,jq) for any positive integers j,q. The exclusion is for all reference indices and multiplicities, not a bounded computation.

articles.name: A projective-line quotient of the Rogalski–Sierra algebra
outside_sections: A projective-line quotient of the Rogalski–Sierra algebra
Alec Kriebel · ORCID 0009-0001-9320-500X · 16 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

article_blocks.text: Alec Kriebel · ORCID 0009-0001-9320-500X · 16 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

For the six-relation presentation R(α, β) in Rogalski and Sierra’s 2010 report and 2012 article, the linear ideal (x₃−x₁, x₄−x₂) has a projective-line twisted homogeneous coordinate ring as its exact quotient. It is a nonzero homogeneous completely prime ideal strictly below the augmentation ideal. This gives negative answers to both printed assertions: uniqueness of the nontrivial graded prime and absence of nontrivial maps to twisted homogeneous coordinate rings. The calculation works over every field whenever β²≠1, hence for all the prescribed algebraically independent parameters. The classical twist machinery is credited; historical priority of this explicit quotient remains unresolved.

A noncommutative algebra can change substantially when two pairs of generators are identified. This note studies one specific identification in the Rogalski–Sierra algebra. The resulting quotient is a familiar twisted coordinate ring of the projective line, with its multiplication written explicitly.

The proof identifies the entire kernel, so the map gives a nonzero completely prime ideal as well as an infinite-dimensional quotient. These supply counterexamples to two literal printed assertions about the original presentation. The construction uses classical machinery, and its historical priority remains unresolved.

Let k be any field and let α, β∈k. Give each generator degree one and define the connected graded associative algebra R=R(α,β)=k⟨x₁,x₂,x₃,x₄⟩/(f₁,…,f₆) by the following six quadratic relations. Products are ordered; the second left factor in both f₅ and f₆ is x₄.
f₁=x₁(αx₁−x₃)+x₃(x₁−αx₃); f₂=x₁(αx₂−x₄)+x₃(x₂−αx₄); f₃=x₂(αx₁−x₃)+x₄(x₁−αx₃); f₄=x₂(αx₂−x₄)+x₄(x₂−αx₄); f₅=x₁(βx₁−x₂)+x₄(x₁−βx₂); f₆=x₁(βx₃−x₄)+x₄(x₃−βx₄).

Theorem 1. For every field k, every α∈k and every β∈k with β²≠1, let I=(x₃−x₁,x₄−x₂) be the two-sided ideal and let σ[s:t]=[s+βt:βs+t] on P¹_k. Then R/I≅k⟨X,Y⟩/(βX²−XY+YX−βY²)≅B(P¹_k,O(1),σ). The map sends x₁,x₃ to s and x₂,x₄ to t, and its kernel is exactly I.

The ideal is homogeneous and completely prime, with 0≠I⊊R₊, where R₊ is the augmentation ideal consisting of positive-degree elements. The quotient is a domain for arbitrary elements, so I is both an ordinary prime and a graded prime. Its degree-n dimension is n+1 for every n≥0, its Hilbert series is (1−z)⁻², and its Gelfand–Kirillov dimension is 2.

The twisted homogeneous coordinate ring uses positive pullbacks: Lₙ=O(1)⊗σ⁎O(1)⊗⋯⊗(σⁿ⁻¹)⁎O(1), Bₙ=H⁰(P¹_k,Lₙ), with L₀=O. For f of degree m, multiplication is f⋆g=f⊗(σᵐ)⁎g. The fixed linear lift gives Lₙ≅O(n), and O(1) is σ-ample.

For algebraically independent α,β over the prime subfield of an uncountable algebraically closed field, β²≠1 automatically. The nontrivial prime I contradicts the printed claim that R₊ is the only nontrivial graded prime. The unital graded surjection onto this infinite-dimensional curve ring contradicts the printed claim that no nontrivial homomorphism to a twisted homogeneous coordinate ring exists. Those assertions impose no injectivity, birationality or lower bound on image dimension.

Substituting x₃=x₁=X and x₄=x₂=Y sends the six defining relations to 0,0,0,0,Q,Q, where Q=βX²−XY+YX−βY². The universal property of free-algebra quotients gives exactly the displayed two-generator quotient. Showing that a relation vanishes in a target would by itself give only a map; the rest of the argument proves there is no additional kernel.

On k[s,t], use the invertible linear automorphism θ(s)=s+βt and θ(t)=βs+t. Its determinant is 1−β². The positive graded twist f⋆g=fθᵐ(g), for f of degree m, is associative, generated in degree one and a domain. It has the same graded vector spaces as the polynomial plane. Its multiplication agrees with the stated projective-line section multiplication.

blocks.text: Let k be any field and let α, β∈k. Give each generator degree one and define the connected graded associative algebra R=R(α,β)=k⟨x₁,x₂,x₃,x₄⟩/(f₁,…,f₆) by the following six quadratic relations. Products are ordered; the second left factor in both f₅ and f₆ is x₄.
f₁=x₁(αx₁−x₃)+x₃(x₁−αx₃); f₂=x₁(αx₂−x₄)+x₃(x₂−αx₄); f₃=x₂(αx₁−x₃)+x₄(x₁−αx₃); f₄=x₂(αx₂−x₄)+x₄(x₂−αx₄); f₅=x₁(βx₁−x₂)+x₄(x₁−βx₂); f₆=x₁(βx₃−x₄)+x₄(x₃−βx₄).

Theorem 1. For every field k, every α∈k and every β∈k with β²≠1, let I=(x₃−x₁,x₄−x₂) be the two-sided ideal and let σ[s:t]=[s+βt:βs+t] on P¹_k. Then R/I≅k⟨X,Y⟩/(βX²−XY+YX−βY²)≅B(P¹_k,O(1),σ). The map sends x₁,x₃ to s and x₂,x₄ to t, and its kernel is exactly I.

The ideal is homogeneous and completely prime, with 0≠I⊊R₊, where R₊ is the augmentation ideal consisting of positive-degree elements. The quotient is a domain for arbitrary elements, so I is both an ordinary prime and a graded prime. Its degree-n dimension is n+1 for every n≥0, its Hilbert series is (1−z)⁻², and its Gelfand–Kirillov dimension is 2.

The twisted homogeneous coordinate ring uses positive pullbacks: Lₙ=O(1)⊗σ⁎O(1)⊗⋯⊗(σⁿ⁻¹)⁎O(1), Bₙ=H⁰(P¹_k,Lₙ), with L₀=O. For f of degree m, multiplication is f⋆g=f⊗(σᵐ)⁎g. The fixed linear lift gives Lₙ≅O(n), and O(1) is σ-ample.

For algebraically independent α,β over the prime subfield of an uncountable algebraically closed field, β²≠1 automatically. The nontrivial prime I contradicts the printed claim that R₊ is the only nontrivial graded prime. The unital graded surjection onto this infinite-dimensional curve ring contradicts the printed claim that no nontrivial homomorphism to a twisted homogeneous coordinate ring exists. Those assertions impose no injectivity, birationality or lower bound on image dimension.

12 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

The classical Robinson sextic is nonnegative, but adding any nonnegative constant does not make it a sum of polynomial squares modulo the ideal of polynomials vanishing on its real tangency variety. This rules out both the exact radical certificate and the positive-constant certificate in the proposed unrestricted replacement of the gradient ideal. The same obstruction applies to the separate-cross-product ideal printed in the original report. Ten zero lines force the low-degree homogeneous parts of all square summands to vanish; an additional coordinate axis then makes the certificate impossible. The proof allows arbitrarily many summands of arbitrary degree and is entirely elementary. We credit the classical form and zero-set method, and make no claim of first bibliographic priority.

A sum of real polynomial squares is always nonnegative. One way to certify that a polynomial is nonnegative is to express it as such a sum, allowing an additional polynomial that vanishes on a chosen set. The choice of that set matters.

This note applies Robinson’s classical sextic to two proposed ideal-only certificates. The polynomial is nonnegative everywhere, yet neither certificate works, even after adding any nonnegative constant. The obstruction permits any finite number of square summands with arbitrary real coefficients and arbitrary finite degrees. It is not a failure found by searching only up to a degree cutoff.
Work in S=ℝ[x,y,z]. For a polynomial f, write f_x, f_y and f_z for its partial derivatives. Define the two ideals separately:
J_f=(y f_x−x f_y, z f_x−x f_z, z f_y−y f_z). K_f=(y f_x, x f_y, z f_x, x f_z, z f_y, y f_z).

For an ideal L, V_ℝ(L) is the set of real points where every polynomial in L vanishes. Let I_ℝ(L) be the full ideal of all real polynomials vanishing on that set, and let ΣS² denote finite sums of squares of real polynomials. The ordinary radical satisfies L⊆√L⊆I_ℝ(L).
The Robinson sextic is R=x⁶+y⁶+z⁶−x⁴y²−x²y⁴−x⁴z²−x²z⁴−y⁴z²−y²z⁴+3x²y²z².
Theorem 1. R is nonnegative on all of ℝ³. For both L=J_R and L=K_R and every real ε≥0, R+ε ∉ ΣS²+I_ℝ(L).

Equivalently, there are no finite m, real polynomials q₁,…,q_m of arbitrary degrees, and h∈I_ℝ(L) with R+ε=∑q_j²+h. No fixed degree bound or bound on the finite summand count is imposed. The theorem includes ε=0 and every positive constant.

Consequently R∉ΣS²+√L, and R+ε∉ΣS²+L for every ε>0, for each of the two ideals. Thus global nonnegativity does not imply either proposed ideal-only certificate. R attains its minimum zero; removing an attainment assumption includes attained examples.

Tangency-minor nonnegativity equivalence. For every real polynomial f in n≥1 variables, nonnegativity on ℝⁿ is equivalent to nonnegativity on the real variety of the minors x_j f_{x_i}−x_i f_{x_j}. No global minimum-attainment or bounded-infimum hypothesis is needed. A negative value away from the origin produces a negative minimum on a compact sphere, where the gradient is parallel to the radius; the origin itself always belongs to the variety. For n=1 there are no minors and the variety is the whole line.

Separate-product diagnostic. In two variables let Q(x,y)=(1−xy)²+y²−1/2 and K_Q=(y Q_x,x Q_y). Then V_ℝ(K_Q)={(0,0)}, where Q=1/2, although Q(2,1/2)=−1/4. Its infimum −1/2 is not attained, since equality would require both y=0 and xy=1; Q(1/u,u)=u²−1/2 approaches that infimum. This is a constant shift of a standard nonattaining example. It concerns only the separate-product reading and does not contradict the tangency-minor equivalence.

The nonnegativity is a classical Schur calculation. Put a=x², b=y² and c=z². The symmetric expression for R can be written as (a−b)²(a+b−c)+c(a−c)(b−c). After ordering a≥b≥c≥0, both terms are nonnegative.

The ten directions (1,s,t), (1,s,0), (1,0,t) and (0,1,t), with each applicable sign independently equal to ±1, give ten whole zero lines of R. Each line lies in both real varieties because the gradient vanishes at every global minimizer. The coordinate axis (u,0,0) also lies in both varieties, and R(u,0,0)=u⁶.

Suppose a certificate existed. On a zero line it would give ε=∑q_j(uv)² for every real u. Each restricted polynomial is bounded and therefore constant. The classical ten-zero cubic argument then forces every square summand’s homogeneous parts of degrees one, two and three to vanish identically. Its constant part is retained; for positive ε it need not be zero.

On the coordinate axis the same certificate gives u⁶+ε=∑q_j(u,0,0)². A restriction of degree above three would contribute a strictly positive highest coefficient that cannot cancel with the other real squares. Thus every restriction has degree at most three. The already-vanishing low-degree parts make every restriction constant, contradicting u⁶+ε. This handles arbitrary finite degrees without assuming the whole variety is finite or the original ideal is radical.

blocks.text: Work in S=ℝ[x,y,z]. For a polynomial f, write f_x, f_y and f_z for its partial derivatives. Define the two ideals separately:
J_f=(y f_x−x f_y, z f_x−x f_z, z f_y−y f_z). K_f=(y f_x, x f_y, z f_x, x f_z, z f_y, y f_z).

For an ideal L, V_ℝ(L) is the set of real points where every polynomial in L vanishes. Let I_ℝ(L) be the full ideal of all real polynomials vanishing on that set, and let ΣS² denote finite sums of squares of real polynomials. The ordinary radical satisfies L⊆√L⊆I_ℝ(L).
The Robinson sextic is R=x⁶+y⁶+z⁶−x⁴y²−x²y⁴−x⁴z²−x²z⁴−y⁴z²−y²z⁴+3x²y²z².
Theorem 1. R is nonnegative on all of ℝ³. For both L=J_R and L=K_R and every real ε≥0, R+ε ∉ ΣS²+I_ℝ(L).

Equivalently, there are no finite m, real polynomials q₁,…,q_m of arbitrary degrees, and h∈I_ℝ(L) with R+ε=∑q_j²+h. No fixed degree bound or bound on the finite summand count is imposed. The theorem includes ε=0 and every positive constant.

Consequently R∉ΣS²+√L, and R+ε∉ΣS²+L for every ε>0, for each of the two ideals. Thus global nonnegativity does not imply either proposed ideal-only certificate. R attains its minimum zero; removing an attainment assumption includes attained examples.

Tangency-minor nonnegativity equivalence. For every real polynomial f in n≥1 variables, nonnegativity on ℝⁿ is equivalent to nonnegativity on the real variety of the minors x_j f_{x_i}−x_i f_{x_j}. No global minimum-attainment or bounded-infimum hypothesis is needed. A negative value away from the origin produces a negative minimum on a compact sphere, where the gradient is parallel to the radius; the origin itself always belongs to the variety. For n=1 there are no minors and the variety is the whole line.

Separate-product diagnostic. In two variables let Q(x,y)=(1−xy)²+y²−1/2 and K_Q=(y Q_x,x Q_y). Then V_ℝ(K_Q)={(0,0)}, where Q=1/2, although Q(2,1/2)=−1/4. Its infimum −1/2 is not attained, since equality would require both y=0 and xy=1; Q(1/u,u)=u²−1/2 approaches that infimum. This is a constant shift of a standard nonattaining example. It concerns only the separate-product reading and does not contradict the tangency-minor equivalence.
