blocks.text: The nonnegativity is a classical Schur calculation. Put a=x², b=y² and c=z². The symmetric expression for R can be written as (a−b)²(a+b−c)+c(a−c)(b−c). After ordering a≥b≥c≥0, both terms are nonnegative.

The ten directions (1,s,t), (1,s,0), (1,0,t) and (0,1,t), with each applicable sign independently equal to ±1, give ten whole zero lines of R. Each line lies in both real varieties because the gradient vanishes at every global minimizer. The coordinate axis (u,0,0) also lies in both varieties, and R(u,0,0)=u⁶.

Suppose a certificate existed. On a zero line it would give ε=∑q_j(uv)² for every real u. Each restricted polynomial is bounded and therefore constant. The classical ten-zero cubic argument then forces every square summand’s homogeneous parts of degrees one, two and three to vanish identically. Its constant part is retained; for positive ε it need not be zero.

On the coordinate axis the same certificate gives u⁶+ε=∑q_j(u,0,0)². A restriction of degree above three would contribute a strictly positive highest coefficient that cannot cancel with the other real squares. Thus every restriction has degree at most three. The already-vanishing low-degree parts make every restriction constant, contradicting u⁶+ε. This handles arbitrary finite degrees without assuming the whole variety is finite or the original ideal is radical.

22 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
Original printed and Zenodo edition: version 1.0.0, dated 22 October 2026. Native record creation is separately recorded in the metadata.

For each fixed field of positive characteristic p, we construct a single compatible symmetric chain of Artinian ideals in two rows of variables, generated from width three. At every width n ≥ 2, its quotient has both the weak and strong Lefschetz properties exactly when p ∤ n − 1. The quadratic quotient is free over the integers, and a determinant for an arbitrary linear form gives the classification over every field extension. In particular, over the fixed infinite field 𝔽ₚ(t) both properties hold and fail at unbounded widths. This gives a negative answer to the unrestricted eventual dichotomies posed by Römer. It gives no negative answer in characteristic zero or in one row.

The weak Lefschetz property asks whether multiplication by one linear form has the largest possible rank between consecutive graded pieces of an Artinian algebra. The strong property asks for the same behavior for every positive power of that one form.

This note gives a single symmetric family whose answer keeps changing as its width grows. Over a field of positive characteristic p, the obstruction recurs whenever n − 1 is divisible by p. The field and the defining rule stay fixed throughout the family.
Fix any field K. For width n ≥ 1, let Rₙ = K[x₁,…,xₙ,y₁,…,yₙ] and 𝔪ₙ = (x₁,…,xₙ,y₁,…,yₙ). Define the homogeneous ideal
Iₙ = 𝔪ₙ³ + (xᵢxⱼ : i ≠ j) + (yᵢyⱼ : 1 ≤ i,j ≤ n) + (xᵢyᵢ : 1 ≤ i ≤ n) + (xᵢyⱼ − xᵢyₖ : i,j,k pairwise distinct).

Here 𝔪ₙ³ includes every cubic monomial, including repeated variables; an empty index condition contributes no generators. The quotient Aₙ = Rₙ/Iₙ is Artinian. Every injection of column sets respects the ideals, so the chain is compatible with simultaneous column permutations in both rows. For every n ≥ 3, Iₙ = (Sym(n)I₃)Rₙ: the entire chain is generated from width three.

For every field K and every n ≥ 2, the Hilbert function is (1,2n,2n), and Aₙ has SLP if and only if it has WLP if and only if (n − 1)1_K ≠ 0. The same classification holds after every field extension, including extensions of finite fields. Width one is a separate case: its Hilbert function is (1,2,1), and it has SLP.

For each prime p, work over the single fixed infinite field K = 𝔽ₚ(t). Among n ≥ 2, exactly the widths n ≡ 1 (mod p) are bad. In particular, both properties hold at n = 2 + kp for every k ≥ 0, and both fail at n = 1 + kp for every k ≥ 1. Both sequences are unbounded. This disproves the unrestricted eventual alternatives in Römer’s question for one fixed field and one fixed two-row chain.

The quadratic quotient is already free over the integers. For n ≥ 2 it has degree-two basis uᵢ = [xᵢ²] and vᵢ = [xᵢyⱼ], where any j ≠ i gives the same vᵢ. For each fixed i, the relations identify these mixed terms without introducing torsion, so this basis survives base change to every field.

For an arbitrary linear form ℓ = Σᵢ(aᵢxᵢ + bᵢyᵢ), multiplication from degree one to degree two has determinant (−1)ⁿ⁻¹(n − 1)∏ᵢaᵢ². At a bad width this vanishes for every choice of coefficients, not just for a symmetric test form. Independently, the nonzero degree-one element Σⱼyⱼ is then killed by every linear form.

At a good width, ℓ = x₁ + ⋯ + xₙ gives an invertible middle-degree map. Its square is Σᵢuᵢ ≠ 0, including in characteristic two. These maps cover all powers with nonzero source and target needed for SLP. The proof uses standard integral linear algebra, rank, determinant and socle methods; the contribution is this explicit chain and its complete classification.

The counterexample uses two rows in fixed positive characteristic. In characteristic zero this particular construction has SLP at every width. It gives no negative answer for arbitrary characteristic-zero chains or for the one-row variant. The width-one exception must not be folded into the n ≥ 2 congruence rule.

The universal written proof establishes the infinite-width and all-field statements. The archive’s finite exact computations supplement that proof. Neither those computations nor bounded literature checks certify exclusive firstness, exhaustive novelty or the present worldwide open status of other variants.

Tim Römer’s original contribution, “Asymptotic properties of invariant chains,” fixes an arbitrary field and an arbitrary fixed number of rows c ≥ 1. Its Artinian-chain question asks whether WLP or SLP eventually always holds or eventually always fails. That contribution is on printed pages 1594–1596 of Oberwolfach Report 31/2020. The separate working-group discussion on pages 1544–1545 focuses on one-row monomial ideals; it is a different scope.

Alexandra Seceleanu and Liana Şega’s “General symmetric ideals,” arXiv:2506.15459v1, gives positive results for general symmetric ideals in one row. Its Theorem B assumes an infinite field of characteristic zero or characteristic greater than n, positive integers d,r, and n ≥ max{d + 1, 1 + (1/r)Σᵢ₌₀ᵈ⁻¹P(i)}, where P(i) is the number of integer partitions of i. Under these hypotheses a general (r,d)-symmetric ideal has WLP. Its chain Theorem 9.2, summarized in Theorem C, assumes characteristic zero, positive d,r with r ≤ P(d), a general starting ideal at a width m sufficiently large for Construction 6.8, and n ≥ m. These hypotheses differ from the fixed-positive-characteristic two-row chain here. The v1 arXiv header is dated 18 June 2025; the PDF’s internal date is 19 June 2025.

David Cook II’s work provides standard background on characteristic-sensitive Lefschetz properties. None of these external theorems is needed in this note’s self-contained proof. The earlier project proof in PR1337 is unpublished. The Oberwolfach DOI identifies the original question; this preprint’s solution DOI is 10.5281/zenodo.23570763.

blocks.text: For each fixed field of positive characteristic p, we construct a single compatible symmetric chain of Artinian ideals in two rows of variables, generated from width three. At every width n ≥ 2, its quotient has both the weak and strong Lefschetz properties exactly when p ∤ n − 1. The quadratic quotient is free over the integers, and a determinant for an arbitrary linear form gives the classification over every field extension. In particular, over the fixed infinite field 𝔽ₚ(t) both properties hold and fail at unbounded widths. This gives a negative answer to the unrestricted eventual dichotomies posed by Römer. It gives no negative answer in characteristic zero or in one row.

blocks.text: The weak Lefschetz property asks whether multiplication by one linear form has the largest possible rank between consecutive graded pieces of an Artinian algebra. The strong property asks for the same behavior for every positive power of that one form.

This note gives a single symmetric family whose answer keeps changing as its width grows. Over a field of positive characteristic p, the obstruction recurs whenever n − 1 is divisible by p. The field and the defining rule stay fixed throughout the family.

blocks.text: Fix any field K. For width n ≥ 1, let Rₙ = K[x₁,…,xₙ,y₁,…,yₙ] and 𝔪ₙ = (x₁,…,xₙ,y₁,…,yₙ). Define the homogeneous ideal
Iₙ = 𝔪ₙ³ + (xᵢxⱼ : i ≠ j) + (yᵢyⱼ : 1 ≤ i,j ≤ n) + (xᵢyᵢ : 1 ≤ i ≤ n) + (xᵢyⱼ − xᵢyₖ : i,j,k pairwise distinct).

Here 𝔪ₙ³ includes every cubic monomial, including repeated variables; an empty index condition contributes no generators. The quotient Aₙ = Rₙ/Iₙ is Artinian. Every injection of column sets respects the ideals, so the chain is compatible with simultaneous column permutations in both rows. For every n ≥ 3, Iₙ = (Sym(n)I₃)Rₙ: the entire chain is generated from width three.

For every field K and every n ≥ 2, the Hilbert function is (1,2n,2n), and Aₙ has SLP if and only if it has WLP if and only if (n − 1)1_K ≠ 0. The same classification holds after every field extension, including extensions of finite fields. Width one is a separate case: its Hilbert function is (1,2,1), and it has SLP.

For each prime p, work over the single fixed infinite field K = 𝔽ₚ(t). Among n ≥ 2, exactly the widths n ≡ 1 (mod p) are bad. In particular, both properties hold at n = 2 + kp for every k ≥ 0, and both fail at n = 1 + kp for every k ≥ 1. Both sequences are unbounded. This disproves the unrestricted eventual alternatives in Römer’s question for one fixed field and one fixed two-row chain.

blocks.text: The quadratic quotient is already free over the integers. For n ≥ 2 it has degree-two basis uᵢ = [xᵢ²] and vᵢ = [xᵢyⱼ], where any j ≠ i gives the same vᵢ. For each fixed i, the relations identify these mixed terms without introducing torsion, so this basis survives base change to every field.

For an arbitrary linear form ℓ = Σᵢ(aᵢxᵢ + bᵢyᵢ), multiplication from degree one to degree two has determinant (−1)ⁿ⁻¹(n − 1)∏ᵢaᵢ². At a bad width this vanishes for every choice of coefficients, not just for a symmetric test form. Independently, the nonzero degree-one element Σⱼyⱼ is then killed by every linear form.

At a good width, ℓ = x₁ + ⋯ + xₙ gives an invertible middle-degree map. Its square is Σᵢuᵢ ≠ 0, including in characteristic two. These maps cover all powers with nonzero source and target needed for SLP. The proof uses standard integral linear algebra, rank, determinant and socle methods; the contribution is this explicit chain and its complete classification.

blocks.text: The counterexample uses two rows in fixed positive characteristic. In characteristic zero this particular construction has SLP at every width. It gives no negative answer for arbitrary characteristic-zero chains or for the one-row variant. The width-one exception must not be folded into the n ≥ 2 congruence rule.

The universal written proof establishes the infinite-width and all-field statements. The archive’s finite exact computations supplement that proof. Neither those computations nor bounded literature checks certify exclusive firstness, exhaustive novelty or the present worldwide open status of other variants.

blocks.text: Tim Römer’s original contribution, “Asymptotic properties of invariant chains,” fixes an arbitrary field and an arbitrary fixed number of rows c ≥ 1. Its Artinian-chain question asks whether WLP or SLP eventually always holds or eventually always fails. That contribution is on printed pages 1594–1596 of Oberwolfach Report 31/2020. The separate working-group discussion on pages 1544–1545 focuses on one-row monomial ideals; it is a different scope.

Alexandra Seceleanu and Liana Şega’s “General symmetric ideals,” arXiv:2506.15459v1, gives positive results for general symmetric ideals in one row. Its Theorem B assumes an infinite field of characteristic zero or characteristic greater than n, positive integers d,r, and n ≥ max{d + 1, 1 + (1/r)Σᵢ₌₀ᵈ⁻¹P(i)}, where P(i) is the number of integer partitions of i. Under these hypotheses a general (r,d)-symmetric ideal has WLP. Its chain Theorem 9.2, summarized in Theorem C, assumes characteristic zero, positive d,r with r ≤ P(d), a general starting ideal at a width m sufficiently large for Construction 6.8, and n ≥ m. These hypotheses differ from the fixed-positive-characteristic two-row chain here. The v1 arXiv header is dated 18 June 2025; the PDF’s internal date is 19 June 2025.

David Cook II’s work provides standard background on characteristic-sensitive Lefschetz properties. None of these external theorems is needed in this note’s self-contained proof. The earlier project proof in PR1337 is unpublished. The Oberwolfach DOI identifies the original question; this preprint’s solution DOI is 10.5281/zenodo.23570763.

article_blocks.text: Alec Kriebel · ORCID 0009-0001-9320-500X
12 October 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
The manuscript is dated 12 October 2026 and prints no version number; 1.0 is the Zenodo version.

Let V be the ordinary, uncompleted complex algebra of all finite-order finite-type invariants of links. We give a principal ideal with a nonempty actual-link zero set whose vanishing ideal strictly contains its radical. The generator is g(4g-1), where g is the sum of squared pairwise linking numbers. The obstruction is a character on the entire algebra, obtained by evaluating the standard twist-restriction polynomial at a nonintegral parameter. This gives a negative answer to the arbitrary-ideal formulation of Bar-Natan's Problem 2.27, as recorded by Ohtsuki; the separate linking-number-generated ideal question is not decided.

A link invariant assigns a number to a collection of intertwined circles. Finite-type invariants form an algebra: they can be added and multiplied. One can ask whether knowing which actual links make an ideal vanish determines that ideal up to taking powers, as in a Nullstellensatz.

This note gives an explicit negative answer to the arbitrary-ideal, actual-link formulation. Its ideal has plenty of actual zeros, including the unlink, yet an invariant vanishing on all those zeros has no positive power in the ideal. The distinction comes from an algebra character that no actual link realizes; it does not contradict the classical Hilbert Nullstellensatz.

For every integer m≥2, let X_m be the oriented, unordered m-component links in S³, including split links. Let V_m be their ordinary, uncompleted unital complex algebra of finite-type invariants, with pointwise operations. Order at most d means that the positive-minus-negative crossing extension vanishes on every link with d+1 double points. Each invariant has some finite order; there is no common order cutoff on the whole algebra and no completion by infinite-order series.

For an ideal A, Z_act(A) means its common zero set among actual links, and J_act(S) means all invariants vanishing on S. The radical rad(A) consists of invariants that have a positive power in A. The always-valid containment is rad(A)⊆J_act(Z_act(A)).

Theorem 1. Set g(L)=Σ_{i<j}lk(L_i,L_j)², f=g(4g−1), and A=fV_m. Then Z_act(A) is exactly the nonempty set of algebraically split links: every pairwise linking number is zero. Moreover g∈J_act(Z_act(A)) but g∉rad(A), so the containment is strict. The unlink belongs to the zero set.

The same construction works in the algebra V on all finite-component links, where each invariant has one finite order valid across that whole domain. The finite-type orders are at most two for g and four for f, uniformly in the number of components. The global argument restricts each such invariant to one fixed-component family; it does not assume that every fixed-component invariant extends to all links.

The construction also works for ordered or labelled links, after forgetting orientations by pullback, and over every characteristic-zero coefficient field. The linking-square expression is unchanged by component permutations or orientation reversals. Its actual integer values are considered before embedding into the coefficient field; no ordering of that field is assumed.

The proof companion also records the integer-valued ring version: restriction gives rational Newton polynomials and a ring homomorphism V_Z→Q, yielding the same obstruction. This is not an arbitrary coefficient-ring or positive-characteristic assertion.

On a crossing-resolution cube, an order-d finite-type invariant has a multilinear representative of degree at most d. Products of orders d and e therefore have order at most d+e. Each pairwise linking number is affine on such a cube, so g has order at most two and f has order at most four.

For an actual link, g is a nonnegative integer, being a sum of squares of integer linking numbers. Thus g(4g−1)=0 exactly when g=0, which is exactly when every pairwise linking number vanishes. These are actual integer linking numbers, not arbitrary complex coordinates. Because the algebra contains the unit and A is generated by f, zeros of f are precisely the common zeros of A.

Let L_n, for every integer n≥0, be the coherently oriented closure of the two-strand braid σ^(2n), with m−2 split unknots added. It has m components and g(L_n)=n². Changing a designated crossing in each added two-crossing block either retains that full twist or cancels the block. The resulting signed resolution cube is the forward difference Δ^r[v(L_n)]. This is a crossing-change argument, not smoothing; every resolution keeps the same component count.

If v has order at most d, then Δ^(d+1)[v(L_n)]=0 for every n≥0. Newton's difference formula gives a unique polynomial P_v(t) of degree at most d agreeing with v(L_n) at all nonnegative integers. Agreement on infinitely many integers shows P_(uv)=P_uP_v and preserves sums and the unit. This constructs a homomorphism on the entire finite-order algebra, rather than assuming a character on C[g] extends to a larger ring.

Evaluate that polynomial formally at one half: χ(v)=P_v(1/2). This is a character on the whole algebra, with χ(g)=1/4 and χ(f)=0. For every N≥1 and every finite-order multiplier h, an equation g^N=fh would imply 4^(−N)=0, which is impossible in characteristic zero. Thus no positive power of g lies in A. The proof has no upper bound on N or on the order of h.

The same contradiction can be read as polynomial divisibility: t^(2N) cannot equal t²(4t²−1)P_h(t), because evaluation at t=1/2 makes the right side zero and the left side nonzero. The finite-order polynomial argument proves the universal statement; the accompanying exact-rational checks support its formulas and conventions.

Formal evaluation at one half is not evaluation on an actual link, including the one-component closure of σ. Actual-link values of g are integers, whereas this character gives 1/4. The counterexample concerns using actual links as the available evaluation points; it is not a failure of the classical Hilbert Nullstellensatz on its usual algebraic spectrum.

The principal ideal A=fV_m is different from the ideal generated by all indexed pairwise linking numbers. That indexed ideal belongs to the ordered or labelled theory, where individual component pairs are distinguished. In that theory the two ideals have the same actual zero set, but g already belongs to the indexed linking-number ideal, so this witness does not decide its radical/vanishing-ideal question.
Algebraically split means that all pairwise linking numbers vanish. It does not mean that the link is geometrically split. The theorem includes split links and does not impose a non-split hypothesis.

No conclusion about completed invariant algebras, homogeneous-ideal variants, positive characteristic, or a knot-only counterexample is asserted. With only one component, g is identically zero, so the displayed witness does not give a knot-only result. Replacing actual links by all algebra characters would change the question.

Polynomiality along twist and braid families is established prior work. The contribution recorded here is its elementary application to the explicit principal ideal and nonempty actual-link zero set. Historical firstness, independent discovery, an exhaustive absence of predecessors and present worldwide openness are not established.

Bar-Natan's Problem 2.27, recorded by Ohtsuki on printed page 422, asks the arbitrary-ideal question using actual links as zeros. The collection has volume year 2002 and was published in 2004. Its separate indexed linking-number example remains distinct from the principal-ideal counterexample here.

The polynomiality input is classical. Stanford–Trapp's Theorem E treats full-twist differences; Eisermann develops finite-type polynomiality and the Newton interpretation. Stoimenow's 2010 Theorem 2.1 and Definitions 2.2–2.3 provide an earlier braid-sequence interface and explicitly credit earlier braiding-sequence work. No new polynomiality method is claimed.

Stoimenow's theorem is read with its local odd-exponent and default non-split conventions. One fixed crossing together with local exponent 2n−1 gives even total exponent 2n. The manuscript's direct singular-link argument independently handles the stated full-twist family and all split components. Jeong–Park's connected-sum polynomiality is a related older route, not silently identified with a varying-linking family.

The source comparison supports these specific classical interfaces, including the exact 2010 theorem and its conventions. It does not certify every earlier or final-version proof, exhaustive literature coverage, or the absence of an earlier equivalent ideal counterexample. These limits do not replace the self-contained all-order proof.
Independent verification, a well-supported primary-source comparison or substantive work toward a journal submission would be welcome. Authorship would reflect actual contributions.

blocks.text: On a crossing-resolution cube, an order-d finite-type invariant has a multilinear representative of degree at most d. Products of orders d and e therefore have order at most d+e. Each pairwise linking number is affine on such a cube, so g has order at most two and f has order at most four.

For an actual link, g is a nonnegative integer, being a sum of squares of integer linking numbers. Thus g(4g−1)=0 exactly when g=0, which is exactly when every pairwise linking number vanishes. These are actual integer linking numbers, not arbitrary complex coordinates. Because the algebra contains the unit and A is generated by f, zeros of f are precisely the common zeros of A.

Let L_n, for every integer n≥0, be the coherently oriented closure of the two-strand braid σ^(2n), with m−2 split unknots added. It has m components and g(L_n)=n². Changing a designated crossing in each added two-crossing block either retains that full twist or cancels the block. The resulting signed resolution cube is the forward difference Δ^r[v(L_n)]. This is a crossing-change argument, not smoothing; every resolution keeps the same component count.

If v has order at most d, then Δ^(d+1)[v(L_n)]=0 for every n≥0. Newton's difference formula gives a unique polynomial P_v(t) of degree at most d agreeing with v(L_n) at all nonnegative integers. Agreement on infinitely many integers shows P_(uv)=P_uP_v and preserves sums and the unit. This constructs a homomorphism on the entire finite-order algebra, rather than assuming a character on C[g] extends to a larger ring.

Evaluate that polynomial formally at one half: χ(v)=P_v(1/2). This is a character on the whole algebra, with χ(g)=1/4 and χ(f)=0. For every N≥1 and every finite-order multiplier h, an equation g^N=fh would imply 4^(−N)=0, which is impossible in characteristic zero. Thus no positive power of g lies in A. The proof has no upper bound on N or on the order of h.

The same contradiction can be read as polynomial divisibility: t^(2N) cannot equal t²(4t²−1)P_h(t), because evaluation at t=1/2 makes the right side zero and the left side nonzero. The finite-order polynomial argument proves the universal statement; the accompanying exact-rational checks support its formulas and conventions.

Formal evaluation at one half is not evaluation on an actual link, including the one-component closure of σ. Actual-link values of g are integers, whereas this character gives 1/4. The counterexample concerns using actual links as the available evaluation points; it is not a failure of the classical Hilbert Nullstellensatz on its usual algebraic spectrum.

The collection has volume year 2002 and was published in 2004. Its separate indexed linking-number example remains distinct from the principal-ideal counterexample here.

The polynomiality input is classical. Stanford–Trapp's Theorem E treats full-twist differences; Eisermann develops finite-type polynomiality and the Newton interpretation. Stoimenow's 2010 Theorem 2.1 and Definitions 2.2–2.3 provide an earlier braid-sequence interface and explicitly credit earlier braiding-sequence work. No new polynomiality method is claimed.

Stoimenow's theorem is read with its local odd-exponent and default non-split conventions. One fixed crossing together with local exponent 2n−1 gives even total exponent 2n. The manuscript's direct singular-link argument independently handles the stated full-twist family and all split components. Jeong–Park's connected-sum polynomiality is a related older route, not silently identified with a varying-linking family.

The source comparison supports these specific classical interfaces, including the exact 2010 theorem and its conventions. It does not certify every earlier or final-version proof, exhaustive literature coverage, or the absence of an earlier equivalent ideal counterexample. These limits do not replace the self-contained all-order proof.

articles.name: Five outgoing centers in a 16-realization cube move
outside_sections: Five outgoing centers in a 16-realization cube move
Alec Kriebel · 15 October 2026 · Unrefereed research note
ORCID · DOI and Zenodo record
Original abstract

We specify six algebraic boundary points, an incoming center, and at least five distinct outgoing centers for a cube move of 16-realizations. Existence follows from strict rational sign bounds for two continuous one-variable residuals. The boundary parameters are uniquely defined real roots of monotone polynomials. This contradicts the at-most-three expectation for construction curves sharing a focus in Remark 4.8 of Melotti–Ramassamy–Thévenin, in the realization setting allowing crossings. The fixed boundary is crossed, so the example concerns no proper embedding. Neither the exact number of centers for this boundary nor a universal maximum is determined.
Overview
A local cube move replaces one central point by another while keeping six boundary points fixed. The quadrilateral rule equates the sums of opposite side lengths raised to a chosen power.

At power 16, this note gives one fixed algebraic boundary with an incoming center and at least five outgoing choices. The same boundary works for all of them; its segments cross, so this is a realization allowing crossings.
Result

Six fixed distinct algebraic points A₁,…,A₆, with both alternating triples noncollinear, admit an incoming center Z and at least five distinct outgoing centers X at α = 16. Every selected center differs from every boundary point.

A quadrilateral PQRS is an α-quad when |P−Q|^α + |R−S|^α = |P−S|^α + |Q−R|^α. The three incoming ordered faces are A₁A₂A₃Z, A₃A₄A₅Z and A₅A₆A₁Z; the three outgoing ordered faces are A₂A₃A₄X, A₄A₅A₆X and A₆A₁A₂X. All six identities hold for the same boundary.

The outgoing centers are at least five intersections of two distinct smooth construction curves sharing the focus A₂. This exceeds the at-most-three expectation for α > 1 in Melotti–Ramassamy–Thévenin, Remark 4.8, p. 811, and the maximum-three conjecture in the crossing-permitted workshop setting, p. 1785. The cited existence theorem is a separate statement.
Why it works
Set A = (0,0), B = (2073/10000,0), C = (4719/10000,64/10000) and λ = 27/1250. The outgoing equations are |X−B|¹⁶ − |X−A|¹⁶ = λ and |X−C|¹⁶ − |X−A|¹⁶ = 1.

With s = |X−A|¹⁶, nonnegative real eighth roots give the three squared distances. An invertible linear system recovers X; one continuous residual G(s) then characterizes the original equations in both directions, retaining all real-branch constraints.

Strict rational signs at 9/10000, 11/10000, 13/10000, 1/2, 1 and 10¹⁶ alternate. The intermediate value theorem supplies a zero in each of five disjoint finite intervals. Different s give different centers; uniqueness within an interval is unnecessary. A concavity estimate controls the remote endpoint without subtracting nearly equal large radicals.

Three uniquely defined real roots of monotone rational polynomials fix the other boundary vertices. Their exact edge-power identities telescope. For this same fixed boundary, a second continuous residual has opposite strict endpoint signs and produces an actual incoming center. The written algebra verifies every incoming and outgoing ordered face, including the dependent third incoming identity.
Exact rational enclosures separate the selected centers from boundary vertices and every line through a boundary pair. A strict orientation pattern proves an interior crossing of [A₁,A₂] and [A₃,A₄].

Each common-focus curve is individually smooth because its powered-distance difference has a nonzero gradient. The boundary point A₃ lies on one curve and has a strictly positive residual for the other, proving that the two curves are distinct sets. This individual regularity does not assert joint transversality of their intersections.

The original standard-library verifier and rational certificate accompany the proof. Its default command recomputes and compares the complete certificate without writing; integer and Fraction arithmetic decide the signs. The existence argument uses the written distance equivalence, monotone boundary definitions, strict signs and exact face identities.
Scope
The fixed boundary crosses. It cannot yield a proper embedding for any choice of central point, and the construction concerns the realization and immersion conventions that permit crossings.

At least five is a lower bound. The exact total for this boundary and a universal maximum are undetermined here. No result for α < 1, root uniqueness within the brackets or joint intersection transversality is asserted.
The note does not establish historical firstness, independence from unknown work or the present worldwide status of stronger questions.
Background and earlier work

Melotti–Ramassamy–Thévenin define the α-quad and cube-move realization setting, including crossed faces. Their Remark 4.8 states the common-focus intersection-count expectation addressed by this construction. The Oberwolfach contribution states the corresponding maximum-three conjecture for crossing-permitted α-immersions.

Weighted-distance and pure-power families predate this note. Ash–Bolker study costs φ(|x−P|)+w(P), including a fourth-power example. Their separate oscillatory cost t+k sin(t) is a different example and does not itself settle this pure-power shared-focus count.

Bourne–Peletier–Roper define p-power costs |x−xᵢ|^p−wᵢ in the author manuscript, Definition 4.12; Bourne–Roper also discuss this established family. At p = 16 with weights (0,λ,1), equality of the three costs is exactly the displayed outgoing system. The contribution here is the explicit fixed-boundary count construction, with its incoming witness and face identities.

Original abstract

For two polytopes, retain the faces of their Minkowski sum whose two canonical summands have positive dimensions and whose dimension is the sum of those dimensions. This is the definition in Payne’s printed Oberwolfach question. Let D be the standard four-simplex and I = [0,1]. For the full-dimensional lattice polytopes D × I and (−D) × I in ℝ⁵, the qualifying-face order complex is a disjoint union of two connected pure graphs, each with 50 vertices and 60 edges. Its rational Betti numbers are (2,22,0,…). Thus both printed assertions, shellability and the homology of a wedge of three-spheres, fail. The shared interval factor deliberately produces a nongeneric example. The argument concerns the printed additive-dimension definition; it does not settle shellability for the different mixed faces used in stable tropical intersections.
Overview

A Minkowski sum adds every point of one polytope to every point of another. Each exposed face has canonical faces from the two summands. The printed question keeps only faces where both summands have positive dimension and their dimensions add exactly.

For two explicit lattice polytopes in five dimensions, the resulting face-inclusion complex splits into two loop-filled graphs. This gives negative answers to both the shellability and sphere-wedge homology assertions in the printed question.
Result
Let D = conv(0,e₁,e₂,e₃,e₄) be the standard four-simplex and I = [0,1]. Both P₁ = D × I and P₂ = (−D) × I are full-dimensional lattice 5-polytopes.

Retain F = F₁ + F₂ when its canonical summands, exposed by the same functional, satisfy dim F₁ > 0, dim F₂ > 0 and dim F = dim F₁ + dim F₂. Form the ordinary order complex: its vertices are qualifying faces and its simplices are nonempty strict chains. No artificial minimum or maximum is adjoined.

This complex is K ⊔ K. Each K is a connected pure graph with 50 vertices and 60 edges, homotopy equivalent to a wedge of eleven circles. The ordinary rational homology is H₀ = ℚ², H₁ = ℚ²² and Hⱼ = 0 for j ≥ 2. The complex is not shellable under either pure or standard nonpure shellability, and it does not have the homology of a wedge of three-spheres.
Why it works

Proper nonempty faces of the simplex difference D−D are indexed by nonempty disjoint subsets A,B of its five vertex labels. Their dimensions add, and inclusion is exactly containment in each label set. The positive-dimension filter keeps the size pairs (2,2), (2,3) and (3,2): 30 minimal faces and 20 maximal faces, with 60 comparabilities and no three-element strict chains. Their graph K is connected.

The common interval factor is decisive. Qualifying faces with a nonzero interval coefficient in their exposing functional form the two endpoint copies of K. With zero coefficient, each summand gains an interval direction but the sum gains only one, so exact dimension additivity fails. The full-base end faces and the whole sum fail the filter too; no qualifying face links the two copies.

Each connected graph has 60−50+1 = 11 independent cycles. In any proposed shelling, the first edge from the second component meets the earlier edges only in the empty face, rather than the required zero-dimensional intersection. This rules out both shellability conventions. Two components and nonzero first homology also rule out the printed sphere-wedge target.
The paper gives the complete analytic face argument. Two exact standard-library checkers accompany it as supplementary verification; the proof does not depend on running them.
Definitions and limits

The shared interval deliberately makes this example nongeneric. Payne’s printed Problem 3 states no general-position condition. No generic-perturbation theorem, minimum-dimension claim, historical firstness or present worldwide openness is asserted.

The exact-additivity filter is different from Adiprasito’s public 2020 manuscript underlying a 2024 article, which requires dim(Σ_{i∈J} Fᵢ) ≥ |J| for every nonempty index subset J. A vertical face with summand dimensions 2 and 2 and sum dimension 3 passes those lower bounds but fails exact additivity. This note does not contradict that stable-intersection theorem or settle its shellability question.

Adiprasito and coauthors’ colorful-Gale “totally mixed” convention instead requires facets of the summands. Hiatt–Simpson–Wang–Wu v2, Section 8, concerns a different Schön subvariety of (ℂ*)⁸ and its tropical link; no identification with this two-summand face poset is supplied.
Earlier work

Canonical Minkowski face decomposition and simplex-difference geometry are classical. Fukuda–Weibel provide the general decomposition statement, and Sturmfels–Tevelev’s scaled opposite tetrahedra give the earlier six-point homology control. That zero-dimensional complex is shellable, so it does not by itself prove nonshellability. The common-interval construction supplies the positive-dimensional disconnected example here.

headings.text: When the local recurrence and equality follow
Two classical examples and the sharp coefficient
The remaining gap and boundary cases

article_blocks.text: Alec Kriebel · 22 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
ORCID · DOI and Zenodo record

For every ordinary unweighted r-differential poset and n ≥ 2, we subtract an explicit nonnegative term from Byrnes's cumulative upper bound for the nth rank size. The term is the cycle rank of the preceding incidence subgraph supported on elements with a singleton successor. Singleton witnesses transfer these cycles into the next incidence graph by replacing stars with trees having the same terminals. The correction can be positive and attained on standard reflected Young-prefix examples, and its coefficient one is sharp. A singleton-successor condition gives the conjectured local recurrence; two such successors give a conditional equality characterization. The result answers the printed request for an improvement of Byrnes's inequality in an incidence-dependent form. It does not prove the general local recurrence, improve the global Fibonacci envelope, or give a combinatorial proof of strict rank growth.

A graded poset is arranged in ranks, with edges recording which elements cover those immediately below. Its rank sizes count the elements at each level. Differential posets satisfy a precise balance between the upward and downward edges.

Byrnes’s cumulative bound limits the size of the next rank using earlier rank sizes. This note subtracts a correction that can be read from the preceding incidence graph. Certain cycles are forced to survive into the next rank, leaving less room for new elements. The correction may be zero; classical examples show that it can also give a strict, attained improvement.

Fix any positive integer r and any ordinary unweighted r-differential poset P: a locally finite poset graded by the nonnegative integers, with one minimum and finite ranks. Its ordinary up and down operators over ℚ satisfy DU−UD = rI at every rank, including rank zero, as an equality of integer incidence counts. Put pⱼ = |Pⱼ|. Zero common covers are allowed; an identity interpreted only modulo a characteristic is not the category used here.
For j ≥ 1, let Bⱼ be the bipartite cover graph on Pⱼ₋₁ ⊔ Pⱼ and let bⱼ = β(Bⱼ), where β(H) = |E(H)|−|V(H)|+c(H) and c(H) counts every component, including isolated vertices.

For n ≥ 2, let S consist of z ∈ Pₙ₋₂ having some a ∈ Pₙ₋₁ with the entire predecessor set pred(a) = {z}. Such an a is a singleton successor of z; this does not mean that z has only one successor. Let Hₛ retain S, every vertex of Pₙ₋₁, and the incident edges between them. Set qₙ = β(Hₛ).
The theorem holds for every such r, P and n: 0 ≤ qₙ ≤ bₙ₋₁ and bₙ ≥ qₙ. Thus, writing Uₙ = 1 + r Σ_{k=0}^{n−2} pₖ + (r−1)pₙ₋₁,
pₙ ≤ Uₙ−qₙ = r pₙ₋₁ + pₙ₋₂ + bₙ₋₁−qₙ.
The correction depends only on the two preceding incidence ranks, before Pₙ is constructed. No additional singleton-support hypothesis is needed for this bound.
The full consecutive-rank incidence graphs are connected. Their edge counts give the exact slack identities pₙ = Uₙ−bₙ and bₙ−bₙ₋₁ = r pₙ₋₁+pₙ₋₂−pₙ.

Choose a singleton witness a_z for each supported z. The common-cover identity supplies upper vertices joining that witness to the other successors of z. Their complete stars form a tree with precisely those terminals. Different supported centers cannot share an internal upper vertex: that would give a common successor to witnesses whose predecessor sets are disjoint.

Consequently all these tree replacements coexist inside the next incidence graph. They preserve the terminal connections and change edge and vertex counts equally, including a one-terminal tree. Retaining all remaining terminal isolates preserves the component count too. Their union therefore has cycle rank qₙ, so the next full graph has at least that cycle rank. The argument works for arbitrary witness choices; finite checks supplement the written proof.

heading.text: When the local recurrence and equality follow

article_blocks.text: If every z ∈ Pₙ₋₂ has at least one singleton successor in Pₙ₋₁, then Hₛ is the whole preceding incidence graph and qₙ = bₙ₋₁. The theorem then gives pₙ ≤ r pₙ₋₁+pₙ₋₂ for every admissible next extension. In particular, the condition holds whenever rank n−1 was formed by reflection-extension; rank n need not itself be reflected.

heading.text: When the local recurrence and equality follow

article_blocks.text: For n ≥ 3, suppose every such z has at least two distinct singleton successors. Equality in the local bound holds if and only if the extension to rank n is reflection-extension, up to relabelling that new rank. The two-singleton and n ≥ 3 hypotheses belong to this equality statement; one witness alone is not asserted to characterize equality.

heading.text: When the local recurrence and equality follow

article_blocks.text: Gaetz–Venkataramana’s established rank-one two-singleton lemma supplies these hypotheses at rank three. Hence for every positive integer r, p₃ ≤ r p₂+r, with equality precisely when rank three is obtained by reflection from rank two. The lemma is credited, rather than presented as new.

heading.text: Two classical examples and the sharp coefficient

article_blocks.text: Wagner reflection adds one upper vertex over each previous neighborhood and r singleton successors over each current element. It preserves the ordinary differential-poset identities and can be repeated indefinitely. The following are classical reflected Young-prefix constructions, used here as witnesses rather than new poset families.

heading.text: Two classical examples and the sharp coefficient

article_blocks.text: For r = 3, take the Y³ prefix with ranks (1,3,9), reflect to obtain rank size 30, and continue reflecting. Here q₃ = b₂ = b₃ = 1: Byrnes’s bound 31 is reduced to the attained bound 30.

heading.text: Two classical examples and the sharp coefficient

article_blocks.text: For r = 1, take Young’s lattice through rank five, reflect twice, and continue reflecting. The ranks are (1,1,2,3,5,7,12,19), with q₇ = b₆ = b₇ = 1. Byrnes’s bound 20 is reduced to the attained bound 19. Both finite prefixes therefore belong to infinite differential posets.

heading.text: Two classical examples and the sharp coefficient

article_blocks.text: In each example pₙ = Uₙ−qₙ with qₙ = 1. Replacing coefficient one by any real c > 1 would demand pₙ ≤ Uₙ−c qₙ < pₙ. Coefficient one is sharp; this does not claim optimality among all possible uses of preceding incidence data.

heading.text: The remaining gap and boundary cases

article_blocks.text: The unremoved allowance is exactly bₙ₋₁−qₙ. In Young’s lattice at n = 6, b₅ = 1 and q₆ = 0: the refined bound is 13, the proposed local bound is 12, and the actual rank size is 11. This is not a counterexample to the local recurrence. The general recurrence would still require bₙ ≥ bₙ₋₁.

heading.text: The remaining gap and boundary cases

article_blocks.text: At n = 2, q₂ = 0 and p₂ ≤ r²+1. For r = 1 the replacement may be a single terminal with no internal vertex. Empty S leaves all Pₙ₋₁ vertices isolated and gives qₙ = 0; b₁ = 0 and no b₀ is assumed.

heading.text: The remaining gap and boundary cases

article_blocks.text: The result does not prove the general local recurrence, improve the global Fibonacci envelope, or provide a combinatorial strict-growth proof. The usual strict-growth statement also has the bottom exception r = 1 with p₀ = p₁ = 1. Weighted or multiple-edge graphs, merely modular commutation and isolated locally commuting layers without a valid bottom rank are outside the theorem.

heading.text: The remaining gap and boundary cases

article_blocks.text: Historical firstness, independence from unknown work and present worldwide openness are not established. The source comparisons are bounded, with version and access limits; a later proof, uninspected publisher edition or unpublished work is not ruled out.

Majumder’s contribution in Oberwolfach Report 23/2018, printed pages 1452–1453, separately asks for an improvement of Byrnes’s cumulative inequality toward the local bound and for a combinatorial strict-growth proof. This note addresses the improvement request in an incidence-dependent form; the request imposes no rank-number-only restriction.

Stanley’s operator framework and Wagner reflection, Byrnes’s cumulative bound and earlier cycle arguments, and Stanley–Zanello’s incidence and hypergraph sums are established background. Cycle-space inclusion and terminal-preserving tree replacement are elementary graph facts. The assertion here is their simultaneous singleton-supported transfer in the ordinary differential-poset setting.

Singleton and crown methods also have Lewis and Miller–Reiner antecedents. Gaetz–Venkataramana’s Proposition 3.4 in the inspected v3 preprint is the exact rank-one lemma used above. Qing and Wright concern related upper-extremal scopes; Miller’s strict-growth work is a different direction. Versioned preprints and the published records are distinguished in the source dossier; no unread final-body identity or exhaustive literature coverage is inferred.

blocks.text: The full consecutive-rank incidence graphs are connected. Their edge counts give the exact slack identities pₙ = Uₙ−bₙ and bₙ−bₙ₋₁ = r pₙ₋₁+pₙ₋₂−pₙ.

Choose a singleton witness a_z for each supported z. The common-cover identity supplies upper vertices joining that witness to the other successors of z. Their complete stars form a tree with precisely those terminals. Different supported centers cannot share an internal upper vertex: that would give a common successor to witnesses whose predecessor sets are disjoint.

Consequently all these tree replacements coexist inside the next incidence graph. They preserve the terminal connections and change edge and vertex counts equally, including a one-terminal tree. Retaining all remaining terminal isolates preserves the component count too. Their union therefore has cycle rank qₙ, so the next full graph has at least that cycle rank. The argument works for arbitrary witness choices; finite checks supplement the written proof.

headings.text: When the local recurrence and equality follow

blocks.text: If every z ∈ Pₙ₋₂ has at least one singleton successor in Pₙ₋₁, then Hₛ is the whole preceding incidence graph and qₙ = bₙ₋₁. The theorem then gives pₙ ≤ r pₙ₋₁+pₙ₋₂ for every admissible next extension. In particular, the condition holds whenever rank n−1 was formed by reflection-extension; rank n need not itself be reflected.

For n ≥ 3, suppose every such z has at least two distinct singleton successors. Equality in the local bound holds if and only if the extension to rank n is reflection-extension, up to relabelling that new rank. The two-singleton and n ≥ 3 hypotheses belong to this equality statement; one witness alone is not asserted to characterize equality.

Gaetz–Venkataramana’s established rank-one two-singleton lemma supplies these hypotheses at rank three. Hence for every positive integer r, p₃ ≤ r p₂+r, with equality precisely when rank three is obtained by reflection from rank two. The lemma is credited, rather than presented as new.

headings.text: Two classical examples and the sharp coefficient

blocks.text: Wagner reflection adds one upper vertex over each previous neighborhood and r singleton successors over each current element. It preserves the ordinary differential-poset identities and can be repeated indefinitely. The following are classical reflected Young-prefix constructions, used here as witnesses rather than new poset families.
For r = 3, take the Y³ prefix with ranks (1,3,9), reflect to obtain rank size 30, and continue reflecting. Here q₃ = b₂ = b₃ = 1: Byrnes’s bound 31 is reduced to the attained bound 30.

For r = 1, take Young’s lattice through rank five, reflect twice, and continue reflecting. The ranks are (1,1,2,3,5,7,12,19), with q₇ = b₆ = b₇ = 1. Byrnes’s bound 20 is reduced to the attained bound 19. Both finite prefixes therefore belong to infinite differential posets.

In each example pₙ = Uₙ−qₙ with qₙ = 1. Replacing coefficient one by any real c > 1 would demand pₙ ≤ Uₙ−c qₙ < pₙ. Coefficient one is sharp; this does not claim optimality among all possible uses of preceding incidence data.

headings.text: The remaining gap and boundary cases

blocks.text: The unremoved allowance is exactly bₙ₋₁−qₙ. In Young’s lattice at n = 6, b₅ = 1 and q₆ = 0: the refined bound is 13, the proposed local bound is 12, and the actual rank size is 11. This is not a counterexample to the local recurrence. The general recurrence would still require bₙ ≥ bₙ₋₁.
At n = 2, q₂ = 0 and p₂ ≤ r²+1. For r = 1 the replacement may be a single terminal with no internal vertex. Empty S leaves all Pₙ₋₁ vertices isolated and gives qₙ = 0; b₁ = 0 and no b₀ is assumed.

The result does not prove the general local recurrence, improve the global Fibonacci envelope, or provide a combinatorial strict-growth proof. The usual strict-growth statement also has the bottom exception r = 1 with p₀ = p₁ = 1. Weighted or multiple-edge graphs, merely modular commutation and isolated locally commuting layers without a valid bottom rank are outside the theorem.

Stanley’s operator framework and Wagner reflection, Byrnes’s cumulative bound and earlier cycle arguments, and Stanley–Zanello’s incidence and hypergraph sums are established background. headings.text: Why least period controls the product
Why a listed return length of six is insufficient

article_blocks.text: Alec Kriebel · 11 October 2026 · Native deposit version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint
ORCID · DOI and Zenodo record

For a noncircular elliptic billiard with a strictly nested nondegenerate confocal elliptical caustic, we prove that the product of ordinary distances from all vertices to either fixed focus is independent of phase if and only if the least period is 2 modulo 4. This proves the least-period interpretation of entry k₁₁₄ in Reznik–Garcia–Koiller's list of unproved invariants and classifies every other primitive period and every repeated traversal. The proof identifies the complete divisor of the focal-distance factor in the classical Jacobi parameter. An exact doubled-triangle example shows why a condition on return length alone is insufficient. The parametrization, identities and divisor method are established tools. This AI-assisted research note is unrefereed.

A billiard trajectory inside an ellipse bounces according to the usual reflection law. In a confocal family, every side touches the same inner ellipse, called the caustic. Moving the starting point changes the polygon’s phase while retaining that caustic.

This note asks when the product of the distances from all polygon vertices to one fixed focus stays unchanged as the phase moves. The answer depends on the least period: the number of bounces before the trajectory first returns. Counting a repeated traversal as a longer list can give the wrong answer.

Fix outer and inner ellipses x²/a²+y²/b²=1 and x²/A²+y²/B²=1, with a>b>0, A>B>0, a>A, b>B and a²−b²=A²−B²=c²>0. The caustic is strictly nested, nondegenerate and confocal. The foci F±=(±c,0) are fixed, and the factors are ordinary positive Euclidean distances from the original billiard vertices, not squared distances or distances from an outer tangent polygon.

For any actual periodic elastic billiard family tangent to that caustic, let n be its primitive least period and set Dₙ±(u)=∏ⱼ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹ |Pⱼ(u)−F±|. Each focal product is independent of phase if and only if n≡2 (mod 4). Every admissible primitive coprime star winding and both orientations are included; n=1 and n=2 cannot occur in this strict elliptical-caustic setting.

For every even least period, Dₙ⁺(u)=Dₙ⁻(u) at each phase. This includes n≡0 (mod 4), when the equal products still vary with phase. Equality between the two foci is a different assertion from phase constancy.

For every integer r≥1, an r-fold traversal gives (Dₙ±)ʳ. Positivity makes this power operation injective, so repetition preserves the primitive constancy class in both directions. For a listed return length N≡2 (mod 4), constancy holds exactly when its least period is even.

heading.text: Why least period controls the product

article_blocks.text: The proof uses Stachel’s classical Jacobi parametrization P(u)=(−a sn u,b cn u), with modulus k=c/A∈(0,1), K=K(k), K′=K(√(1−k²)), cn(v)=B/b and 0<v<K. Here a=A dn(v)/cn(v), and successive vertices are separated by δ=2v=4Kτ/n, where gcd(τ,n)=1 and 0<τ<n/2. Reversing orientation gives the same cyclic subgroup.

heading.text: Why least period controls the product

article_blocks.text: The manuscript checks that the tangent contacts lie inside the actual chords and that the two inward rays satisfy elastic reflection across the normal. Real injectivity modulo 4K makes n the true vertex period. The geometric calculation gives the positive ordinary-distance factors g±(u)=a±c sn u; a>c prevents a hidden sign or square-root convention.

heading.text: Why least period controls the product

article_blocks.text: On the sn torus ℂ/(4Kℤ+2iK′ℤ), the factor g₊ has two simple poles p=iK′ and p+2K, and two distinct simple zeros p−K±v. These are complete, because zero and pole degrees agree. This torus is used for the focal factor; the full complex boundary map need not have the same imaginary period.

heading.text: Why least period controls the product

article_blocks.text: Writing H=⟨δ⟩ for the n-element orbit subgroup, translating the complete divisor through H gives one double zero coset, represented by z=−1/4+τ/(2n), and pole cosets H and 1/2+H. For odd n there are 2n uncancelled simple poles. For even n there are n double poles, cancelled exactly when (−n+2τ)/4 is an integer: precisely n≡2 (mod 4).

heading.text: Why least period controls the product

article_blocks.text: A divisor-free meromorphic function on the compact connected torus is constant. In the other classes a pole remains; the identity theorem transfers that nonconstancy to the physical real family. The half-period identity g₋(u)=g₊(u+2K) gives the second focus and the even-period pointwise equality. This is an all-period proof, rather than an extrapolation from finite checks.

heading.text: Why least period controls the product

article_blocks.text: For n=2m≡2 (mod 4), the positive constant can be evaluated as ∏ⱼ₌₀ᵐ⁻¹ [a²−c² sn²(2jv)]. It has units of lengthⁿ.

heading.text: Why a listed return length of six is insufficient

article_blocks.text: Take a=√15, b=√7, c=√8, A²=135/16 and B²=7/16. The triangle with vertices (a,0), (−3a/4,7/4), (−3a/4,−7/4), and its central reflection, are primitive three-bounce trajectories in the same fixed confocal family. Their side lines x=−A and x±ay=a are tangent to the caustic, their contact points lie inside the segments, and the inward unit rays satisfy the physical reflection law.

heading.text: Why a listed return length of six is insufficient

article_blocks.text: At the fixed focus F₊ their positive primitive products are 15a/2+3c and 15a/2−3c. Traversing each triangle twice produces six listed events, but the two products differ by (15a/2+3c)²−(15a/2−3c)²=90ac=180√30>0.

heading.text: Why a listed return length of six is insufficient

article_blocks.text: Thus a return length of six alone does not force phase constancy. The example distinguishes an unrestricted repeated-list interpretation from a statement explicitly about primitive least period; it does not refute that primitive statement.

For a circle the two foci coincide with its center, every focal distance is the radius a, and every listed N-event product is aᴺ. This is a separate elementary case: the noncircular pole argument is not continued through c=0.

Hyperbolic or degenerate caustics, grazing or two-bounce limits and uniform lower bounds on the size of phase variation are outside the theorem. Ordinary floating-point agreement does not certify constancy, especially when real variation is below numerical resolution. No validated numerical bounds or proof-assistant formalization are claimed.

Reznik, Garcia and Koiller recorded the focal product as k₁₁₄. Their final 2021 Arnold Mathematical Journal article, Fifty New Invariants of N-Periodics in the Elliptic Billiard, defines ordinary vertex-to-focus distances and lists the 2-mod-4 observation in Table 2 with an unknown proof entry. Its text does not explicitly resolve primitive least period versus a return list allowing repetitions. The earlier v11 preprint has the different title Eighty New Invariants; editions are not silently substituted.

Stachel’s published 2022 Theorem 4.3 and equation (4.9) supply the classical parametrization. Standard Jacobi periods, shifts and addition identities, and the general meromorphic Poncelet pole-removal method, retain prior credit. Schwartz, Akopyan–Schwartz–Tabachnikov and Roitman–Garcia–Reznik provide method precedents. The target-specific calculation is the focal divisor and its orbit-coset arithmetic; no new elliptic-function method is claimed.

Other products have different factors: k₁₁₅ concerns vertices of the outer tangent polygon, k₁₁₇ concerns caustic-contact lengths, and k₂₀₂ concerns perpendicular distances to sides. Ferudun’s related unrefereed note addresses k₁₁₅, rather than the original billiard-vertex product here.

The source comparison is bounded. No exclusive historical priority, influence, exhaustive literature coverage or present worldwide openness is certified. The full billiard body of the related Dragović–Gajić article remained unavailable, and the inspected author-site Ferudun body was not authenticated as the exact Zenodo-deposit bytes. These limits do not become claims that the unread material is irrelevant.

blocks.text: A billiard trajectory inside an ellipse bounces according to the usual reflection law. In a confocal family, every side touches the same inner ellipse, called the caustic. Moving the starting point changes the polygon’s phase while retaining that caustic.

This note asks when the product of the distances from all polygon vertices to one fixed focus stays unchanged as the phase moves. The answer depends on the least period: the number of bounces before the trajectory first returns. Counting a repeated traversal as a longer list can give the wrong answer.

headings.text: Why least period controls the product

blocks.text: The proof uses Stachel’s classical Jacobi parametrization P(u)=(−a sn u,b cn u), with modulus k=c/A∈(0,1), K=K(k), K′=K(√(1−k²)), cn(v)=B/b and 0<v<K. Here a=A dn(v)/cn(v), and successive vertices are separated by δ=2v=4Kτ/n, where gcd(τ,n)=1 and 0<τ<n/2. Reversing orientation gives the same cyclic subgroup.

The manuscript checks that the tangent contacts lie inside the actual chords and that the two inward rays satisfy elastic reflection across the normal. Real injectivity modulo 4K makes n the true vertex period. The geometric calculation gives the positive ordinary-distance factors g±(u)=a±c sn u; a>c prevents a hidden sign or square-root convention.

On the sn torus ℂ/(4Kℤ+2iK′ℤ), the factor g₊ has two simple poles p=iK′ and p+2K, and two distinct simple zeros p−K±v. These are complete, because zero and pole degrees agree. This torus is used for the focal factor; the full complex boundary map need not have the same imaginary period.

Writing H=⟨δ⟩ for the n-element orbit subgroup, translating the complete divisor through H gives one double zero coset, represented by z=−1/4+τ/(2n), and pole cosets H and 1/2+H. For odd n there are 2n uncancelled simple poles. For even n there are n double poles, cancelled exactly when (−n+2τ)/4 is an integer: precisely n≡2 (mod 4).

A divisor-free meromorphic function on the compact connected torus is constant. In the other classes a pole remains; the identity theorem transfers that nonconstancy to the physical real family. The half-period identity g₋(u)=g₊(u+2K) gives the second focus and the even-period pointwise equality. This is an all-period proof, rather than an extrapolation from finite checks.
For n=2m≡2 (mod 4), the positive constant can be evaluated as ∏ⱼ₌₀ᵐ⁻¹ [a²−c² sn²(2jv)]. It has units of lengthⁿ.

headings.text: Why a listed return length of six is insufficient

blocks.text: Take a=√15, b=√7, c=√8, A²=135/16 and B²=7/16. The triangle with vertices (a,0), (−3a/4,7/4), (−3a/4,−7/4), and its central reflection, are primitive three-bounce trajectories in the same fixed confocal family. Their side lines x=−A and x±ay=a are tangent to the caustic, their contact points lie inside the segments, and the inward unit rays satisfy the physical reflection law.

At the fixed focus F₊ their positive primitive products are 15a/2+3c and 15a/2−3c. Traversing each triangle twice produces six listed events, but the two products differ by (15a/2+3c)²−(15a/2−3c)²=90ac=180√30>0.

Thus a return length of six alone does not force phase constancy. The example distinguishes an unrestricted repeated-list interpretation from a statement explicitly about primitive least period; it does not refute that primitive statement.

blocks.text: For a circle the two foci coincide with its center, every focal distance is the radius a, and every listed N-event product is aᴺ. This is a separate elementary case: the noncircular pole argument is not continued through c=0.

Hyperbolic or degenerate caustics, grazing or two-bounce limits and uniform lower bounds on the size of phase variation are outside the theorem. Ordinary floating-point agreement does not certify constancy, especially when real variation is below numerical resolution. No validated numerical bounds or proof-assistant formalization are claimed.

blocks.text: Reznik, Garcia and Koiller recorded the focal product as k₁₁₄. Their final 2021 Arnold Mathematical Journal article, Fifty New Invariants of N-Periodics in the Elliptic Billiard, defines ordinary vertex-to-focus distances and lists the 2-mod-4 observation in Table 2 with an unknown proof entry. Its text does not explicitly resolve primitive least period versus a return list allowing repetitions. The earlier v11 preprint has the different title Eighty New Invariants; editions are not silently substituted.

Stachel’s published 2022 Theorem 4.3 and equation (4.9) supply the classical parametrization. Standard Jacobi periods, shifts and addition identities, and the general meromorphic Poncelet pole-removal method, retain prior credit. Schwartz, Akopyan–Schwartz–Tabachnikov and Roitman–Garcia–Reznik provide method precedents. The target-specific calculation is the focal divisor and its orbit-coset arithmetic; no new elliptic-function method is claimed.

Other products have different factors: k₁₁₅ concerns vertices of the outer tangent polygon, k₁₁₇ concerns caustic-contact lengths, and k₂₀₂ concerns perpendicular distances to sides. Ferudun’s related unrefereed note addresses k₁₁₅, rather than the original billiard-vertex product here.

The source comparison is bounded. No exclusive historical priority, influence, exhaustive literature coverage or present worldwide openness is certified. The full billiard body of the related Dragović–Gajić article remained unavailable, and the inspected author-site Ferudun body was not authenticated as the exact Zenodo-deposit bytes. These limits do not become claims that the unread material is irrelevant.

article_blocks.text: Alec Kriebel · 16 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint
ORCID · doi:10.5281/zenodo.23418581

A simple module has no proper nonzero submodule. Its top is its largest quotient that is a direct sum of simple modules. Injectivity and projectivity are different extension and lifting properties. Miyachi’s printed question asks whether a simple top of a Young module forces its associated polynomial injective hull to be projective at some permitted rank.

This note assembles classical representation theory into a family where the Young module itself is simple, but the associated injective hull is never projective. One example occurs in characteristic 3 with the partition (4,1).

For every odd prime p, the Young module labelled by λ = (2p−2,1) in characteristic p is simple, whereas its corresponding polynomial injective hull I_n(λ) is nonprojective for every n≥2. At parameter q=1, this gives a negative answer to the unrestricted formulation of Miyachi’s Conjecture 7 in the 2009 Oberwolfach report. The proof combines classical representation theory with a labelled rank-truncation argument. We include explicit proofs of the local calculations and reproducible supporting checks. Historical priority remains unresolved; no firstness claim is made.

Let p be any odd prime, let k be algebraically closed of characteristic p, and take q=1. Put r=2p−1 and λ=(2p−2,1). In the stable Schur convention Y^λ = F I_N(λ), with N≥r, the Young module Y^λ is simple of dimension 2p−2. Its corresponding injective hull I_n(λ) in degree-r polynomial GL_n(k)-modules, equivalently for the Schur algebra S(n,r), is nonprojective for every integer n≥2.

The broad displayed Conjecture 7 asks for an equivalence between simplicity of top(Y^λ) and projectivity of I_n(λ) for some n≥ℓ(λ). Here ℓ(λ)=2. Simplicity of Y^λ gives a simple top, while the theorem excludes projectivity at every permitted rank. This answers that printed proposal negatively.

The separate stronger proposal uses the constructed Λ_n^i index families. Membership already suffices for projectivity; the theorem therefore excludes membership at every permitted rank and also gives a negative answer to that stronger simple-top criterion. No completeness assertion about the sufficient family is assumed.

Since p does not divide r=2p−1, the natural permutation module k^r splits into its constant line and the augmentation module A=ker(sum). A nonzero vector in a submodule of A has two unequal coordinates; subtracting its image under the corresponding transposition gives a nonzero coordinate difference. Permuting that difference spans A, so A is simple of dimension r−1.

The label is checked at stable rank, rather than inferred at rank two. Sym^(r−1)(k^N)⊗k^N has the two injective summands labelled (r) and λ. Multiplication onto Sym^r(k^N) splits because polarization satisfies mδ=r·id. Its kernel is I_N(λ); on multilinear weight spaces multiplication is coordinate summation. Exactness of F identifies the correctly labelled Young module with A.

At rank two, I_2(λ)=det⊗Sym^(2p−3)(k²). The symmetric power is a nonsplit extension of distinct simple modules: its socle has highest weight (2p−3,0) and dimension 2p−4, and its top has highest weight (p−1,p−2) and dimension 2. After the determinant twist, the labels are (2p−2,1) and (p,p−1). They remain distinct when p=3, even though both dimensions are 2. Thus this injective is not contravariantly self-dual and cannot be projective.

If I_n(λ) were projective at any n≥2, the classical projective-injective theorem would identify it with an indecomposable tilting module T_n(μ). Dominance leaves only μ=(r) or λ, both with at most two parts. Exact truncation of these labelled injective and tilting modules would make I_2(λ) an injective tilting module and hence projective, contradicting the rank-two calculation. This uses the labelled truncation theorems, not preservation of arbitrary projectives by an idempotent functor.

The result concerns algebraically closed characteristic p for odd primes and parameter q=1. Rank one cannot carry this two-part label, and p=2 is outside the theorem. The coefficient argument is for rational algebraic-group modules over the infinite field k, not merely the finite group GL₂(𝔽_p).

The characteristic-zero assumption in the later subsection 0.5 of Miyachi’s contribution belongs to a different method for simple Specht modules; it is not attached to the displayed Conjecture 7. This note does not address a characteristic-zero variant with a nontrivial root-of-unity parameter or refute the separate De Visscher–Donkin classification.

Row p-regularity is different from p-restrictedness, also called column p-regularity here. No projectivity inference from row regularity is used. The theorem supplies the stated all-prime, all-rank conclusion; the accompanying finite computations are supporting evidence rather than a proof of those universal quantifiers.

The natural permutation/augmentation calculation, rank-two structure and Schur-algebra inputs are classical. De Visscher–Donkin supply reciprocity, injective multiplicities, tilting and labelled truncation; Cox–Parker record the stable F I convention. Erdmann–Law’s classical analogue of Proposition 3.1 and Theorem 3.3 give published local-structure antecedents. The contribution here is their explicit assembly into a counterexample to the broad printed proposal.

Historical priority remains unresolved. Coverage of older two-row papers, tables and later work is incomplete. No firstness, certified novelty, new local classification or current worldwide openness is claimed.

Its corresponding injective hull I_n(λ) in degree-r polynomial GL_n(k)-modules, equivalently for the Schur algebra S(n,r), is nonprojective for every integer n≥2.

The broad displayed Conjecture 7 asks for an equivalence between simplicity of top(Y^λ) and projectivity of I_n(λ) for some n≥ℓ(λ). Here ℓ(λ)=2. Simplicity of Y^λ gives a simple top, while the theorem excludes projectivity at every permitted rank. This answers that printed proposal negatively.

The separate stronger proposal uses the constructed Λ_n^i index families. Membership already suffices for projectivity; the theorem therefore excludes membership at every permitted rank and also gives a negative answer to that stronger simple-top criterion. No completeness assertion about the sufficient family is assumed.

blocks.text: Since p does not divide r=2p−1, the natural permutation module k^r splits into its constant line and the augmentation module A=ker(sum). A nonzero vector in a submodule of A has two unequal coordinates; subtracting its image under the corresponding transposition gives a nonzero coordinate difference. Permuting that difference spans A, so A is simple of dimension r−1.

The label is checked at stable rank, rather than inferred at rank two. Sym^(r−1)(k^N)⊗k^N has the two injective summands labelled (r) and λ. Multiplication onto Sym^r(k^N) splits because polarization satisfies mδ=r·id. Its kernel is I_N(λ); on multilinear weight spaces multiplication is coordinate summation. Exactness of F identifies the correctly labelled Young module with A.

At rank two, I_2(λ)=det⊗Sym^(2p−3)(k²). The symmetric power is a nonsplit extension of distinct simple modules: its socle has highest weight (2p−3,0) and dimension 2p−4, and its top has highest weight (p−1,p−2) and dimension 2. After the determinant twist, the labels are (2p−2,1) and (p,p−1). They remain distinct when p=3, even though both dimensions are 2. Thus this injective is not contravariantly self-dual and cannot be projective.

If I_n(λ) were projective at any n≥2, the classical projective-injective theorem would identify it with an indecomposable tilting module T_n(μ). Dominance leaves only μ=(r) or λ, both with at most two parts. Exact truncation of these labelled injective and tilting modules would make I_2(λ) an injective tilting module and hence projective, contradicting the rank-two calculation. This uses the labelled truncation theorems, not preservation of arbitrary projectives by an idempotent functor.

blocks.text: The result concerns algebraically closed characteristic p for odd primes and parameter q=1. Rank one cannot carry this two-part label, and p=2 is outside the theorem. The coefficient argument is for rational algebraic-group modules over the infinite field k, not merely the finite group GL₂(𝔽_p).

The characteristic-zero assumption in the later subsection 0.5 of Miyachi’s contribution belongs to a different method for simple Specht modules; it is not attached to the displayed Conjecture 7. This note does not address a characteristic-zero variant with a nontrivial root-of-unity parameter or refute the separate De Visscher–Donkin classification.

Row p-regularity is different from p-restrictedness, also called column p-regularity here. No projectivity inference from row regularity is used. The theorem supplies the stated all-prime, all-rank conclusion; the accompanying finite computations are supporting evidence rather than a proof of those universal quantifiers.

headings.text: One binary language, including malformed words
An exact source compiler and its cubic cost
A pullback with exactly sh² states
Earlier work and the scope of the contribution

article_blocks.text: Theoretical computer science · Automata · Research note
Alec Kriebel · ORCID: 0009-0001-9320-500X
6 October 2026 · Unrefereed preprint

A finite automaton can describe a language compactly yet require many more states when its nondeterminism is removed, or when the language is complemented. This note transfers two attributed relation-liveness lower bounds to a single binary alphabet, with explicit compilers, exact state counts and a precise treatment of every binary word.

We give explicit fixed-binary-alphabet consequences of OpenAI’s two relation-liveness lower bounds. Encoding each relation on h points by its h² adjacency bits gives a language recognized by a one-way nondeterministic automaton with Nₕ=(3h³−h)/2+2 states. Every equivalent two-way deterministic automaton, and every two-way nondeterministic automaton for its full binary complement, requires 2^{Ω(h)}=2^{Ω(Nₕ^(1/3))} states. We specify all transition rules, including an exact sh²-state pullback for an s-state binary target. The binary language rejects incomplete blocks; a fooling set proves that its one-way nondeterministic state complexity is Θ(h³). The exponential obstructions are inherited from the two upstream theorems; binary adjacency coding is established machinery.

heading.text: One binary language, including malformed words

article_blocks.text: Fix an integer h ≥ 2, let H = {0,…,h−1}, and let Σₕ be the alphabet of all relations on H. A relation on H is encoded by its h² adjacency bits in row-major order: bit t = ph+q records whether the edge (p,q) is present. Relation products are composed in path order, so a sequence is live when some path survives through all its relations. The empty product is the identity relation.

heading.text: One binary language, including malformed words

article_blocks.text: b = h² Lₕ = {relation words whose product is nonempty} Kₕ = enc(Lₕ) ⊆ {0,1}*; enc(ε) = ε.

heading.text: One binary language, including malformed words

article_blocks.text: Every complete b-bit block codes exactly one relation. The language Kₕ is defined on all binary words: it rejects every word whose length is not divisible by h², and otherwise tests the decoded product for liveness. It accepts ε. This strict rejection of incomplete blocks is part of the result, rather than a promise that inputs will be well formed.

heading.text: An exact source compiler and its cubic cost

article_blocks.text: The marked one-way nondeterministic source has one nonaccepting initial state, one accepting state, and two families of scanning states. U(p,t) retains the preceding vertex before choosing an outgoing edge; V(q,t) retains the selected next vertex. Their ranges are

heading.text: An exact source compiler and its cubic cost

article_blocks.text: U(p,t): 0 ≤ p < h, 0 ≤ t < (p+1)h V(q,t): 0 ≤ q < h, q+1 ≤ t < h² Nₕ = (3h³−h)/2 + 2 marked states ordinary epsilon-free 1NFA: Nₕ−1 states.

heading.text: An exact source compiler and its cubic cost

article_blocks.text: At the left marker the source chooses a starting vertex. Within each block, a surviving branch must choose exactly one 1 in that vertex’s row; its final row position cannot simply be skipped. The chosen column becomes the next block’s vertex. Every body-bit move goes right, and only complete block-boundary states can take the accepting stay at the right marker. Thus partial blocks reject, while ε has a two-transition accepting run. The ordinary epsilon-free source combines the first-bit choices in one initial final state and tests acceptance only after consuming the entire word.

heading.text: An exact source compiler and its cubic cost

article_blocks.text: A matching lower bound uses h³ incompatible prefix–suffix cuts, one for each vertex and bit offset. Diagonal pairs encode a live singleton–identity–singleton product. Different-offset crosses have malformed lengths; equal-offset, different-vertex crosses have empty products. Splicing runs with the same cut state would accept a forbidden cross.

heading.text: An exact source compiler and its cubic cost

article_blocks.text: This proves an h³ lower bound for ordinary one-way NFAs and for marked right-only sources, including stays in that right-only model. It is not a cut-state lower bound for arbitrary two-way machines. Consequently this particular strict-block language has one-way nondeterministic state complexity Θ(h³); the claim does not assert optimal source costs across all binary encodings.

All states are counted. The head begins on the left of two distinct endmarkers, which remain distinct and adjacent on empty input. Transitions may be partial and may move left, stay, or move right. Outward moves at markers are disabled. A deterministic target has at most one successor per state-symbol row; a nondeterministic target may have several.

Acceptance means reaching an accepting state by a finite run, initially allowing zero transitions. Missing transitions and nonaccepting infinite runs do not accept. The pullback also preserves positive-run acceptance. There is no hidden halting, reversal, word-length or writable-tape restriction.

heading.text: A pullback with exactly sh² states

article_blocks.text: Given an s-state binary target, the relation-alphabet pullback uses states (q,t), where q is an original target state and t ranges from 0 to b−1. At a relation cell it reads the adjacency bit at phase t. Its simulation rules are:

heading.text: A pullback with exactly sh² states

article_blocks.text: stay t stay

heading.text: A pullback with exactly sh² states

article_blocks.text: right, t < b−1 t+1 stay

heading.text: A pullback with exactly sh² states

article_blocks.text: left, t > 0 t−1 stay
