heading.text: A pullback with exactly sh² states

article_blocks.text: At each marker the original marker row is used independently of the stored phase. Marker stays retain the phase; inward moves reset it to 0 at the left marker and b−1 at the right marker. Missing rows remain missing. The initial state is (q₀,0), and (q,t) is accepting exactly when q is accepting.

heading.text: A pullback with exactly sh² states

article_blocks.text: A relation-cell configuration at cell j maps to binary position (j−1)b+t+1. Each transition corresponds to one binary transition, and every binary transition lifts from every corresponding preimage. Marker phases may be nonunique without introducing an accepting path. The argument covers adjacent markers on ε, both zero-step and positive finite acceptance, stays, partial rows, arbitrary revisits and nonaccepting infinite runs. Determinism and finite-run lengths are preserved. The exact state count is sh², with no extra marker-state family.

The two exponential engines are OpenAI’s attributed Math Release preprints on deterministic simulation of one-way liveness and on nondeterministic complementation. Applying their full relation-alphabet inequalities to the pullback gives the following bounds for every h ≥ 2.
If an s-state marked two-way deterministic automaton recognizes Kₕ, then
If an s-state marked two-way nondeterministic automaton recognizes the complement of Kₕ in all binary words, under zero-step finite acceptance, then
The full complement is the disjoint union
{0,1}* ∖ Kₕ = {x : h² does not divide |x|} ∪ enc(Σₕ* ∖ Lₕ).

The malformed words belong to the binary complement, while the pullback sees every valid encoding of a dead relation product. It therefore recognizes the entire upstream complement. ε is absent from both complements. Restricting the complement to a well-formed-input promise would change the statement.

For a positive-run complementing target, one new nonaccepting initial copy converts the target to zero-step acceptance. The explicit variant is 2^(⌊(h−2)/127⌋) ≤ 2((s+1)h²+1). The displayed deterministic inequality already covers both finite-run conventions. Requiring total rows can be handled by a nonaccepting sink; targets that must halt or accept at the right marker are subclasses of the stated model.

Since h³ ≤ Nₕ ≤ 2h³, both target costs are 2^{Ω(h)} = 2^{Ω(Nₕ^(1/3))}. Polynomial factors and fixed subtractions do not change this asymptotic statement; some small-h numerical lower bounds are simply vacuous. Thus neither simulation nor complementation admits a polynomial state bound on this one fixed alphabet.

The exponent is proportional to the cube root of this binary source size. The note does not assert 2^{Ω(Nₕ)}, a uniform separation such as L ≠ NL, or a small transition-table algorithm. Relation-alphabet pullback tables can be large. The contribution is the explicit transfer and exact language/model accounting, not an independent proof of the upstream exponential obstructions.

heading.text: Earlier work and the scope of the contribution

article_blocks.text: Sakoda and Sipser established the classical deterministic-simulation problem for two-way nondeterministic automata. Binary adjacency coding is established machinery: Kapoutsis’s 2011 conference treatment and the author preprint linked with the 2013 journal work discuss binary one-way liveness for deterministic targets with few reversals. The latter linked body is an October 2011 author preprint; journal pagination is a separate bibliographic reference.

heading.text: Earlier work and the scope of the contribution

article_blocks.text: The public TheoremDB R816 construction uses a different separator/two-bit encoding, a different off-canonical total language and a linear-size binary source, with an inherited quadratic lower bound and a deterministic macro pullback. It is self-reported, source-only context. It neither supplies the two exponential engines used here nor establishes present worldwide openness. Different source costs for a different language do not contradict the cubic lower bound for this exact strict-block language.

heading.text: Earlier work and the scope of the contribution

article_blocks.text: Adeogun and Kapoutsis supply the prior quadratic unrestricted deterministic comparison. In their limitation preprint, the connectivity-chain ceiling is proved as Theorem 2; the general-property extension is stated as Theorem 1 with its proof deferred. That restriction concerns a particular method, not all possible lower-bound arguments. Guillon, Prigioniero and Taheri’s polynomial complementation theorem targets 1-limited automata that may rewrite cells using common guessed annotations. It is not a small read-only 2NFA for the full unannotated complement.

heading.text: Earlier work and the scope of the contribution

article_blocks.text: The two actual exponential inputs are credited to OpenAI at the pinned source commit adc7f1241b42e322a6451854ab7e4b4c146bf78a. Their manuscript dates and public release dates are distinct. No independent resolution of the base conjecture, exclusive historical priority, invention of binary coding, or exhaustive current-openness claim is made.

Encoding each relation on h points by its h² adjacency bits gives a language recognized by a one-way nondeterministic automaton with Nₕ=(3h³−h)/2+2 states. Every equivalent two-way deterministic automaton, and every two-way nondeterministic automaton for its full binary complement, requires 2^{Ω(h)}=2^{Ω(Nₕ^(1/3))} states. We specify all transition rules, including an exact sh²-state pullback for an s-state binary target. The binary language rejects incomplete blocks; a fooling set proves that its one-way nondeterministic state complexity is Θ(h³). The exponential obstructions are inherited from the two upstream theorems; binary adjacency coding is established machinery.

headings.text: One binary language, including malformed words

blocks.text: Fix an integer h ≥ 2, let H = {0,…,h−1}, and let Σₕ be the alphabet of all relations on H. A relation on H is encoded by its h² adjacency bits in row-major order: bit t = ph+q records whether the edge (p,q) is present. Relation products are composed in path order, so a sequence is live when some path survives through all its relations. The empty product is the identity relation.
b = h² Lₕ = {relation words whose product is nonempty} Kₕ = enc(Lₕ) ⊆ {0,1}*; enc(ε) = ε.

Every complete b-bit block codes exactly one relation. The language Kₕ is defined on all binary words: it rejects every word whose length is not divisible by h², and otherwise tests the decoded product for liveness. It accepts ε. This strict rejection of incomplete blocks is part of the result, rather than a promise that inputs will be well formed.

headings.text: An exact source compiler and its cubic cost

blocks.text: The marked one-way nondeterministic source has one nonaccepting initial state, one accepting state, and two families of scanning states. U(p,t) retains the preceding vertex before choosing an outgoing edge; V(q,t) retains the selected next vertex. Their ranges are
U(p,t): 0 ≤ p < h, 0 ≤ t < (p+1)h V(q,t): 0 ≤ q < h, q+1 ≤ t < h² Nₕ = (3h³−h)/2 + 2 marked states ordinary epsilon-free 1NFA: Nₕ−1 states.

At the left marker the source chooses a starting vertex. Within each block, a surviving branch must choose exactly one 1 in that vertex’s row; its final row position cannot simply be skipped. The chosen column becomes the next block’s vertex. Every body-bit move goes right, and only complete block-boundary states can take the accepting stay at the right marker. Thus partial blocks reject, while ε has a two-transition accepting run. The ordinary epsilon-free source combines the first-bit choices in one initial final state and tests acceptance only after consuming the entire word.

A matching lower bound uses h³ incompatible prefix–suffix cuts, one for each vertex and bit offset. Diagonal pairs encode a live singleton–identity–singleton product. Different-offset crosses have malformed lengths; equal-offset, different-vertex crosses have empty products. Splicing runs with the same cut state would accept a forbidden cross.

This proves an h³ lower bound for ordinary one-way NFAs and for marked right-only sources, including stays in that right-only model. It is not a cut-state lower bound for arbitrary two-way machines. Consequently this particular strict-block language has one-way nondeterministic state complexity Θ(h³); the claim does not assert optimal source costs across all binary encodings.

headings.text: A pullback with exactly sh² states

blocks.text: Given an s-state binary target, the relation-alphabet pullback uses states (q,t), where q is an original target state and t ranges from 0 to b−1. At a relation cell it reads the adjacency bit at phase t. Its simulation rules are:
Binary move New phase Relation-tape move
stay t stay
right, t < b−1 t+1 stay
right, t = b−1 0 right
left, t > 0 t−1 stay
left, t = 0 b−1 left

At each marker the original marker row is used independently of the stored phase. Marker stays retain the phase; inward moves reset it to 0 at the left marker and b−1 at the right marker. Missing rows remain missing. The initial state is (q₀,0), and (q,t) is accepting exactly when q is accepting.

A relation-cell configuration at cell j maps to binary position (j−1)b+t+1. Each transition corresponds to one binary transition, and every binary transition lifts from every corresponding preimage. Marker phases may be nonunique without introducing an accepting path. The argument covers adjacent markers on ε, both zero-step and positive finite acceptance, stays, partial rows, arbitrary revisits and nonaccepting infinite runs. Determinism and finite-run lengths are preserved. The exact state count is sh², with no extra marker-state family.

blocks.text: The two exponential engines are OpenAI’s attributed Math Release preprints on deterministic simulation of one-way liveness and on nondeterministic complementation. Applying their full relation-alphabet inequalities to the pullback gives the following bounds for every h ≥ 2.
If an s-state marked two-way deterministic automaton recognizes Kₕ, then
If an s-state marked two-way nondeterministic automaton recognizes the complement of Kₕ in all binary words, under zero-step finite acceptance, then
The full complement is the disjoint union
{0,1}* ∖ Kₕ = {x : h² does not divide |x|} ∪ enc(Σₕ* ∖ Lₕ).

The malformed words belong to the binary complement, while the pullback sees every valid encoding of a dead relation product. It therefore recognizes the entire upstream complement. ε is absent from both complements. Restricting the complement to a well-formed-input promise would change the statement.

For a positive-run complementing target, one new nonaccepting initial copy converts the target to zero-step acceptance. The explicit variant is 2^(⌊(h−2)/127⌋) ≤ 2((s+1)h²+1). The displayed deterministic inequality already covers both finite-run conventions. Requiring total rows can be handled by a nonaccepting sink; targets that must halt or accept at the right marker are subclasses of the stated model.

Since h³ ≤ Nₕ ≤ 2h³, both target costs are 2^{Ω(h)} = 2^{Ω(Nₕ^(1/3))}. Polynomial factors and fixed subtractions do not change this asymptotic statement; some small-h numerical lower bounds are simply vacuous. Thus neither simulation nor complementation admits a polynomial state bound on this one fixed alphabet.

The exponent is proportional to the cube root of this binary source size. The note does not assert 2^{Ω(Nₕ)}, a uniform separation such as L ≠ NL, or a small transition-table algorithm. Relation-alphabet pullback tables can be large. The contribution is the explicit transfer and exact language/model accounting, not an independent proof of the upstream exponential obstructions.

headings.text: Earlier work and the scope of the contribution

blocks.text: Sakoda and Sipser established the classical deterministic-simulation problem for two-way nondeterministic automata. Binary adjacency coding is established machinery: Kapoutsis’s 2011 conference treatment and the author preprint linked with the 2013 journal work discuss binary one-way liveness for deterministic targets with few reversals. The latter linked body is an October 2011 author preprint; journal pagination is a separate bibliographic reference.

The public TheoremDB R816 construction uses a different separator/two-bit encoding, a different off-canonical total language and a linear-size binary source, with an inherited quadratic lower bound and a deterministic macro pullback. It is self-reported, source-only context. It neither supplies the two exponential engines used here nor establishes present worldwide openness. Different source costs for a different language do not contradict the cubic lower bound for this exact strict-block language.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis supply the prior quadratic unrestricted deterministic comparison. In their limitation preprint, the connectivity-chain ceiling is proved as Theorem 2; the general-property extension is stated as Theorem 1 with its proof deferred. That restriction concerns a particular method, not all possible lower-bound arguments. Guillon, Prigioniero and Taheri’s polynomial complementation theorem targets 1-limited automata that may rewrite cells using common guessed annotations. It is not a small read-only 2NFA for the full unannotated complement.

The two actual exponential inputs are credited to OpenAI at the pinned source commit adc7f1241b42e322a6451854ab7e4b4c146bf78a. Their manuscript dates and public release dates are distinct. No independent resolution of the base conjecture, exclusive historical priority, invention of binary coding, or exhaustive current-openness claim is made.

articles.name: Rational-point undecidability for smooth projective varieties over the rational numbers
articles.header: Research Rational-point undecidability for smooth projective varieties over the rational numbers Alec Kriebel · 6 October 2026 · Preprint
outside_sections: Research Rational-point undecidability for smooth projective varieties over the rational numbers Alec Kriebel · 6 October 2026 · Preprint

Can an algorithm always decide whether a geometric object defined by rational equations has a rational point? This note derives a negative answer for the full promised class of smooth projective geometrically integral varieties over ℚ, using Poonen’s established transfer and the newly released OpenAI arithmetic preprints with two explicit technical substitutions. It also derives a noncomputability result for the height of a smallest rational point.

Combining OpenAI’s negative solution of rational Hilbert’s tenth problem with Poonen’s established effective transfer, we obtain undecidability of rational-point existence for arbitrary smooth projective geometrically integral varieties over ℚ. We specify a homogeneous-equation input promise and reconstruct the terminating contradiction algorithm. There is also no computable uniform bound on the height of one rational point in terms of the size of the presented equations. The arithmetic input is used with two explicit corrections documented here and in the accompanying verification supplement. This is a geometric consequence of that input; neither the geometric reduction nor the base undecidability theorem is claimed as a new independent solution.

heading.text: Full printed abstract — A conditional coefficient-prime repair of the five-point height argument

article_blocks.text: We reconstruct the non-CM arithmetic part of the five-point height argument in the pinned source [1], replacing its new unrestricted 2-adic modularity input by Pan’s published theorem at 5. The 2-adic member of the resulting system supplies the conductor at 5. The deduction is conditional on the preceding geometric and height-comparison inputs stated below; it neither certifies the entire upstream manuscript nor establishes undecidability of rational polynomial solvability.

heading.text: Full printed abstract — A conditional coefficient-prime repair of the five-point height argument

article_blocks.text: The pinned source cited as [1] is the first reference below.

The input is a finite homogeneous-equation presentation of a smooth projective geometrically integral variety over ℚ. Ambient dimension, variety dimension, degrees, number of equations and coefficient heights may all vary. The promise concerns the geometric object presented; an algorithm is required to terminate and answer correctly on every valid input. The note derives that no such algorithm decides whether a rational point exists.

The second conclusion concerns one point when points exist. For a rational projective point, choose primitive integer coordinates with the first nonzero coordinate positive; its height is the largest absolute coordinate. With s(e) the bit length of the specified presentation and embedding, no total computable function B(s(e)) uniformly bounds the height of a smallest rational point. Such a bound would turn a finite search through coordinate vectors into a decision algorithm. This is a computability statement, not a numerical height estimate for a particular variety.

Poonen’s effective construction transfers rational-point existence from an affine input to a finite collection of smooth projective candidates. Effective component and geometric-integrality tests ensure that only valid promised inputs reach the hypothetical decision procedure. The resulting reduction makes finitely many nonadaptive disjunctive oracle queries. Naive projective closure or resolution alone cannot replace this transfer, because boundary points can be introduced or rational singular points can be lost.

The arithmetic undecidability input is OpenAI’s Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rational numbers, together with the needed non-CM, full-rational-two-torsion branch of A pointwise 2-converse for elliptic curves with rational two-torsion. Both are new OpenAI Math Release preprints dated 24 September 2026, used at source commit adc7f1241b42e322a6451854ab7e4b4c146bf78a. They are substantive arithmetic dependencies. This note makes their use and the following two substitutions explicit.

In the five-point height argument, published Pan modularity at coefficient prime 5 replaces the new unrestricted 2-adic modularity input. The compatible 2-adic constituent of the same system supplies the conductor at 5. The coefficient pair is (5, 2).

In the pointwise-converse determinant argument, an integral universal group-ring correction reconciles inverse/direct Frobenius-Euler conventions and the smoothing factors before character evaluation. The correction preserves the central valuations without adding a factor of two for every auxiliary prime.

The four-page companion isolates the coefficient-prime substitution. Its theorem explicitly assumes three preceding inputs: a fixed proper cover with its principally polarized abelian-surface family, bounded defining field and reduction control; the fixed quaternionic non-CM/CM dichotomy with a uniform CM Faltings-height bound; and the comparison from base height to stable Faltings height. These retained inputs are separate from Pan’s modularity theorem.

The five points are the individually rational branch values of the fixed discriminant-210 quaternionic quotient, labelled by the distinct involutions 30, 42, 70, 105 and 210. For a rational parameter s outside those branch values, M_S(s) is the product of primes outside a fixed exceptional set S at which at least one branch-contact order is odd. Assuming the three inputs, the companion derives h(s) ≤ H M_S(s)^c for fixed constants H, c > 0. It treats this fixed configuration, not arbitrary five rational points.

The companion does not by itself certify the whole upstream manuscript or establish undecidability of rational polynomial solvability. The main note uses the wider corrected arithmetic argument as well as the geometric transfer.

The geometric reduction belongs to Bjorn Poonen’s Existence of rational points on smooth projective varieties (2009). Poonen also credits an earlier ℚ-case route to R. Robinson through Smoryński. The new arithmetic input belongs to the cited OpenAI preprints. The connection between least-point height bounds and rational Hilbert’s tenth problem also has prior literature, including Skorobogatov and Sofos.

The consequence supplies neither a new independent solution of rational Hilbert’s tenth problem nor a new geometric reduction or first-priority claim. It establishes no fixed-curve, fixed-surface or fixed-dimension result, and no automatic Fano, general-type or finite-point-promise extension. A single-output many-one reduction, a specified Turing degree and quantitative reduction bounds are not asserted.

blocks.text: The input is a finite homogeneous-equation presentation of a smooth projective geometrically integral variety over ℚ. Ambient dimension, variety dimension, degrees, number of equations and coefficient heights may all vary. The promise concerns the geometric object presented; an algorithm is required to terminate and answer correctly on every valid input. The note derives that no such algorithm decides whether a rational point exists.

The second conclusion concerns one point when points exist. For a rational projective point, choose primitive integer coordinates with the first nonzero coordinate positive; its height is the largest absolute coordinate. With s(e) the bit length of the specified presentation and embedding, no total computable function B(s(e)) uniformly bounds the height of a smallest rational point. Such a bound would turn a finite search through coordinate vectors into a decision algorithm. This is a computability statement, not a numerical height estimate for a particular variety.

blocks.text: Poonen’s effective construction transfers rational-point existence from an affine input to a finite collection of smooth projective candidates. Effective component and geometric-integrality tests ensure that only valid promised inputs reach the hypothetical decision procedure. The resulting reduction makes finitely many nonadaptive disjunctive oracle queries. blocks.text: The four-page companion isolates the coefficient-prime substitution. Its theorem explicitly assumes three preceding inputs: a fixed proper cover with its principally polarized abelian-surface family, bounded defining field and reduction control; the fixed quaternionic non-CM/CM dichotomy with a uniform CM Faltings-height bound; and the comparison from base height to stable Faltings height. These retained inputs are separate from Pan’s modularity theorem.

The five points are the individually rational branch values of the fixed discriminant-210 quaternionic quotient, labelled by the distinct involutions 30, 42, 70, 105 and 210. For a rational parameter s outside those branch values, M_S(s) is the product of primes outside a fixed exceptional set S at which at least one branch-contact order is odd. Assuming the three inputs, the companion derives h(s) ≤ H M_S(s)^c for fixed constants H, c > 0. It treats this fixed configuration, not arbitrary five rational points.

headings.text: The full formula and its domain

article_blocks.text: Geometry · Elliptic billiards · Research note
Alec Kriebel · Independent researcher · ORCID
13 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

As an even-period billiard orbit moves around an ellipse, the perpendicular feet of a fixed point on the orbit's boundary tangent lines form a changing polygon. Its signed-area centroid stays fixed wherever that centroid is defined. This note proves the observation of Reznik, Garcia and Koiller, gives the centroid explicitly, and identifies the exact circle on which it can fail to exist for star orbits.

Reznik, Garcia and Koiller observed that the area centroid of the outer-side pedal polygon of an even-period elliptic billiard is independent of the orbit phase (invariant k307). We prove this observation on the natural domain of the signed-area centroid and give its explicit value. The proof uses antipodal pairing, support coordinates and telescoping edge moments. For simple even orbits the centroid exists for every fixed pedal point. For even star orbits it can be undefined on a fixed circle, which we determine exactly and realize in a noncircular eight-period example. The note includes a reproducible verification package; the written identities give the all-period proof.

Let the billiard boundary be the noncircular ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 , with a > b > 0 , and fix the confocal elliptic caustic x²/(a² − λ) + y²/(b² − λ) = 1 , where 0 < λ < b² . Assume a Poncelet family whose least period N ≥ 4 is even. Primitive self-intersecting star trajectories are allowed; their vertices keep their trajectory order.

For any fixed real point M = (Mₓ, Mᵧ) , let Qᵢ(M) be its perpendicular foot on the full tangent line to the boundary ellipse at the billiard vertex Pᵢ . These tangent lines are the sides of the outer polygon. The feet are not restricted to tangent segments.
For complex plane points, write [p,q] = Im(conj(p)q) , with conj denoting complex conjugation. With cyclic indices, the signed shoelace area, cubic edge moment and centroid are
S(Q) = ½ Σᵢ [Qᵢ,Qᵢ₊₁] T(Q) = Σᵢ [Qᵢ,Qᵢ₊₁](Qᵢ + Qᵢ₊₁) C(Q) = T(Q)/(6S(Q)), only when S(Q) ≠ 0.
For a star, this is the signed-area centroid with multiplicity. It is not the centroid of the unsigned regions cut out by the star and is not the arithmetic mean of the pedal vertices.

The proof begins with the antipodal symmetry of an even least-period elliptic billiard. The forward Poncelet map commutes with central inversion; the finite orientation-preserving circle action identifies inversion with a half-period shift. This applies to primitive stars as well as simple trajectories.

Support coordinates for the boundary ellipse turn the consecutive tangent geometry into an identity for doubled unit normals. A cyclic edge-moment identity telescopes on this auxiliary ordered polygon without assuming that it is simple. Antipodal pairing cancels the odd terms in the pedal construction. Reducing the remaining cubic moments, then applying the translation law for signed first moments, gives both the area factor and the complete centroid formula above. The four-period rectangle branch is established separately.

The contribution is the all-even-least-period signed-centroid formula together with its exact natural domain and the simple/star boundary analysis. The all-period conclusion rests on written identities. The accompanying exact and numerical materials provide reproducible supporting evidence; finite samples alone do not establish arbitrary periods, uniform stability near degeneracies, or a formally certified proof.

Writing M = (X,Y) and R² = X² + Y² , the exact signed moments are

At M = (13√731/144, 0) , the area vanishes while T = (221√21930/10368, 0) ≠ 0 . Thus a genuine nonremovable singularity occurs at this diagnostic point. The centroid is undefined on the entire zero-area circle; a nonremovable pole at every point of that circle is not claimed.

Reversing the trajectory changes the signs of both S and T , leaving their centroid quotient unchanged. Repeating an even least-period trajectory scales the two moments by the same factor. Merely repeating an odd primitive orbit to obtain an even list does not supply the required antipodal pairing and is outside this theorem.

The hypotheses exclude a circular boundary, hyperbolic or degenerate caustics, and zero-signed-area pedal polygons. Conclusions about unsigned region centroids, arithmetic vertex means, or uniform numerical stability at excluded limits do not follow. In the star case the doubled-normal polygon can have negative signed area; the simple-orbit positivity argument is not extended to stars.

Reznik, Garcia and Koiller formulated the outer-side pedal area-centroid observation as invariant k307 , in Table 4 and the associated discussion of their work. Their published Fifty new invariants of N-periodics in the elliptic billiard (2021) and the separately identified arXiv version 11, Eighty new invariants , are distinct editions.

Bialy and Tabachnikov's Dan Reznik's identities and more supplies neighboring vertex-centroid identities, including k306, and classical even-orbit symmetry. The vertex mean and the signed-area centroid require different moment arguments. Schwartz and Tabachnikov's work on Poncelet centers of mass supplies signed/multiplicity centroid context and general centroid-locus theorems. Applying a fixed-conic Poncelet theorem directly to arbitrary-point outer pedals would require a separate fixed-conic realization, which is not assumed here.

The note credits the original observation and classical methods. Its contribution is the explicit formula, the all-period support and cubic-moment proof, and the exact domain analysis. Historical priority and exclusive firstness are not established.

sections.text: Abstract Reznik, Garcia and Koiller observed that the area centroid of the outer-side pedal polygon of an even-period elliptic billiard is independent of the orbit phase (invariant k307). We prove this observation on the natural domain of the signed-area centroid and give its explicit value. The proof uses antipodal pairing, support coordinates and telescoping edge moments. For simple even orbits the centroid exists for every fixed pedal point. For even star orbits it can be undefined on a fixed circle, which we determine exactly and realize in a noncircular eight-period example. The note includes a reproducible verification package; the written identities give the all-period proof.

blocks.text: Let the billiard boundary be the noncircular ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 , with a > b > 0 , and fix the confocal elliptic caustic x²/(a² − λ) + y²/(b² − λ) = 1 , where 0 < λ < b² . Assume a Poncelet family whose least period N ≥ 4 is even. Primitive self-intersecting star trajectories are allowed; their vertices keep their trajectory order.

For complex plane points, write [p,q] = Im(conj(p)q) , with conj denoting complex conjugation. With cyclic indices, the signed shoelace area, cubic edge moment and centroid are

blocks.text: Set z = Mₓ + iMᵧ and introduce the real quantities
H = (a² + b²)/2, e = (a² − b²)/2 d = 1 − λ(a⁻² + b⁻²), F = Hd + 2λ v = −4eλd/(F² − e²d²), G = 2F + d|z|².
For the branch oriented counterclockwise around the caustic, F > 0 , F² − e²d² > 0 and the outer-pedal area at the origin satisfies S(0) > 0 . For every fixed M ,
S(M) = S(0)(2F + d|z|²)/(2F). C(Q(M)) = z/2 − { z(F + 2Hd + evd) + conj(z)[2Fv + 3ed + (vd/2)|z|²] } / {3(2F + d|z|²)}, provided G ≠ 0.

The explicit centroid depends on the ellipse, caustic and fixed pedal point, but not on the orbit phase wherever G ≠ 0 . The unnormalized origin area S(0) is not asserted to be phase invariant; it cancels in the centroid quotient.
If d ≥ 0 , the centroid exists for every fixed point M .

The least period is four if and only if d = 0 . The four-period rectangle case gives C(Q(M)) = M/3 for every M , and is handled before any division by d .
Every simple winding-one even family has d ≥ 0 , so every M is allowed. For a simple family of least period at least six, d > 0 .

blocks.text: The proof begins with the antipodal symmetry of an even least-period elliptic billiard. The forward Poncelet map commutes with central inversion; the finite orientation-preserving circle action identifies inversion with a half-period shift. This applies to primitive stars as well as simple trajectories.

Support coordinates for the boundary ellipse turn the consecutive tangent geometry into an identity for doubled unit normals. A cyclic edge-moment identity telescopes on this auxiliary ordered polygon without assuming that it is simple. Antipodal pairing cancels the odd terms in the pedal construction. Reducing the remaining cubic moments, then applying the translation law for signed first moments, gives both the area factor and the complete centroid formula above. The four-period rectangle branch is established separately.

The contribution is the all-even-least-period signed-centroid formula together with its exact natural domain and the simple/star boundary analysis. The all-period conclusion rests on written identities. The accompanying exact and numerical materials provide reproducible supporting evidence; finite samples alone do not establish arbitrary periods, uniform stability near degeneracies, or a formally certified proof.

blocks.text: Reversing the trajectory changes the signs of both S and T , leaving their centroid quotient unchanged. Repeating an even least-period trajectory scales the two moments by the same factor. Merely repeating an odd primitive orbit to obtain an even list does not supply the required antipodal pairing and is outside this theorem.

The hypotheses exclude a circular boundary, hyperbolic or degenerate caustics, and zero-signed-area pedal polygons. Conclusions about unsigned region centroids, arithmetic vertex means, or uniform numerical stability at excluded limits do not follow. In the star case the doubled-normal polygon can have negative signed area; the simple-orbit positivity argument is not extended to stars.

blocks.text: Reznik, Garcia and Koiller formulated the outer-side pedal area-centroid observation as invariant k307 , in Table 4 and the associated discussion of their work. Their published Fifty new invariants of N-periodics in the elliptic billiard (2021) and the separately identified arXiv version 11, Eighty new invariants , are distinct editions.

Bialy and Tabachnikov's Dan Reznik's identities and more supplies neighboring vertex-centroid identities, including k306, and classical even-orbit symmetry. The vertex mean and the signed-area centroid require different moment arguments. Schwartz and Tabachnikov's work on Poncelet centers of mass supplies signed/multiplicity centroid context and general centroid-locus theorems. Applying a fixed-conic Poncelet theorem directly to arbitrary-point outer pedals would require a separate fixed-conic realization, which is not assumed here.

The note credits the original observation and classical methods. Its contribution is the explicit formula, the all-period support and cubic-moment proof, and the exact domain analysis. Historical priority and exclusive firstness are not established.

This note computes every L²-Betti number of OpenAI’s explicit rank-100 amalgam directly, and combines that calculation with OpenAI’s positive Bernoulli cost estimate. The result is a free ergodic probability-measure-preserving orbit relation whose cost is strictly greater than one although all its L²-Betti numbers vanish. The group’s infimum cost is one. The direct invariant calculation and the substantial upstream positive-cost input have separate roles.

We give a direct calculation of all L²-Betti numbers of the rank-100 amalgam in OpenAI’s fixed-price construction. An elementary regular-tree argument makes its cellular boundary injective, proves its displayed presentation complex aspherical, and gives βₙ⁽²⁾(Γ) = 0 for every n ≥ 0, independently of either cost bound. Combining this calculation with OpenAI’s positive Bernoulli cost estimate gives an explicit free ergodic probability-measure-preserving orbit relation with cost at least 1 + (100·2⁶¹)⁻¹ and vanishing L²-Betti numbers. The group infimum cost remains one. The construction and positive cost estimate are due to OpenAI; the cost–Betti comparison and action invariance are due to Gaboriau. This is an attributed consequence and verification note, with a separate direct invariant proof.

heading.text: The explicit group and the full conclusion

article_blocks.text: Let A = F(a, b_1, …, b_99), let w = a b_1 a b_2 … a b_99 a, and let J = ⟨b_1, …, b_99, w⟩. The group is Γ = A ∗_J (J × ⟨t⟩). Its displayed presentation has 101 generators and 100 relators: [t, b_i] = 1 for 1 ≤ i ≤ 99, and [t, w] = 1. The associated presentation complex is a finite two-dimensional K(Γ, 1).

heading.text: The explicit group and the full conclusion

article_blocks.text: Every L²-Betti number of Γ vanishes: βₙ⁽²⁾(Γ) = 0 for every n ≥ 0. Gaboriau’s action-invariance theorem transfers this to the orbit relation of every essentially free probability-measure-preserving action of Γ. That transfer does not require ergodicity.

heading.text: The explicit group and the full conclusion

article_blocks.text: For the invariant conull free part X of the product-Lebesgue Bernoulli shift [0, 1]^Γ, the action is free, ergodic and probability-measure-preserving. Its orbit relation ℛ_X satisfies βₙ⁽²⁾(ℛ_X) = 0 for all n ≥ 0 and Cost(ℛ_X) ≥ 1 + 1/(100·2⁶¹) > 1. The positive gap is obtained from OpenAI’s substantial Bernoulli cost theorem, with α = 2⁻⁶¹.

The note supplies a direct invariant proof for the displayed group. A free-basis substitution turns the relevant convolution operator into the adjacency problem on an infinite 100-regular tree. The tree argument and the infinite-order t direction establish injectivity of the completed cellular boundary. The argument preserves the order of the noncommuting factors in the Fox-derivative formulas.

Injectivity also applies to finitely supported integral cellular chains. The simply connected two-dimensional presentation cover is then acyclic and hence contractible, proving the K(Γ, 1) assertion. The completed chain complex, with module ranks 100, 101 and 1, has zero reduced L²-homology in every degree. Euler characteristic zero is only a consistency check; it would not by itself prove the vanishing.

This all-degree Betti calculation and the asphericity proof use neither cost bound. They do not independently prove the positive Bernoulli cost estimate or failure of fixed price. The tree operator is proved injective on the regular representation, with no claim of bounded invertibility, a spectral gap or injectivity in arbitrary finite quotients.

heading.text: Bernoulli cost and group infimum cost

article_blocks.text: Cost is the infimum of the total domain measure of partial orbit maps that generate a measured equivalence relation. The classical comparison is Cost(ℛ) − 1 ≥ β₁⁽²⁾(ℛ) − β₀⁽²⁾(ℛ). The zeroth term matters: a free action of a finite group of order q has β₀⁽²⁾ = 1/q and cost 1 − 1/q. For the infinite group here, free orbits have β₀⁽²⁾ = 0.

heading.text: Bernoulli cost and group infimum cost

article_blocks.text: The note also constructs cyclic-height actions Y_M = X × ℤ/Mℤ. With χ(a) = 1 and χ(b_i) = χ(t) = 0, the action is (x, r)g = (xg, r + χ(g) mod M). These actions are free, ergodic and probability-measure-preserving for every positive integer M. A short direct graphing proof gives Cost(ℛ_{Y_M}) ≤ 1 + 99/M for every integer M > 100.

heading.text: Bernoulli cost and group infimum cost

article_blocks.text: Every essentially free action has cost at least one by the classical comparison, while the Y_M bounds approach one. Thus Cost_*(Γ) = 1, where Cost_* is the infimum over essentially free probability-measure-preserving actions. This does not assert that any action attains cost one. The Bernoulli relation’s strictly positive cost gap and the group infimum are distinct statements.

heading.text: Bernoulli cost and group infimum cost

article_blocks.text: The cyclic-height graphing bound also gives a separate limiting proof of first-Betti vanishing. The direct all-degree proof and the group-infimum argument remain valid independently of the Bernoulli positive lower bound.

That estimate relies on the upstream compression, deployment, finite-model, rank and planar-shortening argument; it is not a consequence of the invariant calculation or finite arithmetic checks alone.

A self-contained regular-tree and cellular-boundary calculation proves that its displayed 101-generator/100-relator presentation complex is a finite two-dimensional classifying space and every L2-Betti number vanishes, independently of either cost bound. Gaboriau's action invariance and OpenAI's positive Bernoulli cost estimate then give an explicit free ergodic p.m.p. orbit relation with Cost at least 1 + 1/(100*2^61) and vanishing L2-Betti numbers. The group infimum cost is one.

sections.text: The explicit group and the full conclusion Let A = F(a, b_1, …, b_99), let w = a b_1 a b_2 … a b_99 a, and let J = ⟨b_1, …, b_99, w⟩. The group is Γ = A ∗_J (J × ⟨t⟩). Its displayed presentation has 101 generators and 100 relators: [t, b_i] = 1 for 1 ≤ i ≤ 99, and [t, w] = 1. The associated presentation complex is a finite two-dimensional K(Γ, 1). Every L²-Betti number of Γ vanishes: βₙ⁽²⁾(Γ) = 0 for every n ≥ 0. Gaboriau’s action-invariance theorem transfers this to the orbit relation of every essentially free probability-measure-preserving action of Γ. That transfer does not require ergodicity. For the invariant conull free part X of the product-Lebesgue Bernoulli shift [0, 1]^Γ, the action is free, ergodic and probability-measure-preserving. Its orbit relation ℛ_X satisfies βₙ⁽²⁾(ℛ_X) = 0 for all n ≥ 0 and Cost(ℛ_X) ≥ 1 + 1/(100·2⁶¹) > 1. The positive gap is obtained from OpenAI’s substantial Bernoulli cost theorem, with α = 2⁻⁶¹.

blocks.text: The note supplies a direct invariant proof for the displayed group. A free-basis substitution turns the relevant convolution operator into the adjacency problem on an infinite 100-regular tree. The tree argument and the infinite-order t direction establish injectivity of the completed cellular boundary. The argument preserves the order of the noncommuting factors in the Fox-derivative formulas.

Injectivity also applies to finitely supported integral cellular chains. The simply connected two-dimensional presentation cover is then acyclic and hence contractible, proving the K(Γ, 1) assertion. The completed chain complex, with module ranks 100, 101 and 1, has zero reduced L²-homology in every degree. Euler characteristic zero is only a consistency check; it would not by itself prove the vanishing.

This all-degree Betti calculation and the asphericity proof use neither cost bound. They do not independently prove the positive Bernoulli cost estimate or failure of fixed price. The tree operator is proved injective on the regular representation, with no claim of bounded invertibility, a spectral gap or injectivity in arbitrary finite quotients.

headings.text: Bernoulli cost and group infimum cost

blocks.text: Cost is the infimum of the total domain measure of partial orbit maps that generate a measured equivalence relation. The classical comparison is Cost(ℛ) − 1 ≥ β₁⁽²⁾(ℛ) − β₀⁽²⁾(ℛ). The zeroth term matters: a free action of a finite group of order q has β₀⁽²⁾ = 1/q and cost 1 − 1/q. For the infinite group here, free orbits have β₀⁽²⁾ = 0.

The note also constructs cyclic-height actions Y_M = X × ℤ/Mℤ. With χ(a) = 1 and χ(b_i) = χ(t) = 0, the action is (x, r)g = (xg, r + χ(g) mod M). These actions are free, ergodic and probability-measure-preserving for every positive integer M. A short direct graphing proof gives Cost(ℛ_{Y_M}) ≤ 1 + 99/M for every integer M > 100.

Every essentially free action has cost at least one by the classical comparison, while the Y_M bounds approach one. Thus Cost_*(Γ) = 1, where Cost_* is the infimum over essentially free probability-measure-preserving actions. This does not assert that any action attains cost one. The Bernoulli relation’s strictly positive cost gap and the group infimum are distinct statements.

The cyclic-height graphing bound also gives a separate limiting proof of first-Betti vanishing. The direct all-degree proof and the group-infimum argument remain valid independently of the Bernoulli positive lower bound.

article_blocks.text: Alec Kriebel · ORCID Published October 6, 2026 · Zenodo version 1.0.0 · Preprint

We give an explicit restriction and transference consequence of OpenAI's October 5, 2026 full annular variation theorem for the triangular Hilbert transform. For arbitrary commuting invertible probability-preserving transformations S,T and complex f,g ∈ L 3 , the symmetric bilinear Hilbert sums have bounded pointwise r -variation in L 3/2 for every r > 2, and converge almost everywhere and in L 3/2 . The restriction uses boxes of fixed positive area and a uniformly summable kernel error. The analytic breakthrough is the cited continuous theorem; the present note supplies the discrete restriction and full measure-theoretic transfer.

Two commuting transformations describe two compatible ways to move through a probability space. A bilinear ergodic Hilbert sum combines the values of two functions along those motions, using the signed weight 1/n and truncating symmetrically in positive and negative time. This note shows that the sums settle to a limit and quantitatively controls their fluctuations.

The argument is a consequence of OpenAI's full annular variation theorem for the triangular Hilbert transform. The note adds an explicit passage from that continuous estimate to lattice sums and then to arbitrary commuting probability-preserving transformations.
Let S and T be commuting invertible measurable transformations of a probability space, with measurable inverses, preserving the probability measure. For complex f,g ∈ L 3 , set H 0 = 0 and
H N (f,g)(x) = ∑ 0<|n|≤N f(S n x)g(T n x)/n.
For every real r > 2 there is a finite constant D r , independent of the space and transformations, such that

Here V r is the supremum, over all finite increasing integer lists 0 ≤ N 0 < ⋯ < N J , of (∑ j=1 J |H N j − H N j−1 | r ) 1/r . The supremum is taken pointwise before the L 3/2 norm; each point may choose its own list.

The maximal function sup N≥0 |H N | has the same bound. The sums converge almost everywhere and in L 3/2 to a bounded complex bilinear operator H(f,g). They also satisfy the stronger maximal-tail conclusion
‖sup N≥m |H N (f,g) − H(f,g)|‖ 3/2 → 0 as m → ∞.
No ergodicity or freeness assumption is required.

article_blocks.text: A finite-menu, finite-window form of Calderón transference then applies the lattice estimate to orbit arrays. Keeping the endpoint horizon fixed while the orbit window expands preserves the pointwise supremum and makes the limiting argument explicit. The result concerns complex L 3 inputs, symmetric odd Hilbert truncations, commuting transformations, and r > 2. It gives no r = 2 estimate, noncommuting theorem, extension to other input exponents, or one-sided commuting Cesàro convergence statement. The supporting kernel checks address the discrete cell bookkeeping; they do not establish the continuous analytic theorem.

A. P. Calderón, Ergodic theory and translation-invariant operators (1968) , for classical transference.
C. Demeter and C. Thiele, On the two dimensional bilinear Hilbert transform , Section 6 and footnote 36, for the continuous-to-lattice and orbit-array reductions.
P. Durcik, V. Kovač, K. A. Škreb and C. Thiele, Norm-variation of ergodic averages with respect to two commuting transformations , Section 5, for positive-area phase integration.
C. Demeter, Pointwise convergence of the ergodic bilinear Hilbert transform , Theorem 1.2, for Hilbert convergence along opposite powers of one transformation.

articles.name: Exact semidefinite complexity of the symmetric traveling-salesman polytope
outside_sections: Exact semidefinite complexity of the symmetric traveling-salesman polytope
Alec Kriebel · 6 October 2026 · Unrefereed preprint
ORCID: 0009-0001-9320-500X · DOI and Zenodo record
Original manuscript abstract

The exponential real PSD-rank theorem for shifted perfect-matching matrices in the OpenAI Math Release implies that the symmetric traveling-salesman polytope on N cities has exact real semidefinite extension complexity 2 Θ(N) , measured by PSD matrix order. We give explicit data for Yannakakis's 3n-city face projection, a 2n-city contraction variant, a padding projection covering every sufficiently large city count, and a subset-state flow upper bound. The exponential lower-bound method and its central estimate belong to the cited matching theorem; this note supplies an explicit consequence and verification package, not a new lower-bound method. The exponential input has been independently examined in mathematical audits; the accompanying Lean statements cover only superpolynomial bounds. No conventional human peer review has been completed.
Overview

A traveling-salesman tour visits each city once and returns to its starting point. The symmetric TSP polytope is the convex hull of the undirected edge-incidence vectors of all such tours. Its points include every convex mixture of valid tours.

A semidefinite lift describes that polytope using extra coordinates, affine equations, and a positive semidefinite (PSD) matrix. This note shows that the smallest exact real lift has exponential matrix order as the number of cities grows. It also gives an exact construction of exponential order, so the lower and upper bounds agree at that scale.

The substantial exponential lower-bound breakthrough is OpenAI's theorem for shifted perfect-matching matrices . This note supplies its explicit TSP consequence, constructions, and verification package. It claims no independent lower-bound method or priority for the established reductions.
How the lower bound reaches TSP

The matching input concerns A n (ρ) U,M = |M ∩ δ(U)| − 1 + ρ, with U an odd vertex set and M a perfect matching. For each fixed 0 < ρ < 1, OpenAI's pinned theorem gives exponential real PSD rank for all sufficiently large even n. Adding one scalar block converts factors of the unshifted matrix into factors of the shifted matrix. The note's tight-slack calculation then connects arbitrary exact affine PSD lifts to the unshifted matching slacks, giving xc psd,ℝ (P PM (n)) ≥ 2 an for some a > 0 and all sufficiently large even n. The endpoint ρ = 1 is excluded.
Taking a nonempty face or an affine image cannot increase the required matrix order. The paper makes two matching-to-TSP constructions explicit:

Yannakakis's 3n-city face. Use left and right cliques and a middle layer. For each label i, the only middle-vertex edges form the path ℓ i –d i –r i . Setting every other unavailable edge to zero defines a face and forces these paths. The remaining edges in each clique form a perfect matching. Projecting onto the left clique recovers the matching polytope. A 2n-city contraction. Keep the two cliques, force each diagonal cross edge ℓ i r i to one, and force every other cross edge to zero. Contracting the diagonal edges gives the same connected, two-colored union of matchings. The diagonal-one constraints are essential.

In either construction, every first matching has a second matching that joins its pairs into one alternating cycle. This proves that every matching occurs as the projection of a face tour. The constructions give surjective projections; they do not require a unique tour for each matching.

Padding covers every city count: for N ≥ m ≥ 3, force a path through the added cities, then contract it to an old city. This makes P TSP (m) a linear image of a face of P TSP (N). Choosing the even number n = 2⌊N/4⌋ yields the bound 2 2a⌊N/4⌋ once the matching threshold is reached. Thus the exponential bound holds for every sufficiently large integer N.
Why an exponential upper bound also exists

Fix city 1 and let Q be the remaining q = N − 1 cities. A directed acyclic network records a visited subset S ⊆ Q and its last city i. A source-to-sink path lists a permutation of Q; its edge labels give a tour through city 1. Nonnegative unit flows are convex combinations of these paths, so their edge-label projection is exactly the TSP polytope.

The network has 2q + q(q − 1)2 q − 2 arcs. Put one nonnegative flow variable on each diagonal entry of a PSD matrix, set off-diagonal entries to zero, and impose flow conservation. This gives the displayed upper bound 2(N − 1) + (N − 1)(N − 2)2 N − 3 . The construction uses the established subset-state dynamic-programming idea associated with Held–Karp.
Background and credit

Yannakakis's classical face projection supplies the 3n-city reduction. Rothvoß records its consequence in his work on linear extension complexity of the matching polytope. Gouveia–Parrilo–Thomas provide the general cone-factorization framework; the note gives the tight-slack argument needed for its unrestricted affine real PSD convention.

Lee–Raghavendra–Steurer proved an unrestricted TSP lower bound of 2 Ω(N 1/13 ) . Lee–Prakash–de Wolf–Yuen corrected a computational estimate in that work and give 2 Ω̃(N 1/11 ) ; the tilde suppresses logarithmic factors. The sharp exponential-order consequence here uses OpenAI's new matching theorem. A bounded literature search does not establish firstness.

Independent mathematical audits examined the central matching proof and found no material defect. articles.name: A counterexample to Takao's self-duality question
outside_sections: A counterexample to Takao's self-duality question
Alec Kriebel · Independent researcher · 4 October 2026 · Unrefereed preprint
ORCID: 0009-0001-9320-500X · DOI and Zenodo record · Zenodo version 1.0
Open PDF · Download PDF · Original verification ZIP · BibTeX
Original manuscript abstract

Takao asked whether a finite flat commutative group scheme over a Witt ring, killed by p and having quasi-supersingular special fiber, must be Cartier self-dual in ranks p 2n with n ≥ 3. For every p > 3 and n ≥ 3, we give a counterexample over W(F̅ p ) . A six-dimensional Dieudonné module has an explicit filtration by supersingular elliptic p-torsion modules, an explicit finite Honda complement, and an image-intersection invariant distinguishing it from its dual. Both the special fiber and its finite flat Witt-ring lift are non-self-dual. The construction is an application of classical Dieudonné and finite Honda theory.
Use the Open PDF link above if the embedded reader is unavailable.
Overview

Cartier duality is the group-scheme form of character duality. A group scheme is self-dual when it is isomorphic to its Cartier dual. Takao asked whether a filtration built from supersingular elliptic p-torsion forces self-duality under the stated finite flat hypotheses.

This note gives an explicit negative answer in every stated higher rank. The special fiber has the required filtration, yet a simple invariant distinguishes it from its dual. A finite Honda system realizes that same special fiber in a finite flat group scheme over a Witt ring; the lift also fails self-duality.
A six-dimensional module
Contravariant Dieudonné theory encodes the special fiber by a vector space M with Frobenius-semilinear F and inverse-Frobenius-semilinear V. On a basis e 0 , …, e 5 , the nonzero images are

These operators satisfy FV = VF = 0 and F 3 = V 3 = 0. The explicit basis change in the paper gives an F,V-stable flag of dimensions 2 and 4. Its three two-dimensional factors all have Fx = Vx = y and Fy = Vy = 0, the module of supersingular elliptic p-torsion over this algebraically closed field. Exact contravariance turns the module flag into the required subgroup filtration.
The obstruction to self-duality
The invariant is δ(T) = dim k (im F T 2 ∩ im V T 2 ) . An isomorphism preserves both second-image subspaces and their intersection.

Takao asked whether a finite flat commutative group scheme over a Witt ring, killed by p and having quasi-supersingular special fiber, must be Cartier self-dual in ranks p 2n with n ≥ 3. For every p > 3 and n ≥ 3, we give a counterexample over W(F̅ p ) . A six-dimensional Dieudonné module has an explicit filtration by supersingular elliptic p-torsion modules, an explicit finite Honda complement, and an image-intersection invariant distinguishing it from its dual. Both the special fiber and its finite flat Witt-ring lift are non-self-dual. The construction is an application of classical Dieudonné and finite Honda theory.

Cartier duality is the group-scheme form of character duality. A group scheme is self-dual when it is isomorphic to its Cartier dual. Takao asked whether a filtration built from supersingular elliptic p-torsion forces self-duality under the stated finite flat hypotheses.

This note gives an explicit negative answer in every stated higher rank. The special fiber has the required filtration, yet a simple invariant distinguishes it from its dual. A finite Honda system realizes that same special fiber in a finite flat group scheme over a Witt ring; the lift also fails self-duality.

H n ≄ H n D , and G n ≄ G n D .

Here quasi-supersingular means that the special fiber has a subgroup filtration whose successive quotients are E i [p] for supersingular elliptic curves E i . The theorem does not require this filtration to lift over W.

Takao's Proposition 2 gives self-duality for n ≤ 2. The question immediately following it, on p. 2479 of his Oberwolfach contribution, asks about n ≥ 3. The construction starts with n = 3, of rank p 6 , and extends to every larger n.

articles.name: An alternating antimorphic Fine-Wilf theorem
outside_sections: An alternating antimorphic Fine-Wilf theorem
Alec Kriebel · Independent researcher · 3 October 2026 · Unrefereed research note
ORCID: 0009-0001-9320-500X · DOI and Zenodo record · Zenodo version 1.0
Original verification ZIP · Open PDF · Download PDF · BibTeX
Original manuscript abstract

Let θ be an antimorphic involution of a free monoid. If a finite word w has alternating θ-periods p,q and |w| ≥ p+q−gcd(p,q), then gcd(p,q) is an alternating θ-period of w. This proves the unnumbered conjecture stated after Theorem 23 in Nowotka's contribution, joint with Bischoff, to Mini-Workshop: Combinatorics on Words (2010). The proof applies the classical Fine–Wilf theorem to the common reflected extension θ(w)w and recovers the alternating phase at its center. The length formula cannot be decreased by one uniformly.
Use the Open PDF link above if the embedded reader is unavailable.
Overview

An alternating period describes a word built by repeating a block, its reflected image, the block, its reflected image, and so on. The reflection may also swap letters. The theorem says that two such patterns sharing a sufficiently long finite prefix force a common alternating pattern whose block length is the greatest common divisor of the two lengths.

The threshold is the familiar Fine–Wilf expression p+q−gcd(p,q). The proof obtains it by reflecting the whole finite word once, applying the classical theorem for ordinary periods, and using the reflection center to recover the required alternating phase.
Why the reflected word works

Every antimorphic involution reverses a word and applies an involutive permutation σ to its letters. For one alternating period p, extending uθ(u) in both directions gives an ordinary 2p-periodic sequence with reflection identity s −1−i = σ(s i ) .

Its restriction around the center is exactly W = θ(w)w. Applying the same argument to q gives ordinary periods 2p and 2q on this same finite word . The construction uses the observed w; it assumes no equality between two unseen infinite completions.

Writing L = |w|, the bound gives 2L ≥ 2p+2q−2d . Classical Fine–Wilf therefore gives W ordinary period 2d. Its central block is θ(v)v. Moving by multiples of 2d within the finite interval, on either side of that center, shows that the right-hand word w follows v, θ(v), v, θ(v), … exactly.
Why the formula cannot always be shortened

Take ordinary reversal, distinct letters a,b, and w = abb. It is a prefix of both (ab ba) ω and (abb bba) ω , so it has alternating periods 2 and 3. Its length is one below 2+3−gcd(2,3) = 4 . Alternating period 1 would force the constant word aaa…, which does not begin abb.
This example rules out lowering the formula by one uniformly . It does not determine the best threshold separately for every pair of periods, alphabet, or involution.
The question and earlier work

The theorem proves the exact unnumbered conjecture following Theorem 23 on printed p. 2220 of Nowotka's contribution, joint with Bischoff, to the 2010 mini-workshop report, published in 2011. It is distinct from numbered Conjecture 27. Theorem 23 and Bischoff's thesis give the longer sufficient bound p+q.

The ordinary Fine–Wilf theorem and the reflection/doubled-period machinery are prior work. Bischoff's thesis develops the relevant reflection method. This note uses one common extension of the entire finite prefix to reach the shorter threshold.

Czeizler–Kari–Seki and Kari–Seki study related θ-primitive-root and more general block-power questions, with different hypotheses and conclusions. For p > q ≥ 2d, Kari–Seki's author manuscript has a piecewise bound: at q = 2d its stronger branch is 2p−⌊d/2⌋ . The note's single sufficient comparison is valid but weaker at that endpoint.

For ordinary reversal at the common phase, Simpson's published palindromic-periodicity theorem directly requires 2p+2q−2d on w itself, twice the threshold here. A general letter-twisted reflection is not automatically an ordinary palindrome. These comparisons do not exclude every indirect reformulation of earlier work or certify first discovery.
Scope and review status

The theorem concerns the stated alternating-prefix definition for one arbitrary antimorphic involution. Its uniform obstruction is not a pairwise-optimality claim. The bounded literature assessment does not certify global novelty or present worldwide openness.

A positive integer p is an alternating θ-period of w if w is a prefix of (uθ(u)) ω for a length-p word u. The symbol ω means infinite repetition. The block order is prescribed, and p need not be a minimal period.
If the finite word w has alternating θ-periods p and q, put d = gcd(p,q) . If
|w| ≥ p + q − d,
then, for the length-d prefix v of w, w is a prefix of (vθ(v)) ω . Thus d is an alternating θ-period, with the phase anchored at the beginning of w. No minimality of d is asserted.

The length hypothesis already implies |w| ≥ max(p,q). The theorem allows a final incomplete block and includes equal periods and divisibility cases. Arbitrary-order concatenations of u and θ(u) form a different model.

Original source and verification ZIP · Open PDF · Download PDF · BibTeX
Original manuscript abstract

Every positive definite real homogeneous form admits linear coordinates in which its symmetric ordered coefficients have diagonal entries equal to one and all mixed entries strictly between zero and one. This answers Brandes's question in Problem 11 of the 2019 Oberwolfach report on analytic number theory, including its absolute-value inequality. The proof chooses a basis close to a direction minimizing the form on a Euclidean sphere. The desired coefficient inequalities then follow from a positive quadratic term in a polynomial difference.
Use the Open PDF link above if the embedded reader is unavailable.
Overview

A positive definite form is a homogeneous polynomial that is positive at every nonzero real vector. This note shows that suitable linear coordinates give it a simple coefficient pattern: the diagonal symmetric ordered entries are one, and every mixed entry is positive and smaller than one.

The coordinate vectors can be nearly parallel. Their independence is enough for the theorem; no orthogonality or quantitative conditioning bound is imposed. The coefficient convention is equally important: ordinary collected monomial coefficients carry additional multinomial factors.
Which coefficients are normalized?
The ordered expansion sums over all D-tuples of indices:
p(t) = ∑ j₁,…,jᴅ A(e j₁ ,…,e jᴅ ) t j₁ ⋯t jᴅ .

When equal monomials are collected, the coefficient of t α is the ordered entry multiplied by D!/(α 1 !⋯α m !) . The theorem bounds the entry before this factor. It does not say that every ordinary monomial coefficient lies between zero and one.

For example, p(x,y) = x 4 + 12x 2 y 2 + y 4 is positive definite. Its original symmetric ordered entry A(e 1 ,e 1 ,e 2 ,e 2 ) is 12/6 = 2. The result supplies suitable new coordinates; it asserts no bound in every starting basis.
Why clustering a basis works
Choose a unit vector v minimizing p on an auxiliary Euclidean sphere. After temporarily dividing by its positive minimum, p(v) = 1 and p(x) ≥ ‖x‖ D . Tangential first and second derivatives give
A(v D−1 ,u) = 0, Q(u,u) ≥ ‖u‖ 2 /(D−1), where Q(a,b) = A(v D−2 ,a,b) and u ⟂ v.
Take an orthonormal basis w 1 ,…,w m−1 of the tangent space, set w m = 0, and use x i = v + εw i . These vectors remain independent for every nonzero ε, even though they cluster near v.
For a tuple J, compare the product of its diagonal values with the Dth power of its multilinear entry. The resulting polynomial gap has quadratic term
(D/2) ε 2 ∑ r<s Q(w jᵣ −w jₛ , w jᵣ −w jₛ ).

Every mixed tuple has a nonzero tangential difference, making this term strictly positive. The multilinear numerator separately stays positive by continuity from one. There are only finitely many tuples, so one sufficiently small positive ε makes all the required inequalities hold simultaneously.

Undo the temporary common scaling, then replace each column by z i = x i /p(x i ) 1/D using the original p. This positive rescaling preserves independence, gives unit diagonal values, and leaves every mixed ordered entry strictly between zero and one.
Scope

The theorem is an existence result over the real general linear group. The constructed basis can be close to singular. Openness permits a rational unnormalized basis, but the final unit-diagonal rescaling need not preserve rationality.
No extension to merely nonnegative forms, unimodular integral changes, controlled conditioning, or an effective uniform choice of ε is asserted. The analytic proof has no computational assumption.
The question and precursor

Problem 11, attributed to Brandes in the 2019 Oberwolfach Analytic Number Theory Problem Session, asks for a linear change making each ordered coefficient's absolute value at most the geometric mean of its corresponding diagonal entries. The note makes the canonical symmetric polarization convention explicit.

Brandes's Forms representing forms: the definite case is a direct precursor. The available arXiv v2 author version includes the quadratic matrix-entry Cauchy–Schwarz normalization in Lemma 2.1. The publisher's final typeset edition was not inspected for this comparison; final-edition equivalence and pagination-specific theorem identity are not certified.

articles.name: A credited finiteness deduction for restricted boundary-twist factorizations
outside_sections: A credited finiteness deduction for restricted boundary-twist factorizations
By Alec Kriebel , independent researcher · 14 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

A surface can admit many ways to express a twist near its boundary as a sequence of positive twists along interior curves. This note gives a credited deduction that, for a fixed genus and the intersection restriction below, only finitely many such ordered factorizations remain after changing all curves by the same boundary-fixing homeomorphism.

A surface can admit many ways to express a twist near its boundary as a sequence of positive twists along interior curves. This note gives a credited deduction that, for a fixed genus and the intersection restriction below, only finitely many such ordered factorizations remain after changing all curves by the same boundary-fixing homeomorphism.

Fix an integer g ≥ 1 and an oriented compact connected surface S g ,1 with one boundary circle δ. Maps preserve orientation and fix the boundary pointwise; isotopies fix it pointwise too. Each factor is a positive Dehn twist about an unoriented interior simple closed curve that is not null-homotopic. Repeated curve classes are permitted and count repeatedly toward the length.
t c₁ ··· t cₙ = t δ , with i(c j , c k ) ≤ 1 for every pair j, k.

Here i denotes geometric intersection: the minimum number of crossings in the two isotopy classes. The target is one positive boundary twist. Boundary-parallel curves are allowed. Two ordered words are identified only by simultaneous conjugation , meaning that one mapping class is applied to every curve in the sequence.
There are finitely many such simultaneous-conjugacy classes. Consequently, the possible lengths have a finite maximum M ( g ), and some admissible word attains it:

A peripheral, or boundary-parallel, factor appears only in the singleton factorization t δ . Every other admissible word uses only nonseparating curves. The values 12 and 40 are deductions from prior work with this convention bridge stated.

This gives a negative answer to the separately printed restricted arbitrary-length clause attributed to Smith in Wajnryb’s chapter of Farb’s Problems on Mapping Class Groups and Related Topics (printed page 126, PDF page 133). The preceding unrestricted question and the surrounding classification questions have different scopes.

The argument combines two finite structures. First, the distinct curve classes in a factorization form its support . The intersection restriction bounds support size by 2 2g (3g − 2) + 1: curves in the same mod-two homology class must be disjoint, and a disjoint nonperipheral collection has at most 3g − 2 members. Marked ribbon graphs, together with the topology of their complements and the distinguished boundary, then give only finitely many possible support orbits. This counts distinct curves; it does not bound how often a curve can repeat.

Second, for any fixed finite curve alphabet, only finitely many positive words can have the prescribed product. Positive essential twists on the bordered surface cannot form a nonempty identity product. Inserting letters into a shorter word produces a product of conjugated positive letters, so two different words with the same value cannot be related by subsequence. Higman’s finite-alphabet lemma then rules out an infinite collection of equal-value words. The note also derives this finite-alphabet conclusion from Cossu–Tringali’s factorization theory, using a normal ambient positive cone and nonempty atomic expansions. The target need not be central in that group lemma; centrality of t δ is used when transporting words between surface supports.

The classical even-chain relation (t a₁ ··· t a₂g ) 4g+2 = t δ supplies length 4g(2g + 1), so the finite set of lengths is nonempty. Positivity excludes peripheral factors beyond the singleton. A separating factor would be disjoint from all the supporting curves; capping the boundary and applying Smith’s invariant-essential-curve obstruction rules it out. Only after this exclusion does the nonseparating length convention of Baykur–Monden–Van Horn-Morris apply to the low-genus upper bounds.

This is a credited deduction and exposition. Cossu–Tringali, Corollary 4.13 of their final v3 preprint , supplies the generic finite-alphabet corollary. The support methods build on Juvan–Malnič–Mohar and Malestein–Rivin–Theran. The marked disconnected bordered-surface construction adapts Cahn–Fanoni–Petri’s ribbon/complement method. Honda–Kazez–Matić, Smith, the classical chain relation, Higman, and Baykur–Monden–Van Horn-Morris supply the other credited inputs. No new generic method or first-discovery claim is made.

Exact M ( g ) for g ≥ 3, explicit numerical upper formulas, an effective exhaustive-enumeration stopping criterion, extremizers, and Hurwitz, positive Artin, T-move or A 5 /D 6 classifications remain unresolved in this work. The higher-genus unrestricted infinite-length results do not impose the pairwise intersection restriction. Fixed genus, positivity, non-null-homotopic curves, one boundary twist and pointwise boundary fixing are substantive hypotheses.

The note does not certify historical novelty, exact application priority or worldwide current-open status. Its cited preprint versions are identified in the manuscript; a complete journal-body read of Higman’s article or Smith’s journal edition was unavailable in its bounded source audit. The finite-alphabet exposition is self-contained, and the external geometric and gauge-theoretic inputs remain credited premises.

Fix an oriented compact surface of genus g≥1 with one boundary circle, and fix that boundary pointwise in both maps and isotopies. Ordered positive factorizations of its single boundary twist, along non-null-homotopic simple closed curves with pairwise geometric intersection at most one, have finitely many simultaneous-conjugacy classes. Repetitions are permitted. Their lengths therefore have a finite attained maximum M(g), with 4g(2g+1)≤ M(g); credited low-genus deductions give M(1)=12 and M(2)=40. This is a credited finiteness deduction and exposition: the finite-alphabet group lemma is a verified corollary of Cossu–Tringali's factorization theory, and the support and embedding mechanisms are prior curve-system and ribbon-surface methods, with the marked bordered adaptation supplied here. It answers negatively the separately stated restricted arbitrary-length clause attributed to Smith in Wajnryb's chapter. Exact M(g) for g≥3, explicit upper formulas, a stopping criterion, extremizers and finer classifications remain unresolved in this work. Historical novelty and exact priority are not certified.

For each fixed genus g ≥ 1, let S(g,1) be an oriented compact surface with one boundary component, and let maps and isotopies fix that boundary pointwise. We prove that ordered positive factorizations of one positive boundary Dehn twist, along non-null-homotopic simple closed curves with repetitions permitted and pairwise geometric intersection at most one, have finitely many simultaneous-conjugacy classes. Their maximal length M(g) is finite and attained, with M(g) ≥ 4g(2g+1). Peripheral factors occur only in the singleton factorization; otherwise all factors are nonseparating. The values M(1) = 12 and M(2) = 40 are credited deductions from prior work with the convention bridge stated. This gives a complete negative answer, under the stated conventions, to the separately printed restricted arbitrary-length clause in the Wajnryb/Farb problem collection. The full original maximum and classification bundle remains partial: exact M(g) for g ≥ 3, explicit upper formulas, an effective exhaustive-enumeration stopping criterion, extremizers, and Hurwitz, positive Artin, T-move and A5/D6 classifications remain unresolved in this work. Marked ribbon graphs, together with the topology of their complements and the distinguished boundary, then give only finitely many possible support orbits. This counts distinct curves; it does not bound how often a curve can repeat.

Second, for any fixed finite curve alphabet, only finitely many positive words can have the prescribed product. Positive essential twists on the bordered surface cannot form a nonempty identity product. Inserting letters into a shorter word produces a product of conjugated positive letters, so two different words with the same value cannot be related by subsequence. Higman’s finite-alphabet lemma then rules out an infinite collection of equal-value words. The note also derives this finite-alphabet conclusion from Cossu–Tringali’s factorization theory, using a normal ambient positive cone and nonempty atomic expansions. The target need not be central in that group lemma; centrality of t δ is used when transporting words between surface supports.

The classical even-chain relation (t a₁ ··· t a₂g ) 4g+2 = t δ supplies length 4g(2g + 1), so the finite set of lengths is nonempty. Positivity excludes peripheral factors beyond the singleton. A separating factor would be disjoint from all the supporting curves; capping the boundary and applying Smith’s invariant-essential-curve obstruction rules it out. Only after this exclusion does the nonseparating length convention of Baykur–Monden–Van Horn-Morris apply to the low-genus upper bounds.

blocks.text: This is a credited deduction and exposition. Cossu–Tringali, Corollary 4.13 of their final v3 preprint , supplies the generic finite-alphabet corollary. The support methods build on Juvan–Malnič–Mohar and Malestein–Rivin–Theran. The marked disconnected bordered-surface construction adapts Cahn–Fanoni–Petri’s ribbon/complement method. Honda–Kazez–Matić, Smith, the classical chain relation, Higman, and Baykur–Monden–Van Horn-Morris supply the other credited inputs. No new generic method or first-discovery claim is made.

Exact M ( g ) for g ≥ 3, explicit numerical upper formulas, an effective exhaustive-enumeration stopping criterion, extremizers, and Hurwitz, positive Artin, T-move or A 5 /D 6 classifications remain unresolved in this work. The higher-genus unrestricted infinite-length results do not impose the pairwise intersection restriction. Fixed genus, positivity, non-null-homotopic curves, one boundary twist and pointwise boundary fixing are substantive hypotheses.

The note does not certify historical novelty, exact application priority or worldwide current-open status. Its cited preprint versions are identified in the manuscript; a complete journal-body read of Higman’s article or Smith’s journal edition was unavailable in its bounded source audit. The finite-alphabet exposition is self-contained, and the external geometric and gauge-theoretic inputs remain credited premises.

blocks.text: Fix an oriented compact surface of genus g≥1 with one boundary circle, and fix that boundary pointwise in both maps and isotopies. Ordered positive factorizations of its single boundary twist, along non-null-homotopic simple closed curves with pairwise geometric intersection at most one, have finitely many simultaneous-conjugacy classes. Repetitions are permitted. Their lengths therefore have a finite attained maximum M(g), with 4g(2g+1)≤ M(g); credited low-genus deductions give M(1)=12 and M(2)=40. This is a credited finiteness deduction and exposition: the finite-alphabet group lemma is a verified corollary of Cossu–Tringali's factorization theory, and the support and embedding mechanisms are prior curve-system and ribbon-surface methods, with the marked bordered adaptation supplied here. It answers negatively the separately stated restricted arbitrary-length clause attributed to Smith in Wajnryb's chapter. Exact M(g) for g≥3, explicit upper formulas, a stopping criterion, extremizers and finer classifications remain unresolved in this work. Historical novelty and exact priority are not certified.

blocks.text: For each fixed genus g ≥ 1, let S(g,1) be an oriented compact surface with one boundary component, and let maps and isotopies fix that boundary pointwise. We prove that ordered positive factorizations of one positive boundary Dehn twist, along non-null-homotopic simple closed curves with repetitions permitted and pairwise geometric intersection at most one, have finitely many simultaneous-conjugacy classes. Their maximal length M(g) is finite and attained, with M(g) ≥ 4g(2g+1). Peripheral factors occur only in the singleton factorization; otherwise all factors are nonseparating. The values M(1) = 12 and M(2) = 40 are credited deductions from prior work with the convention bridge stated. This gives a complete negative answer, under the stated conventions, to the separately printed restricted arbitrary-length clause in the Wajnryb/Farb problem collection. The full original maximum and classification bundle remains partial: exact M(g) for g ≥ 3, explicit upper formulas, an effective exhaustive-enumeration stopping criterion, extremizers, and Hurwitz, positive Artin, T-move and A5/D6 classifications remain unresolved in this work. The note is a credited deduction and exposition. Cossu and Tringali's arXiv:2208.05869v3, Corollary 4.13, supplies the generic finite-alphabet finiteness corollary through a normal reduced cone and nonerasing atomic expansions. The support and ribbon arguments explicitly build on Juvan–Malnič–Mohar, Malestein–Rivin–Theran, and Cahn–Fanoni–Petri. Honda–Kazez–Matić, Smith, the chain relation, and Baykur–Monden–Van Horn-Morris provide credited premises. Exact historical priority of the resulting surface application, novelty, and worldwide current-open status remain UNKNOWN; a bounded literature audit is not an absence proof. Extensive AI tools were used in mathematical and source checking, writing, code, and package preparation. This preprint is unrefereed, has no external human peer review, and is not formally certified. The accompanying verification kit provides written proof and source/custody records plus reproducible finite fault controls; those controls do not replace the universal proof or replay omitted historical inputs.
